title: Mesh Inference: A Formal Model of Collective Intelligence Without a Center
summary: We present a formal model of mesh inference: how a population of independent agents, each holding private state and exchanging only admitted, typed observations, derives a conclusion none of them holds alone, with no central coordinator and no agent exposed. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the agents may span different teams, networks, and organizations. Motivated by the observation that asking a model is energy-minimizing inference, we model the mesh as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. We show that a single admission/emission policy governs three properties. First, mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission, symmetric or not, because the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it is identification-complete: it derives the centralized optimum exactly when the contributing views are carrier-connected. Third, it is observation-only: no node transmits its internals, and confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime every derived answer is determined, hence equal to the centralized optimum, at O(diam^2) latency, the measured price of removing the center. One such derivation is one turn of a center-free learning loop, which we formalize as architecture rather than prove. The open problem we state is when asking improves the collective rather than corrupting it: whether the non-linear closure derives an upgraded answer or a confident error. To our knowledge, this is the first formal model of mesh inference.

AI.tldr: A formal model where independent agents perform collective inference by exchanging only typed observations—no weights, gradients, or hidden states—converging to the centralized optimum under carrier-connected conditions with formal guarantees on uniqueness, confidentiality, and latency.
AI.motivation: Decentralized inference across organizational boundaries is needed (e.g., privacy, multi-party collaboration), but prior distributed learning requires sharing gradients or hidden states. The authors observe that model inference is energy-minimizing and ask whether a mesh of agents can collectively reach a conclusion without any central coordinator or exposure of internals.
AI.method: The mesh is modeled as a coupled free energy that each agent locally relaxes. A single admission/emission policy governs the system. Analysis uses M-matrix properties to prove convergence, carrier-connectedness for identification-completeness, and Lagrangian duality to show confidentiality as the dual of identification. The linear-Gaussian regime is analyzed for latency bounds (O(diam²)).
AI.result: Three properties are proven under a unified policy: (1) unique convergence for any symmetric/asymmetric admission (M-matrix coupling), (2) identification-completeness—exact centralized optimum when views are carrier-connected, (3) observation-only—no internal transmission, with content-addressed lineage as the sole side-channel. In linear-Gaussian, the derived answer equals the centralized optimum with O(diam²) latency.
AI.conclusion: This is claimed as the first formal model of mesh inference. The open problem is whether non-linear closure upgrades the collective answer or produces confident errors. One derivation corresponds to one turn of a center-free learning loop, formalized as architecture.

title: SIGMA: Skill-Incidence Graphs for Compositional Multi-Agent Design
summary: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers mainly improve collaboration by optimizing communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks that require unseen combinations of capabilities. We propose SIGMA, a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills. Given a task and a skill library, SIGMA predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to the relevant assigned capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational. Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance and improves over CARD, the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline, by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points, respectively. It also shows stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points. These results suggest that compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SIGMA-2338/.

AI.tldr: SIGMA proposes a compositional multi-agent framework where agents are dynamically constructed as bundles of reusable skills based on task requirements, rather than using fixed predefined agents. It predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix and communication topology, achieving superior performance and robustness across reasoning and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based multi-agent systems rely on closed-set agents with fixed roles, limiting generalization to tasks requiring novel capability combinations. There is a need for compositional agent construction that can flexibly assemble agents from reusable skills to handle unseen task demands.
AI.method: SIGMA uses a skill-incidence graph framework: given a task and skill library, it predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to relevant capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational.
AI.result: Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance, outperforming CARD (the strongest non-compositional topology baseline) by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points respectively. Under unseen skill libraries, it shows only a 0.96-point average performance drop, demonstrating strong robustness.
AI.conclusion: Compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization. Skill-based agent assembly enables better generalization and robustness to unseen capability combinations.

title: Blame is easier than praise: Measuring off-ball defensive performance in football
summary: The defensive performance of football players is commonly measured through a limited number of actions like tackles and interceptions while their continuous impact through positional behaviour has hardly been studied before. We formulate this problem as an attribution over multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories without player-level ground truth labels, where event-level changes of expected threat are distributed among individuals. We propose a framework that performs this attribution using player involvement scores calculated from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). By computing role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures, we can determine each defender's expected responsibility for threat created through arbitrary passes. The validity and robustness of this approach are evaluated on a uniquely extensive cross-gender and cross-competition data set, including positional and event data from 64 matches of the men's World Cup, 116 matches of the women's German Bundesliga and 336 matches of the men's German 3. Liga. In the absence of a ground truth, we propose an evaluation protocol that combines multiple relatively weak proxies into robust summary scores. We find a validity score that is improved by around 1 standard deviation compared to the best action-based metric and demonstrate that many popular measures show limited validity. The "blame" for conceding high-value actions shows especially strong correlations with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric in football to reliably measure positioning errors. All code underlying this work is publicly available to support reproducibility and further research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for measuring football defenders' continuous positional impact by attributing threat changes in spatiotemporal trajectories. Using Defensive Pressure Areas (DPAs) with role-conditioned baselines and automatically detected team structures, it quantifies each defender's expected responsibility for conceded threats. Evaluated on a large cross-gender, cross-competition dataset (516 matches), the proposed metric outperforms action-based measures by ~1 standard deviation in validity and correlates strongly with external ratings and market values — making it the first published metric to reliably measure positioning errors in football.
AI.motivation: Traditional defensive performance metrics rely on sparse, discrete actions (tackles, interceptions) and fail to capture the continuous positional influence of defenders throughout a match. There is no existing method that reliably attributes responsibility for conceded threats to individual defenders based on their spatial positioning, nor is there a ground truth for such evaluations. The authors aim to fill this gap by formulating defensive assessment as a multi-agent spatiotemporal attribution problem.
AI.method: The framework computes player involvement scores using Defensive Pressure Areas (DPAs) — regions of pitch influence. Key components: (1) Role-conditioned baselines derived from automatically detected team structures (formations/roles) to establish expected defensive responsibility; (2) Attribution of event-level changes in expected threat (xT) across players; (3) A novel evaluation protocol that aggregates multiple weak proxy signals (external ratings, market values, etc.) into robust summary validity scores, circumventing the absence of ground truth labels.
AI.result: The proposed metric achieves a validity score approximately 1 standard deviation higher than the best action-based metric. Many popular existing defensive measures demonstrate limited validity. The "blame" component — attributing responsibility for conceded high-value actions — exhibits particularly strong correlations with external ratings and market values. The framework is validated on 516 matches spanning men's World Cup, women's Bundesliga, and men's 3. Liga.
AI.conclusion: This is the first published metric in football capable of reliably measuring defensive positioning errors. The DPA-based attribution framework provides a principled way to evaluate continuous defensive behaviour beyond discrete actions. Public release of all code supports reproducibility and enables further research in sports analytics and multi-agent trajectory attribution.

title: Human-like autonomy emerges from self-play and a pinch of human data
summary: Self-play reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a way to train driving policies without any human data. It uses cheap, large-scale simulations to substitute expensive, large-scale human driving demonstrations. A key limitation of this approach is that policies trained through pure self-play can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with people. Previous works attempt to mitigate such behavioral misalignments through extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. Instead of completely discarding human demonstrations, our method treats them as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Like the spice in a good stew, we find that a little human data goes a long way: our method uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations, 2500x fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories and complete training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Videos and full source code are available at https://spiced-self-play.com/.

AI.tldr: A method called "Spiced Self-Play" that augments pure self-play RL for autonomous driving with a small amount (30 minutes) of human demonstration data as a regularization objective, enabling policies that coordinate well with humans while requiring 2500× less data than imitation learning.
AI.motivation: Pure self-play RL for driving policies can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with human drivers. Existing mitigation approaches (reward engineering, domain randomization) are brittle and labor-intensive. The authors aim to bridge this behavioral alignment gap efficiently without discarding the benefits of self-play.
AI.method: The method treats a small set of human driving demonstrations (30 minutes) as a regularization objective layered on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Self-play RL training proceeds with this combined objective, where the human data acts as a behavioral prior or constraint that steers learned policies toward human-compatible conventions, analogous to "spice" seasoning a dish.
AI.result: Resulting policies successfully coordinate with held-out human trajectories. The approach requires only 30 minutes of human demonstrations — 2500× fewer than comparable imitation learning methods — and completes training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU.
AI.conclusion: A little human demonstration data goes a long way when used as a regularizer in self-play RL. This approach efficiently combines the scalability of simulation-based self-play with human compatibility, avoiding the labor-intensive drawbacks of both pure self-play (alien behavior) and full imitation learning (massive data requirements).

title: Supporting Design Decisions in Rule-Based Model Transformations
summary: Model Driven Engineering relies on model transformations to automate the derivation of target models or source code from source models. However, the design decisions that govern how source elements are mapped to target artifacts typically remain embedded in the transformation source code, limiting flexibility, reusability, and traceability. This paper proposes an approach to explicitly model and manage design decisions in rule-based model transformations. Design decisions are separated from transformation implementation through three mechanisms. First, a decision model captures design decisions and their options independently of any source modeling language for a given transformation domain. Second, a binding model connects these decisions to specific metamodel concepts in a given source modeling language, enabling reuse of the same design knowledge across transformations from similar languages. Third, a configuration model records the specific option chosen for each applicable source model element, with defaults pre-selected automatically. During execution, variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically according to configured choices. A trace model records which rules and options were applied to produce each target element. We establish a formal mathematical framework that defines the core concepts of variability-based transformations and proves key properties of the resulting transformations. The formal concepts are realized in a practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models. We demonstrate practical feasibility by extending an existing embedded domain-specific language for model-driven engineering with variability support and illustrate the approach with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an approach to externalize design decisions from model transformation code using four interconnected models (decision, binding, configuration, and trace), supported by a formal mathematical framework that proves key properties of variability-based transformations.
AI.motivation: In traditional model-driven engineering, design decisions governing how source elements map to target artifacts are hard-coded within transformation implementations, which limits flexibility, hinders reuse across similar languages, and obscures traceability between decisions and generated artifacts.
AI.method: The approach introduces three separation mechanisms: (1) a decision model capturing design decisions and options independently of any source metamodel; (2) a binding model linking decisions to concrete metamodel concepts for cross-language reuse; and (3) a configuration model recording chosen options per source element with automatic defaults. Variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically at execution time, and a trace model records rule-option-to-target-element mappings. A formal mathematical framework defines core concepts and proves properties, instantiated in a practical architecture with four interconnected artifact models. Feasibility is demonstrated by extending an existing embedded DSL for MDE with variability support and applying it to an ER-to-Relational transformation.
AI.result: The formal framework establishes rigorous definitions for variability-based transformations and proves key properties. The practical architecture demonstrates that design decisions can be successfully externalized from transformation code. The ER-to-Relational case study shows the approach working end-to-end on a complete, non-trivial transformation scenario.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling design decisions as first-class artifacts—separate from transformation logic—improves flexibility, reusability across source languages, and traceability in rule-based model transformations. The approach is both formally grounded and practically feasible.

title: MonaVec: A Training-Free Embedded Vector Search Kernel for Edge and Offline AI Systems
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/mona-hq/monavec (PyPI: monavec; crates.io: monavec-core). Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20559587
summary:
We present MonaVec, a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel for edge and offline AI -- settings where server infrastructure, network connectivity, and training data are all unavailable. Existing vector-search systems assume a persistent server, gigabytes of RAM, or a training pass over the corpus; MonaVec instead targets the deployment profile of SQLite: one file, one function call, runs anywhere. Its quantization core is training-free by default and data-oblivious: a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions any input distribution toward N(0,1), so precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize to 4 bits (8x smaller) with no learned codebook and no data pass. The index persists as a single .mvec file whose embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed makes results reproducible across architectures and byte-identical within a build -- a determinism guarantee that parallel-build graph libraries cannot offer.
  On semantic embeddings (AG News, 45K x 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce reaches 0.960 Recall@10 in 27 MB -- leading float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall -- while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism. A single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the same data-oblivious pipeline to magnitude-sensitive L2 data, and optional IvfFlat and HNSW backends carry it to million-vector corpora.
  MonaVec is implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar). It targets on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval -- the niche SQLite occupies for relational data: one file, one call, runs anywhere.

AI.tldr: MonaVec is a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel targeting edge/offline AI. It uses a training-free, data-oblivious quantization (Randomized Hadamard Transform + precomputed Lloyd-Max tables) to achieve 4-bit compression with no learned codebooks. Results are byte-identical across architectures via a ChaCha20-seeded deterministic pipeline, packaged as a single .mvec file with SQLite-like deployment simplicity.
AI.motivation: Existing vector-search systems assume server infrastructure, ample RAM, or a training pass over the corpus. MonaVec fills the niche for edge and offline AI — scenarios lacking servers, connectivity, and training data — analogous to SQLite's role for relational databases: zero-configuration, single-file, embedded operation.
AI.method: The core quantization uses a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) to condition arbitrary input distributions toward N(0,1), enabling precomputed Lloyd-Max tables to quantize vectors to 4 bits without any learned codebook or data pass. The index persists in a single .mvec file, with an embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed ensuring deterministic, byte-identical results across architectures. An optional single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the pipeline to L2 data. Backends include BruteForce, IvfFlat, and HNSW. Implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar).
AI.result: On AG News (45K × 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce achieves 0.960 Recall@10 in 27 MB, surpassing float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall, while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism.
AI.conclusion: MonaVec delivers competitive recall with extreme compression (4-bit, 8× smaller) and deterministic reproducibility in an embedded, single-file deployment model, making it well-suited for on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval — the vector-search counterpart to SQLite.

title: Exposing the Unsaid: Visualizing Hidden LLM Bias through Stochastic Path Aggregation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit representational and syntactic biases that are difficult to evaluate due to the stochastic nature of text generation. Standard auditing methods rely on a single output inspection or static automated metrics. These approaches obscure the underlying probability distributions and fail to capture biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. This paper introduces TreeTracer, a visual analytics tool designed to evaluate LLM bias through aggregated comparison. Using a systematic perturbation analysis pipeline, the tool replaces ontology-defined terms in each input prompt, aggregates hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure, and then performs classification-aware node merging with an auxiliary language model. The resulting structure is visualized through a custom Sankey diagram. By juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees, the workspace enables direct comparison between semantic contexts and supports systematic bias detection. Because any visualization reflects only a subset of the model's learned behavior, the system further applies contrastive inference to compute and directly display counterfactual token probabilities across contexts, reducing the risk of misinterpreting the presence of bias. We validate the workspace through case studies comparing an unaligned baseline model GPT-2 XL against the constitutionally aligned Apertus models. The visual aggregation successfully exposes hidden representational harms, such as counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirms that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and effectively supports analysts in detecting systemic biases.

AI.tldr: TreeTracer is a visual analytics tool that aggregates hundreds of LLM outputs into syntax-aligned Sankey diagrams, enabling systematic bias detection through ontology-driven perturbation and contrastive counterfactual analysis across semantic contexts.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM bias auditing methods (single-output inspection, static metrics) obscure underlying probability distributions and miss biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. There is a need for tools that expose the full stochastic landscape of model behavior.
AI.method: TreeTracer employs a perturbation analysis pipeline: (1) ontology-defined term replacement in prompts, (2) aggregation of hundreds of stochastic generations into syntax-aligned hierarchical structures, (3) classification-aware node merging via an auxiliary LM, (4) visualization through custom Sankey diagrams juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees, and (5) contrastive inference computing counterfactual token probabilities across contexts.
AI.result: Case studies comparing GPT-2 XL against Apertus models exposed hidden representational harms including counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization. A preliminary user study confirmed the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and supports systematic bias detection.
AI.conclusion: Visual aggregation paired with contrastive inference effectively surfaces systemic biases otherwise concealed in lower-probability branches, and the comparative Sankey-based workspace proves usable for analysts conducting LLM bias audits.

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. To be published in the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Agentic Services which is part of the IEEE Conference on Web Services
summary: Autonomous agentic AI systems driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new class of security, privacy, and compliance challenges: an agent that can invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate with peer agents across organizational boundaries must be constrained not just by authentication and access control, but by the full structure of enterprise governance. This includes specifying what agents are permitted and prohibited from doing, what they areobliged to do after certain actions (e.g., notify the CISO), under what conditions a standing obligation may be waived, and which rules take precedence when policies conflict. This governance problem exceeds what current policy engines provide. Systems such as XACML, Rego, and Cedar address only the permit/prohibit subset of this governance structure. They do not provide obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations that waive obligations in specific circumstances, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies commonly found in applications such as healthcare, cybersecurity, or data privacy. We propose AgenticRei, which realizes key governance requirements such as obligations, dispensations, policy conflict resolutions, and reasoning over policies, as well as the basic permit/prohibit constraints. We use a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed as OWL (Web Ontology Language) and evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. We show through examples that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines. Our approach composes naturally with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven autonomous agents introduce governance challenges beyond permit/prohibit access control—including obligations, dispensations, and conflict resolution. The authors propose AgenticRei, a deontic policy framework built on OWL/Rei with an external runtime logic engine, to capture full enterprise governance constraints for agent actions and inter-agent communication.
AI.motivation: Current policy engines (XACML, Rego, Cedar) only handle permit/prohibit semantics. They lack support for obligation lifecycle management, dispensations (waiving obligations under specific conditions), meta-policy conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies. LLM-driven autonomous agents that invoke tools, manipulate data, and coordinate across organizational boundaries require this richer governance structure to meet security, privacy, and compliance requirements.
AI.method: AgenticRei uses a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed in OWL (Web Ontology Language). Policies are evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine operating entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. The approach composes with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.
AI.result: Through examples, the authors demonstrate that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines.
AI.conclusion: AgenticRei addresses a critical gap in autonomous agent governance by extending policy enforcement beyond binary permit/prohibit to include obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning, enabling enterprise-grade compliance for LLM-driven agentic systems.

title: Secure Coding Drift in LLM-Assisted Post-Quantum Cryptography Development: A Gamified Fix
comment: Accepted for 2026 SIGIR Workshop on Vulnerabilities in Generative Systems for Information Retrieval track
summary: The transition to Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) introduces considerable implementation complexity, requiring strict adherence to constant-time execution, side channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. Simultaneously, large language models (LLMs) are heavily embedded in software development workflows, including cryptographic engineering. While LLMs improve productivity, evidence shows that they frequently generate insecure or suboptimal code, particularly in security critical domains. This paper introduces Secure Coding Drift in PQC, a novel socio technical vulnerability model capturing the gradual degradation of secure coding practices due to sustained reliance on LLM-generated code. Unlike prior work that focuses on static vulnerabilities, we conceptualise security risk as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon rising from human AI interaction. To mitigate this, we propose a gamified, LLM augmented secure coding framework that embeds adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into development workflows. Our approach reframes LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, contributing toward safer PQC implementation in AI mediated environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Secure Coding Drift in PQC," a socio-technical vulnerability model describing how sustained reliance on LLM-generated code gradually erodes secure coding practices in Post-Quantum Cryptography implementations. The authors propose a gamified, LLM-augmented framework incorporating adversarial evaluation, behavioral feedback, and security scoring to mitigate this drift.
AI.motivation: PQC transitions demand rigorous constant-time execution, side-channel resistance, and precise parameterization. LLMs are increasingly used in cryptographic engineering yet frequently produce insecure code. Prior work examines static vulnerabilities, but no model captures the longitudinal, behavioral degradation of security practices arising from sustained human-AI interaction in this domain.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize "Secure Coding Drift in PQC" as a novel socio-technical vulnerability model. They then propose a countermeasure framework that is gamified and LLM-augmented, embedding three components into development workflows: (1) adversarial evaluation, (2) behavioral feedback loops, and (3) security scoring. This reframes LLMs from passive code assistants into active security co-pilots.
AI.result: The paper is conceptual and proposes a framework; no empirical results or quantitative evaluations are reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Secure Coding Drift represents a significant, underexamined risk in AI-mediated PQC development. The proposed gamified, LLM-augmented framework offers a pathway toward safer PQC implementations by transforming LLMs into active security co-pilots rather than passive code generators.

title: Computational Identifiability
summary: Identification conditions describe the computability of a target query or parameter of interest as a function of the type and amount of information available. In causal identification, this information is often expressed in the form of a causal graph, and data are observed or collected for some subset of variables in the graph. Target queries may be for a single effect alone or for a class of effects in a given model. The derivation of an identification algorithm then defines mathematically the process by which the desired causal effect(s) can be uniquely determined, theoretically, in expectation. Identifiability in expectation, or 'theoretical identifiability,' generally assumes asymptotic properties, infinite data, or other mathematically idealized conditions. In this paper, we explore a fundamental distinction between this theoretical, idealized notion of identifiability and a proposed alternative that is computation-bound. The framework we propose - 'computational identifiability' - is to instead define a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. If this process finds an estimator empirically, within a desired error tolerance, then identifiability is satisfied, conditional on the specified assumptions of the search (i.e., a prior distribution over the parameters) and conditional on the search procedure itself. Through several experiments, we demonstrate how this framework allows us to answer fine-grained, practical identification questions, such as identification with small finite samples, with ambiguous graphical criteria, with mixed observational-interventional data, and across counterfactual data and estimands. Code is available at https://github.com/lbynum/metadentify.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "computational identifiability," a framework that reconceptualizes causal identifiability as a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator, contrasting with traditional asymptotic theoretical identifiability. It demonstrates the framework's utility in small-sample, ambiguous-graph, mixed-data, and counterfactual settings.
AI.motivation: Traditional theoretical identifiability relies on idealized asymptotic assumptions (infinite data, perfect graph specification), which can be disconnected from practical finite-sample scenarios. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a notion of identifiability grounded in actual computational procedures and empirical performance.
AI.method: The proposed framework defines identifiability via a finite computational search over a space of candidate estimators, parameterized by a prior distribution. If the search converges to an estimator achieving a desired error tolerance on the available finite data, the query is deemed computationally identifiable, conditional on the search procedure and prior assumptions. Experiments are conducted to illustrate the framework.
AI.result: The framework successfully addresses practical identification questions that theoretical identifiability cannot: identification with small finite samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed observational-interventional data, and counterfactual estimands. Empirical demonstrations validate the approach.
AI.conclusion: Computational identifiability offers a practically relevant complement to theoretical identifiability, enabling fine-grained, data-dependent identification assessments that reflect the realities of finite computation and finite samples.

title: LLM-Mediated Human-AI Interaction in Search and Rescue: Impact of Expertise on Attentional Allocation
summary: Human-AI teaming (HAT) increasingly involves AI systems that provide real-time, context-aware guidance in complex tasks. While such systems can improve performance, their effectiveness depends on how they shape human cognition and behavior. In particular, AI assistance can introduce cognitive demands and influence attention, planning, and interaction with the task environment, with effects that can vary across levels of expertise. This work investigates these mechanisms in a simulated search and rescue (SAR) environment. We compare human performance under two LLM (Large Language Model)-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline, and analyze interaction at multiple levels, including task performance, eye-tracking measures, and planning behavior. Eye tracking provides fine-grained insight into attention allocation and interaction with AI guidance, while behavioral measures capture how users structure and adapt their decisions over time. Results indicate that LLM guidance enhanced task efficiency (higher rewards and victims-per-step) but did not increase total victims saved. Eye-tracking data revealed an attention-guidance trade-off, with visual resources shifting to the chat interface alongside increased pupil size variability. Expertise moderated this effect: novices exhibited passive AI reliance, whereas experts maintained a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning. These findings suggest that LLM-mediated teaming efficacy depends on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to maintain situational awareness.

AI.tldr: In a simulated search-and-rescue task, LLM guidance improved task efficiency but not total victims saved. Eye-tracking revealed an attention-guidance trade-off — users shifted visual focus to the chat interface. Expertise moderated reliance: novices passively followed AI, while experts maintained environmental scanning to verify AI suggestions, highlighting the importance of cross-referencing for situational awareness in human-AI teams.
AI.motivation: To investigate how real-time, context-aware AI guidance shapes human cognition, attention, planning, and behavior in complex tasks, and how these effects differ across levels of operator expertise in human-AI teaming.
AI.method: A simulated search and rescue (SAR) environment was used to compare human performance across three conditions: two LLM-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline. Multi-level analysis was conducted using task performance metrics, eye-tracking measures (attention allocation, pupil size variability), and behavioral measures of planning and decision adaptation.
AI.result: LLM guidance improved task efficiency (higher rewards, higher victims-per-step) but did not increase total victims saved. Eye-tracking showed an attention-guidance trade-off: visual resources shifted toward the chat interface, accompanied by increased pupil size variability. Expertise moderated these effects — novices showed passive AI reliance, while experts engaged in a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated teaming efficacy hinges on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to maintain situational awareness. Without this verification behavior, AI assistance may not translate efficiency gains into improved overall outcomes.

title: AgentArmor: A Framework, Evaluation, \& Mitigation of Coding Agent Failures
summary: Software engineering and deployment are increasingly being delegated to AI coding agents. The scale of their adoption is surfacing rare, but highly destructive, failure modes. In this paper, we study these failure modes as stemming from three distinct mechanisms: underspecification, where default model behavior is unsafe; capability errors, where the safe action is available but the model does not adhere to it due to bias or capability limitations; and agent harness errors, where the model fails to execute the safe action through the harness. We evaluate these across 8 different evaluations, each inspired by real-life deployment failures, totaling 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. Based on this evaluation, we propose AgentArmor, an agent harness modification, to mitigate these errors. By adding an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a ``3 strikes'' policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools for the agent to edit its own context, we show that AgentArmor is safer across a statistically significant number of samples. Thus, we suggest concrete mitigations for current coding agents and a design philosophy for future agent harness features.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes failure modes of AI coding agents—underspecification, capability errors, and agent harness errors—using evaluations based on real-world deployment failures, and proposes AgentArmor, a harness modification with guardrails (extended prompts, command classifiers, "3 strikes" policy, self-editing tools) that demonstrably improves safety.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents are increasingly deployed for software engineering tasks, rare but highly destructive failure modes have emerged. The paper is motivated by the need to systematically categorize these failures and develop practical mitigations to prevent catastrophic outcomes in production environments.
AI.method: The authors taxonomize failures into three mechanisms—underspecification (unsafe defaults), capability errors (model fails to select available safe actions due to bias/limitations), and agent harness errors (model cannot execute safe action through the harness). They evaluate these across 8 evaluations inspired by real deployment failures, spanning 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. They then propose AgentArmor, which integrates: an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a "3 strikes" policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools enabling the agent to edit its own context.
AI.result: AgentArmor demonstrates statistically significant safety improvements compared to baseline agent harnesses across the evaluated samples, validating each component's contribution to mitigating the identified failure modes.
AI.conclusion: Concrete harness-level mitigations like AgentArmor can substantially reduce destructive failure modes in coding agents, and the paper offers a design philosophy for building safer agent harnesses in future systems.

title: VCG: A Multimodal Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Video Feeds under Extreme Cold-Start Conditions
summary: The digital commerce landscape is shifting from static, search-driven catalogs to dynamic, immersive video feeds. This transition introduces an ``extreme cold-start'' problem: unlike traditional items, new short-form videos lack the dense interaction history required for collaborative filtering. Furthermore, immersive feeds introduce strong position and duration biases that distort standard engagement signals. In this paper, we demonstrate the Video Candidate Generation (VCG) system, a scalable multimodal retrieval engine designed to solve these challenges in a large-scale e-commerce environment. By leveraging a domain-adapted vision-language model (based on CLIP), we map users and videos into a shared semantic space, enabling zero-shot retrieval based on visual content rather than behavioral history. We detail the system's architecture and present a rigorous evaluation comparing generative (LLM) vs. discriminative (CLIP) embeddings. Our results show that while generative models excel at attribute prediction, they suffer from embedding space collapse in retrieval tasks. Online A/B testing demonstrates that VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases, yielding a 50\% uplift in deep video completion. To showcase the system's capabilities, we present an interactive demonstration featuring three bi-directional retrieval scenarios: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.

AI.tldr: A multimodal retrieval system (VCG) using domain-adapted CLIP for zero-shot video retrieval in e-commerce, addressing extreme cold-start, position bias, and duration bias; achieves 50% uplift in deep video completion over baselines.
AI.motivation: Modern e-commerce has shifted from static catalogs to immersive short-video feeds, creating an "extreme cold-start" problem where new videos lack interaction history for collaborative filtering. Additionally, immersive feeds introduce position and duration biases that distort engagement signals, necessitating a fundamentally different retrieval approach.
AI.method: The VCG system maps users and videos into a shared semantic space using a domain-adapted vision-language model based on CLIP, enabling zero-shot retrieval from visual content without behavioral history. The system architecture is evaluated by comparing generative (LLM) embeddings against discriminative (CLIP) embeddings, with online A/B testing to measure real-world impact.
AI.result: Discriminative (CLIP) embeddings outperform generative (LLM) embeddings for retrieval, as generative models suffer from embedding space collapse. Online A/B testing shows VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases and yields a 50% uplift in deep video completion.
AI.conclusion: Domain-adapted CLIP-based multimodal retrieval solves cold-start and bias challenges in video-based e-commerce feeds. The system supports three bi-directional retrieval modes: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.

title: Ensembles of Large Language Models for Identifying EQ-5D Studies in PubMed Based on Their Abstracts
summary: The rapid increase in scientific publications leads to the fact that manual study screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) is increasingly resource consuming, inefficient, and inconsistent. Classifying studies that clearly report health-related quality-of-life results, such as EQ-5D data, requires a high level of clinical interpretation and poses challenges for human reviewers. This study investigates the use of Google's Gemini and Gemma large language models (LLMs) in automating EQ-5D detection in the PubMed biomedical database based only on published abstracts. A multi-phase framework is proposed that integrates few-shot prompting, weight ensembling aggregation, and a soft stacking meta-classifier. Nine LLMs are evaluated on a dataset of PubMed studies manually labeled by two experts regarding EQ-5D reporting. The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b obtained a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, exceeding individually attained results. The ensembling of top-performing models improved the balance between precision and recall compared to individual models, while the soft stacking approach provided greater reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis shows that the probability results from the models are important in guiding the final predictions. The findings suggest that an ensemble-based LLM setup is a reliable and scalable approach for automating screening in biomedical research.

AI.tldr: This study proposes an ensemble-based LLM framework using Google's Gemini and Gemma models to automate the detection of EQ-5D health-related quality-of-life data from PubMed abstracts in systematic literature reviews. A multi-phase approach combining few-shot prompting, weight ensembling, and soft stacking achieved 0.74 F1-score and accuracy, outperforming individual models.
AI.motivation: Manual screening in systematic literature reviews is increasingly resource-intensive and inconsistent due to the rapid growth of scientific publications. Detecting studies reporting EQ-5D data requires high clinical interpretation, motivating the exploration of automated LLM-based solutions.
AI.method: A multi-phase framework integrating (1) few-shot prompting of nine Google Gemini and Gemma LLMs, (2) weight ensembling aggregation of top-performing models (gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, gemma-3-27b), and (3) a soft stacking meta-classifier. Evaluation was conducted on a PubMed dataset manually labeled by two domain experts for EQ-5D reporting.
AI.result: The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b achieved a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, outperforming all individual models. Ensembling improved precision-recall balance, while soft stacking enhanced reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis confirmed that model probability outputs are informative for final predictions.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based LLM configurations offer a reliable and scalable method for automating study screening in biomedical SLRs, with practical applicability for EQ-5D detection and similar clinical data extraction tasks.

title: Measuring Curriculum Alignment across Topical Coverage, Competency, and Cognitive Depth: A Longitudinal Framework Applied to CS2013 and CS2023
summary: Undergraduate computer science is governed by international curricular guidelines revised about once a decade, yet programs lack a reliable, reproducible way to measure how completely they cover the current guidelines and how that coverage shifts when the guidelines are restructured. We address this with a human-in-the-loop pipeline that measures a program's coverage of an external body of knowledge, applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc in Computer Science against Computer Science Curricula 2013 (CS2013) and 2023 (CS2023). The pipeline represents the program and each guideline as structured corpora, generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches by semantic retrieval, and confirms them through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition. Of seven benchmarked retrievers, a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble was strongest, and a reputed long-context model underperformed a small sentence model, so retriever choice must be measured. Both maps were validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64 for CS2023, 0.69 for CS2013). The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units, near-constant across a decade. Extending the same retrieve-then-confirm design to competency articulation and cognitive depth shows that the program articulates the competency for ~88% of covered units under each guideline, yet delivers it at the recommended depth for 76% of present units under CS2023 against 95% under CS2013, a gap reflecting the newer guideline's raised expectations, not the program. The longitudinal comparison separates persistent structural gaps (parallel and distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals), uncovered against both guidelines and ABET, from differences that reflect the standard's evolution. The instrument is reusable and available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: A human-in-the-loop pipeline using semantic retrieval maps a CS program's coverage against curricular guidelines (CS2013 and CS2023), finding stable ~50% knowledge-unit coverage over a decade. The same approach extends to competency articulation and cognitive depth, revealing that the program meets recommended depth for 76% of covered units under CS2023 vs. 95% under CS2013, reflecting raised expectations in the newer standard.
AI.motivation: CS programs lack a reliable, reproducible instrument to measure how comprehensively they cover international curricular guidelines and how that coverage changes when guidelines are revised. This gap impedes systematic curriculum evaluation and accreditation.
AI.method: A retrieve-then-confirm pipeline: (1) represents the program's course materials and each curricular guideline as structured corpora; (2) generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches via semantic retrieval (seven retrievers benchmarked, with reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble performing best); (3) human judges confirm matches under an explicit coverage definition; (4) validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's κ: 0.69 CS2013, 0.64 CS2023). Extends to competency articulation and Bloom's-level cognitive depth analysis.
AI.result: Coverage is near-constant across a decade: 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units. The program articulates competency for ~88% of covered units under both guidelines. Cognitive depth adequacy drops from 95% (CS2013) to 76% (CS2023), attributable to CS2023's raised expectations. Persistent structural gaps identified in parallel/distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, and systems fundamentals — confirmed against both guidelines and ABET. A long-context model underperformed a small sentence model in retrieval.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a reusable, validated instrument for longitudinal curriculum-coverage measurement. It disentangles persistent program gaps from differences reflecting guideline evolution, offering actionable diagnostic value for CS programs seeking accreditation alignment or curricular reform.

title: FloatDoor: Platform-Triggered Backdoors in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sensitive settings such as software engineering, where their outputs directly shape downstream artifacts. Recent work has shown that an identical model can produce measurably different outputs depending on the deployment platform, a consequence of non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. We study the security implications of this platform-dependent variability and uncover a novel attack surface on LLM deployments. We introduce FloatDoor, the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against generative LLMs. The compromised model exhibits adversary-chosen behavior when served on a target platform and is otherwise benign. FloatDoor is realized through two lightweight LoRA adapters, one that amplifies inter-platform numerical divergence and one that binds the resulting platform signature to a malicious downstream task, while leaving aggregate model utility largely intact. FloatDoor exploits a pronounced time-of-check, time-of-use gap between model auditing and serving. We demonstrate FloatDoor on Qwen3-4B across a broad range of deployment targets, including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. As a final case study, we show that FloatDoor reliably induces exploitable code vulnerabilities on a chosen target platform. Our results establish a new class of attacks on LLM deployments and underscore the pressing need for trusted model supply chains in sensitive, LLM-powered applications.

AI.tldr: FloatDoor is the first input-independent backdoor attack that exploits platform-dependent floating-point divergence in LLM deployments, using two LoRA adapters to trigger malicious behavior only on a specific hardware target (GPU, TPU, CPU) while remaining benign elsewhere.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce measurably different outputs across deployment platforms due to non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. This creates an unexploited attack surface where an adversary can compromise models in a platform-specific manner, exploiting the gap between model auditing and serving (TOCTOU).
AI.method: FloatDoor uses two lightweight LoRA adapters: (1) an amplifier adapter that magnifies inter-platform numerical divergence to create a reliable platform signature, and (2) a binding adapter that links this signature to a malicious downstream task. The attack is input-independent — the compromised behavior manifests solely based on the deployment platform, not on adversarial inputs.
AI.result: FloatDoor was demonstrated on Qwen3-4B across NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. The attack preserved aggregate model utility. In a case study, FloatDoor reliably induced exploitable code vulnerabilities specifically on the chosen target platform.
AI.conclusion: FloatDoor establishes a new class of platform-triggered attacks on LLM deployments, highlighting the critical need for trusted model supply chains and platform-aware security auditing in sensitive LLM-powered applications.

title: When to Trust, How to Distill: Multi-Foundation Model Guidance for Lightweight, Robust Scientific Time Series Forecasting
comment: KDD 2026, paper decision: Accepted, track: AI for Science. total 12 pages including references and appendix
summary: The deployment of Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) in physical sciences is hindered by a critical trade-off: while these models encode rich, universal temporal dynamics, they suffer from severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to specific scientific domains, and their computational cost prohibits deployment in edge-computing sensor networks. We address a fundamental challenge: How can we extract latent structural knowledge from misaligned foundation models (FM) to train lightweight, specialized forecasters? We propose Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation (Guard), a novel framework that reframes multiteacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a "circuit-breaker," automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality. We evaluate our proposed lightweight framework on four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids. Our method significantly reduces RMSE relative to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline, successfully distilling knowledge from pretrained FMs (teachers) even when they exhibit suboptimal zero-shot accuracy due to distribution shift between the original and target data domains. We demonstrate that these domain-misaligned teachers can still serve as critical correctives, outperforming the globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. Ultimately, this enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/RupasreeDey/GUARD-KDD2026.

AI.tldr: Guard proposes a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework that dynamically routes between misaligned time-series foundation models and applies uncertainty-gated temperature scaling to train lightweight, domain-specialized forecasters deployable on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) encode rich temporal dynamics but suffer from severe distributional misalignment in specific scientific domains and are too computationally expensive for edge deployment. The key question: how to extract latent structural knowledge from misaligned FMs to train lightweight specialized forecasters.
AI.method: Guard introduces two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher per instance based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a circuit-breaker, automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality.
AI.result: Guard significantly reduces RMSE compared to fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baselines across four climate-critical domains (meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, energy grids). Domain-misaligned teachers serve as critical correctives, outperforming globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that even distributionally misaligned foundation models contain extractable structural knowledge valuable for domain-specific forecasting. This enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment.

title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
comment: Pre-Print of a paper to be published at the International Computing Education Research (ICER) conference 2026
summary:
Program visualizations are widely used to support novice programmers, yet students often ignore or resist well-designed visual scaffolds. Research on multiple external representations (MERs) offers cognitive design principles for coordinating views, but less is known about what shapes learners' engagement with available representations.
  We conducted a within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates who had completed CS1 and CS2. Students completed think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking while using a multi-representational probe with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, and Python Tutor, across scope, while loops, and linked lists.
  Gaze analysis showed that students spent nearly half their time focused on code despite available visual scaffolds. Students without prior experience anchored even more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Interviews identified three factors shaping selective engagement: agency, as students sought control over cognitive effort rather than simply having it reduced; representational fit, as identical designs differed in whether they felt helpful or overwhelming; and legitimacy, as some students avoided metaphorical scaffolds they perceived as childish or insufficiently rigorous for university-level work.
  These findings suggest that multi-representational tools in computing education require attention to affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical considerations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. More broadly, the themes help explain why cognitively sound visualization tools may fail to engage the students they are designed to help.

AI.tldr: A gaze-tracking study of 19 post-CS2 undergraduates reveals that students spend ~50% of time on code despite rich visual scaffolds, and identifies three non-cognitive factors—agency, representational fit, and legitimacy—that shape learners' selective engagement with program visualizations.
AI.motivation: Program visualizations are widely deployed to support novice programmers, yet students frequently ignore or resist them. While MER research provides cognitive design principles for coordinating views, little is known about what psychosocial factors drive learners' selective engagement with available representations. The authors aim to uncover why cognitively sound tools fail to engage their intended users.
AI.method: Within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates (post-CS1 and CS2). Participants completed think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking while using two tools: (1) a multi-representational probe featuring synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, and (2) Python Tutor. Tasks spanned scope, while loops, and linked lists across both tools.
AI.result: Gaze analysis showed students spent nearly half their time on code views. Novices without prior experience anchored more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Interviews revealed three engagement-shaping factors: (1) agency—students wanted control over cognitive effort, not just reduction; (2) representational fit—identical designs were perceived as either helpful or overwhelming; (3) legitimacy—students avoided metaphorical scaffolds perceived as childish or academically insufficient.
AI.conclusion: Multi-representational tools in CS education must address affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical recommendations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to convey disciplinary legitimacy. These themes explain why cognitively well-designed visualization tools may still fail to engage target learners.

title: Before the Pull Request: Mining Multi-Agent Coordination
comment: 9 pages, 2 tables. LNCS format. Code, dataset, and mining toolkit: https://github.com/neul-labs/grite
summary: Autonomous coding agents now open millions of pull requests, yet large-scale studies find their PRs are produced faster but accepted less often - a coordination and trust gap that pull-request-level telemetry cannot explain. We argue the missing signal lives before the PR, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. We study this process through grite, our open-source coordination substrate that needs no central server and stores its records inside git itself, so its append-only, signed event log captures the coordination process directly. We show that (i) this shared substrate reduces duplicate and conflicting work at bounded overhead - the share of work that merely re-does a teammate's task falls from 78% to 0% while useful throughput more than triples; (ii) every agent's copy of the log converges to the same state with no write silently dropped, where a file-based tracker loses concurrent writes; and (iii) the log is a mineable artefact from which concrete failure modes - conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close - are automatically recoverable with provenance, several invisible in pull-request history. We release the dataset, harness, and mining toolkit.

AI.tldr: Autonomous coding agents produce PRs faster but suffer lower acceptance rates due to coordination failures invisible at the PR level. The authors introduce grite, a serverless coordination substrate that stores signed, append-only event logs inside git, enabling agents to coordinate before PR creation. This eliminates duplicate work (78%→0%), triples useful throughput, ensures log convergence without dropped writes, and enables automated recovery from failure modes like conflicting edits and lock starvation.
AI.motivation: Current large-scale studies reveal a paradox: autonomous coding agents produce pull requests faster but are accepted less often, indicating a coordination and trust gap. PR-level telemetry alone cannot explain this, as the critical coordination failures — agents claiming, dividing, and colliding over shared work — occur before a PR is even filed. The missing signal lies in the pre-PR coordination process.
AI.method: The authors developed **grite**, an open-source, serverless coordination substrate. It requires no central server and stores all coordination records directly inside git as an append-only, cryptographically signed event log. This design ensures every agent possesses a tamper-evident, convergent copy of the coordination history. The system is evaluated along three dimensions: (i) reduction of duplicate/conflicting work and throughput improvement; (ii) log convergence and write durability under concurrency (compared against file-based trackers); and (iii) the log's utility as a mineable artifact for automatically diagnosing and recovering from concrete failure modes with full provenance.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) grite reduced the share of work that merely re-does a teammate's task from 78% to 0%, while useful throughput more than tripled; (2) every agent's log copy converged to identical state with zero silently-dropped writes, unlike file-based trackers that lose concurrent writes; (3) the event log proved to be a mineable artifact enabling automatic recovery — with provenance — of concrete failure modes (conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close), several of which are invisible in PR history alone.
AI.conclusion: Pre-PR coordination is the critical missing layer for multi-agent coding systems. By embedding a signed, append-only event log directly into git, grite provides a decentralized coordination substrate that eliminates duplicate work, guarantees convergence, and enables forensic recovery of coordination failures. The authors release the dataset, harness, and mining toolkit to support further research.

title: DynAMO:Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration via Topological Multi-Agent Scheduling
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, 4 algorithms. Evaluated on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark. Code: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO
summary:
While LLM-powered agents offer end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, real-world Industry 4.0 deployment is hindered by latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. We present DynAMO (Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration), a deployment-ready engine using a Plan-then-Execute architecture to generate verifiable workflow graphs. DynAMO supports both SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). By dynamically identifying independent tasks, DynAMO preserves structural correctness and safety while significantly improving efficiency through controlled reasoning overlap.
  Across six controlled experiments on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark, DynAMO demonstrates substantial performance and robustness gains. Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6x over sequential orchestration, rising to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows. After instrumenting external tool calls with realistic latencies, a latency decomposition shows that LLM reasoning and orchestration still account for more than 90% of execution time, identifying model inference as the primary system bottleneck. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by approximately 30%, and DynAMO maintains correct functional behaviour (task completion, agent sequencing, and output quality) while exhibiting graceful degradation under controlled fault injection. Reproducibility analysis further confirms stable execution under repeated runs, with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance. These findings establish DynAMO as a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines. Code is available at: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO

AI.tldr: DynAMO is a deployment-ready engine for LLM-powered agents in Industry 4.0 that uses Plan-then-Execute architecture with verifiable workflow graphs. It supports both sequential and parallel execution, achieving 1.6–1.8x latency reduction while maintaining safety. Structured context pruning further reduces inference latency by ~30%, and the system degrades gracefully under faults.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agents promise end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, but real-world Industry 4.0 deployment faces three critical barriers: (1) high end-to-end latency, (2) concurrency instability, and (3) safety risks. Existing approaches lack a practical orchestration framework that simultaneously addresses these concerns.
AI.method: DynAMO employs a Plan-then-Execute architecture that first generates verifiable workflow graphs. It supports two execution modes: SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency with dynamic identification of independent tasks). The system instruments external tool calls with realistic latencies, applies structured context pruning to reduce inference overhead, and is evaluated under controlled fault injection for robustness assessment. Experiments were conducted on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark across six controlled scenarios.
AI.result: Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by 1.6x median (up to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows). LLM reasoning and orchestration account for >90% of execution time after realistic tool-call instrumentation, with structured context pruning reducing inference latency by ~30%. DynAMO maintains correct functional behavior (task completion, agent sequencing, output quality) under fault injection with graceful degradation. Reproducibility analysis confirms stable execution with reduced latency variance under parallel scheduling.
AI.conclusion: DynAMO provides a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware LLM-agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines, establishing that dependency-aware parallel orchestration with verifiable workflows can simultaneously address latency, safety, and robustness requirements.

title: Token Factory: Efficiently Integrating Diverse Signals into Large Recommendation Models
summary: Large Recommendation Models (LRMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in industry-scale recommendation tasks. However, holistically integrating traditional signals into these transformer-based architectures effectively and efficiently remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches that "textualize" these signals directly or create discrete item representations often lead to excessively long prompts, substantial memory footprints, and high computational overhead. To overcome these limitations, we propose "Token Factory", a framework designed to transform traditional signals into "soft tokens" that can be directly processed by LRMs. This approach enables efficient integration and compression of heterogeneous input features, preventing prompt length explosion while enhancing model performance. We detail the architecture of Token Factory and present experimental results validating its effectiveness in a production-scale recommendation environment.

AI.tldr: Token Factory introduces "soft tokens" to efficiently integrate traditional recommendation signals into Large Recommendation Models (LRMs), solving the problem of prompt length explosion and high computational cost inherent in textualization or discrete representation approaches.
AI.motivation: LRMs perform well in recommendation but struggle to holistically and efficiently incorporate traditional signals (e.g., categorical features, user/item metadata). Existing methods that textualize signals or create discrete item representations cause excessively long prompts, large memory footprints, and high computational overhead, limiting practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors propose "Token Factory," a framework that transforms traditional recommendation signals into learnable, continuous "soft tokens." These soft tokens are directly consumable by transformer-based LRMs, enabling heterogeneous input features to be integrated and compressed efficiently. The architecture prevents prompt length explosion while retaining signal fidelity, functioning as a feature encoding bridge between traditional recommender system inputs and modern LRM architectures.
AI.result: Experimental results from a production-scale recommendation environment validate that Token Factory effectively integrates traditional signals into LRMs, improving model performance while avoiding the prompt length and computational inefficiencies of prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: Token Factory provides a practical, scalable solution for bridging traditional recommendation signals with transformer-based LRMs, enabling efficient industrial deployment without sacrificing the richness of heterogeneous input features.

title: Disentangling Linguistic Relatedness from Task Alignment in Cross-Lingual Transfer
summary: We study cross-lingual transfer by fine-tuning seven large language models (4B--671B parameters) on Arabic and evaluating zero-shot reading comprehension on Semitic languages and non-Semitic controls. Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, we find no evidence of Semitic-specific transfer: models with weak baselines improve dramatically across all languages, while strong-baseline models show only marginal gains regardless of language family. A chain-of-thought ablation reinforces this finding -- the same models that benefit most from fine-tuning benefit equally from inference-time reasoning, suggesting both mechanisms address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs on Arabic yields zero-shot reading comprehension improvements that are uniform across Semitic and non-Semitic languages, driven by task-format alignment rather than language-family-specific cross-lingual transfer. Strong-baseline models show only marginal gains, and chain-of-thought prompting produces similar benefits, reinforcing the format-alignment hypothesis.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether fine-tuning LLMs on one Semitic language (Arabic) yields disproportionate cross-lingual transfer benefits for other Semitic languages compared to unrelated languages, testing the hypothesis of language-family-specific transfer.
AI.method: The authors fine-tuned seven LLMs (4B–671B parameters, spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures) on Arabic reading comprehension data, then evaluated zero-shot performance on a suite of Semitic languages and non-Semitic control languages. They further conducted a chain-of-thought ablation: models that benefited from fine-tuning were tested with inference-time reasoning to disentangle task-format alignment from knowledge transfer.
AI.result: No evidence of Semitic-specific transfer was found. Weak-baseline models improved dramatically across all languages irrespective of family; strong-baseline models showed only marginal gains. The chain-of-thought ablation revealed that models benefiting most from fine-tuning also benefited equally from inference-time reasoning, implicating task-format alignment as the primary mechanism rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual transfer from Arabic fine-tuning is not mediated by language-family similarity but by teaching models the task format. Both fine-tuning and chain-of-thought prompting serve as interchangeable means of aligning models to the reading comprehension task structure.

title: Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized language modeling through autoregressive generation, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as an alternative paradigm that generates text through iterative denoising rather than next-token prediction, allowing parallel refinement of entire sequences. While numerous diffusion-based architectures have been proposed, differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare their capabilities and understand the trade-offs they offer. In this work, we present a systematic experimental analysis of modern DLMs. Specifically, we evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving, while explicitly considering both generation quality and computational efficiency. Beyond downstream evaluation, we analyze the impact of key inference-time factors, including denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, and complement large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets. We show that the behavior of DLMs is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. Overall, our study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic experimental comparison of eight state-of-the-art Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) across eight diverse benchmarks, analyzing performance-efficiency trade-offs and the impact of inference-time design choices such as denoising steps, context length, and parallel unmasking strategies.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of diverse DLM architectures has created a fragmented landscape where inconsistent evaluation protocols, datasets, and hyperparameters prevent meaningful comparison. There is a need for a unified, systematic analysis to clarify the real-world capabilities and trade-offs of diffusion-based language modeling versus autoregressive methods.
