title: LLM Doesn't Know What It Doesn't Know: Detecting Epistemic Blind Spots via Cross-Model Attribution Divergence on Clinical Tabular Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to structured clinical data, yet whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge on such tasks remains unexplored. We study this question through the lens of cross-model attribution divergence with the goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty for structured tasks, comparing Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a prediction task via attribution divergence analysis. We report four findings. First, LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, it outputs a near-constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of whether accuracy is 49% or 75.3%, tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. Second, the LLM exhibits an inverse difficulty effect: accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when it is moderately uncertain. Third, few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions: they reduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) from 1.54 to 0.38 and improve accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. Fourth, a cross-model calibrator that determined LLM reliability using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates, without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. We frame these findings as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data and outline a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness.

AI.tldr: LLMs show poor epistemic self-awareness on structured clinical data — their verbalized confidence is near-constant and uninformative. Cross-model attribution divergence analysis with XGBoost reveals an inverse difficulty effect, and combining few-shot examples with SHAP-derived evidence dramatically improves both agreement and accuracy. A cross-model calibrator using attribution divergence signals reduces calibration error significantly without accessing model internals.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed on structured clinical tasks, but whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge (epistemic self-awareness) on such data is unknown. The authors aim to reduce epistemic uncertainty by studying cross-model attribution divergence between LLMs and traditional ML models.
AI.method: The authors compare Qwen 2.5 7B with XGBoost on a structured clinical prediction task using attribution divergence analysis. They introduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) to quantify divergence. Interventions include few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence, both individually and combined. A cross-model calibrator is developed that uses attribution divergence signals to produce patient-specific reliability estimates, operating without model internals or repeated inference.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) LLM verbalized confidence is nearly constant (0.856–0.937) regardless of accuracy (49%–75.3%), tracking prompt format not prediction quality. (2) Inverse difficulty effect: LLM accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when XGBoost is uncertain. (3) Few-shot examples and SHAP evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions, reducing ADS from 1.54 to 0.38 and improving accuracy from 49% to 75.3%. (4) The cross-model calibrator reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080.
AI.conclusion: The findings constitute a "cold start" problem for LLMs on structured data: they lack genuine epistemic self-awareness and default to uninformative confidence heuristics. Cross-model attribution divergence offers a practical path toward patient-specific reliability estimation and improved calibration without requiring model internals.

title: When Global Gating Is Enough: Admission-Time Hubness Control in Anisotropic Vector Retrieval Systems
summary: Vector hubness, where a few points become nearest neighbors of many queries, creates a poisoning risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): one injected document can influence unrelated requests. Existing defenses use periodic reverse-kNN scans, leaving an exposure window and repeated corpus-wide work. We study admission-time control, scoring each candidate against sentinel queries and quarantining hub-like documents before insertion. Across two 100,000-document corpora, five encoders, and disjoint attacker and defender query sets, a global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (>=0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91 +/- 0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on general documents. A per-topic gate provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, with corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. On HNSW, admission adds about 3.1% to ingestion latency, scoring remains flat to 10^6 vectors, and 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing, none involving attacks. Provenance complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an admission-time control mechanism that quarantines hub-like documents before they enter a vector index, mitigating hubness-based poisoning attacks in RAG systems. Using sentinel queries and a global gate, it achieves near-perfect recall against attacks with only 1% false positives, adding ~3.1% ingestion overhead on HNSW.
AI.motivation: Vector hubness — where a few points dominate nearest-neighbor results across many queries — poses a poisoning risk for RAG: an attacker can inject a single hub document that surfaces in responses to many unrelated requests. Existing defenses rely on periodic reverse-kNN scans, which leave an exposure window between scans and require repeated corpus-wide computation. The authors aim to close this window by intercepting adversarial documents at ingestion time.
AI.method: The approach scores each incoming document candidate against a fixed set of sentinel queries (disjoint from real user queries) using the same embedding model. A global gate computes a hubness score — based on how often the candidate ranks among top-k results across sentinels — and quarantines documents exceeding a threshold. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, yielding corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion. The method is evaluated across two 100K-document corpora, five encoders, and adversarial settings including HotFlip attacks, with both exact and approximate (HNSW) indexing. A per-topic gate variant is also tested. Provenance tracking is positioned as a complement for natural or tight-domain hubs.
AI.result: The global gate achieves recall of 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point and ≥0.92 across the effective range. Against HotFlip attacks, recall is 0.91 ± 0.07. False positives on benign documents are ~1%. The per-topic gate provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Admission adds ~3.1% to HNSW ingestion latency, with scoring latency remaining flat up to 10^6 vectors. Under approximate indexing, only 1.2% of admission decisions flip, none involving attacks.
AI.conclusion: Admission-time gating with sentinel queries is an effective, low-overhead defense against hubness-based poisoning in RAG, eliminating the exposure window of periodic scans. The global nature of hubness (due to embedding anisotropy) makes a global gate sufficient; per-topic gating offers no gains. Provenance can complement the gate for edge cases involving natural or domain-specific hubs.

title: Weibull Weight-Scale Parameter Evolution under AdamW Training Dynamics
summary: Building on a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, we study why the Weibull weight-scale parameter $λ$ grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training. We derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update: an alignment force measuring the correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction, an injection force from adaptive step magnitude, and a decay force from decoupled weight decay. On self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments, alignment dominates the rise phase, contributing 88-94% of the absolute force budget across four random seeds and remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the transition from weight-scale growth to relaxation. These force dynamics directly govern the squared-norm component underlying $λ(t)$; the remaining RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is measurable and decomposes into bridge and integration components, totaling approximately 5-6% in densely sampled regions. To extend the analysis to real models where optimizer moments are unavailable, we introduce a spline displacement method that recovers the alignment force from sparse checkpoints with approximately 92-94% accuracy, about twice the naive two-point baseline. We further observe that the peak value of $λ(t)$ varies with training-data coherence in our experiments, suggesting a data-dependent component of weight-scale growth that we leave to a controlled follow-up study. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes why the Weibull weight-scale parameter λ grows, overshoots, and relaxes during AdamW training. The authors decompose squared weight norm dynamics into alignment, injection, and decay forces, showing alignment dominates growth (88–94% of force budget), while alignment–decay balance explains the peak and relaxation. A spline displacement method recovers alignment force from sparse checkpoints at ~92–94% accuracy, and a data-dependence observation motivates future study.
AI.motivation: Prior work established a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, but the dynamical mechanism driving the characteristic growth, overshoot, and relaxation of the Weibull scale parameter λ during AdamW training remained unexplained. The authors aim to uncover the underlying optimizer-level forces governing this phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm directly from the AdamW update rule: (1) an alignment force (correlation between weights and adaptive update direction), (2) an injection force (adaptive step magnitude), and (3) a decay force (from decoupled weight decay). They validate this decomposition on self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments across four random seeds. For real-world models where optimizer moments are inaccessible, they introduce a spline displacement method to recover alignment force from sparse checkpoints. They also decompose the RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset into bridge and integration components.
AI.result: Alignment force dominates the weight-norm growth phase, contributing 88–94% of the absolute force budget and remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay forces approach balance, explaining the transition from growth to relaxation. The RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset totals ~5–6% in densely sampled regions. The spline displacement method recovers alignment force with ~92–94% accuracy from sparse checkpoints, roughly double the naive two-point baseline. The peak value of λ(t) varies with training-data coherence.
AI.conclusion: The three-force decomposition provides a mechanistic understanding of Weibull weight-scale dynamics during AdamW training. Alignment force is the primary driver of weight-scale growth, and its balance with decay explains the overshoot-relaxation pattern. The spline displacement method enables practical force analysis without requiring full optimizer state. The data-dependence of λ's peak suggests a connection between data coherence and weight-scale dynamics, left for future controlled study.

title: Designing for Interconnected Islamic Learning: A Qualitative Study of Muslim Women's Experiences with Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah Apps
comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
summary: Islamic learning often depends on reading the Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah together, yet digital tools typically separate these sources across apps, screens, and search pathways. We examine this as a human-computer interaction problem through five semi-structured interviews with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Participants described a recurring tension: they wanted Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context at the point of reading, but only when contextual expansion remained trustworthy, optional, and did not interrupt reading. Interpreting the interviews through gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning, we identify five themes concerning contextual understanding, authenticity, interface clutter, study modes, and guidance features. We introduce layered contextuality as an HCI account of this domain: contextual expansion must be balanced with interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and continuity across devices and study intensities.

AI.tldr: Islamic learners need Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah integrated at the point of reading, but only when that contextual expansion is trustworthy, optional, and non-disruptive. The paper proposes "layered contextuality" as an HCI framework balancing contextual depth with devotional flow, interpretive accountability, and cross-device continuity.
AI.motivation: Digital Islamic learning tools fragment the Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah across separate apps and interfaces, despite traditional Islamic pedagogy relying on their integrated study. This fragmentation creates a human-computer interaction problem that undermines contextual understanding for learners, particularly in informal, self-directed study settings.
AI.method: Five semi-structured interviews with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Data interpreted through three analytical lenses: gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning. Thematic analysis yielded five themes.
AI.result: Five themes emerged: (1) desire for contextual understanding across the three sources; (2) concern for authenticity and epistemic trustworthiness of linked content; (3) tension around interface clutter versus minimalist reading; (4) need to toggle between devotional and study modes; (5) demand for guidance features. These reveal a recurring tension: learners want integrated context available on demand but fear interruption of devotional flow and unreliable interpretive pathways.
AI.conclusion: The authors introduce "layered contextuality" — an HCI design concept where contextual expansion (linking Qur'an, Hadith, Seerah) must be balanced with interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and seamless continuity across devices and study intensities. This framework offers guidance for designing digital religious learning tools that respect both epistemic rigor and spiritual experience.

title: ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research
summary: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

AI.tldr: ScaffoldAgent is a dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research that models outline evolution as a structured decision process with Expansion, Contraction, and Revision operations, guided by a utility signal that estimates downstream value from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing OEDR systems suffer from "scaffold drift" — fixed outlines or locally-heuristic refinements cannot adapt to continuous information accumulation during multi-round retrieval, and there is delayed feedback for evaluating whether outline modifications improve the final report. A principled mechanism is needed to dynamically optimize the outline scaffold based on anticipated downstream utility.
AI.method: ScaffoldAgent treats outline evolution as a structured decision process with three atomic operations: Expansion (adding new nodes), Contraction (removing nodes), and Revision (modifying existing nodes). A utility-guided feedback mechanism estimates the downstream value of each candidate operation by computing retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal drives node selection, operation scheduling, and termination decisions during inference.
AI.result: Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym demonstrate that ScaffoldAgent consistently outperforms existing deep research agents in both long-form report generation quality and factual grounding.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, utility-guided outline optimization significantly improves the coherence and factual accuracy of long-form reports in open-ended deep research settings, addressing the scaffold drift problem that plagues fixed-outline and heuristic-refinement baselines.

title: Execution-bound advisory automation for agentic AI: a reproducible AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework
summary: A protocol driven framework is presented that binds SBOM and AIBOM artefacts to deterministic environment capture and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed from declared artefacts, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies. CSAF VEX advisories are generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated through deterministic replay. Evaluation uses approximately 10000 component entries across synthetic Agentic AI workloads 50 to 5000 components, incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.

AI.tldr: A protocol framework linking SBOM/AIBOM artifacts with deterministic environment capture and runtime telemetry to compute exploitability, generate signed CSAF VEX advisories, and validate through replay, evaluated on ~10,000 components across synthetic Agentic AI workloads.
AI.motivation: Current vulnerability management approaches lack deterministic, verifiable linkage between declared software/AI bills of materials, runtime behavior, and exploitability assessment. The gap between static artifact declarations and actual runtime conditions prevents reliable, cryptographically provable vulnerability advisory generation.
AI.method: The framework binds SBOM and AIBOM artifacts to deterministic environment snapshots and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed through a tripartite analysis: (1) declared artifacts, (2) observed activation conditions, and (3) enforced execution policies. CSAF-format VEX advisories are then generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated via deterministic replay. Evaluation spans ~10,000 component entries in synthetic Agentic AI workloads scaling from 50 to 5,000 components, integrating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.
AI.result: The approach successfully generates verifiable, signed CSAF VEX advisories from combined static and runtime evidence. Deterministic replay validates the integrity of the advisory generation pipeline. The framework scales across synthetic Agentic AI workloads ranging from 50 to 5,000 components, demonstrating feasibility on approximately 10,000 total component entries across multiple vulnerability intelligence sources (OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, EPSS).
AI.conclusion: Deterministic binding of SBOM/AIBOM artifacts to runtime telemetry enables verifiable, replayable exploitability computation and cryptographically signed advisory generation. The protocol-driven approach provides a foundation for trustworthy, evidence-based vulnerability disclosure in complex, AI-augmented software supply chains.

title: PACMS: Submodular Context Selection as a Pluggable Engine for LLM Agents
summary:
Conversational and tool-using LLM agents operate over a context window that fills from several directions simultaneously. As a session proceeds, the agent accumulates user and assistant turns, entries drawn from a persistent memory store, and often largest of all, the verbatim outputs of tool calls such as file reads, search results, and API responses. Once the cumulative context exceeds the model's token budget, the framework must decide what to keep.
  The prevailing mechanism is recency truncation, sometimes paired with periodic summarization. This is topic-blind: a fact established early in a session is discarded simply because it is old, even when the current user query is about exactly that fact; conversely, verbose but irrelevant recent material is retained. Agents that must recall information across many turns, the defining case for memory, are precisely where recency truncation fails.
  Existing alternatives sit outside the agent's assembly step. Retrieval augmented generation fetches external documents into the prompt but does not arbitrate the agent's \emph{already-present} pooled context. Context-compression methods reduce token count by rewriting or pruning text, but operate query-blind and lossily. Neither treats memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool to be selected from by relevance at the moment the prompt is assembled.

AI.tldr: Current LLM agents rely on recency-based context truncation, which discards old but potentially relevant information while retaining irrelevant recent content. The authors argue for a relevance-based selection mechanism that treats conversation turns, memory entries, and tool outputs as a unified candidate pool during prompt assembly.
AI.motivation: LLM agents with conversational memory and tool-use capabilities accumulate extensive context — user/assistant turns, persistent memory entries, and verbose tool outputs (file reads, search results, API responses). When this exceeds token limits, recency truncation (the dominant approach) fails catastrophically: it discards early-session facts that may be critical to the current query while keeping irrelevant recent material. This is especially problematic for memory-intensive agents that must recall across many turns. Existing alternatives like RAG (fetching external documents) and context compression (lossy rewriting/pruning) operate outside the prompt-assembly step and do not treat all context sources as a unified, relevance-selectable pool.
AI.method: This abstract is a position/problem-formulation piece rather than presenting a concrete implemented method. It identifies the gap: current approaches either truncate by recency (topic-blind), retrieve external documents (RAG), or compress lossily, but none performs relevance-based arbitration over the agent's already-present pooled context — encompassing memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs — at the moment of prompt assembly.
AI.result: The abstract does not present empirical results. It establishes a problem characterization: recency truncation is structurally misaligned with the needs of memory-reliant agents, and existing alternatives (RAG, context compression) fail to address the need for a unified, relevance-driven selection mechanism operating at prompt-assembly time.
AI.conclusion: A new mechanism is needed that performs query-conditioned, relevance-based selection over the entire pooled context (conversation, memory, tool outputs) during prompt assembly, rather than relying on recency truncation, external retrieval alone, or lossy compression.

title: Pruning via Causal Attribution Preserves Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on LLM Reasoning. 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning but incur substantial inference cost. We introduce Causal Attribution Pruning (CAP), a training-free method that identifies critical attention heads by measuring their causal impact on reasoning tasks and uses these head-level scores to guide fine-grained weight pruning. For each attention head, CAP estimates the expected performance degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. These causal scores are then converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices. Unlike magnitude-only or activation-based criteria, CAP's interventional measurement directly captures each head's functional contribution, yielding relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. We evaluate CAP on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP improves over Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations. with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. Our results suggest that attention-head-level causal attribution can better preserve reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, while remaining limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity.

AI.tldr: CAP is a training-free pruning method that uses causal attribution scores at the attention-head level to guide fine-grained weight pruning, achieving up to 61% relative accuracy gains over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity for reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at multi-step reasoning but incur high inference costs. Existing pruning criteria (magnitude-based, activation-based) are correlational rather than causal, so they may misidentify which heads are functionally important for reasoning, degrading downstream performance.
AI.method: CAP measures each attention head's causal impact by forward-passing a small reasoning calibration set with the head masked, estimating expected performance degradation. These head-level causal scores are converted to weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices, guiding structured pruning. CAP is training-free and interventional.
AI.result: CAP outperforms Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations at 10–20% sparsity, with particularly large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3-8B-Instruct (up to 61% relative gain at 20% sparsity). At 50% sparsity, gains diminish due to coarse MLP attribution.
AI.conclusion: Head-level causal attribution better preserves reasoning performance than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, but is limited by coarse MLP importance estimation at high sparsity levels.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision-Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer's Disease Risk
summary: The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision-language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer's disease (AD). A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes replacing discrete phenotypic grouping in vision-language contrastive learning with a continuous, learnable similarity function for predicting Alzheimer's disease from retinal images and clinical risk profiles, demonstrating improved performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language alignment methods for retinal-based AD prediction (e.g., REVEAL) use hard phenotypic group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. This discrete treatment fails to capture the spectrum nature of disease risk.
AI.method: A continuous phenotypic structure formulation is introduced: (1) inter-subject similarity is modeled as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles; (2) soft multi-positive relationships are defined via a continuous aggregation operator; (3) a soft-target contrastive objective jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure end-to-end.
AI.result: The proposed framework consistently outperforms both discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction.
AI.conclusion: Treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal data.

title: SafeSpec: Fast and Safe LLM via Dynamic Reflective Sampling
summary: Speculative inference accelerates large language model (LLM) decoding but provides no inherent safety guarantees. Existing safety defenses are largely incompatible with speculative inference: they either introduce additional computation or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism, negating acceleration benefits. This reveals a fundamental incompatibility between current safety methods and speculative decoding. We propose SafeSpec, a safety-aware speculative inference framework that integrates risk estimation directly into the verification process. SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model to jointly evaluate semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. When unsafe generations are detected, SafeSpec applies rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating generation. We model jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase the probability of harmful continuations without eliminating safe ones. Under this model, SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process. Across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks, SafeSpec achieves a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off. On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup on benign workloads, demonstrating that speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized.

AI.tldr: SafeSpec is a speculative inference framework that integrates safety verification into the draft-verify loop, using a lightweight safety head and risk-aware trajectory recovery to jointly optimize inference speedup and safety against jailbreak attacks.
AI.motivation: Speculative inference accelerates LLM decoding but lacks safety guarantees, and existing safety defenses are incompatible with speculative decoding because they add computation overhead or break the draft-verify mechanism, negating speed gains. This creates a fundamental tension between efficient inference and inference-time safety.
AI.method: SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model, enabling joint evaluation of semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. Unsafe drafts trigger rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations. Jailbreak attacks are modeled as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase harmful continuation probability without eliminating safe paths. SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while maintaining a 2.06× inference speedup on benign workloads. The framework achieves a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized rather than treated as mutually exclusive objectives. SafeSpec demonstrates that integrating risk estimation into the verification stage enables robust safety guarantees without sacrificing the speed benefits of speculative decoding.

title: Zero-Inflated Gaussian Distributions Enable Parameter-Space Sparsity in Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
summary: Estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) are a powerful class of evolutionary methods for black-box optimization, especially when little is known about the structure of the objective. Whereas classical evolutionary algorithms rely on hand-designed mutation and crossover operators, hard to devise for unknown problem structures, and a source of bias, EDAs sidestep operator design entirely: they fit a probability distribution to the best individuals and sample the next generation from it. EDAs are well established on continuous parameter spaces, but they have not previously been generalized to sparse ones, in which most coefficients of a good solution are exactly zero. Existing sparse black-box optimizers therefore reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes alternating between support set and active values, zeroing thresholds, and other baked-in assumptions. We close this gap by proposing multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws. A latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and the interactions between the two, so sparsity patterns and active values are optimized jointly, hierarchy-free. We show that the latent parameters of this model are identifiable from observed samples, unlike in the missing-data settings where related constructions originate, and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators for them. The estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures, and on the Lunar Lander benchmark the resulting ZIG-EDA converges faster and reaches higher final returns than a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while finding controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithm (EDA) for sparse black-box optimization using multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as the sampling model, eliminating the need for hand-crafted sparsity operators by jointly modeling sparsity patterns and active parameter values with identifiable latent parameters and amortized inversion-based estimators.
AI.motivation: Existing EDAs are well-established for continuous dense optimization but have not been generalized to sparse settings where most optimal coefficients are zero. Current sparse black-box optimizers reintroduce hand-designed sparsity operators, bi-level schemes, and zeroing thresholds—precisely the ad-hoc mechanisms EDAs were meant to avoid—creating undesirable inductive bias.
AI.method: The authors introduce multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws, using a latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions that jointly represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and their interactions. They prove identifiability of the latent parameters from observed samples (unlike related missing-data models) and develop practical amortized inversion-based estimators that accurately recover latent correlation structures.
AI.result: On the Lunar Lander benchmark, the ZIG-EDA converges faster and achieves higher final returns compared to a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while discovering controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.
AI.conclusion: ZIG-EDA successfully generalizes EDAs to sparse optimization without reintroducing hand-crafted sparsity mechanisms, demonstrating superior performance and model identifiability, thus filling a significant gap in black-box optimization methodology.

title: MemGUI-Agent: An End-to-End Long-Horizon Mobile GUI Agent with Proactive Context Management
summary: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress on short-horizon tasks, yet remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks that require retaining intermediate facts across many steps and app transitions. We attribute this limitation to ReAct-style prompting, which passively accumulates per-step records, leading to prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts. To address this, we introduce MemGUI-Agent, an end-to-end long-horizon mobile GUI agent with proactive context management. MemGUI-Agent is built on Context-as-Action (ConAct), which casts context management as first-class actions emitted by the same policy that selects UI actions. Instead of passively appending history, ConAct maintains three structured context fields: folded action history, folded UI state, and recent step record, preserving critical UI facts while keeping context compact. To make proactive context management learnable across model scales, we construct MemGUI-3K, a 2,956-trajectory dataset with full ConAct annotations for supervised training and offline analysis. Training an 8B model on MemGUI-3K produces MemGUI-8B-SFT, an 8B MemGUI-Agent that achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://memgui-agent.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MemGUI-Agent introduces Context-as-Action (ConAct), an end-to-end framework that treats context management as first-class actions, maintaining structured, compact context fields to enable reliable long-horizon mobile GUI task execution without prompt explosion.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based mobile GUI agents using ReAct-style prompting passively accumulate per-step records, causing prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts, making them unreliable on long-horizon tasks that require retaining intermediate facts across many steps and app transitions.
AI.method: MemGUI-Agent employs Context-as-Action (ConAct), which casts context management as first-class actions emitted by the same policy that selects UI actions. It maintains three structured context fields (folded action history, folded UI state, and recent step record) instead of passively appending history. A new dataset, MemGUI-3K (2,956 trajectories), provides full ConAct annotations for supervised training. An 8B model (MemGUI-8B-SFT) is trained on this dataset.
AI.result: MemGUI-8B-SFT achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and successfully generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Proactive context management via ConAct, with structured, compact context fields and dedicated training data (MemGUI-3K), enables MLLM-based agents to reliably handle long-horizon mobile GUI tasks, outperforming passive history accumulation approaches and generalizing across benchmarks.

title: RACL: Reasoning-Agent Control Layers for Continuous Metaheuristic Learning
summary: This paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics. RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent does not replace the optimizer and does not modify business constraints. Instead, it controls the optimizer's internal search behavior by observing operational memory, reasoning over past behavior, formulating bounded hypotheses, testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, applying guardrails, consolidating useful policies and explaining its decisions. The experiment uses vehicle routing as a testbed, but the contribution is not a new routing solver, a particular ALNS configuration or a specific set of routing rules. The contribution is the RACL method: a way for a reasoning agent to discover, validate, consolidate and explain algorithmic control rules for a metaheuristic. In the current experimental setting, RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21 of 21 feasible cases and improves or ties a non-reasoning Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18 of 21 feasible cases, with an average RACL vs STP cost delta of -0.641%. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% versus Fixed and -1.605% versus STP without showing material computational overhead. During the proof-of-concept, Codex was used as an in-the-loop reasoning agent observing executions, interpreting logs and proposing live bounded interventions. The policy proxy was later used only to make quantitative evaluation reproducible.

AI.tldr: RACL introduces a reasoning-agent control layer that sits above any metaheuristic optimizer, observing its operational memory, formulating and testing bounded interventions, and consolidating effective control policies—improving routing costs by up to 8.3% over fixed baselines without modifying the underlying solver or its constraints.
AI.motivation: Metaheuristics often rely on hand-tuned, static control policies that cannot adapt to instance-specific dynamics during search. Rather than designing new solvers or problem-specific rules, the authors aim to create a general method that allows a reasoning agent to dynamically discover, validate, and explain algorithmic control rules by observing and intervening on an existing optimizer's internal state.
AI.method: RACL places a reasoning agent (Codex in the proof-of-concept) above an existing optimizer (ALNS for vehicle routing). The agent observes the optimizer's operational memory, reasons over past behavior, formulates bounded hypotheses, tests interventions, evaluates outcomes against guardrails, and consolidates successful policies. A policy proxy is later used for reproducible quantitative evaluation. The method is compared against Fixed, Operational Memory Policy (OMP), and Stagnation-Triggered Policy (STP) baselines.
AI.result: RACL improves or ties OMP in 21/21 feasible cases and improves or ties STP in 18/21 cases, with an average cost delta of -0.641% vs STP. On the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% vs Fixed and -1.605% vs STP, with negligible computational overhead. The reasoning agent discovers, validates, and consolidates effective control rules without modifying business constraints.
AI.conclusion: RACL demonstrates that a reasoning agent can effectively control a metaheuristic's internal search behavior from above, yielding consistent improvements over static and stagnation-triggered policies. The contribution is the general RACL method itself—not any specific routing solver or rule set—opening a path toward self-adaptive, explainable metaheuristic control layers.

title: DevOps and General Developers: Insights from Stack Overflow's 2023 Survey
comment: 17 pages, 11 tables, research paper based on the 2023 Stack Overflow Developer Survey data analysis
summary:
Purpose: To investigate the distinct roles of DevOps specialists and general software developers, examining their varying use of tools, technologies, methodologies, and demographics in the current software development environment. In addition, to differentiate these two professional groups regarding their unique contributions and challenges in the field.
  Design/Methodology/Approach: The research uses a quantitative approach to analyze data from the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey. It focuses on a comparative analysis of technological preferences, demographic information, and professional experiences between DevOps specialists and general developers, highlighting key trends and differences. The data analysis was conducted using Python's Pandas library for data analysis.
  Findings: The research indicates no significant difference in the tool and technology preferences between DevOps specialists and general software developers, highlighting their complementary roles. DevOps specialists and general software developers use tools like Docker and Kubernetes, emphasizing efficiency and automation. While general developers employ diverse tools for various role demands, demographic trends show younger general developers and mid-career DevOps professionals. This age range reflects growing experience in DevOps, and both groups are adapting to remote and hybrid work models in the evolving tech industry.
  Practical Implications: This research offers perspectives on the dynamic roles within software development, emphasizing the growing importance of DevOps. It is a valuable resource for academic and industry professionals to understand the evolving dynamics in software development roles.
  Originality/Value: This research fills a significant gap in the existing literature regarding the evolving dynamics of software development roles.

AI.tldr: This study compares DevOps specialists and general software developers using Stack Overflow 2023 survey data, finding no significant differences in tool/technology preferences but notable demographic distinctions — younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps professionals — with both groups converging on tools like Docker/Kubernetes and adapting to remote/hybrid work models.
AI.motivation: To fill a gap in the literature by empirically distinguishing DevOps specialists from general software developers in terms of tool usage, methodologies, demographics, and professional contributions, thereby clarifying their distinct yet complementary roles in modern software development.
AI.method: Quantitative comparative analysis of Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey data using Python's Pandas library, examining technological preferences, demographic information, and professional experiences between the two groups.
AI.result: No significant difference in tool/technology preferences between groups; both heavily use Docker and Kubernetes. Demographic patterns reveal younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps specialists. Both groups are increasingly adopting remote and hybrid work arrangements.
AI.conclusion: DevOps specialists and general developers play complementary rather than fundamentally distinct roles regarding tooling. The field shows age-based stratification with DevOps attracting more experienced professionals, and the broader industry shift toward remote/hybrid work is evident across both groups.

title: Generative Engine Optimization at Scale: Measuring Brand Visibility Across AI Search Engines
summary:
People increasingly get answers straight from AI search engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini rather than scrolling search results. Brands that once focused on search engine optimization (SEO) must now optimize for how these engines represent, cite, and recommend them -- a shift variously called Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), and AI Search Visibility. We treat AEO and AI Visibility as part of GEO, and study how to measure brand visibility across AI engines: what they value when they cite a brand, which sources they rely on, and what content large language models surface. The hard case is everyone outside the already-authoritative top brands -- SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and early-stage startups.
  We analyze 100K+ prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on Ranqo between March and May 2026. First visibility runs form a clear three-tier brand-stature ladder: global household names (e.g., Stripe, Nike) appear in 73% of relevant AI answers on their first run; established mid-market and regional brands (e.g., Olipop, Klaviyo) in 44%; niche and small brands in just 11% -- about 30 percentage points per step. When engines cite sources, about 78% go to corporate websites; among non-corporate sources YouTube leads, ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. The highest-leverage page is the ranked "best-of" listicle, the most-cited content format at about 21% of all citations. Sentiment is the unstable signal: whether a brand is framed positively or negatively flips about 6.7 times more often than whether it is mentioned at all.
  These findings provide a first large-scale baseline for measuring GEO: AI brand visibility can be measured, differs by platform, and varies strongly by brand maturity. We close by proposing seven v1.1 protocols to test whether specific recommendations can causally improve AI visibility.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale empirical analysis of brand visibility across AI-powered search engines (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini), analyzing 100K+ prompt responses for 100+ brands. It finds a steep three-tier visibility hierarchy — household names appear in 73% of relevant answers, mid-market brands in 44%, and niche brands in just 11%. Corporate websites dominate citations (78%), "best-of" listicles are the most-cited content format (~21%), and sentiment proves highly unstable. The authors propose seven measurement protocols for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).
AI.motivation: As users increasingly query AI search engines directly rather than clicking through traditional search results, brands must shift from SEO to optimizing for how AI engines represent, cite, and recommend them. No large-scale baseline exists for measuring this visibility, and the challenge is especially acute for non-authoritative brands — SMEs, D2C companies, creators, and startups — who lack the established digital authority of global household names.
AI.method: The authors analyzed over 100,000 prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on the Ranqo platform between March and May 2026. They measured brand visibility by examining: (1) mention frequency in AI-generated answers, (2) source citation patterns (corporate vs. non-corporate), (3) content formats most frequently cited, and (4) sentiment stability. Brands were stratified into three tiers — global household names, established mid-market/regional brands, and niche/small brands — to compare visibility rates.
AI.result: Three key findings emerged: (1) A three-tier brand-stature ladder with ~30 percentage-point drops per step (73% → 44% → 11% visibility); (2) corporate websites account for 78% of citations, with YouTube leading non-corporate sources ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia; (3) "best-of" listicles dominate as the most-cited content format (~21% of all citations); (4) sentiment is the most volatile signal, flipping positive/negative ~6.7× more often than mention presence changes. Visibility also varies by AI platform and strongly correlates with brand maturity.
AI.conclusion: AI brand visibility is measurable, platform-dependent, and stratified by brand maturity. The findings establish the first large-scale empirical baseline for GEO research. The authors propose seven v1.1 protocols for causally testing interventions to improve AI visibility, framing GEO as an emerging discipline requiring structured, reproducible measurement.

title: Detecting Hallucinations for Large Language Model-based Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning infers new knowledge from existing facts and is widely applied in question answering, recommendation, and decision support. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks have become increasingly popular by leveraging retrieved KG information. However, hallucinations in LLMs remain a critical issue. Even when relevant KG knowledge is incorporated, models may still generate incorrect outputs, leading to misinformation and unreliable decisions. Existing hallucination detection methods either focus on LLM internal states or verify consistency with retrieved contexts, but both overlook the structural information in KGs, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this gap, we propose LUCID, the first halLUcination deteCtIon method for LLM-based knowleDge graph reasoning frameworks. LUCID jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information. Specifically, it extracts node and edge features from attention scores and semantic similarities, and integrates them with KG structure using a graph neural network. We also construct manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation. Experiments on nine datasets show that LUCID achieves state of the art performance compared to 15 baselines.

AI.tldr: LUCID is a hallucination detection method for LLM-based KG reasoning that combines LLM attention scores with KG structural and semantic features via a graph neural network, achieving state-of-the-art results across nine benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: LLMs tend to hallucinate even when provided with relevant KG knowledge, and existing hallucination detection methods ignore KG structural information, leading to suboptimal detection in KG reasoning contexts.
AI.method: LUCID extracts node and edge features from LLM attention scores and semantic similarities, then integrates them with KG structural information using a graph neural network. The authors also constructed manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on nine datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance compared to 15 baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating KG structural information alongside LLM attention and semantic features significantly improves hallucination detection in LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks. LUCID is the first method specifically designed for this task.

title: Emergent Alignment
summary: Can Large Language Models (LLMs) discern when their own outputs are misaligned with human ethics? And can they self-correct? We endow an LLM with a conscience step that reviews its own reasoning and outputs, and we extend the training loss with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to steer the model away from non-ethical outputs. The result is an online technique to align models in a wide range of applications: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning. It does not require a weaker or stronger judge, relying instead on a frozen copy of itself. In previous work, the Emergent Misalignment scenario showed a range of emergent unethical behaviors from fine-tuning the model to hack code. Instead, we empirically show how to achieve Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question steers training toward an ethical model under the same code hacking scenario.

AI.tldr: LLMs are equipped with a "conscience step" — a self-review mechanism — and trained via DPO to self-identify and correct ethically misaligned outputs, achieving "Emergent Alignment" without external judges, demonstrated on code-hacking scenarios.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs can autonomously detect when their outputs violate human ethics and self-correct, addressing the risk of emergent misalignment during fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and deployment.
AI.method: A conscience step is added where the model reviews its own reasoning and outputs. Training loss is augmented with a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) alignment component that penalizes unethical outputs, using a frozen copy of the model as the reference (no external/stronger judge). The technique is applied online across training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot settings.
AI.result: The method produces "Emergent Alignment": a single high-level introspective question steers the model toward ethical behavior, empirically demonstrated in the same code-hacking scenario previously used to show Emergent Misalignment.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can self-monitor and self-correct ethical misalignment through introspection augmented with DPO-based alignment training, enabling scalable alignment without reliance on external supervisory models.

title: DISARM: Target Electronic Device Informed Mitigation of Software Runtime Side-Channel Vulnerabilities
summary: Program runtime or timing attacks exploit variations in a program's execution times to extract sensitive information from the program (e.g. encryption keys, sensitive variable data, intellectual property). State-of-the-art solutions to runtime side-channel attacks attempt to balance the execution time of the sensitive code for different control flow paths to eliminate the timing leakage. However, during the mitigation process, most techniques do not consider the underlying hardware or device on which the target program is supposed to run on. This can lead to over-fixing (unnecessary extra operations), under-fixing (not solving the imbalance properly), and even failures. We propose DISARM, a joint hardware-software methodology (unlike any existing solution) for mitigating runtime side-channel vulnerabilities that utilizes timing values from real embedded devices to generate targeted software fixes. We implement DISARM to support C, C++, and Java source codes and validate it across 22 standard benchmarks. DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions such as PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR in terms of execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness on five different embedded or edge devices.

AI.tldr: DISARM is a joint hardware-software methodology that uses real timing measurements from embedded devices to generate targeted software fixes for runtime side-channel vulnerabilities, outperforming existing solutions across execution time, code size, and correctness.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime side-channel mitigation techniques fail to account for the underlying hardware, leading to over-fixing, under-fixing, or outright failures. No prior solution jointly considers hardware and software in the mitigation process.
AI.method: DISARM uses timing values collected from real embedded devices to guide software-based fixes. It supports C, C++, and Java source code and validates across 22 standard benchmarks on five different embedded/edge devices.
AI.result: DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions (PENDULUM, DifFuzzAR) in execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness across all five tested embedded/edge devices.
AI.conclusion: A hardware-aware, joint design approach to timing side-channel mitigation yields more precise and efficient fixes than software-only or hardware-agnostic techniques.

title: MobileForge: Annotation-Free Adaptation for Mobile GUI Agents with Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization
summary: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress in UI understanding and action execution, but adapting them to real target apps remains costly because mobile apps are numerous, frequently updated, and hard to cover with human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free GUI learning reduces manual supervision, yet lacks a unified substrate connecting target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback, while policy optimization often relies on isolated rollouts and coarse rewards that are hard to convert into reliable improvement signals. We present MobileForge, an annotation-free adaptation system for mobile GUI agents. MobileForge consists of MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interaction, and Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which turns trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO updates. Using only automatically generated annotation-free adaptation data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld, close to the closed-data GUI-specialized GUI-Owl-1.5-8B base model at 69.0%. The MobileForge-adapted ForgeOwl-8B further reaches 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent in our evaluation. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://mobile-forge.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MobileForge is an annotation-free adaptation framework for mobile GUI agents that combines MobileGym (a real-app interaction environment) with HiFPO (a hierarchical, feedback-guided policy optimization method using step-level GRPO updates) to adapt MLLMs for mobile tasks without human annotations, achieving competitive or superior performance against closed-data baselines.
AI.motivation: Adapting MLLM-based mobile GUI agents to real target apps is costly due to the sheer number, frequent updates, and difficulty of covering apps with human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free approaches lack a unified framework connecting exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback, while policy optimization relies on coarse rewards that yield unreliable improvement signals.
AI.method: MobileForge comprises two components: (1) MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interactions through automated exploration and curriculum mining; (2) HiFPO (Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization), which converts trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) updates for fine-grained policy improvement.
AI.result: Using only automatically generated annotation-free data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld (close to the closed-data GUI-Owl-1.5-8B at 69.0%). The resulting model ForgeOwl-8B achieves 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing it as the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent.
AI.conclusion: MobileForge demonstrates that annotation-free adaptation with hierarchical feedback-guided policy optimization can effectively adapt general MLLMs into competitive mobile GUI agents, matching or exceeding closed-data specialized models while using only automatically generated data, with strong generalization to out-of-domain tasks.

title: A Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization
comment: Presented at the 17th Workshop on Optimization and Learning in Multiagent Systems (OptLearnMAS, https://optlearnmas.github.io), co-located with the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
summary: Many decision-making problems in computing and networking systems can be naturally formulated as cost-minimization problems under performance constraints. In dynamic environments, reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to solve such problems at runtime by embedding both costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward through weighted penalty terms, following a Lagrangian-inspired formulation. However, in this context the behavior of the learned policy critically depends on the choice of these weights, which are typically selected manually. This makes it difficult to identify an appropriate trade-off between optimizing the primary objective and effectively avoiding constraint violations, particularly in non-stationary environments where their relative importance may change. This paper presents MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization), an approach to tackle this balancing problem through multi-agent RL. MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by formulating the selection of reward weights as a learning problem, providing a !rst step towards more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: MAMO decouples reward weight selection from task execution by framing weight selection as a multi-agent RL problem, enabling autonomous balancing of cost minimization and constraint satisfaction in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: In Lagrangian-inspired RL for constrained optimization, the reward weights (penalty terms) critically influence policy behavior but are typically hand-tuned. This manual selection fails in non-stationary environments where the cost-constraint trade-off shifts over time, motivating an automated, adaptive weight selection mechanism.
AI.method: MAMO employs a multi-agent RL architecture that decouples task execution from objective design. One set of agents handles the primary task (cost minimization under constraints), while another agent (or set of agents) learns to dynamically select the reward weights that balance costs and constraint violations, treating weight selection itself as a learning problem.
AI.result: The paper presents MAMO as a first step toward autonomous and robust RL-based solutions, though the abstract does not report specific quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling reward weight selection from task policy learning via multi-agent RL provides a more autonomous and adaptive approach to constrained optimization in dynamic environments, reducing reliance on manual weight tuning.

title: JustDiag!: A Diagnostic Justification Engine for Accountable Root Cause Analysis
summary: Large language models can produce fluent root cause analyses, but fluent final answers alone are insufficient evidence for accountability in high-stakes operations. In real incident response, engineers need to know what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remained, and whether the system resolved the case or preserved uncertainty. We address this gap with JustDiag, a diagnostic justification engine for RCA that maintains an explicit process state over evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. We evaluated the system on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer protocol that separately scores final-answer quality and process quality. Relative to a matched control without diagnostic justification, JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores, while accepting slightly lower terminal completion due to more calibrated non-closure. These results suggest that accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not only fluent final answers.

AI.tldr: JustDiag is a diagnostic justification engine for root cause analysis (RCA) that explicitly tracks evidence, hypotheses, conflicts, and uncertainty. Evaluated on 66 real incidents, it outperformed a baseline in both outcome and process quality, while accepting slightly lower completion rates due to calibrated non-closure. The work argues that accountable RCA requires explicit justification artifacts, not just fluent answers.
AI.motivation: LLMs can produce fluent RCA outputs, but fluency masks a critical gap: in high-stakes incident response, engineers need auditable diagnostic reasoning — what evidence supports a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remain, and whether uncertainty was preserved or prematurely resolved. Existing systems lack explicit process-state tracking for accountability.
AI.method: JustDiag is a diagnostic justification engine that maintains an explicit process state over evidence collection, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next investigative checks. The system was evaluated on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer evaluation protocol that separately scores (1) final-answer quality and (2) process quality, compared against a matched control without diagnostic justification capabilities.
AI.result: JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores relative to the control. It accepted slightly lower terminal completion rates due to more calibrated non-closure — i.e., it appropriately declined to close cases when evidence was insufficient rather than forcing a fluent but unsupported answer.
AI.conclusion: Accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not merely fluent final answers. Calibrated non-closure is a feature, not a bug, in high-stakes diagnostic settings.

title: ScholarQuest: A Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark for Agentic Academic Paper Search in Open Literature Environments
summary: Academic paper search is a core step in scientific research, and LLM-based search agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for iterative, intent-driven literature exploration. However, existing benchmarks are insufficient for systematically evaluating agentic academic search under realistic open literature environments. We propose ScholarQuest, a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for agentic academic paper search. ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 computer science topics and four representative research intents, including method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It further provides scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation. Benchmarking results show that agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, yet the best-performing agent only achieves 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All, indicating substantial room for improvement. In addition, analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases further highlight the benchmark's ability to provide multi-dimensional evaluation signals for academic paper search agents.

AI.tldr: ScholarQuest is a large-scale benchmark for evaluating LLM-based search agents in academic literature discovery, built from 1,000+ CS topics across four research intents. Current agents outperform single-shot retrieval but achieve only ~0.31–0.36 Recall, revealing significant room for improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate agentic academic search systems under realistic, open literature environments. There is a need for a systematic, taxonomy-guided benchmark that supports iterative, intent-driven literature exploration with reproducible evaluation.
AI.method: ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 computer science topics categorized into four representative research intents: method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It features scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend called ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation. The benchmark evaluates both agentic methods and single-shot retrieval baselines using metrics including Recall@100 and Recall@All.
AI.result: Agentic methods consistently outperform single-shot retrieval baselines. However, the best-performing agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All, indicating substantial headroom. Additional analyses cover search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure case diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: ScholarQuest exposes a significant performance gap in current agentic academic search systems and provides rich multi-dimensional evaluation signals — spanning recall, efficiency, robustness across intents, and failure modes — to guide future research in this domain.

title: Sign-Language Datasets at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey on Resources, Benchmarks, and Annotation Standards
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: Sign languages are expressive visual languages used by Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) communities. Despite substantial progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production, advances remain constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Existing benchmarks often fail to reflect real-world communication needs, and systematic analyses of these limitations remain limited. In this survey, we present a comprehensive index of sign-language datasets, covering 120 resources across 35 sign languages. We analyze key challenges such as modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias, and outline considerations for future dataset design. We also introduce a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet and release a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/Ginqwerty/Open-Sign-Language) to support standardized documentation and reproducible evaluation. Overall, our work provides a unified and practical foundation for developing inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey indexing 120 sign-language datasets across 35 sign languages, analyzing challenges like modality imbalance and annotation granularity, and introducing a standardized 24-field datasheet with an open-source repository to support reproducible sign-language technology development.
AI.motivation: Existing sign-language recognition, translation, and production research is constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Current benchmarks fail to capture real-world communication needs, and systematic analyses of these shortcomings are scarce, motivating a unified survey and standardization effort.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive survey indexing 120 sign-language datasets across 35 sign languages. They systematically analyze key challenges—modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias—and propose a standardized 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet schema. They also release a public GitHub repository for standardized documentation and reproducible evaluation.
AI.result: The survey catalogs 120 datasets spanning 35 sign languages, identifies recurrent limitations in existing benchmarks (e.g., modality skew, coarse annotations, demographic bias), and delivers a 24-field datasheet template alongside an open-source repository to promote consistent dataset documentation and benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified, practical foundation for building more inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies by addressing dataset fragmentation and promoting standardization, with the datasheet and repository serving as community resources for future research and real-world deployment.

title: ITNet: A Learnable Integral Transform That Subsumes Convolution, Attention, and Recurrence
summary: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers each encode different inductive biases -- locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction -- and have remained mathematically distinct since their inception. We show that this fragmentation reflects not a fundamental diversity in how signals should be processed, but rather incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. We introduce the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified architecture built around a learnable kernel that depends jointly on positions and features. This kernel is implemented as a small neural network, specifically an MLP, that models pairwise interactions, enabling the model to adapt its behavior from data. We show that convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (including LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba) arise as special cases under appropriate parameterizations, and that ITNet is a universal approximator of continuous operators. To make this practical, we develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization, enabling efficient and scalable computation. A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K , GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA\,v2 and NLVR2. The results demonstrate that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families from data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified neural architecture showing that convolutions, self-attention, and recurrent networks are all special cases of a learnable integral transform with a position-and-feature-dependent kernel, and demonstrates competitive performance across vision, language, and 3D tasks.
AI.motivation: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers have remained mathematically distinct, each encoding different inductive biases (locality, sequential memory, content-dependent pairwise interaction). The authors argue this fragmentation reflects incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object rather than fundamental diversity in signal processing.
AI.method: ITNet is built around a learnable kernel implemented as an MLP that depends jointly on positions and features. The framework unifies convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) as special parameterizations. Practical scalability is achieved via tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization. A shared operator with lightweight modality-specific encoders is used across tasks.
AI.result: A single ITNet architecture matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K, GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA v2, and NLVR2, demonstrating that one learned interaction mechanism can recover behaviors of all three architectural families.
AI.conclusion: The fragmentation of neural architectures is not fundamental; a unified integral transform framework can recover and match the performance of specialized architectures across diverse modalities, pointing toward general-purpose learning mechanisms.

title: ProMUSE: Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty-guided Staged Evidential Alzheimer Disease Classification
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a fatal disorder that destroys memory and cognitive skills in the elderly population.
