Most treatments for AD are effective in the early stage, leading to an increasing demand for early AD diagnosis. AD diagnosis increasingly relies on multimodal data such as clinical assessments, structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging. However, MRI and PET acquisition remain costly and not universally accessible, making full-modality inference impractical in real-world clinical workflows. We propose ProMUSE, a Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty Guided Staged Evidential Network that adaptively determines when additional modalities are necessary, helping reduce the overall cost of data acquisition while maintaining accuracy. ProMUSE first performs evidential classification using low-cost clinical data and quantifies uncertainty via a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, ProMUSE progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty through Dempster-Shafer theory to obtain a calibrated multimodal prediction. This staged acquisition strategy enables accurate diagnosis while minimizing reliance on expensive imaging. Experiments on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks demonstrate that ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50-90%, yielding substantial cost savings. These results highlight ProMUSE as a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening.

AI.tldr: ProMUSE is a staged evidential network for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis that starts with low-cost clinical data and only requests expensive MRI/PET scans when prediction uncertainty is high, reducing imaging usage by 50–90% while maintaining accuracy competitive with full-modality baselines.
AI.motivation: MRI and PET imaging are costly and not universally accessible, yet critical for AD diagnosis. A practical clinical workflow needs to balance diagnostic accuracy with resource efficiency by adaptively determining when expensive modalities are truly necessary.
AI.method: ProMUSE performs evidential classification on clinical data using a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model to quantify uncertainty. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, it progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty via Dempster-Shafer theory for calibrated multimodal prediction.
AI.result: On ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS datasets across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks, ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy versus full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50–90%, yielding substantial cost savings.
AI.conclusion: ProMUSE is a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening, demonstrating that staged modality acquisition guided by evidential uncertainty can dramatically lower diagnostic costs without sacrificing accuracy.

title: AI Conversational Interviewing: Scaling Up Semi-Structured and In-depth Interviews
summary: Public opinion research has long faced a trade-off between depth and scale: standardized surveys enable large-scale measurement but restrict respondents to researcher-defined categories, obscuring the diversity of unexpected considerations that underlie public sentiment. More conversational interviews provide richer insights through open-ended probing, but their reliance on trained human interviewers has kept them difficult to scale. This study introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a method for collecting open-ended public opinion data at scale, pursuing three objectives: to demonstrate the analytical value of conversational text data for questions beyond the reach of closed-ended items; to assess the method's practical viability through participants' own evaluations; and to inform implementation by experimentally comparing voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice interview modes. We conducted a study combining an AI-led interview with a standardized survey on migration policy among 571 respondents recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel. The findings establish AI Conversational Interviewing as a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit. The conversational transcripts surface considerations and reasoning that a comprehensive standardized battery does not capture such as markedly different mental models of migration among subgroups with similar attitudes levels. Among respondents who completed the interview, evaluations of the AI interview were at or above those of the standardized survey across modes, although completion itself varied by condition. By releasing open data and open-source pipeline materials, the study contributes to a growing literature on harnessing artificial intelligence to expand the methods of public opinion measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a scalable method for collecting open-ended public opinion data, comparing voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice AI interview modes against standardized surveys among 571 respondents. Results show AI interviews surface reasoning and mental models that closed-ended surveys miss, and participants rate the AI interview experience at or above the standardized survey.
AI.motivation: Public opinion research faces a fundamental trade-off: standardized surveys achieve scale but constrain respondents to researcher-defined categories, while conversational interviews yield richer insights but are expensive and difficult to scale due to reliance on trained human interviewers. The authors aim to resolve this tension by leveraging AI to conduct open-ended interviews at scale.
AI.method: The authors conducted a study with 571 respondents (recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel) combining an AI-led conversational interview with a standardized survey on migration policy. Three AI interview modes were experimentally compared: voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice. The study pursued three objectives: demonstrating analytical value of conversational data, assessing participant evaluations of the method, and comparing implementation modes.
AI.result: AI Conversational Interviewing transcripts revealed considerations and reasoning (e.g., divergent mental models of migration among subgroups with similar attitude levels) not captured by comprehensive standardized batteries. Participants rated the AI interview experience at or above the standardized survey across all modes. However, completion rates varied by experimental condition.
AI.conclusion: AI Conversational Interviewing is a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit, capable of surfacing nuanced public reasoning at scale. The authors contribute open data and open-source pipeline materials to support further research on AI-augmented public opinion measurement.

title: Phoenix: Safe GitHub Issue Resolution via Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: We present Phoenix, a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues from triage through pull-request creation, combining seven layered safety controls with a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy. Phoenix decomposes the work across six specialized agents. Planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst and Pull Request (PR) agent, all coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before a pull request is opened. On a 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite. run on the production webhook path, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of instances with no pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs; this curated slice is not directly comparable to full-split leaderboard results, and we discuss the limits of the comparison. A complementary pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories yields 100% correctness preservation (CP; mean 122s on the hard tier). Manual inspection shows that about half of the resulting pull requests are well-targeted fixes. The other half place code at incorrect paths, a planner localization limitation we are addressing with retrieval. We also report the deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI) that motivated each safety mechanism.

AI.tldr: Phoenix is a multi-agent LLM system with seven safety controls that resolves GitHub issues from triage to PR creation using six specialized agents, achieving 75% oracle resolution on a curated SWE-bench Lite slice and 100% correctness preservation on 42 real issues.
AI.motivation: Automated issue resolution systems face deployment risks such as regressions, incorrect code placement, and CI failures. The authors seek to build a production-safe system that combines layered safety mechanisms with effective multi-agent coordination to resolve real-world GitHub issues reliably.
AI.method: Phoenix employs six specialized agents (Planner, Reproducer, Coder, Tester, Failure Analyst, PR Agent) coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Seven layered safety controls are integrated throughout the pipeline. A baseline-aware test evaluation strategy checks every change against a baseline test run before opening any pull request.
AI.result: On a 24-instance curated slice of SWE-bench Lite (production webhook path), Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% with zero pass-to-pass regressions. A pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories achieved 100% correctness preservation (mean 122s on hard tier). Manual inspection revealed roughly half the PRs are well-targeted; the other half suffer from incorrect code path localization.
AI.conclusion: Phoenix demonstrates effective multi-agent issue resolution with strong safety guarantees, though planner localization remains a key limitation. The authors are addressing this with retrieval-based improvements. Each safety mechanism was motivated by real deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI).

title: OpenRath: Session-Centered Runtime State for Agent Systems
summary: Modern agent systems often suffer from fragmented runtime state: transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately and become difficult to inspect or reproduce. OpenRath addresses this issue with a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent, multi-session systems. The analogy concerns the role of a central first-class runtime abstraction, not tensor computation. Its core abstraction is Session, the runtime value passed between agents and workflows. A Session is branchable, inspectable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable. It records conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence, while defining where memory interactions enter the runtime record. Since this state is carried by the same value used in program execution, fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations rather than states reconstructed from external traces. OpenRath further defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector, with Selector turning control flow into runtime-routed decisions. This report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Its claims are limited to controlled runtime properties, while broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are left for follow-on evaluation. The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition.

AI.tldr: OpenRath proposes a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent systems centered on a first-class runtime abstraction called Session, which unifies fragmented runtime state (transcripts, tool effects, lineage, memory) into a branchable, inspectable, and replayable value, enabling explicit fork/merge/replay operations rather than post-hoc state reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Modern agent systems suffer from fragmented runtime state—transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded disparately, making inspection and reproduction difficult. This fragmentation undermines auditability and composability of multi-agent, multi-session systems.
AI.method: OpenRath introduces a programming model centered on Session as a first-class runtime value passed between agents and workflows. Session is branchable, inspectable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable, recording conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence. The model also defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector abstractions—Selector turns control flow into runtime-routed decisions. Fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations on Session rather than states reconstructed from external traces.
AI.result: The report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Claims are deliberately limited to controlled runtime properties; broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are deferred to follow-on evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition, unifying previously fragmented state into a single inspectable and composable abstraction.

title: ELVA: Exploring Ranking-Driven Universal Multimodal Retrieval
summary:
Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via contrastive learning has become a mainstream paradigm for improving the performance of Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR). However, previous works have ignored the grain blindness when adapting the contrastive paradigm into retrieval tasks. Grain blindness refers to the tendency of the model to overlook grain-level information contained in the query, which is crucial for effectively handling complex queries. This stems from contrastive learning treating samples as a binary classification (positive/negative), while ignoring the different information carried by each negative sample. To address this, we argue that negatives should be treated differently according to their similarity to the positive sample, enabling the model to learn distinct grain information from each negative. In this paper, we introduce a simple but effective framework, called ELVA, a novel rule-based RL framework that mitigates grain blindness through ranking-driven MLLMs. 1) Instead of relying on reward models, we extend Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
  (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, allowing the model to explore new ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels. 2) By utilizing rule-based rewards, our approach jointly optimizes the ranking of negative samples while enlarging the similarity gap between positive and negative. To more precisely measure grain blindness, we further introduce MRBench, a new benchmark specifically designed for multi-grain query scenarios. ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results across standard retrieval benchmarks, and its notable 13.1% improvement on MRBench further demonstrates its effectiveness in alleviating grain blindness.

AI.tldr: ELVA is a rule-based RL framework that addresses "grain blindness" in multimodal retrieval — the phenomenon where contrastive learning treats all negatives uniformly, ignoring the varying similarity levels among them. It extends RLVR to retrieval, using rule-based rewards to rank negatives by similarity and widen the positive-negative gap. A new benchmark, MRBench, measures multi-grain query handling, where ELVA achieves a 13.1% improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing contrastive learning approaches for Universal Multimodal Retrieval suffer from "grain blindness": the model treats all negative samples as equally negative (binary classification) and fails to capture the fine-grained, grain-level information that distinguishes negatives by their varying degrees of similarity to the positive. This impairs handling of complex, multi-grain queries.
AI.method: The authors propose ELVA, a rule-based reinforcement learning framework. Key components: (1) Extending Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to retrieval, enabling exploration of ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels. (2) Rule-based reward design that jointly optimizes negative sample ranking orders and enlarges the similarity gap between positives and negatives. They also introduce MRBench, a benchmark for multi-grain query evaluation.
AI.result: ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results on standard retrieval benchmarks. On MRBench, the newly proposed multi-grain benchmark, ELVA yields a notable 13.1% improvement, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating grain blindness.
AI.conclusion: Treating negatives with differential importance based on their similarity to positives — operationalized through rule-based RL — effectively alleviates grain blindness in multimodal retrieval. The approach yields substantial gains on both standard and multi-grain benchmarks.

title: Quantifying Aleatoric Uncertainty of In-Context Learning for Robust Measure of LLM Prediction Confidence
summary: In-Context Learning (ICL) allows LLMs to adapt to new tasks from a few demonstrations, but its reliability remains a concern: predictions are highly sensitive to both prompt design and the model's ability to understand the context, obscuring whether failures arise from data properties or model limitations. Uncertainty decomposition-separating aleatoric from epistemic sources-is particularly crucial in this setting, yet existing methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture the unique dynamics of ICL. To address this, we introduce a concept of self-function vectors, built upon Bayesian views and the mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors leverage internal model representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, thereby enabling a direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework and circumventing the reliance on brittle input or decoding manipulations. Given the lack of established benchmarks and suitable evaluation protocols, we also propose the first and rigorous evaluation protocol, in which data is manipulated in controlled ways so as to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely and separately from epistemic uncertainty. With this new evaluation framework, initially grounded in synthetic tasks for conceptual development and subsequently extended to real-world datasets, we show that our proposed methodology can measure uncertainty of LLM predictions made under ICL more reliably than existing alternative methods. Moreover, we show it can be used as a practical tool for trustworthy-related applications, such as hallucination detection. Our findings pave a new direction for connecting the quantitative view of uncertainty with the mechanistic understanding of model behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "self-function vectors" — a Bayesian and mechanistic interpretability-based method for decomposing uncertainty in In-Context Learning (ICL). It separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty by leveraging internal model representations of the latent concept learned during prompting. The authors also propose the first rigorous evaluation protocol with controlled data manipulations to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely. The method demonstrates superior reliability over existing approaches and shows practical utility for hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: ICL reliability is undermined by high sensitivity to prompt design and model comprehension, making it difficult to disentangle whether failures stem from inherent data ambiguity (aleatoric) or model limitations (epistemic). Existing uncertainty decomposition methods are designed for standard generation tasks and fail to capture ICL's unique dynamics. A principled, ICL-specific uncertainty quantification framework is thus critically needed.
AI.method: The authors propose self-function vectors grounded in Bayesian principles and mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting using internal model representations, enabling direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework while avoiding brittle input or decoding manipulations. They also introduce a rigorous evaluation protocol where data is systematically manipulated to isolate and quantify aleatoric uncertainty separately from epistemic uncertainty, initially on synthetic tasks and then on real-world datasets.
AI.result: The proposed methodology measures uncertainty of LLM predictions under ICL more reliably than existing alternatives, as demonstrated through the new evaluation framework. Additionally, the method proves effective for practical trustworthy-AI applications, notably hallucination detection.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new direction connecting quantitative uncertainty estimation with mechanistic understanding of model behavior in ICL. The self-function vector approach provides a principled, reliable uncertainty decomposition tool that advances both theoretical understanding and practical trustworthiness of LLMs deployed in few-shot settings.

title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
summary: Recent position papers argue that the classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive large language model (LLM) agents and call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that can unlock new agent capabilities such as proactive clarification seeking and shared mental-model building. Practical deployment constraints -- black-box APIs, interactive latency budgets, and the absence of labeled trajectories -- rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the most viable family for surfacing such signals at deployment time. We answer this call with a simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), enabling the agent to ask for clarification when the task specification is ambiguous. To evaluate it, we introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, and systematically compare the proposed decomposition against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B) on these variants together with the standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Averaged across the five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM, and leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, indicating that the gains generalize beyond a single LLM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prompt-based decomposition separating action confidence from request uncertainty (u) for LLM agents, enabling proactive clarification under underspecified tasks. Evaluated on two new clarification-augmented benchmarks across five LLM backbones, the method substantially outperforms ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM), with gains generalizing across models.
AI.motivation: Existing aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty frameworks are inadequate for interactive LLM agents. Deployment constraints (black-box APIs, latency budgets, no labeled trajectories) preclude logprob-based, multi-sampling, or training-based uncertainty estimation, leaving prompt-based methods as the only viable option. The work responds to calls for underspecification-aware, decomposed, communicable uncertainty representations that enable proactive clarification seeking.
AI.method: A prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u). When request uncertainty is high (ambiguous task specification), the agent proactively asks for clarification rather than guessing. Evaluation uses two newly introduced benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification, ALFWorld-Clarification) with 50% deliberately underspecified tasks. The method is systematically compared against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B), plus standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection.
AI.result: Averaged across five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM. It leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, demonstrating cross-model generalization.
AI.conclusion: The prompt-based decomposition of action confidence and request uncertainty is effective and generalizable for enabling LLM agents to recognize underspecified tasks and seek clarification, outperforming existing uncertainty estimation baselines across diverse model backbones and benchmarks.

title: Low-Cost Multi-Precision Systolic Arrays for Accelerating FHE NTTs on AI ASICs
summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) ensures robust data privacy but suffers from prohibitive computational overhead. Accelerating FHE on AI hardware like Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) is promising, yet fundamentally limited by a precision mismatch: TPUs are optimized for 8-bit arithmetic, whereas FHE and its critical parts such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), demand high precision. Current approaches bridge this gap using matrix decomposition to execute NTT computations on low-precision matrix engines. However, reconstructing the full-precision results requires shift-and-add accumulation that does not match the dataflow of matrix multiplication. This forces offloading full-precision reconstruction from matrix engines to vector processors that disrupts the matrix multiplication dataflow, creating significant performance bottleneck. To resolve this limitation, we propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array in sync with low-precision matrix multiplication under a uniform dataflow. Synthesized at 7nm with OpenRoad, our design incurs negligible hardware overhead. Cycle-accurate simulations using SCALE-Sim demonstrate that natively executing NTTs on the proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33x speedup, for transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16 on 128x128 matrix engines, successfully enabling standard AI hardware to support high-precision FHE acceleration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that enables native full-precision output reconstruction within TPU-like matrix engines, eliminating the bottleneck of offloading reconstruction to vector processors. The design achieves at least 1.33× speedup for NTT transforms on standard AI hardware with negligible area overhead.
AI.motivation: TPUs are optimized for low-precision (8-bit) matrix multiplication, but FHE workloads (specifically the Number Theoretic Transform) require high precision. Existing approaches use matrix decomposition followed by shift-and-add reconstruction, but this reconstruction step disrupts the matrix multiplication dataflow when offloaded to vector processors, creating a severe performance bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors design a multi-precision systolic array that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array, synchronized with low-precision matrix multiplication under a unified dataflow. The design is synthesized at 7nm using OpenRoad and evaluated via cycle-accurate simulations with SCALE-Sim, targeting 128×128 matrix engines with NTT transform sizes from 2^12 to 2^16.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33× speedup compared to baseline approaches that offload reconstruction to vector processors. Hardware overhead is negligible. The design successfully bridges the precision gap, enabling standard AI hardware (TPUs) to accelerate high-precision FHE workloads.
AI.conclusion: Native in-array full-precision reconstruction eliminates the vector processor bottleneck, making it feasible to efficiently accelerate high-precision FHE on commodity AI accelerators with minimal hardware modifications.

title: cAPM: Continual AI-Assisted Pace-Mapping with Active Learning
summary: Ventricular tachycardia is a life-threatening rhythm disorder and a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Pace-mapping is a clinical procedure for identifying the intervention target during catheter ablation of VT. It requires clinicians to pace different sites in the ventricles and rapidly interpret the resulting electrocardiograms to determine where to pace next or whether a target site has been identified. Active learning AI models have been proposed to guide clinicians to the next pacing site, showing promise in reducing the number of pacing sites and improving the efficiency of pace-mapping. Existing methods require retraining each target without the ability to transfer knowledge across multiple VTs within the same patient or across patients. We introduce cAPM for continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping to capture and transfer knowledge accumulated from past pace-mapping data to reduce the number of pace-mapping data needed for future target VTs. This is made possible by a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, an active-learning strategy that refines this surrogate model by selecting the most informative pacing site for each target, and a continual learning strategy to do so sequentially while retaining knowledge from prior targets. Evaluated on an in-silico testbed consisting of sequentially-presented localization tasks across different physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM with and without replay of past data samples achieved an 81% probability of localizing within clinical tolerance (5 mm accuracy) using 4.5 pace-mapping sites, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving 38% probability using 13.7 pacing sites. These results provide a strong basis for preparing cAPM towards in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies where it can be used to guide pace-mapping.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces cAPM, a continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping framework that transfers knowledge across multiple ventricular tachycardia (VT) localization tasks. By combining a task-agnostic surrogate neural network with active learning and continual learning strategies, cAPM achieves 81% localization probability within 5mm accuracy using only 4.5 pacing sites, dramatically outperforming the state-of-the-art active learning method (38% with 13.7 sites).
AI.motivation: Existing AI-assisted pace-mapping methods require retraining from scratch for each VT target within the same patient, failing to leverage knowledge accumulated from prior pace-mapping procedures. This inefficiency leads to excessive pacing sites and prolonged procedures. The authors aim to enable knowledge transfer across multiple VT localization tasks to reduce the number of pacing sites needed for future targets.
AI.method: cAPM integrates three components: (1) a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology; (2) an active-learning strategy that sequentially selects the most informative next pacing site to refine the surrogate model for each target VT; and (3) a continual learning strategy that retains knowledge from prior targets while sequentially adapting to new ones, optionally using replay of past data samples to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
AI.result: Evaluated on an in-silico testbed with sequentially-presented VT localization tasks across varying physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM (with and without replay) achieved an 81% probability of localizing within 5 mm clinical tolerance using only 4.5 pace-mapping sites. In contrast, the state-of-the-art active-learning baseline achieved only 38% probability while requiring 13.7 pacing sites.
AI.conclusion: cAPM demonstrates that continual learning combined with active learning can substantially reduce the data burden for VT pace-mapping by transferring knowledge across targets. These results provide a strong foundation for advancing cAPM toward in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies.

title: Editorial Alignment: A Participatory Approach to Engaging Editorial Expertise in LLM-mediated Knowledge Dissemination
summary: The emergence of LLM-driven information services is reshaping the conditions under which public knowledge institutions operate, threatening to absorb the editorial function these institutions exist to exercise. While LLMs offer powerful new affordances for knowledge dissemination, editorial authority is challenged by pretrained LLMs that arrive already aligned with the values and dissemination strategies of their commercial developers. This paper investigates editor participation in re-aligning LLM interfaces to editorial standards through design workshops, in a case study where we design and implement an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface with a Nordic public knowledge institution. We introduce editorial alignment as a design practice within Participatory AI, framing AI alignment as a design process and positioning the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial practice and values into alignment objectives for technical implementation. Last, we discuss how editorial alignment can create space for ongoing participation and give editors agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "editorial alignment" as a participatory design practice for re-aligning LLM interfaces with editorial standards, demonstrated through a case study with a Nordic public knowledge institution where editors co-designed an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven information services threaten to absorb the editorial function of public knowledge institutions by imposing the commercial values and dissemination strategies embedded in pretrained models, undermining institutional editorial authority.
AI.method: The authors conducted design workshops with editors from a Nordic public knowledge institution, using Participatory AI methods to co-design and implement an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface. They frame editorial alignment as a design practice where editorial standards are translated into alignment objectives, treating the editorial standard as a design artefact.
AI.result: The case study demonstrates that editorial participation in re-aligning LLM interfaces is feasible and productive, yielding a functioning LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface aligned with institutional editorial standards rather than commercial defaults.
AI.conclusion: Editorial alignment creates space for ongoing participation and grants editors meaningful agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination. It reframes AI alignment as a participatory design process rather than a purely technical problem, situating editorial standards as negotiable design artefacts within Participatory AI.

title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

AI.tldr: When LLMs act as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their biases spread between agents. The paper introduces "Contagion Networks" to measure this propagation, finding consistent bias transfer (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]) among homogeneous DeepSeek-chat agents, which is 3–5× weaker than cross-model contagion. Increasing evaluator committee size from 1 to 3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as evaluators in multi-agent systems, yet systematic evaluation biases can propagate through agent networks, distorting collective decision-making. There is no formal framework for measuring or mitigating this bias contagion effect.
AI.method: The authors propose "Contagion Networks," a formal framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation. They conduct controlled 3-agent experiments using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based). The Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ₃ is measured, and propagation regimes are defined by the spectral radius ρ(Γ_N). Committee-size ablation (k=1 to k=3) tests mitigation efficacy.
AI.result: Evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]) even within the same underlying model. Homogeneous-model contagion coefficients are 3–5× weaker than prior cross-model findings (MM-EPC: γ ≈ 0.85–1.3), placing them in the "suppression regime." Increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.conclusion: LLM evaluator biases propagate measurably even among homogeneous agents, but at substantially lower rates than cross-model settings. Committee-based evaluation serves as an effective mitigation strategy. The open-source Contagion Network framework is released to support further research.

title: FAPO: Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization of Multi-Step LLM Pipelines
summary: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail through interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, so prompt-only optimization can miss bottlenecks in the chain. We present FAPO (Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization), a framework that lets Claude Code optimize an LLM pipeline inside a standardized codebase. FAPO evaluates a pipeline, inspects intermediate steps, diagnoses failures, proposes scoped changes, and validates variants repeatedly to optimize against a score function. It first tries prompt edits and, only when prompt optimization appears insufficient, changes chain structure within the permitted scope when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 model-benchmark comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean $\pm$ trial-standard-deviation ranges, and the mean FAPO-GEPA gain is +14.1 pp. In the six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where prompt-first search escalated to structural changes, FAPO wins all six with a mean gain of +33.8 pp. FAPO also improves performance on security tasks: on CTIBench-RCM, a security CVE-to-CWE task, prompt-only FAPO lifts test accuracy by +4.0 pp on GPT-5, +7.1 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct, and +2.0 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning. These results position FAPO as a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks.

AI.tldr: FAPO is a fully autonomous framework that optimizes entire LLM pipelines by diagnosing failures across retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps. It first tries prompt edits, then escalates to structural changes when prompt optimization is insufficient. Across six benchmarks, FAPO outperforms the GEPA baseline in 15/18 comparisons (+14.1 pp mean gain), with particularly strong results (+33.8 pp) when structural changes are needed, and also improves security task performance.
AI.motivation: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail due to complex interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting components. Prompt-only optimization approaches miss structural bottlenecks in the chain. A method that can autonomously diagnose and fix both prompt-level and structure-level issues is needed.
AI.method: FAPO (Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization) uses Claude Code to iteratively optimize LLM pipelines within a standardized codebase. The framework: (1) evaluates the pipeline against a score function, (2) inspects intermediate steps, (3) diagnoses failure modes, (4) proposes scoped changes, and (5) validates variants. It employs a two-tier strategy: first attempting prompt edits, and only when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck does it modify chain structure within permitted scope.
AI.result: FAPO beats baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean ± trial-standard-deviation ranges, with a mean FAPO-GEPA gain of +14.1 pp. In six HoVer and IFBench comparisons requiring structural changes, FAPO wins all six with +33.8 pp mean gain. On CTIBench-RCM (security CVE-to-CWE), prompt-only FAPO improves accuracy by +4.0 pp (GPT-5), +7.1 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct), and +2.0 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning).
AI.conclusion: FAPO represents state-of-the-art pipeline optimization for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks, demonstrating that autonomous, attribution-driven optimization spanning both prompts and chain structure yields significant and consistent improvements over prompt-only baselines.

title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, existing graph-based integration methods, such as graph serialization and graph neural networks, either suffer from scalability issues or exploit only local graph information. On the other hand, existing semantic tokenization methods typically rely on heuristics and lack explicit supervision signals, which may lead to inaccurate or suboptimal semantic representations. To address these limitations in user interest context modeling, we propose G2Rec, a scalable framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization for industrial-scale generative recommendation. Overall, G2Rec enables recommendation models to capture holistic and semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth user interests, thereby providing more comprehensive and accurate modeling of user behavior contexts in industrial sequential recommendation. Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of G2Rec over existing methods.

AI.tldr: G2Rec is a scalable generative recommendation framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with supervised semantic item tokenization, enabling models to capture semantically grounded user interest prototypes without ground-truth interest labels.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods face two key limitations: (1) graph-based integration methods (e.g., graph serialization, GNNs) either lack scalability or capture only local graph information; (2) semantic tokenization methods rely on heuristics without explicit supervision, leading to suboptimal semantic representations. These shortcomings hinder effective simultaneous injection of user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts.
AI.method: G2Rec combines holistic graph-based co-engagement modeling with supervised semantic tokenization into a unified framework. It leverages global graph structure to capture comprehensive user co-engagement patterns while employing explicitly supervised semantic tokenization to produce accurate item representations, all designed for industrial-scale deployment.
AI.result: Online deployment across multiple product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that G2Rec outperforms existing generative recommendation methods.
AI.conclusion: G2Rec effectively addresses the dual challenges of scalable graph integration and reliable semantic tokenization in generative recommendation, delivering superior performance in both offline benchmarks and real-world industrial deployments.

title: Granularity-Regulated Adaptive Computational Efficiency for Optimal Verification in Test-Time Scaling
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs) by investing additional compute at inference time. A central component of TTS is the \emph{verifier}, which selects or scores candidate solutions to guide the search process. While prior work has explored the benefit of verification, a fundamental question remains underexplored: \emph{what is the optimal granularity of verification under a given compute budget?} Coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) and fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) represent two extremes, yet neither alone achieves compute-optimality across all regimes. In this paper, we establish a unified theoretical framework, called \textbf{GRACE} (\underline{G}ranularity-\underline{R}egulated \underline{A}daptive \underline{C}omputational \underline{E}fficiency), that characterizes the optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. We prove that there exists a phase transition: fine-grained verification dominates when either the compute budget is large or the problem is hard, whereas coarse-grained verification is preferred in the low-budget, easy-problem regime. Our theory unifies Best-of-$N$, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework, and motivates an adaptive granularity strategy that provably achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier. Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborate all four theoretical claims, with our adaptive strategy outperforming fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1\% accuracy at matched compute.

AI.tldr: GRACE provides a theoretical framework showing optimal verification granularity in test-time scaling depends on compute budget and problem difficulty, with a phase transition from coarse-grained to fine-grained verification. An adaptive strategy achieves the Pareto frontier, outperforming fixed baselines by up to 3.1%.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling relies on verifiers to guide search over candidate solutions, but the field lacks a principled understanding of the optimal granularity of verification (coarse outcome-level vs. fine process-level) under a given compute budget. Neither ORMs nor PRMs alone achieve compute-optimality across all regimes.
AI.method: The authors propose GRACE, a unified theoretical framework that formulates optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. They prove a phase transition phenomenon and unify Best-of-N, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework. An adaptive granularity strategy is derived that provably attains the compute-performance Pareto frontier.
AI.result: Empirical validation on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborates all four theoretical claims. The adaptive granularity strategy outperforms fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1% absolute accuracy at matched compute budgets.
AI.conclusion: There exists a phase transition in optimal verification granularity: fine-grained verification (PRM-style) dominates under large compute budgets or hard problems; coarse-grained verification (ORM-style) is preferable under low budgets or easy problems. An adaptive strategy that adjusts granularity per-problem achieves compute-optimality.

title: Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops
summary: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the "narration gap" in LLM-solver hybrid pipelines, where a language model translates a formal solver's output into natural language. It shows that certificate gating preserves soundness, but adversarial prompt injection can invert verified conclusions across phrasings; hardened prompts reduce but cannot eliminate this vulnerability.
AI.motivation: SAT/SMT solvers provide sound, verifiable answers, but when embedded in LLM reasoning pipelines, the soundness guarantee can be lost during the narration step—the phase where the solver's output is translated into a user-facing answer. Prior work has neglected this narration gap, motivating a formal and empirical investigation.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure, (2) evaluate five open-source models under prompt injection attacks, testing certificate gating and adversarial rephrasing, and (3) assess mitigation via hardened prompts against both static and adaptive adversaries.
AI.result: Certificate gating ensures the solver's verdict remains sound. However, an adversary can invert a verified conclusion through varied phrasings and communication channels. Hardened prompts significantly reduce injection success but fail to eliminate it entirely, and the system remains vulnerable under adaptive attacks.
AI.conclusion: In the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not extend to the final answer the user reads. The narration step constitutes a critical weak link where formal soundness guarantees can be subverted, and current mitigations are insufficient against adaptive adversaries.

title: FFinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming
summary: Existing safety benchmarks target general adversarial scenarios but miss finance-specific risks. Financial LLMs face regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion that require targeted evaluation. We introduce FinRED, an expert-guided red-teaming framework for financial LLM safety evaluation developed with financial experts. FinRED uses a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global standards (e.g., FATF and EU DORA) to threats ranging from regulatory evasion to complex fraud, integrated with a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) through an expert-defined schema. Rigorous expert validation confirms seed plausibility and realism for meaningful LLM safety evaluation. We also provide an expert-validated, finance-specific rubric that goes beyond disclaimer checks, aligns more closely with human experts than static one-size-fits-all rubrics, and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. Aligned with internationally adopted risk-management and information-security standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 27001), FinRED is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI) regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation in real financial services. To mitigate dual-use risks, the dataset, generation pipeline, prompt template, and evaluation framework are gated for qualified researchers at https://github.com/selectstar-ai/FinRED-paper and https://huggingface.co/datasets/datumo/FinRED.

AI.tldr: FinRED is an expert-guided red-teaming framework for evaluating financial LLM safety, featuring a two-level taxonomy aligned with global regulatory standards (FATF, EU DORA), a scalable pipeline for generating context-rich behavioral prompts from real financial documents, and a finance-specific evaluation rubric that reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. It is deployed in South Korea's FSI regulatory sandbox.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks fail to capture finance-specific risks such as regulatory violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion. Financial LLMs require targeted evaluation frameworks that address these domain-specific threats beyond general adversarial scenarios.
AI.method: FinRED introduces a two-level taxonomy that maps international standards (FATF, EU DORA, ISO/IEC 27001) to concrete threats (regulatory evasion, complex fraud). It employs a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) via an expert-defined schema, with rigorous expert validation of seed plausibility. The framework also provides a finance-specific evaluation rubric that improves alignment with human expert judgment compared to generic rubrics.
AI.result: The finance-specific rubric significantly improves evaluation accuracy, reducing critical false negatives from 28 to 12 compared to static one-size-fits-all approaches. Expert validation confirms the plausibility and realism of generated behavioral prompts. The framework is operationally deployed in South Korea's FSI regulatory sandbox for real financial services evaluation.
AI.conclusion: FinRED fills a critical gap in financial LLM safety evaluation by providing a domain-specific, standards-aligned red-teaming framework with validated prompts and rubrics. It demonstrates practical deployability in real regulatory settings, with gated access to mitigate dual-use risks.

title: Protein Representation Learning with Secondary-Structure and Energy-Filtered Hydrogen-Bond Graphs
summary: Graph-based representations are widely used in protein modeling, yet many existing approaches rely primarily on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially reflect the principles governing protein folding. Proteins instead adopt complex three-dimensional conformations organized around secondary structure elements, such as $α$-helices and $β$-sheets, which encode recurring local motifs and stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions. In this work, we introduce a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning. Residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments, and graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by their energetic strength. This design enables the model to capture both local structural context and long-range couplings that are central to protein stability and function. We evaluate the proposed approach on commonly used protein benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods. In addition, the resulting graph representations offer enhanced biological interpretability, as the learned connectivity aligns with established structural motifs. These findings suggest that incorporating secondary structure and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning. The code is released at https://github.com/mohamedmohamed2021/SSProNet

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SSProNet, a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning that builds graphs using hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by energetic strength and augments node features with secondary structure assignments, outperforming existing graph-based methods while offering improved biological interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based protein representations rely mostly on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which fail to adequately capture the principles of protein folding — specifically the secondary structure elements (α-helices, β-sheets) and stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions that are central to protein stability and function.
AI.method: The authors propose a graph neural network where: (1) residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments (α-helix, β-sheet, loop/coil), and (2) graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by their energetic strength, rather than simple distance cutoffs. This design captures both local structural context and long-range couplings.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods on commonly used protein benchmarks. The learned graph connectivity also aligns with established structural motifs, demonstrating enhanced biological interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating secondary structure information and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning, and the approach is made publicly available as open-source code.

title: Organizing in the Digital Age: Understanding Community, Challenges, and Consequences in Digitally-facilitated Labor Organizing
summary: The contemporary American labor force is highly dispersed, necessitating the use of digital communication tools to bridge spatial and temporal gaps in union organizing. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how workers within various labor unions utilize digital, text-based communication platforms -- including Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack -- for labor organizing. Through 17 qualitative interviews, we examine the challenges and opportunities presented by digital organizing, identifying both technical and social obstacles. Our findings reveal that although digital tools are integral to contemporary labor successes, they also introduce new complexities, such as navigating technical security, managing information overload, and building trust and consensus. Based on these insights, we draw connections to broader understandings of digital organizing and the role of digital tools in unions.

AI.tldr: A qualitative interview study (n=17) examining how U.S. labor unions use digital text-based platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing, revealing that while these tools are crucial for modern union success, they also create challenges around security, information overload, and trust-building.
AI.motivation: The U.S. labor force is geographically dispersed, creating spatial and temporal gaps that traditional face-to-face organizing cannot bridge. Digital communication tools have become necessary infrastructure for union organizing, yet their specific affordances, challenges, and sociotechnical dynamics remain underexplored in the labor context.
AI.method: The authors conducted 17 qualitative semi-structured interviews with workers across multiple labor unions who actively use digital, text-based communication platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing activities. Data were analyzed through qualitative thematic analysis to identify recurring challenges and opportunities.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) Technical security navigation — workers struggle with platform security, surveillance risks, and maintaining operational security while organizing. (2) Information overload — the volume and velocity of digital communication can overwhelm organizers and dilute strategic messaging. (3) Trust and consensus-building — establishing interpersonal trust and reaching collective agreement proves more difficult in text-based, asynchronous environments compared to in-person settings. Despite these frictions, digital tools were deemed integral to contemporary labor successes.
AI.conclusion: Digital organizing platforms are a double-edged sword for labor unions: indispensable for coordination across dispersed workforces, yet they introduce sociotechnical complexities that require new literacies and strategies. The authors connect these findings to broader scholarship on digital organizing, arguing that tool adoption must be accompanied by deliberate practices addressing security, information management, and relational trust.

title: StaminaBench: Stress-Testing Coding Agents over 100 Interaction Turns
summary: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing. Unlike the prevailing fraction-of-tasks-solved metric, this matches real vibe-coding where sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns. In StaminaBench, agents implement a REST API server and modify it across a tunable number of procedurally generated follow-up change requests - 100 in our experiments, resulting in codebases of up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement, ensuring reproducibility and reliability; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, both constrained to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and the server run in an isolated environment and communicate with the benchmark through HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. We evaluate six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each and find that: (1) all the tested models fail within 5-6 turns, confirming that vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent and allowing it to retry improves passed turn count by up to 12x; and (3) a good harness is required for strong performance: stronger models exhibit up to a 6x gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail with any harness. We release the benchmark and the generated tasks to enable further research into multi-turn coding agent behavior. Benchmark code and data: github.com/amazon-science/StaminaBench.

AI.tldr: StaminaBench evaluates coding agents' endurance over 100 consecutive change requests on a REST API codebase, revealing that all tested models fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback, but passing test results back to the agent improves performance up to 12x, and harness quality creates up to a 6x performance gap between the same model.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks measure agent performance on task completion rates (fraction of tasks solved), which fails to capture real-world "vibe-coding" scenarios where developers and agents engage in long, multi-turn sessions spanning dozens or hundreds of iterative change requests. The authors aim to fill this gap by introducing a metric for agent stamina — the ability to sustain correctness over extended interaction sequences.
AI.method: StaminaBench procedurally generates a REST API server implementation task followed by 100 structured change requests drawn from either hardcoded or LLM-driven samplers. All tests are generated programmatically without LLM involvement for reproducibility. The agent and server run in an isolated, black-box, language-agnostic environment communicating via HTTP. Six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs are evaluated across 20 scenarios, comparing performance with and without test feedback loops.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Without test feedback, all tested models fail within 5–6 consecutive turns due to accumulating bugs. (2) Feeding test pass/fail feedback back to the agent and allowing retries increases the number of successfully passed turns by up to 12×. (3) Harness quality significantly amplifies model capability — stronger models show up to a 6× performance gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail regardless of harness.
AI.conclusion: Sustained multi-turn coding performance (stamina) is a critical but underexplored dimension of coding agent evaluation. Test feedback loops and robust agent harness design are essential for long-horizon reliability. The authors release StaminaBench as an open-source benchmark to spur further research into multi-turn agent behavior.

title: Cost-Optimal LLM Routing with Limited User Feedback under User Satisfaction Guarantees
summary: Inference costs for large language model (LLM) applications are rapidly growing, driven by surging demand and rising infrastructure cost. Users expect high-quality responses, and in commercial settings this is formally codified in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), creating a fundamental tension between cost and quality. Recent progress on cost-aware LLM request routing has shown potential to resolve this tension, but existing approaches rely on complete feedback signals, offline training, extensive per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity. We introduce SLARouter, an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy from the sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. SLARouter provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance. Experiments across a wide range of LLM benchmarks show that SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without the need for per-benchmark tuning, reducing operating cost by up to 2.2x over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: SLARouter is an online LLM request routing algorithm that learns cost-optimal policies from sparse, one-sided user feedback, providing theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance while reducing operating costs by up to 2.2× over baselines without per-benchmark tuning.
AI.motivation: LLM inference costs are escalating due to demand and infrastructure expenses, while users demand high-quality responses codified in SLAs — creating a cost-quality tension. Existing cost-aware routing approaches suffer from requiring complete feedback, offline training, per-workload tuning, and lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity.
AI.method: SLARouter is an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy using only sparse, one-sided user feedback (typical in production). It operates at inference time and provides theoretical guarantees for cost optimality and strict SLA compliance without requiring per-workload tuning.
AI.result: Across diverse LLM benchmarks, SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without per-benchmark tuning and reduces operating costs by up to 2.2× compared to existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: SLARouter effectively resolves the cost-quality tension in LLM serving by enabling online, adaptive routing with SLA guarantees, leveraging only sparse production feedback to achieve significant cost savings.

title: Trustworthy Multi-Agent Systems: Mitigating Semantic Drift with the Argent Signaling Protocol
summary:
When multi-agent LLM systems produce bad answers, not all failures are equal: some answers are grounded in the right material but incomplete, while others are simply ungrounded and should be stopped. Current retry strategies treat both cases identically (try again and hope for the best), leaving human supervisors unable to tell whether a retry was warranted or whether the system should have halted instead.
  We introduce the Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP), a compact machine-readable header that accompanies every AI-generated response with structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index that classifies the evidentiary basis of each claim. These signals enable a controller to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures and route each case differently.
  We evaluate ASP in two modes. In standalone mode, a 27-question document-grounded QA benchmark over the Array BioPharma/Ono license agreement compares baseline prompts against ASP-instrumented controller actions across three local GGUF models. On Qwen~(0.8B), ASP improves pass rate from 11.1% to 33.3% and mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; on Dobby~(8B), ASP produces 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; on SmolLM3~(3B), ASP alternates between repair and containment per question. Aggregate improvement is meaningful (12/81 to 21/81 passes). In multi-agent mode, an ASP sidecar sits between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent; the sidecar blocks 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from reaching the downstream agent (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).

AI.tldr: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) adds structured quality signals (@Certainty, @Grounding, @Stochasticity, and an assumption index) to AI-generated responses, enabling a controller to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures. Evaluated on a document-grounded QA benchmark, ASP improved pass rates (e.g., Qwen 0.8B: 11.1%→33.3%) and blocked 100% of ungrounded outputs in a multi-agent setting.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM systems treat all failures identically via blind retry, wasting compute on ungrounded outputs that should be halted rather than retried. Human supervisors cannot distinguish whether a retry was warranted or the system should have stopped. A mechanism is needed to classify failure types and route them appropriately.
AI.method: The authors propose ASP, a machine-readable header with four signals: @Certainty, @Grounding, @Stochasticity, and an assumption index classifying each claim's evidentiary basis. A controller uses these signals to route failures into repair (retry) or containment (halt). Evaluation uses a 27-question QA benchmark over a legal contract, tested in standalone mode (three GGUF models: Qwen 0.8B, Dobby 8B, SmolLM3 3B) and multi-agent mode (ASP sidecar between retrieval and decision agents).
AI.result: Standalone: Qwen 0.8B pass rate improved from 11.1% to 33.3%, mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; Dobby 8B achieved 4 fail-to-pass recoveries (33.3%→44.4%); SmolLM3 3B alternated between repair and containment. Aggregate passes rose from 12/81 to 21/81. Multi-agent: the ASP sidecar blocked 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs (24/27 blocked, zero ungrounded propagations).
AI.conclusion: ASP provides a lightweight, interoperable signaling layer that allows AI systems to communicate failure types, enabling intelligent routing between retry and halt. This improves both answer quality and system safety by preventing ungrounded information from propagating downstream.

title: Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why
summary: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5\% of extractions, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80\% to 99\%.

AI.tldr: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at University Medicine Essen that extracts structured clinical information from heterogeneous patient documents. It addresses metadata gaps, temporal reasoning, and cross-document dependencies that cause standard RAG to fail. In a lymphoma registry study with 7,326 clinician judgments, 96.5% of extractions were accepted.
AI.motivation: Patient data is fragmented across hundreds of documents with incomplete or absent document-level metadata. Standard RAG systems fail due to poor temporal reasoning, inability to handle cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata — yet AI systems critically need this metadata for effective retrieval and triage.
AI.method: The authors developed ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction), an on-premise agentic retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. It reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in specific source passages, enabling clinician verification. The system's architectural decisions are explicitly traced to the metadata gap problem. Evaluation was conducted via an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study where nuclear-medicine physicians verified every extracted value against its cited sources.
AI.result: Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5% of extractions overall. Per-type acceptance rates ranged from 80% to 99%, demonstrating strong but variable performance across different information categories.
AI.conclusion: An agentic architecture with explicit source grounding can achieve clinically acceptable extraction performance (96.5% acceptance) on real-world, heterogeneous patient data, overcoming the limitations of standard RAG approaches in healthcare settings.

title: AutoTam: Specifying Secure Protocol Implementations with Tamarin Model Generation
summary:
Formal verification is a challenging but important task for ensuring the security of cryptographic protocols. While modern protocol verification tools significantly reduce verification effort, modelling remains challenging to practitioners without a background in formal verification. In addition, transferring verification results to a concrete protocol implementation requires expert knowledge.
  In this paper, we present a novel language-first method for verification of trace properties using a domain-specific language for protocol implementations. We target the Tamarin prover for verification, and we prove that verified universal trace properties translate back to the implementation. We additionally integrate symbolic execution in order to analyse the memory safety of protocol implementations. We use our tool to implement and generate accurate models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol, and for the WireGuard VPN protocol. Our WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using our interpreter, and achieves acceptable performance. We formally prove our implementations secure using a combination of symbolic execution and verification of the generated Tamarin models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a language-first approach that uses a domain-specific language (DSL) for implementing cryptographic protocols, which automatically generates Tamarin models for formal verification of trace properties, with verified properties translating back to the implementation. Symbolic execution is also integrated for memory safety analysis. The approach is validated on a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard VPN.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of cryptographic protocols is critical for security but remains challenging for practitioners without formal methods expertise. Two key pain points are: (1) modelling protocols for verification tools is difficult and error-prone, and (2) transferring verification results to concrete implementations requires expert knowledge, creating a gap between verified models and running code.
AI.method: The authors propose a language-first method: a domain-specific language (DSL) for writing protocol implementations from which Tamarin prover models are automatically generated. They prove that verified universal trace properties in Tamarin translate back to the implementation. Additionally, they integrate symbolic execution to analyse memory safety of the protocol implementations. The approach combines both symbolic execution and formal verification of generated Tamarin models.
AI.result: The tool was used to implement and generate accurate Tamarin models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and the WireGuard VPN protocol. The WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using their interpreter and achieves acceptable performance. Both implementations were formally proven secure using the combined approach.
AI.conclusion: The language-first, DSL-based approach successfully bridges the gap between protocol implementation and formal verification, enabling practitioners to obtain verified security guarantees without deep expertise in formal methods. The WireGuard case study demonstrates practical viability through interoperability and acceptable performance.

title: Physics-Informed Discovery of Yield Functions in Plasticity via Convex Neural Representations
summary: Identifying anisotropic yield functions remains challenging since yielding is not directly observed in full-field mechanical measurements, directional calibration can require many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for discovering yield functions from full-field displacement data and reaction force data, without stress observations, plastic strain measurements, direct yield surface data, or a prescribed parametric yield function. The framework identifies the yield function as a mechanically constrained constitutive component inside elastoplastic stress integration, rather than through direct stress-space supervision. The yield function is represented by a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one while imposing the assumed tension-compression symmetry, and this neural yield function is trained with a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. The proposed framework is validated using finite element (FE) benchmark studies with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions, assessing yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability through plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment. This study provides a mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration.
