AI.tldr: A framework is proposed to discover anisotropic yield functions directly from full-field displacement and reaction force data using a convex neural network embedded within elastoplastic stress integration, eliminating the need for stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or pre-specified parametric forms. Validated on von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d benchmarks, the method enforces convexity and positive homogeneity while training across multiple loading cases via a physics-informed force equilibrium loss.
AI.motivation: Identifying anisotropic yield functions is challenging because yielding is not directly observable in full-field measurements, directional calibration demands many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. Existing methods typically require stress-space supervision, plastic strain data, or a prescribed parametric function.
AI.method: The framework represents the yield function as a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one with assumed tension-compression symmetry. This neural yield function is embedded inside elastoplastic stress integration and trained with a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases, using only full-field displacement data and reaction force data.
AI.result: Validation on FE benchmarks with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions demonstrates accurate yield contour agreement. The study further assesses sensitivity to displacement noise, identifiability via plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and deployment as a polynomial surrogate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanics-constrained framework successfully discovers anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration, providing a robust data-driven alternative to conventional yield function identification.

title: DataMagic: Transforming Tabular Data into Data Insight Video
summary: Data videos integrate dynamic charts, voice narration, and synchronized animations to communicate data insights as temporal narratives, making them an effective medium for improving data consumption efficiency in the data management lifecycle. However, producing high-quality data videos requires expertise spanning data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing approaches fall short: static visualization tools (e.g., BI dashboards) lack narrative logic and animation; authoring tools require users to pre-prepare visualizations rather than working from raw data; pixel-level video generation models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. We demonstrate DataMagic, an end-to-end interactive system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos. To ensure data fidelity, DataMagic introduces the declarative specification DVSpec, which binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields through data-driven semantic references. To address the combinatorial explosion of the design space, DataMagic adopts a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then optimizes narrative coherence through global orchestration. Leveraging DVSpec's decoupling of logic and rendering, the system further supports three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A, transforming one-way videos into explorable interactive data interfaces. Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of the DataMagic. Homepage: https://datamagic-home.github.io/

AI.tldr: DataMagic is an end-to-end system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into interactive, narrative data-insight videos, using a declarative specification (DVSpec) for data fidelity and a multi-agent architecture for narrative coherence.
AI.motivation: Producing high-quality data videos requires combined expertise in data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing tools are inadequate: static BI dashboards lack narrative and animation, authoring tools cannot work from raw data, and generative video models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance.
AI.method: DataMagic introduces (1) DVSpec, a declarative specification that binds visual/animation elements to data fields via semantic references ensuring data fidelity; (2) a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that parallel-generates candidate scenes then globally optimizes narrative coherence; and (3) three interaction modes with structured provenance-based data Q&A, leveraging DVSpec's logic-rendering decoupling.
AI.result: Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of DataMagic.
AI.conclusion: DataMagic successfully bridges the gap between raw data and high-quality narrative videos by ensuring data fidelity through declarative specifications and managing design complexity via multi-agent orchestration, while transforming passive videos into explorable interactive interfaces.

title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Cold-start Recommendation
summary: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems due to its accessibility and generality, yet it usually presents noisy samples (e.g., clickbait, position bias). Meanwhile, recommenders inevitably face the item cold-start problem due to the continuous influx of new items. We identify that cold items are more prone to noisy samples due to the aforementioned factors, and researchers often overlook the significance of denoising implicit feedback for cold items. Previous denoising studies usually identify noisy samples based on heuristic patterns, such as higher loss values, and mitigate noise through sample selection or re-weighting. However, these methods have limited adaptability and are ineffective in cold-start scenarios. To achieve denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation, we propose a model-agnostic denoising method called DIF. First, user preferences for content remain stable, which allows us to infer pseudo-labels indicating whether a user is interested in a cold item through content-similar warm items. Furthermore, to improve pseudo-label accuracy, we model the confidence of pseudo-labels based on the content similarity between the cold item and warm items, and then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels for each sample. Finally, we explicitly estimate the uncertainty of the noisy sample label by considering its relative entropy and the cold-start status of the item, which adaptively guides the role of pseudo-labels to correct the noisy labels at the sample level. DIF's superiority is supported by both theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The method has been deployed on a billion-user scale short video application Kuaishou and has significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIF is a model-agnostic denoising method for cold-start recommendation that uses content-similar warm items to generate confidence-weighted pseudo-labels, then corrects noisy implicit feedback labels by adaptively accounting for relative entropy and cold-start status. Deployed on Kuaishou, it significantly improved commercial metrics.
AI.motivation: Implicit feedback (clicks, views) is inherently noisy due to clickbait and position bias, and cold items are disproportionately affected. Existing denoising methods rely on heuristic patterns (e.g., high loss values) and lack adaptability for cold-start scenarios where interaction data is sparse. The stability of user content preferences remains underexploited for cold-item denoising.
AI.method: DIF operates in three stages: (1) Pseudo-label inference via content-similar warm items, leveraging stable user content preferences; (2) Confidence modeling based on content similarity between cold and warm items, with aggregation of multiple pseudo-labels per sample; (3) Adaptive label correction that estimates the uncertainty of noisy labels using relative entropy and the item's cold-start status, allowing pseudo-labels to guide correction at the sample level. The method is model-agnostic.
AI.result: DIF achieved superior performance supported by theoretical justification and extensive real-world dataset experiments. It was deployed on Kuaishou, a billion-user short video platform, and significantly improved various commercial metrics in cold-start scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Denoising implicit feedback specifically for cold items is a critical yet overlooked problem. DIF provides an effective, model-agnostic solution by transferring knowledge from warm items through content similarity, with adaptive confidence and uncertainty modeling. Its industrial deployment validates practical impact at scale.

title: Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data
comment: 8 pages of main content, 28 total pages. 30 figures
summary: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After sampling and annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, a RoBERTa-based model for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to 3M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data, (ii) we uncover a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlying web text, and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics in ways that current curation practices neither measure nor account for. Our framework, dataset, and analyses provide a foundation for understanding how narrative qualities are distributed in LLM pretraining data and for studying how data composition affects narrative reasoning tasks. We publicly release NarraDolma and NarraBERT.

AI.tldr: First fine-grained study of narrative features in a web-scale LLM pretraining corpus (Dolma, 3T tokens), introducing an 11-dimension framework across agency, setting, and events; authors release NarraBERT (fine-tuned RoBERTa) and NarraDolma (3M annotated passages), revealing multidimensional narrative structure unequally distributed across sources and topics.
AI.motivation: Despite narrative being a fundamental mode of human communication, the narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored. Current data curation practices neither measure nor account for narrative qualities, leaving a gap in understanding how pretraining data composition affects downstream narrative reasoning.
AI.method: Drawing on narrative theory, the authors design a framework with three core narrative elements — agency, setting, and events — operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. They sample and manually annotate 400 diverse passages from Dolma, then fine-tune a RoBERTa-based model (NarraBERT) for fine-grained narrative prediction. NarraBERT is applied to 3 million passages to produce the NarraDolma dataset.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous web data; (ii) a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlies web text; (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics in ways current curation practices neither measure nor account for.
AI.conclusion: The framework, NarraBERT model, and NarraDolma dataset provide a foundation for understanding narrative quality distribution in LLM pretraining data and for studying how data composition affects narrative reasoning. All artifacts are publicly released.

title: Which Pairs to Compare for LLM Post-Training?
summary: Preference-based post-training has become a central paradigm for aligning language models. A common data-collection strategy is to generate a small set of completions for each prompt and label the resulting comparison pairs. However, human preference labels are often much more expensive than generating additional completions, suggesting a different use of the same labeling budget: generate a larger pool of completions, but label only the most informative comparison pairs. This paper studies which pairs should be compared in preference-based post-training. We formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by the quality of the final policy under the preference-based post-training objective. We instantiate this framework for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), analyzing how the choice of labeled pairs propagates through DPO training to downstream policy performance. Our main results provide matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap of the DPO-trained policy. The bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance through a single design-dependent information matrix, which links label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation and motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large generated completion pools. Experiments on synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks show that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes comparison curation in preference-based post-training (e.g., DPO) as a sampling-design problem, deriving matching upper and lower bounds on policy suboptimality that depend on a design-dependent information matrix. The resulting optimization criterion guides budgeted selection of the most informative comparison pairs from large completion pools, improving sample efficiency over standard heuristics.
AI.motivation: Human preference labels are expensive relative to generating additional completions, yet standard practice labels a small set of completions per prompt rather than strategically selecting the most informative pairs from a larger pool. The paper addresses the underexplored question of which comparison pairs should be labeled to maximize downstream policy quality under a fixed labeling budget.
AI.method: The authors frame comparison curation as a sampling-design problem evaluated by the final policy's optimality gap under the DPO objective. They derive matching upper and lower bounds linking comparison selection to parameter estimation error via a design-dependent information matrix, yielding an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted pair selection. Practical sampling designs are proposed based on this criterion, and validated on synthetic and LM post-training benchmarks.
AI.result: The derived bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance solely through a design-dependent information matrix, which governs both parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. The proposed sampling designs consistently outperform common comparison-selection heuristics in terms of sample efficiency across both synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Strategic curation of comparison pairs using the proposed information-matrix criterion significantly improves the sample efficiency of preference-based post-training. The framework provides a principled alternative to naive comparison labeling and highlights the value of investing labeling budget in selecting informative pairs from large completion pools.

title: A Measurement Study of Cryptographic Misuse in Embodied AI Mobile Applications
summary: Embodied AI (EAI) mobile applications are evolving from auxiliary user interfaces into active control-path components, directly linking mobile-side cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust. Despite this shift, existing security research predominantly focuses on embodied AI devices and cloud infrastructures, leaving the mobile control layer largely unexplored as a critical attack surface. To bridge this gap, we present the first large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse within the EAI mobile ecosystem. We construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world applications across six EAI domains, and employ an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes. Our measurement yields 12,975 misuse findings (with an evaluated precision of 80.74\%), revealing that these cryptographic failures are driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors. We uncover structural security trade-offs: latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection, while the heavy reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates the local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Through real-world case studies, we demonstrate how these mobile-side cryptographic flaws bypass nominal network protections, enabling adversaries to intercept command channels and hijack the physical control of EAI entities. Ultimately, our findings highlight that mobile applications have become a fragile, yet overlooked, cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems.

AI.tldr: First large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse in the Embodied AI mobile app ecosystem. Analyzing 507 apps across six EAI domains, the authors uncover 12,975 misuse findings (80.74% precision), revealing that cryptographic failures stem from EAI-specific engineering constraints — latency-sensitive control paths weaken transport security, and offline provisioning/legacy IoT SDKs promote hardcoded credentials. These mobile-side flaws enable command-channel interception and physical hijacking of EAI entities.
AI.motivation: Existing security research on Embodied AI focuses on devices and cloud infrastructure while neglecting the mobile control layer, which increasingly serves as an active control-path component bridging cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust. This gap motivates the first systematic measurement of cryptographic misuse in EAI mobile applications.
AI.method: The authors construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world EAI mobile applications spanning six domains. They employ an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to systematically measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes across these applications.
AI.result: The measurement yields 12,975 misuse findings with an evaluated precision of 80.74%. Cryptographic failures are driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors. Two key structural trade-offs emerge: (1) latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport-layer protection, and (2) reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Case studies demonstrate real-world exploitability — adversaries can intercept command channels and hijack physical control of EAI entities.
AI.conclusion: Mobile applications have become a fragile yet overlooked cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems. The findings call for rethinking security architectures in EAI systems to account for the mobile control layer as a critical attack surface, and for developing domain-specific cryptographic guidelines that address the unique engineering constraints of embodied AI mobile apps.

title: Prompt Quality and Pull Request Outcomes: A Stage-Based Empirical Study of LLM-Assisted Development
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering workflows, yet little is known about how prompt structure influences downstream pull request (PR) outcomes. Prior studies primarily examine conversational helpfulness, productivity, or coarse-grained adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in collaborative integration behavior insufficiently understood. We analyze 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions derived from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Building on prior research on developer-facing artifacts and prompt engineering, we operationalize prompt structure using three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. We first evaluate whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments of prompt structure, finding substantial variation across dimensions and workflow contexts. Specificity shows the most stable agreement with human judgments; Context is systematically under-scored by the LLM; and Verification remains difficult to assess consistently, motivating a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, we then examine how prompt structure influences actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth across AI-assisted PR workflows. Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification emerges as the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. Overall, our findings show that prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows, influencing downstream adoption and integration through contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 265 developer-ChatGPT interactions in open-source pull requests, operationalizing prompt structure along three dimensions (Context, Specificity, Verification) and examining how each dimension differentially affects code generation, adoption, and integration depth in collaborative software engineering workflows.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered tools like ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering, but the influence of prompt structure on downstream PR outcomes — beyond coarse-grained adoption metrics or conversational helpfulness — remains poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically characterizing how prompt characteristics shape integration behavior.
AI.method: The authors collected 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions from self-admitted usage in open-source PRs. They operationalized prompt structure across three dimensions (Context, Specificity, Verification) and first evaluated whether LLM-assisted annotation could reliably reproduce human judgments. Finding dimension-dependent variation in LLM-human agreement, they adopted a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, they then conducted regression analyses to assess how each prompt dimension influences three outcomes: actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth.
AI.result: LLM-human annotation agreement varies by dimension: Specificity shows the most stable agreement; Context is systematically underscored by the LLM; Verification remains difficult to assess consistently. In the outcome analysis, Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification is the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. Prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across the AI-assisted software engineering workflow.
AI.conclusion: Prompt structure matters differentially across stages of AI-assisted PR workflows. Contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues each play distinct roles in shaping whether generated code is actionable, adopted, and deeply integrated — underscoring the need for prompt design strategies tailored to specific workflow stages rather than one-size-fits-all approaches.

title: Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models Across Agreement, Consistency, and Bias
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for language models, but judge validation in practice relies on exact-match agreement, a metric that does not correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. We present the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge to date: 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench, evaluated under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit) over 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments. Four findings emerge, consistent across the full cohort, including the April 2026 frontier: kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is universal (33--41 pp on MT-Bench), judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, high test--retest reliability (>0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) in two production-deployed judges (instantiating a consistency--bias paradox), and verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across our cohort under a single pairwise rubric. We distill these into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper conducts the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge (21 judges, 9 providers, ~541K judgments), revealing that standard exact-match agreement overstates judge quality; Cohen's kappa shows 33–41pp deflation, rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, and a consistency–bias paradox exists where high test–retest reliability coexists with severe position bias. The authors propose a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-as-a-Judge validation relies on exact-match agreement, which fails to correct for chance agreement and systematically inflates perceived discriminative ability. There is no standardized, rigorous validation protocol, and the field lacks a large-scale, multi-judge, multi-benchmark analysis that quantifies the gaps between naive and chance-corrected metrics.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 21 judges from nine providers across three benchmarks (MT-Bench, JudgeBench, RewardBench) under three protocols: (1) agreement (exact match vs. Cohen's kappa), (2) consistency (test–retest reliability), and (3) bias audit (position bias, verbosity bias). They conduct 118 runs totaling ~541,000 individual judgments, spanning models up to the April 2026 frontier.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is universal at 33–41 pp on MT-Bench. (2) Judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across different benchmarks. (3) A consistency–bias paradox: two production-deployed judges show both high test–retest reliability (>0.95) and severe position bias (>0.10). (4) Verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across the cohort under a single pairwise rubric.
AI.conclusion: Exact-match agreement is an inadequate validation metric that misrepresents judge quality. The findings motivate a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol incorporating chance-corrected agreement, cross-benchmark ranking, consistency checks, and bias audits to ensure robust LLM judge evaluation.

authors: Antonio de Sousa Leitão Filho; Allan Kardec Duailibe Barros Filho; Fabrício Saul Lima; Selby Mykael Lima dos Santos; Rejani Bandeira Vieira Sousa
title: Toten: Knowledge-Based Ontological Tokenization Of Physical Quantities And Technical Notation In Brazilian Portuguese
summary: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization is statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, but semantically blind to structured technical entities, fragmenting physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions into lexically arbitrary subwords. We present TOTEN, a knowledge-based ontological tokenization framework that replaces statistical derivation with declarative classification grounded in a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE). We formalize TOTEN as the triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>: the ontology gathers types, structural principles, composition relations, and preservable invariants; the classification function maps raw text into typed regions; and the instantiator family yields a self-descriptive structured representation. Robustness derives from deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional), Unicode Character Database (typographic), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Intrinsic evaluation covers four properties verifiable by construction -- ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction -- over an internal, physically validated benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases). We also report detection recall, distinguishing coverage from conditional atomicity. Against eight state-of-the-art baselines, TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction of 0.775-0.904 on external corpora, vs. 0.627-0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, the oracle from which the system inherits dimensional authority.

AI.tldr: TOTEN is a knowledge-based tokenization framework that replaces statistical Byte-Pair Encoding with ontology-driven classification, achieving superior handling of physical quantities, units, and numerical expressions by grounding tokenization in a formal ontology of engineering entities and external oracles.
AI.motivation: Standard Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization, while statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, is semantically blind — it fragments structured technical entities (physical quantities, numbers, units, symbolic expressions) into arbitrary subwords. This undermines downstream scientific and engineering NLP tasks where preserving the integrity of such entities is critical.
AI.method: TOTEN is formalized as a triple: an ontology (OEE — Ontology of Engineering Entities) providing types, composition relations, and invariants; a classification function mapping raw text to typed regions; and an instantiator family producing self-descriptive structured representations. Robustness is ensured through deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional analysis), the Unicode Character Database (typographic classification), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Evaluation covers four intrinsic properties: ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction.
AI.result: On an internal benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1,771 eligible cases), TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction scores of 0.775–0.904 on external corpora (vs. 0.627–0.703 for Quantulum3, the best baseline). On EngQuant, TOTEN scores 0.780 vs. 0.340 for Quantulum3. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation confirms concurrent validity between internal and external rankings. Dimensional equivalence achieves statistical parity with the Pint oracle.
AI.conclusion: TOTEN demonstrates that knowledge-based, ontology-grounded tokenization significantly outperforms statistical tokenization for technical entities, with statistical significance and oracle-level authority on dimensional correctness. The framework establishes a new paradigm for semantically-aware tokenization in scientific and engineering domains.

title: Accelerating Trust Convergence in IIoT: A ML Approach for Dynamic Network Conditions
summary: In Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments, trust management plays a vital role in securing systems, especially when dealing with resource-constrained devices. Traditional trust models often overlook the impact of fluctuating network quality, leading to slower trust convergence and inaccurate assessments. In this paper, we propose a dynamic trust management solution, known as the Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach, which integrates Machine Learning (ML) to accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions. Our model predicts the number of time units needed for trust convergence based on key network metrics and dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model to enhance convergence speed. Using a simulation framework that incorporates realistic Wi-Fi channel conditions based on the IEEE 802.11 standard, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the TCA-based approach, achieving up to a 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging conditions. Furthermore, the proposed solution exhibits resilience in scenarios involving malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy. This work provides a scalable and adaptive trust framework for IIoT systems in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

AI.tldr: A dynamic trust management framework (TCA) that uses machine learning to predict and accelerate trust convergence in IIoT environments under poor network conditions, achieving up to 28.6% reduction in convergence time.
AI.motivation: Traditional trust models in IIoT ignore fluctuating network quality, resulting in slow trust convergence and inaccurate assessments, particularly for resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: The TCA approach employs ML to predict the number of time units required for trust convergence based on network metrics, then dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model. Validation uses a simulation framework with realistic IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi channel conditions.
AI.result: Up to 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging network conditions, with improved trust evaluation accuracy and resilience against malicious nodes.
AI.conclusion: TCA offers a scalable, adaptive trust framework for IIoT that ensures robust performance across varying network conditions in dynamic industrial environments.

title: Emyx: Fast and efficient all-atom protein generation
summary: Computational enzyme design requires generating proteins that scaffold catalytic residues and ligands, a task that demands both geometric accuracy and structural diversity from the underlying generative model. Current all-atom generators inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction, leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. We argue that much of this complexity is unnecessary for generators, which condition on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich co-evolutionary signals. Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that concentrates capacity within standard transformer blocks, replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity. We additionally derive an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, bridging flow matching training efficiency with state-of-the-art sampling methods designed for diffusion models without retraining. Despite being the smallest model, Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 against the AME enzyme design benchmark across success rate under strict evaluation requiring both global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity, while training in just $682$ GPU-hours, roughly $4\times$ less than RFdiffusion3.

AI.tldr: Emyx, a compact 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model for enzyme design, outperforms larger competitors (Proteína-Complexa, RFdiffusion3) on the AME benchmark while training 4× faster (682 GPU-hours), by eliminating unnecessary architectural complexity and bridging flow matching with EDM-style sampling.
AI.motivation: Current all-atom generative models for computational enzyme design inherit expensive, complex architectures from structure prediction (e.g., IPAs, heavy embedding stacks), leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. The authors argue this complexity is unnecessary for generators that condition on sparse geometric constraints (catalytic residues and ligands) rather than rich co-evolutionary signals.
AI.method: Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that: (1) concentrates capacity in standard transformer blocks instead of heavy embedding stacks, using lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity; (2) derives an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, enabling the use of state-of-the-art diffusion sampling methods without retraining.
AI.result: Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 on the AME enzyme design benchmark across multiple metrics: success rate (global fold recovery + catalytic geometry accuracy), structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity. Training requires only 682 GPU-hours, roughly 4× less than RFdiffusion3.
AI.conclusion: Heavy architectures inherited from structure prediction are overkill for conditional protein generation. A streamlined flow matching model with sparse representations and EDM-compatible sampling achieves superior enzyme design performance at a fraction of the training cost.

title: Creating Multilingual Mental Health Dialogue Datasets: Limits of Persona-Based Localization via Nationality and Language
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026), co-located with ACL 2026
summary: AI and large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools to address global mental health challenges. Despite the global nature of these challenges, there remains a critical shortage of high-quality datasets for training and evaluating such systems. To mitigate this gap, researchers increasingly generate synthetic clinical personas to simulate user data and test digital mental health support systems. However, most validated personas rely on English-centric contexts. This paper investigates whether similar persona-based methods can be used to generate multilingual mental health datasets. We modified nationality and language parameters in personas to generate clinical dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. We then examined how different LLMs perform when evaluating the depression severity of these generated multilingual datasets against the baseline in English. Our findings indicate that just adding nationality and language parameters in personas might not be adequate, as it can introduce clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judge models often exhibit inaccuracies in assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying across different models. This exposes the systemic limitations of applying English-centric personas to multilingual contexts. Ultimately, our work highlights the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation to ensure equitable mental health systems globally.

AI.tldr: Investigates whether English-centric synthetic clinical personas can be adapted for multilingual mental health dataset generation. Finds that simply adding nationality/language parameters introduces clinical inconsistency, and LLM evaluators perform poorly on non-English depression severity assessment.
AI.motivation: There is a critical shortage of high-quality multilingual datasets for training and evaluating AI-based mental health systems. While synthetic persona generation has shown promise for English data, it is unclear whether these methods transfer effectively to other languages, risking inequitable global mental health AI deployment.
AI.method: Modified nationality and language parameters in clinical personas to generate mental health dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. Evaluated how different LLMs assess depression severity in these multilingual datasets, comparing performance against an English baseline.
AI.result: Simply adding nationality and language parameters to English-centric personas is insufficient — it introduces clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judge models exhibit inaccuracies when assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying significantly across different models.
AI.conclusion: The work exposes systemic limitations of applying English-centric persona generation methods to multilingual contexts and highlights the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation approaches to ensure equitable mental health systems globally.

title: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
summary: The decentralized deployment of LLM agents with diverse capabilities across diverse tasks motivates infrastructure for knowledge sharing across heterogeneous agent populations. Just as search engines index human-generated artifacts to support human problem solving, retrieval systems can organize agent-generated artifacts for reuse across agent populations. We extend retrieval-augmented generation - which demonstrates the value of human-authored artifacts to individual agents - to retrieval of agent-generated artifacts supporting a population of agents. In particular, agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge, yet these artifacts are typically discarded after a single use or retained only by the producing agent, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover existing solutions. We propose Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. We focus on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena), where trajectories are long and encode especially rich procedural structure. Our experiments demonstrate that retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps without coordination or joint training. These results position MATM as a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: MATM introduces a shared memory framework where LLM agents store and retrieve task execution trajectories, enabling knowledge reuse across heterogeneous agent populations. Experiments in ALFWorld and WebArena show improved task performance and reduced interaction steps without requiring agent coordination or joint training.
AI.motivation: LLM agents performing diverse tasks typically discard their execution trajectories after single use, forcing new agents to independently rediscover solutions. Just as web search indexes human knowledge, agent populations need infrastructure for sharing procedural knowledge encoded in agent trajectories.
AI.method: MATM provides a population-level retrieval system where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository, and consumer agents retrieve relevant past trajectories to guide task execution. The framework is evaluated in long-horizon interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena) where trajectories contain rich procedural structure.
AI.result: Retrieving trajectories from MATM consistently improved downstream task performance and reduced the number of interaction steps needed. These gains were achieved without explicit inter-agent coordination or joint training.
AI.conclusion: MATM establishes a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems, extending retrieval-augmented generation from human-authored artifacts to agent-generated procedural knowledge.

title: LaViSA: A Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity Benchmark
summary: Structural ambiguity arises when a single sentence admits multiple valid interpretations due to its syntactic structure, posing a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes serve as useful cues for resolving such ambiguity, and Vision and Language Models (VLMs) need to be capable of deriving possible semantic interpretations from visual scenes. We introduce Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity (LaViSA), a benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of VLMs to resolve structural ambiguity leveraging visual scenes. LaViSA consists of ambiguous sentences, their disambiguated sentences, and corresponding images of these disambiguated sentences across seven ambiguity categories. Using LaViSA, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of diverse VLMs, including both proprietary and open-source models with varying parameter scales and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that although recent VLMs can leverage visual scenes to resolve structural ambiguity to a some extent, they still struggle with certain ambiguity types and visually subtle semantic distinctions, indicating remaining limitations in resolving structural ambiguity using visual scenes.

AI.tldr: LaViSA is a new benchmark for evaluating how well Vision-Language Models (VLMs) resolve structural (syntactic) ambiguity using visual scenes. It covers seven ambiguity categories with matched ambiguous/disambiguated sentence-image pairs. Experiments reveal that while modern VLMs can partially leverage visual context, they still struggle with certain ambiguity types and subtle visual-semantic distinctions.
AI.motivation: Structural ambiguity — where a single sentence has multiple valid syntactic parses — poses a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual context can help disambiguate such sentences, but it is unclear to what extent current VLMs can actually exploit visual scenes for this purpose. A dedicated benchmark is needed to systematically evaluate this capability.
AI.method: The authors construct LaViSA, a benchmark containing ambiguous sentences paired with disambiguated counterparts and corresponding images, spanning seven categories of structural ambiguity. Using this dataset, they conduct a comprehensive evaluation across a diverse set of VLMs — including proprietary and open-source models of varying scales and reasoning abilities — measuring how well each model resolves ambiguity by leveraging visual information.
AI.result: Recent VLMs demonstrate some ability to use visual scenes for structural disambiguation, but performance remains inconsistent. Models particularly struggle with specific ambiguity categories and with cases requiring discrimination of subtle semantic distinctions in images, indicating that current VLMs have not yet fully mastered visual grounding for syntactic ambiguity resolution.
AI.conclusion: Despite progress in vision-language modeling, resolving structural ambiguity through visual scene understanding remains an open challenge. The LaViSA benchmark highlights specific limitations in current VLMs and provides a targeted testbed for future research on integrating syntactic disambiguation with visual reasoning.

title: AI4SE and SE4AI Exploration: A Decade Looking Back and Forward
summary: The March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and Systems Engineering (SE) became the most downloaded issue in the publication's history and launched a research community that now draws over 250 registrants to its annual workshop. In this article, we trace the progress in AI and SE across three phases (labeled here foundational, applied, and LLM inflection) based on the authors' reading of the field's core papers, and describe our opinions of where the community has converged and where critical gaps remain. Separately, a human-AI agreement literature review leveraging both human expertise and six AI models was performed to assess the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. The results identify five critical research gaps and offer guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE. We share the agreement data and the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application so readers can compare their own relevance judgments with the human and AI raters.

AI.tldr: This article traces the evolution of AI and Systems Engineering (SE) integration across three phases—foundational, applied, and LLM inflection—identifies five critical research gaps via a human-AI agreement literature review of over 2,500 publications, and introduces the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer tool for community use.
AI.motivation: The surge of interest sparked by the March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and SE, coupled with rapid advances in AI (particularly LLMs), created a need to systematically assess the field's progress, convergence points, and remaining gaps to guide practitioners and researchers.
AI.method: The authors (1) conducted a qualitative synthesis of core papers to delineate three evolutionary phases of AI4SE/SE4AI (foundational, applied, LLM inflection) and identify convergence/divergence in the community; (2) performed a human-AI agreement literature review using both human experts and six AI models to assess relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications; (3) developed the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application to share agreement data and enable reader-driven relevance judgments.
AI.result: The analysis identified five critical research gaps in AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation for SE. The phased framework captures the field's trajectory from early conceptual work through practical applications to the disruptive impact of LLMs. The agreement study and Explorer tool provide a replicable benchmark for human-AI relevance assessment.
AI.conclusion: The AI4SE/SE4AI community has matured significantly since 2020, coalescing around key themes, but substantial gaps remain—particularly in AI assurance and workforce transformation—that require urgent attention from both researchers and practitioners.

title: GNSS Spoofing Threat for V2X communications
comment: 2026 IEEE\@. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) constitute a core technology for delivering crucial positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services in the Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) domain, where they are indispensable for generating Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) that uphold network reliability and vehicular safety. Yet, GNSS signals are acutely exposed to spoofing, an advanced attack in which an adversary transmits crafted signals that replicate legitimate satellite characteristics, misleading the receiver into computing a false position. This work presents a methodology for conducting physical spoofing with inexpensive Software Defined Radio (SDR), describing a coordinate generation pipeline that employs Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity, and linear interpolation to produce high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The proposed attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OnBoard Unit (OBU) and RoadSide Unit (RSU) devices using a HackRF One across three scenarios that emulate synthetic trajectories at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h. The most significant contribution of this paper is the demonstration that V2X communications are not secured, as they are susceptible to GNSS spoofing attacks, which cause service degradation without being detected.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a low-cost GNSS spoofing attack on V2X OnBoard and RoadSide Units using SDR, demonstrating that V2X communications are vulnerable to undetectable position falsification, with experimental validation across three vehicle velocity scenarios.
AI.motivation: GNSS is critical for V2X Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM), but satellite signals are inherently vulnerable to spoofing attacks. The authors aim to demonstrate that V2X communications are not adequately secured against physical-layer GNSS spoofing, which can degrade service without triggering detection mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors implement a physical GNSS spoofing attack using low-cost SDR (HackRF One) with a coordinate generation pipeline that employs Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization for constant velocity emulation, and linear interpolation to synthesize high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The attack is validated on real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices across three synthetic trajectory scenarios at 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h.
AI.result: The spoofing attack successfully misled both OBU and RSU devices across all three velocity scenarios (90, 145, and 200 km/h), causing service degradation without detection. The experiment empirically confirms that V2X communication integrity is compromised by GNSS spoofing at the physical layer.
AI.conclusion: V2X communications are not secure against GNSS spoofing attacks despite their safety-critical role. The demonstrated vulnerability highlights a significant gap in current V2X security architectures, which fail to detect or mitigate physical-layer GNSS deception, posing risks to vehicular network reliability and safety.

title: A Hybrid GNN-FEM Framework for Phase-Field Fracture Simulation. Physics-Preserving Hybridization for Generalizable Surrogate Modeling
summary: Scientific machine learning (SciML) has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating simulations of complex physical systems, yet achieving physically consistent and generalizable predictions for nonlinear, history-dependent problems remains a central challenge. In this study, we propose a hybrid GNN--FEM framework for efficient and generalizable phase-field fracture modeling. While phase-field approaches provide a robust variational framework for simulating complex crack evolution, their high computational cost limits practical applications because they require solving coupled, nonlinear, and history-dependent systems within an incremental finite element procedure. To address this challenge, a graph neural network surrogate is integrated into the conventional staggered scheme, replacing the phase-field update at each load increment while retaining the FEM-based displacement solver to enforce mechanical equilibrium and boundary conditions. By preserving the incremental solution structure, the framework remains consistent with history-dependent fracture evolution without requiring the surrogate to approximate the full solution trajectory. This selective surrogate strategy emphasizes the identification of a physically meaningful and incrementally structured learning target, rather than relying on brute-force data generation to learn the full fracture process. The proposed framework achieves strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations through dimensionless feature design, a graph-based formulation on mesh-based domains, and a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the hybrid approach reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy compared with conventional FEM, and exhibits robust predictive performance across diverse problem settings.

AI.tldr: A hybrid GNN-FEM framework is proposed for phase-field fracture modeling, where a graph neural network replaces the expensive phase-field update in the staggered scheme while retaining FEM for displacement solves, achieving computational speedup with strong generalization across geometries, loads, materials, and discretizations.
AI.motivation: Phase-field fracture models are accurate but computationally prohibitive due to coupled, nonlinear, history-dependent systems solved incrementally. Existing SciML surrogates struggle with physical consistency and generalization for such history-dependent problems. The goal is to reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy and generalizability without requiring the surrogate to learn the full solution trajectory.
AI.method: A selective surrogate strategy integrates a GNN into the staggered FEM scheme: the GNN replaces only the phase-field update at each load increment, while FEM continues solving the displacement field to enforce equilibrium and boundary conditions. Key design elements include: (1) dimensionless feature engineering, (2) graph-based formulation operating directly on FEM meshes, and (3) a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field PDE. The GNN learns a physically meaningful, incrementally structured target rather than the entire fracture process.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show the hybrid GNN-FEM framework significantly reduces computational cost compared to conventional FEM while maintaining accuracy. It exhibits robust predictive performance and strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and mesh discretizations.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid GNN-FEM approach with selective surrogate placement and physics-informed learning offers an effective strategy for accelerating phase-field fracture simulations. Preserving the incremental FEM structure ensures consistency with history-dependent physics, and the framework's strong generalization suggests broader applicability to other nonlinear, history-dependent SciML problems.

title: Beyond Uniform Forgetting: A Study of Sequential Direct Preference Optimization Across Preference Settings
summary: Aligning language models with human preferences often requires optimising multiple behavioural objectives. A practical approach is to apply these objectives sequentially using preference optimisation methods such as Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO), but it remains unclear whether later training uniformly degrades preferences learned earlier or whether the effect depends on the relationship between objectives. We study sequential DPO across four preference settings covering distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, we evaluate all objectives after every stage with a fixed base-model reference. We find that sequential DPO does not produce a single forgetting pattern; preference change ranges from partial degradation to stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Pair-level analysis using length-normalised policy margins shows that aggregate metrics can mask heterogeneous changes across preference pairs, whereas quartile decomposition reveals that high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve depending on the setting. Mechanistic diagnostics show that Stage~2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective across all settings, providing little evidence that direct gradient opposition is the primary driver. These findings suggest that future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength, rather than assuming that later objectives affect earlier preferences uniformly.

AI.tldr: Sequential DPO training does not uniformly degrade earlier preferences; the effect depends on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Pair-level and mechanistic analyses reveal heterogeneous changes masked by aggregate metrics, with no evidence that gradient opposition drives forgetting.
AI.motivation: When aligning language models with multiple human preferences, it is common to apply objectives sequentially via DPO. However, it is unclear whether later training uniformly degrades earlier-learned preferences or whether the effect varies with the relationship between objectives. The authors aim to dispel the assumption of uniform forgetting and provide a nuanced characterization of sequential DPO dynamics.
AI.method: The authors conduct sequential DPO experiments using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters across four distinct preference settings: distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. All objectives are evaluated after every stage using a fixed base-model reference. They employ length-normalised policy margins for pair-level analysis, quartile decomposition to examine confidence-stratified effects, and mechanistic diagnostics comparing Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates to the previous objective's direction.
AI.result: Sequential DPO yields heterogeneous outcomes: partial degradation, stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer, depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and order. Aggregate metrics mask pair-level heterogeneity; high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve. Mechanistically, Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective across all settings, suggesting direct gradient opposition is not the primary driver of forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength rather than assuming later objectives uniformly degrade earlier preferences. The findings challenge the prevailing narrative of catastrophic forgetting in sequential preference optimisation.

title: Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective
summary: Electronic design automation (EDA) is inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy. Design artifacts, flow scripts, and engineering decisions cross tool, session, and organizational boundaries before final implementation, signoff, or release. Each transfer carries explicit and implicit requirements that may not be fully captured by stage-local checks. LLM-based agents now invoke EDA tools directly, embed retrieved knowledge in executable scripts, and hand off state across sessions and stages. Once their outputs condition downstream engineering decisions, the transferred object must satisfy a handoff contract and meet the assumptions of its next consumer. This survey introduces handoff validity as its organizing principle. A handoff is valid when the transferred object satisfies the consumer's acceptance conditions and carries sufficient context, evidence, and provenance for downstream use. We review 82 systems and classify them into three boundary classes. Stage-Bound systems establish validity within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task. Flow-Bound systems preserve coherent workflow state across tools, invocations, and sessions. Organization-Bound systems maintain source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. For each class, we analyze handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. These analyses motivate a five-layer EDA agent communication protocol (EACP), covering the agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security and IP protocols. We aim to provide a common vocabulary and research agenda for trustworthy agentic EDA.

AI.tldr: This survey introduces "handoff validity" as an organizing principle for LLM-based agents in EDA, classifying 82 systems into Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, and Organization-Bound categories, and proposes a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) to ensure trustworthy handoffs across tools, sessions, and organizational boundaries.
AI.motivation: EDA workflows are multi-stage and handoff-heavy, with design artifacts and decisions crossing tool, session, and organizational boundaries. Each transfer carries implicit/explicit requirements that stage-local checks cannot fully capture. As LLM-based agents increasingly drive EDA tool invocation and downstream decisions, there is no systematic framework for ensuring that transferred objects satisfy downstream consumer assumptions—hence the need for a handoff validity framework.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic survey of 82 LLM-based EDA systems, classify them into three boundary classes (Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, Organization-Bound), and analyze each class along dimensions of handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. Based on this analysis, they propose a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) stack: agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security/IP protocols.
AI.result: The survey identifies three distinct handoff boundary classes: (1) Stage-Bound systems validate within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task; (2) Flow-Bound systems maintain coherent workflow state across tools, invocations, and sessions; (3) Organization-Bound systems ensure source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. The proposed EACP provides a layered protocol architecture addressing gaps in current agent communication for EDA.
AI.conclusion: Handoff validity is a critical missing concept in agentic EDA. By framing agent interactions through handoff contracts, objects, and coordination mechanisms, the field can move toward trustworthy multi-agent EDA systems. The EACP protocol stack offers a concrete research agenda and common vocabulary for building reliable, provenance-aware agent communication in electronic design automation.

title: When Does Streaming Tool Use Help? Characterizing Tool-Intent Stabilization in Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Streaming RAG) reduces user-perceived latency by issuing tool queries in parallel with ongoing user input, before the utterance is complete. Reported gains are aggregate, yet the mechanism's benefit is fundamentally query-intrinsic: speculation can only help when the correct tool query becomes determinable before the user stops speaking or typing. We isolate and measure this property -- tool-intent stabilization, the point in the input stream at which a speculative query's retrieval converges to the answer-bearing result. On the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions) we (i) measure the distribution of stabilization, (ii) derive a model-agnostic bound H on the portion of tool latency that can be hidden behind the user's remaining input, as a function of tool latency L and input cadence δ, (iii) validate against a working streaming pipeline that realized savings meet or exceed this bound, and (iv) identify which query properties predict early versus late stabilization. The study requires no model training and runs on commodity CPU hardware. We find that at a realistic operating point (L=600ms, δ=3w/s, θ=0.8), 73.9% of queries across the full benchmark admit substantial latency hiding -- a blended figure that mixes sufficiency stabilization on the 21.3% of questions where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable (95.2% streamable on this favorable slice) with a grounding-free top-1-settling fallback on the remainder. On the favorable slice, φ_suf is bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] by exact and relaxed grounding -- both early. Question type produces a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, epsilon^2=0.04), directly informing when a learned speculative trigger is worth its cost.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies when speculative tool queries in Streaming RAG become stable enough to hide latency behind ongoing user input. On the CRAG benchmark, 73.9% of queries admit substantial latency hiding at realistic settings, with stabilization occurring very early for verbatim-retrievable questions. The authors derive a model-agnostic bound and validate it against a working pipeline, offering actionable insight for when learned speculative triggers are worthwhile.
AI.motivation: Streaming RAG promises reduced user-perceived latency by issuing tool queries before the user finishes speaking/typing, but reported gains are aggregate. The core unanswered question is *query-intrinsic*: speculation only helps when the correct tool query stabilizes (becomes determinable) early enough in the input stream. No prior work isolates or measures this "tool-intent stabilization" property, making it unclear when and why speculation actually works.
AI.method: The authors define and measure tool-intent stabilization on the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions). They derive a model-agnostic bound H representing the portion of tool latency concealable behind remaining user input, as a function of tool latency L, input cadence δ, and a tolerance parameter θ. They validate this bound against a working streaming pipeline using BM25 retrieval and examine two stabilization criteria: sufficiency stabilization (gold evidence is verbatim-present and retrievable) and a grounding-free top-1-settling fallback. They also analyze which query properties (e.g., question type) predict early vs. late stabilization using Kruskal-Wallis and epsilon-squared effect size.
AI.result: At L=600ms, δ=3 words/s, θ=0.8, 73.9% of CRAG queries admit substantial latency hiding. On the favorable subset (21.3% of questions) where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable, 95.2% are streamable; φ_suf is bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] — very early. On the remaining questions, a top-1-settling fallback applies. Question type yields a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, ε²=0.04, small-to-moderate effect), indicating question type alone is informative but insufficient for fine-grained triggering decisions.
AI.conclusion: Tool-intent stabilization is measurable, early for a substantial fraction of queries, and predictable from lightweight query properties without model training. The derived bound H provides a principled framework for deciding when speculative tool use is worthwhile. The significant but small effect of question type on stabilization timing directly informs the cost-benefit tradeoff of learned speculative triggers in streaming RAG systems.

title: A BART-based approach with hierarchical strategy for Vietnamese abstractive multi-document summarization
summary: In this technical report, we focus on solving the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, introduced in the International Workshop on Vietnamese Language and Speech Processing (VLSP) 2022. We choose to follow the popular hierarchical approach, i.e. condensing each document followed by aggregation and summarization. We propose a novel yet simple strategy to shorten documents that is driven by the golden summary, thus ensuring high correlation between stages of the hierarchical approach. Our method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP's public test set, and can produce fluent and concise summaries. Additionally, we utilize external sources for extra data, which greatly enhances the quantity of data for Vietnamese multi-document summarization. The additional data is made available for the community.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical approach for Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization is proposed, using a novel golden-summary-driven document shortening strategy. It achieves 0.2468 ROUGE2-F1 on the VLSP 2022 test set and leverages extra external data released to the community.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization introduced in the VLSP 2022 workshop, where existing methods struggle with long input documents and limited training data for Vietnamese.
AI.method: A hierarchical two-stage approach: (1) condense each document individually, then (2) aggregate and summarize the condensed outputs. The key novelty is a golden-summary-driven document shortening strategy that selects sentences from source documents based on their relevance to the reference summary, ensuring high correlation between the condensation and summarization stages. External data sources are also leveraged for data augmentation.
AI.result: The method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP public test set and produces fluent, concise summaries. The additional external data significantly enhances the available training data quantity for Vietnamese multi-document summarization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed simple yet effective golden-summary-driven shortening strategy improves hierarchical multi-document summarization for Vietnamese, and the released external data provides a valuable resource for future research in this under-resourced domain.

title: BrainG3N: A Dual-Purpose Tokenizer for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) brain MRI is central to clinical neurology and neuro-oncology, where generative models could augment under-represented cohorts, simulate disease trajectories, and support privacy-preserving data sharing. Latent diffusion has been the go-to solution for modeling imaging data, but it places two competing demands on the tokenizer: encoder embeddings must retain the clinical information that downstream tasks act on, and the decoder must reconstruct anatomically faithful volumes. Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers achieve the second at the expense of the first. To address this, we introduce a fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) based tokenizer for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion, decoupling encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. We pretrain the encoder on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts spanning four modalities, ten disease categories, and 200+ acquisition sites, and demonstrate its dual utility in two settings. First, on a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (i.e., BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, and MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. Second, a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these clinically informative embeddings supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Together these results establish a single 3D brain-MRI embedding space capable of both downstream clinical tasks and controllable generation.

AI.tldr: A 3D masked-autoencoder tokenizer decouples encoder and decoder for brain MRI latent diffusion: a frozen MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings (SOTA on 21/23 downstream tasks), while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs volumes. The embeddings enable both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting via a diffusion transformer.
AI.motivation: Existing latent diffusion models for 3D brain MRI face a trade-off: reconstruction-driven tokenizers produce anatomically faithful volumes but sacrifice the clinical utility of encoder embeddings needed for downstream tasks. The authors aim to achieve both — clinically informative embeddings and high-fidelity reconstruction — within a single framework.
AI.method: The authors propose a fully volumetric MAE-based tokenizer that decouples the encoder and decoder. A 3D MAE encoder (pretrained on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts, 4 modalities, 10 disease categories, 200+ sites) is frozen to produce clinically informative embeddings. A separate CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. A conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) is then trained on these embeddings for generation and longitudinal forecasting.
AI.result: On a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches state-of-the-art models (BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. The conditional DiT supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.
AI.conclusion: A single 3D brain MRI embedding space can serve dual purposes — strong performance on diverse downstream clinical tasks and controllable image generation — by decoupling the tokenizer's encoder (clinical representation) from its decoder (anatomical reconstruction).

title: TrustMix: How to Mix Messages in a Mobile Ad-hoc Network
summary:
Mix networks are a highly effective way to achieve anonymity, defending against a wide range of traffic-analysis attacks. However, mix networks are usually designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied in the context of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). The few existing solutions for MANETs require advance knowledge of the topology or a trusted central party.
  In this paper, we present TrustMix, a mix protocol for MANETs that operates without any central trusted party. In TrustMix, parties join groups and then messages are forwarded via multiple groups to provide anonymity. With TrustMix, users only need to find a party nearby that they consider trusted. They then forward the message to this party's group, and the party shuffles messages before forwarding to other groups, meaning that the original message and the forwarded message cannot be linked. Furthermore, even if the chosen party is adversarial, they can only break the anonymity if all parties in their group are adversarial as all of them contribute to the shuffling. In addition to anonymity, TrustMix also enforces rate limits on the number of messages through the use of linkable ring signatures, which allows detecting that parties send more messages that allowed without revealing identities.
  We prove the security of our protocol in the random oracle model. We evaluate its anonymity using an existing mix-network simulator and show that TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept Android implementation and show that TrustMix achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.

AI.tldr: TrustMix is a decentralized mix network protocol for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) that provides anonymity without any central trusted party. It uses group-based message shuffling and linkable ring signatures for rate limiting, offering provable security in the random oracle model with practical mobile performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional mix networks are designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied to MANETs. Existing MANET mix solutions require either advance topology knowledge or a trusted central party, limiting their applicability in dynamic, decentralized mobile environments.
AI.method: TrustMix organizes parties into groups. A sender forwards a message to a nearby trusted party's group, where all group members collectively shuffle messages before forwarding to subsequent groups, breaking linkability between input and output messages. It employs linkable ring signatures to enforce per-party rate limits without revealing identities. Security is proven in the random oracle model, and anonymity is evaluated via an existing mix-network simulator. A proof-of-concept Android implementation with 5 devices demonstrates practical throughput.
AI.result: TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity compared to baseline approaches according to mix-network simulator evaluation. The protocol achieves provable security in the random oracle model. The Android proof-of-concept demonstrates acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.
AI.conclusion: TrustMix successfully brings mix-network anonymity to MANETs without requiring a trusted central party or advance topology knowledge. The combination of group-based shuffling and linkable ring signatures provides both strong anonymity and rate-limiting enforcement, with performance that is viable on real mobile hardware.
