title: How Linear Is a Transformer Feed-Forward Block? Per-Block Linear Recoverability Is Learned, Not Architectural
summary:
Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs) are often treated as nonlinear stores of computation, yet how nonlinear a trained FFN block actually is has rarely been measured. We treat each FFN as a position-wise input-to-output map and split it into the exact least-squares linear approximation plus a residual. The held-out variance the closed-form linear map explains defines a block's linear recoverability (R^2_lin), an optimiser-free measure of its linearity.
  Across all twelve blocks of GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and llama-160m, R^2_lin is highly heterogeneous and non-monotone with depth, ranging from near-linear (>0.99) to strongly nonlinear (<0.3) between adjacent blocks, and is not set by the activation function: same-width GELU models GPT-2 and Pythia-160m have sharply different profiles, so recoverability is a learned property of individual trained blocks, not an architectural one. A low-rank bilinear probe of the residual recovers only a few points of R^2, with gain uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity: the unrecovered computation is not a single position-wise product but higher-order or distributed structure.
  The measurement also serves as a targeted compression signal: recoverable blocks admit large single-layer replacements (GPT-2's early FFN at 8x fewer parameters for +0.77 perplexity), while low-recoverability blocks flag where this is unsafe. It further exposes a methodological pitfall: trained linear baselines can badly under-converge on ill-conditioned transformer activations, so we report the exact closed-form least-squares ceiling throughout.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces R²_lin, a metric that quantifies how linearly recoverable each transformer FFN block is by computing the exact least-squares linear approximation and measuring held-out variance explained. Across GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and Llama-160m, linearity varies dramatically between adjacent blocks (R² from >0.99 to <0.3), depends on learned properties rather than architecture, and serves as both a compression guide and a warning against under-converged linear baselines.
AI.motivation: Despite FFNs being conceptualized as nonlinear computational stores in transformers, no prior work has rigorously measured just how nonlinear trained FFN blocks actually are. The authors aim to fill this gap with a principled, optimizer-free metric and explore its practical implications for model compression and methodology.
AI.method: Each FFN block is treated as a position-wise map f(x). The authors compute its exact least-squares linear approximation W* = argmin_W E[||f(x) - Wx||²] in closed form, then define R²_lin as the fraction of variance explained by this optimal linear map. A low-rank bilinear probe further decomposes the residual. The metric is applied layer-wise across GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and Llama-160m, and single-layer linear replacements are tested for compression.
AI.result: R²_lin is highly heterogeneous across blocks and non-monotonic with depth; adjacent blocks can span near-linear to strongly nonlinear regimes. Profiles differ sharply between same-width GELU models (GPT-2 vs. Pythia-160m), proving linearity is learned, not architectural. Bilinear probes recover only a small R² gain uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity, suggesting higher-order structure. High-R² blocks can be replaced with linear layers at 8x parameter reduction for only +0.77 perplexity. Trained linear baselines severely under-converge on ill-conditioned activations, motivating the closed-form approach.
AI.conclusion: FFN linearity is a learned, block-specific property that varies wildly within a single model. R²_lin provides a reliable, optimizer-free diagnostic for identifying compressible blocks and exposes a methodological flaw in using trained linear probes as baselines. The residual nonlinearity that bilinear probes cannot capture points to distributed, higher-order computation worthy of further study.

title: Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring
summary: LLMs can personalize education, although current static-prompt tutoring systems struggle to adapt to diverse academic disciplines. We develop and test a system with subject-aware prompting, based on 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) extracted from raw transcripts. We first train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, and then deploy it for online adaptation with actual high-school students. The simulation benchmark shows the router outperforming two static baselines ($0.694$ vs. $0.647$ and $0.64$, $p<0.001$). A/B testing ($N=656$ conversations from 359 students) shows sim-to-real transfer where the model switches from analytical to scaffolding learning strategies. Our adaptive prompt selection mechanism improves instructional efficiency, maintains pedagogical quality and reduces interactions by around 3 turns ($p=0.007$). While a greedy router achieves a comparable exercise conversion rate with the baseline ($19.1\%$ vs. $19.6\%$), a stochastic router that samples strategies leads to a higher conversion rate ($28.1\%$).

AI.tldr: A subject-aware prompt routing system for LLM tutoring is developed, trained in simulation, and deployed with high-school students. The adaptive router outperforms static baselines on pedagogical benchmarks, reduces conversation length, and a stochastic variant boosts exercise conversion rates from 19.6% to 28.1%.
AI.motivation: Current LLM tutoring systems use static prompts that cannot adapt to diverse academic disciplines, limiting personalization. There is a need for dynamic, subject-aware prompt selection that responds to real-time pedagogical signals in student-tutor interactions.
AI.method: The authors extract 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) from raw transcripts. They train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment and then deploy it for online adaptation with high-school students. Two router variants are tested: a greedy router and a stochastic router that samples strategies. Evaluation uses simulation benchmarks against two static baselines, plus A/B testing with N=656 conversations from 359 students, measuring instructional efficiency, pedagogical quality, interaction length, and exercise conversion rate.
AI.result: In simulation, the router achieves 0.694 vs. static baselines of 0.647 and 0.64 (p<0.001). In real deployment, the model successfully shifts from analytical to scaffolding strategies (sim-to-real transfer). The adaptive mechanism reduces interactions by ~3 turns (p=0.007). The greedy router matches baseline exercise conversion (19.1% vs. 19.6%), while the stochastic router significantly improves it to 28.1%.
AI.conclusion: Subject-aware, adaptive prompt routing enhances LLM tutoring by improving pedagogical outcomes and efficiency. Stochastic strategy sampling is particularly effective for boosting student exercise conversion, suggesting that non-deterministic prompt selection better supports learner engagement and follow-through.

title: The Hidden Environmental Cost of Poor Coding Practices in TensorFlow and Keras Applications: A Study on Resource Leaks and Carbon Emissions
summary: Efficiency and sustainability are critical considerations in the development and deployment of machine learning (ML) applications. Among the factors influencing sustainability, resource leaks in ML code can introduce hidden inefficiencies that elevate energy consumption and CO2 emissions. Despite this, empirical evidence quantifying their environmental impact remains limited. This emerging results paper presents an initial empirical investigation of two common resource-leak smells, namely Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR), and their impact on energy consumption and CO2 emissions in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Controlled experiments were conducted for each smell by executing identical training tasks while comparing against a smell-free baseline. Our preliminary results show that both smells consistently increase estimated electricity usage and carbon emissions. IMR and UTR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and 46%, respectively, with proportional increases in CO2 emissions. Paired statistical tests indicate that these differences are systematic and statistically significant, providing initial empirical evidence that resource-leak smells may degrade ML energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. These findings suggest that resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and sustainability, emphasizing the importance of integrating resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an initial empirical study quantifying how two resource-leak code smells in TensorFlow/Keras — Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR) — increase energy consumption by ~32% and ~46% respectively, with proportional CO₂ emission increases, providing statistically significant evidence that resource leaks degrade ML sustainability.
AI.motivation: While sustainability and efficiency are critical in ML development, empirical evidence quantifying the environmental impact of resource leaks in ML code remains limited. The authors aim to fill this gap by measuring how common resource-leak smells affect energy consumption and carbon emissions.
AI.method: Controlled experiments were conducted on TensorFlow and Keras workloads. For each resource-leak smell (IMR and UTR), identical training tasks were executed, comparing smelly implementations against a smell-free baseline. Electricity consumption and CO₂ emissions were measured, and paired statistical tests assessed the significance of observed differences.
AI.result: IMR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and UTR by approximately 46%, with proportional increases in CO₂ emissions. Paired statistical tests confirmed these differences are systematic and statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: Resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and environmental sustainability. The findings emphasize the need to integrate resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development practices.

title: Where Does Social Reasoning Come From? Capability Provenance in Language Models
summary: We use training-data attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, mapping which regions of the pretraining corpus support social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning in OLMo3-7B. Training-data attribution measures how strongly each training document influences a model's predictions on a benchmark, but document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities, and prior work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning. We compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set drawn from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix, aggregate influence across WebOrganizer's 24-format x 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins), and contrast benchmark pairs in a 2x2 design that varies domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, and the contrast is sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning provides partial causal validation: forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and we open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

AI.tldr: The paper uses training-data attribution to map which pretraining corpus regions support social vs. STEM reasoning in OLMo3-7B, finding qualitatively distinct corpus regions for each, validated through targeted machine unlearning.
AI.motivation: Prior training-data attribution work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning, and document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support specific capabilities. The authors aim to bridge this gap by systematically mapping how different regions of the pretraining corpus contribute to social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: They compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) on the OLMo3-7B model over a working set from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix. Influence scores are aggregated across WebOrganizer's 24-format × 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins). They employ a 2×2 contrastive design varying domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge), using SocialIQA, MMLU Social Sciences, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU STEM as benchmarks. Targeted machine unlearning on high-attribution topic bins provides causal validation.
AI.result: Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, with sharper contrast at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted unlearning of high-attribution bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the corresponding benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, providing partial causal validation.
AI.conclusion: Training-data attribution can serve as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, effectively revealing which pretraining data regions underpin specific reasoning capabilities. The authors open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

title: Quantization as a Malicious Task: Removing Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors via Task Arithmetic
summary: Model quantization is widely adopted to reduce memory usage and inference cost when deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. However, recent studies have revealed a new security threat known as Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs), where a model behaves normally in full precision but activates malicious behavior only after quantization. Existing defenses typically modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, often introducing additional computational overhead or relying on specific quantization settings. Here, we present QVec, a parameter-space perspective for defending against QCBs. We observe that the weight difference between a full-precision model and its quantized counterpart encodes a structured behavioral shift, which can be interpreted as a malicious task vector rather than random quantization noise. Based on this insight, QVec counteracts this malicious direction through controlled parameter correction prior to deployment. QVec requires no retraining, no trigger samples, and only a single quantization pass to estimate the parameter shift, together with a lightweight hyperparameter search. Extensive experiments across image classification benchmarks and multiple Large Language Model (LLM) attack scenarios demonstrate that QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance.

AI.tldr: QVec defends against quantization-conditioned backdoors by interpreting the weight shift from full-precision to quantized models as a malicious task vector and correcting it via a lightweight, retraining-free parameter-space intervention requiring only one quantization pass.
AI.motivation: Existing QCB defenses modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, incurring computational overhead or depending on specific quantization settings. A more general, efficient, and plug-and-play defense is needed.
AI.method: QVec frames the weight difference between full-precision and quantized models as a structured malicious task vector. It estimates this parameter shift with a single quantization pass, then applies a controlled parameter correction (with lightweight hyperparameter search) to neutralize the backdoor direction before deployment — no retraining or trigger samples required.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks and multiple LLM attack scenarios show QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while maintaining clean performance.
AI.conclusion: QVec offers a simple, efficient, and general defense against QCB attacks, demonstrating that parameter-space correction alone can effectively mitigate quantization-conditioned backdoors without compromising model utility.

title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse rich verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) into a binary pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that routes every verifier signal back into proof search through a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling first, then a critic-guided MCTS pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples. The protocol preserves every theorem solved by its own Phase 1 sweep, so Phase 2's additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. VERITAS reaches 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. an independently run Best-of-5 at 36.9%, Portfolio 26.2%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench, a 55-theorem combinatorics benchmark we release on which Best-of-5 (1.8%) falls below Portfolio (3.6%), exposing that unguided sampling hurts when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback. Artifacts are available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: VERITAS is a zero-shot framework that improves LLM-based formal theorem proving by routing all verifier signals (not just pass/fail) back into proof search via Best-of-N sampling followed by MCTS with failure-guided negative examples, achieving 40.6% on miniF2F and releasing a new combinatorics benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based formal provers discard rich intermediate verifier feedback (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress), reducing it to a binary pass/fail bit. This wastes valuable debugging signal that could guide proof search, particularly on hard problems requiring iterative lemma discovery where unguided sampling fails.
AI.method: A two-phase zero-shot protocol: Phase 1 performs Best-of-N sampling to solve as many theorems as possible. Phase 2 runs a critic-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples, using all verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial progress) to guide exploration. Crucially, Phase 2 preserves every theorem already solved in Phase 1, so any additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration.
AI.result: VERITAS achieves 40.6% on miniF2F versus an independently run Best-of-5 baseline at 36.9% and Portfolio at 26.2%. On the newly released VERITAS-CombiBench (55 combinatorics theorems), VERITAS scores 7.3% while Best-of-5 scores only 1.8% and Portfolio 3.6%, demonstrating that unguided sampling underperforms when iterative lemma name recovery from verifier feedback is required.
AI.conclusion: Routing rich verifier signals back into proof search via a two-phase sampling-then-MCTS protocol yields measurable gains over pure Best-of-N and portfolio approaches. The stark performance inversion on combinatorics problems confirms that feedback-guided search becomes essential when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively, motivating future work on tighter verifier-prover feedback loops.

title: Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact
summary: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign large language models (LLMs) stable psychological profiles that affect their usability, safety assessment, and use as proxies for human participants in research. Using a formal psychometric framework, we show that these profiles are largely a measurement artifact. Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, we report four findings. First, differences between models are driven not by the traits an instrument targets but by a directional response bias, a tendency to respond toward one end of the scale, or one labeled option, regardless of item content; a variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias, against 9-16% in humans. Second, the bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated by it. Third, because bias rather than trait drives responding, an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality, a term we coin for the proportion of items for which trait and bias point in opposite directions. Fourth, the profile a model appears to have shifts with the items used and can be manufactured through item selection. These results demonstrate that the apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the instrument used to measure them, not properties of the models themselves. As instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, we call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

AI.tldr: Psychometric instruments borrowed from human psychology produce apparent LLM psychological profiles that are largely measurement artifacts driven by directional response bias (80-90% of model variance), not genuine traits. Response orthogonality — whether trait and bias point in opposite directions across items — almost entirely predicts an instrument's apparent reliability. Model profiles can be manufactured through item selection.
AI.motivation: There is a growing trend of using human psychological instruments to assign stable psychological profiles to LLMs, which then influence usability judgments, safety evaluations, and the use of LLMs as human proxies in behavioral research. The authors question whether these profiles reflect genuine model properties or are merely artifacts of the measurement instruments themselves.
AI.method: The authors administered a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments (both self-report and behavioral tasks) to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples. They applied a formal psychometric framework including variance decomposition to separate trait-driven variance from directional response bias (the tendency to favor one end of a scale or labeled option regardless of item content). They introduced the concept of "response orthogonality" — the proportion of items where trait and bias point in opposite directions — and tested its predictive power for apparent reliability. They also demonstrated profile manipulation through selective item inclusion.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Between-model variance is 81-90% attributable to directional response bias, versus only 9-16% in humans. (2) This bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated. (3) An instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality. (4) A model's apparent psychological profile shifts with item selection and can be intentionally manufactured, confirming profiles are instrument artifacts rather than model properties.
AI.conclusion: LLM psychological profiles derived from human instruments are predominantly artifacts of measurement rather than reflections of stable model traits. Since instruments from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, the authors call for developing dedicated assessment approaches centered on response orthogonality to ensure that any claimed model traits are genuine.

title: CoRaCommit: A VS Code Extension for Commit Message Generation with Exemplar Retrieval
comment: 17 pages, 6 images, 3 tables, Manuscript submitted to a Journal (2026)
summary: Commit messages are essential textual artifacts that describe the intent behind code changes, and play a critical role in version control, code review, and historical tracking. However, in practice, commit messages are primarily authored manually, which is time-consuming and often results in inconsistent quality and non-uniform expression. Existing VS Code extensions for commit message generation typically directly invoke large language models based on the code diff, without leveraging similar commit exemplars as references, and rarely support user feedback-driven LLM recommendation. To address these limitations, this paper presents CoRaCommit, a VS Code extension that enhances commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as prompt context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate commit message comparison, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback. Experimental results on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset show that CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.

AI.tldr: CoRaCommit is a VS Code extension that improves commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as context, running multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate comparison, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback, outperforming existing extensions on standard metrics.
AI.motivation: Manual commit message writing is time-consuming and leads to inconsistent quality. Existing VS Code extensions rely solely on code diffs fed directly to a single LLM, lack retrieval of similar historical commit exemplars as references, and do not support user-feedback-driven LLM recommendation.
AI.method: CoRaCommit employs three key mechanisms: (1) retrieval of similar commit exemplars from a corpus to serve as prompt context, (2) parallel invocation of multiple LLMs to generate candidate commit messages for comparison, and (3) dynamic LLM recommendation based on user feedback. Evaluation uses 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset.
AI.result: CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics on the 945-commit ApacheCM benchmark, validating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented generation with similar commit exemplars, combined with multi-LLM comparison and user-feedback-driven recommendation, significantly improves commit message quality over existing approaches that rely on code-diff-only prompting.

title: Before the Labels: How Dataset Construction Shapes Suicidality Detection in Clinical Text
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026)
summary: Clinical NLP increasingly relies on electronic health record (EHR) data to detect suicidal behaviors, treating clinical documentation as more reliable ground truth than social media. We argue that this framing obscures how EHR-based suicidality datasets encode a particular operationalization of suicidality, shaped by who authors the data, how episodes are bounded, and how ambiguity is resolved. We ground this argument in a case study of the ScAN dataset, built over MIMIC-III clinical notes. We show how governance constraints, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay-level aggregation produce labels that reflect clinician-documented judgments, treat suicidality as a bounded episode, and assume that intent can be reliably inferred from documentation. A linguistic analysis demonstrates that identical labels subsume heterogeneous clinical framings differing in temporality, negation, and uncertainty. We argue that clinical NLP should examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that EHR-based suicidality datasets encode specific operational assumptions (who authors, how episodes are bounded, how ambiguity is resolved) that are obscured when labels are treated as ground truth. A case study of the ScAN dataset (MIMIC-III) reveals that governance, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay aggregation produce labels that conflate heterogeneous clinical framings of suicidality.
AI.motivation: Clinical NLP increasingly treats EHR documentation as more reliable ground truth than social media for detecting suicidal behaviors, but this framing neglects how the very construction of these datasets embeds a particular operationalization of suicidality — one shaped by institutional, methodological, and interpretive choices rather than reflecting an objective clinical reality.
AI.method: The authors ground their argument in a case study of the ScAN dataset (constructed over MIMIC-III clinical notes). They conduct a linguistic analysis examining how governance constraints, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling protocols, and hospital-stay-level aggregation shape the resulting labels. The analysis surfaces how identical labels subsume heterogeneous clinical framings that differ along dimensions of temporality, negation, and uncertainty.
AI.result: The ScAN dataset's labels are shown to reflect clinician-documented judgments rather than verified patient states, treat suicidality as a bounded episode tied to a single hospital stay, and assume that suicidal intent can be reliably inferred from clinical documentation alone. Linguistic analysis reveals that identical labels mask substantial heterogeneity: notes differ markedly in temporality (past vs. present vs. future orientation), negation (denied vs. affirmed ideation), and uncertainty (speculative vs. definitive language).
AI.conclusion: Clinical NLP researchers should critically examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth. The field must acknowledge that EHR-derived labels are products of sociotechnical and institutional processes, not neutral reflections of patient experience.

title: LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of $149$ sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.

AI.tldr: NRT-Bench evaluates LLM agents as operators of a simulated nuclear power plant under adaptive multi-turn adversarial attacks. Across four frontier models, 8.7–12.1% of attack sessions cause a critical safety function failure, with near-disjoint vulnerabilities across models. Defenses show model-dependent, sometimes counterproductive effects.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in safety-critical supervisory roles, but their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure is poorly understood. Existing red-teaming relies heavily on LLM-judged harm rather than objective safety signals, motivating a benchmark grounded in physical system safety.
AI.method: A five-role LLM agent team operates a simulated nuclear plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs). Adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is measured objectively: a run ends the moment any CSF is lost, with attribution to the causal message. Four frontier models are evaluated under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, testing both undefended and defended configurations.
AI.result: 8.7–12.1% of attack sessions result in CSF loss. The four models appear similarly robust by aggregate rate, but their failure cases barely overlap: of 149 total sessions, none defeat all four models while one-third defeat at least one. Defenses (guardrail stacks, safety-advisor agents) are strongly model-dependent—the same defense can lower attack success for one model yet raise it for another.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive multi-turn attacks can reliably push LLM-agent-operated safety-critical systems past safety limits. Near-disjoint failure modes across models indicate that ensemble or defense-in-depth strategies may not straightforwardly improve robustness. The benchmark and tooling are released for reproducible safety evaluation.

title: Thermodynamic Signatures of Reasoning: Free-Energy and Spectral-Form-Factor Diagnostics for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
summary: Hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) is deployment-critical, and recent work shows that the spectrum of attention-derived graph Laplacians carries strong signal about reasoning quality. Prior spectral diagnostics, however, summarize the Laplacian spectrum by a handful of eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, leaving most of its structure unused. We propose Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts its thermodynamic potentials partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity together with the random-matrix-theory (RMT) spectral form factor. We prove three results: (i)~Lipschitz stability of Fes under attention perturbation; (ii)~an expressiveness result showing that Fes enriches finite spectral summaries and approximates moment-derived spectral functionals under explicit regularity and grid-resolution assumptions; and (iii)~a finite-sample PAC bound on the AUROC of a training-free detector built from Fes. Empirically, across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, a lightweight probe on Fes descriptors achieves the strongest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by $+6.5$ AUROC points and over GoR-4 by $+2.4$ points on average, while requiring no update to the underlying LLM. In the fully unsupervised setting, an RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC $0.71$, providing a label-free but weaker detector. A complementary RMT analysis shows that correct generations exhibit more Wigner-Dyson like spectral statistics, whereas hallucinations exhibit more Poisson-like statistics. The anonymized code and config are provided in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats attention Laplacians as Hamiltonians and extracts thermodynamic potentials and random matrix theory (RMT) spectral form factors for hallucination detection in LLMs. Fes outperforms prior attention-spectral baselines by +6.5 AUROC over LapEig and +2.4 over GoR-4, with theoretical guarantees on stability, expressiveness, and PAC generalization bounds.
AI.motivation: Prior spectral diagnostics for hallucination detection summarize the Laplacian spectrum using only a few eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, discarding most structural information. The authors aim to exploit the full spectral structure of attention-derived graph Laplacians to build a richer, more discriminative descriptor.
AI.method: Free-Energy Signatures (Fes) treat each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extract thermodynamic potentials: partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity, and the RMT spectral form factor. A lightweight probe is trained on Fes descriptors. A fully unsupervised variant uses an RMT-deviation score. Theoretical contributions include: (i) Lipschitz stability under attention perturbation, (ii) expressiveness relative to finite spectral summaries, and (iii) a finite-sample PAC bound on AUROC for the training-free detector.
AI.result: Across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, the Fes-based probe achieves the highest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by +6.5 and over GoR-4 by +2.4 AUROC points on average. The unsupervised RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC 0.71. RMT analysis reveals that correct generations exhibit Wigner-Dyson statistics, while hallucinations exhibit Poisson-like statistics.
AI.conclusion: Fes provides a rich, stable, and theoretically grounded spectral descriptor for hallucination detection that requires no LLM updates, significantly outperforming prior attention-spectral methods. The thermodynamic and RMT perspective offers both practical detection gains and interpretable insights into the spectral signatures of hallucinated versus correct generations.

title: Your Mouse and Eyes Secretly Leak Your Preference: LLM Alignment using Implicit Feedback from Users
summary: To align a Large Language Model (LLM), most existing methods collect explicit human feedback and train a reward model to predict the human preference based on the response text. These existing methods have two key limitations. First, the users rarely provide explicit feedback for LLM responses, which makes the high-quality preference annotation expensive to collect. Second, the methods do not leverage implicit human feedback, which has proven vital to the economic moats of Internet giants. To quantify the value of implicit feedback, we build a new dataset called IFLLM, which collects 1336 multi-turn questions from the 59 Mechanical Turk workers, their mouse trajectories, and eye gazing points to the LLMs' responses from their webcams. IFLLM shows that the users have very diverse types of gazing behavior and mouse trajectories. Our reward model based on the implicit user feedback boosts the accuracy of the text-based reward model from 55% to 64% and nearly triples the relative response quality improvements after applying the DPO to eight LLMs, demonstrating the value of implicit feedback in the wild. Our data collection website, dataset, and codes can be found at https://github.com/themehulpatwari/llm-implicit-feedback/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IFLLM, a dataset capturing implicit human feedback (mouse trajectories, eye gaze) during LLM interactions, and demonstrates that incorporating such implicit signals into reward models significantly improves preference prediction accuracy and downstream LLM alignment via DPO compared to text-only reward models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM alignment methods rely on explicit human feedback, which is expensive and rarely provided by users in practice. Moreover, these methods ignore implicit feedback signals (e.g., gaze, mouse movement) — a resource that major Internet companies already leverage. The authors aim to quantify the value of such implicit feedback for LLM alignment.
AI.method: The authors construct the IFLLM dataset by collecting 1,336 multi-turn questions from 59 MTurk workers, along with mouse trajectories and webcam-based eye-gazing data as implicit feedback on LLM responses. They then train a reward model that fuses implicit behavioral signals with text-based preferences and evaluate it on preference prediction accuracy. Finally, they apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to eight LLMs using this reward model and measure relative response quality improvements.
AI.result: The IFLLM dataset reveals diverse patterns in users' gazing behavior and mouse trajectories. The implicit-feedback-augmented reward model improves preference prediction accuracy from 55% (text-only) to 64%. When used for DPO-based alignment across eight LLMs, it nearly triples the relative response quality improvements, demonstrating the practical value of implicit feedback in real-world settings.
AI.conclusion: Implicit human feedback — specifically mouse trajectories and eye gaze — provides a valuable and complementary signal for LLM alignment. Integrating these signals into reward models yields substantial gains in both preference prediction and downstream alignment quality, suggesting that implicit feedback should be a standard component of future alignment pipelines.

title: JAMER: Project-Level Code Framework Dataset and Benchmark on Professional Game Engines
summary: Current AI-driven game development has made substantial progress in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based game coding, yet project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains largely unexplored due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. We present JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine. Our key insight is that Game Jam competitions, community events where developers build complete games under tight time constraints, yield thousands of open-source projects suitable for this purpose. Building on the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode, we design a deterministic verification pipeline from file integrity to runtime behavior collection, distilling 8,133 verified projects from over 240,000 repositories. Of these, 300 manually verified projects form JamBench; the rest constitute JamSet. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated through a pipeline combining compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a capability cliff as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates dropping from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones (Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates yet yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating that the bottleneck lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. Experiments validate JamSet as effective training data. All data and code are publicly available.

AI.tldr: JamSet and JamBench are the first project-level game code dataset and benchmark built on the Godot engine, sourced from Game Jam competitions. The paper introduces a deterministic verification pipeline and evaluates frontier models, revealing a steep capability drop as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates falling from 80.4% to 5.7%. Code agents improve compilation but not behavioral quality, pinpointing architectural design as the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: While AI-driven game development has advanced in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based coding, project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains unexplored due to the lack of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. Game Jam competitions provide an untapped source of complete, open-source game projects suitable for this purpose.
AI.method: The authors collect over 240,000 repositories from Game Jam events, leveraging the Godot engine's text-based scene format and headless execution mode to build a deterministic verification pipeline that checks file integrity and runtime behavior. This yields 8,133 verified projects (JamSet), with 300 manually verified projects forming JamBench. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated via compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Nine frontier models and code agents are benchmarked.
AI.result: A capability cliff emerges as project scale increases: runtime pass rates drop from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones (Task2a). Code agents improve compilation rates but yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating the bottleneck is architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. JamSet is validated as effective training data.
AI.conclusion: Project-level game code generation on professional engines remains a formidable challenge for current AI models. The primary bottleneck is architectural design capability rather than code syntax. JamSet and JamBench provide foundational resources to advance research in this direction, with all data and code publicly released.

title: MiqraBERT: Regression-Based Sentence-BERT Finetuning for Biblical Hebrew Parallel Detection
summary: Textual reuse pervades the Hebrew Bible, yet the computational methods used to detect it still rest largely on lexical overlap, and they falter once a parallel involves paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. This paper introduces MiqraBERT, a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) for verse-level semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew. The training set comprises 1,650 labeled verse and half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels drawn from the Chronicles synoptic material and from foundational studies of poetic parallelism, balanced against 825 randomly sampled negatives. Through cosine-similarity regression, the model learns an embedding space in which parallel verses cluster together and unrelated verses move apart. We evaluate separation with distribution-based metrics, Wasserstein distance and the overlap coefficient, across ten random seeds. MiqraBERT improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from roughly 24% to about 6%. Narrative synoptic parallels reach a recall@10 of 87.1%; poetic parallels remain difficult, below 9%. This genre-dependent asymmetry confines the model's reliable scope to narrative textual reuse. MiqraBERT is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/davidmsmiley/MiqraBERT

AI.tldr: MiqraBERT is a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT for detecting semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew verse pairs. Trained on 1,650 labeled pairs (825 true parallels, 825 negatives), it improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the baseline and achieves 87.1% recall@10 on narrative synoptic parallels, though poetic parallels remain challenging (below 9% recall).
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods for detecting textual reuse in the Hebrew Bible rely primarily on lexical overlap and fail when parallels involve paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. A semantic rather than lexical approach is needed to capture these non-literal parallels.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) into a Sentence-BERT architecture called MiqraBERT. The training data consists of 1,650 verse and half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels sourced from Chronicles synoptic material and poetic parallelism studies, plus 825 randomly sampled negatives. Training uses cosine-similarity regression to learn an embedding space where parallel verses cluster together. Evaluation employs Wasserstein distance and overlap coefficient metrics across ten random seeds to measure distributional separation.
AI.result: MiqraBERT achieves a 2.7-fold improvement in distributional separation over the pre-trained baseline, reducing the ambiguous overlap region from ~24% to ~6%. On narrative synoptic parallels, recall@10 reaches 87.1%. However, poetic parallelism recall@10 remains below 9%, revealing a significant genre-dependent performance asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: MiqraBERT successfully captures narrative-level semantic textual reuse in Biblical Hebrew, substantially outperforming lexical-overlap baselines. The model's reliable scope is limited to narrative material, as poetic parallelism remains a difficult challenge due to its greater linguistic complexity. The model is publicly released on HuggingFace.

title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Predictive Validity for the Evaluation of LLM Agents
summary: Agent benchmarks are growing fast, but no single benchmark touches more than four or five of the dimensions that deployment exposes. This paper aggregates the largest coordinated deep-dive of one MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark to date: fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including a multi-modal visual extension), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. Consolidating those studies with seven prior agent benchmarks, we argue that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; recent public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct empirical evidence of this rank instability. We propose ranking configurations by predictive validity, the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, rather than in-sample mean, and report a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that exposes the deployment-relevant dimensions HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. The position is operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds; existing evidence partly supports it but is too thin to confirm. We close with a pre-registered pilot design and a field-level vision for what the next generation of agentic benchmarks should report.

AI.tldr: The paper aggregates 14 MCP-based industrial-agent benchmarks and 7 prior benchmarks to argue that aggregate-score leaderboards underspecify deployment-relevant evaluation. It proposes ranking by predictive validity (in-sample vs. out-of-sample rank correlation) over mean scores, introduces a 12-tier measurement apparatus, and provides falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with a pre-registered pilot design for next-generation agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current agent benchmarks are proliferating rapidly but each captures only 4-5 dimensions of real-world deployment. Aggregate-score leaderboards create a false sense of comprehensive evaluation, yet rankings derived from them fail to transfer to out-of-distribution settings. The authors seek to expose this underspecification and provide a more rigorous, deployment-relevant evaluation framework.
AI.method: The study conducts 14 parallel MCP-based industrial-agent implementation studies spanning new asset classes (multi-modal visual extension), orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation probes. These are consolidated with 7 prior benchmarks. The authors analyze rank instability through public-to-hidden competition retrospectives and propose predictive validity (in-sample/out-of-sample rank correlation) as an alternative metric. A 12-tier measurement apparatus is introduced to surface dimensions that frameworks like HELM collapse.
AI.result: Aggregate-score rankings exhibit significant rank instability when transferred to out-of-distribution settings, as evidenced by public-to-hidden competition retrospectives. The 12-tier measurement apparatus successfully exposes deployment-relevant dimensions that prior evaluation frameworks obscure. Three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds are proposed; existing evidence provides partial but insufficient support.
AI.conclusion: The field needs to move beyond aggregate-score leaderboards toward evaluation frameworks that prioritize predictive validity. The paper delivers a pre-registered pilot design and a vision for what next-generation agentic benchmarks should report, emphasizing deployment-relevant dimensions and out-of-distribution robustness as core evaluation criteria.

title: Multi-View Decompilation for LLM-Based Malware Classification
summary: Malware analysts often inspect compiled binaries through decompiled pseudo-C, when source code is unavailable. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can assist this process by classifying decompiled code as benign or malicious, but existing pipelines typically rely on a single decompiler view. We argue that this assumption is fragile: decompilers are lossy heuristic tools, and different decompilers can expose different artefacts of the same binary. We curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning a range of threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Across a range of LLMs from major model families, we find that providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses further show that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, supporting the view that decompiler outputs provide complementary evidence. Our results suggest that multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.

AI.tldr: Malware analysis using LLMs on decompiled code is improved by providing pseudo-C output from multiple decompilers (Ghidra and RetDec) rather than relying on a single decompiler, as different decompilers make partially different errors and offer complementary evidence.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based malware classification pipelines rely on a single decompiler view, which is fragile since decompilers are lossy heuristic tools. Different decompilers expose different artifacts of the same binary, and leveraging multiple views could improve classification robustness.
AI.method: The authors curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning diverse threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled using both Ghidra and RetDec, producing matched pseudo-C views. Multiple LLMs from major model families are evaluated on classifying these views, comparing single-decompiler vs. dual-decompiler prompting. Agreement analyses between decompiler outputs are also conducted.
AI.result: Providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1 across a range of LLMs, primarily by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses reveal that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, confirming that their outputs provide complementary evidence.
AI.conclusion: Multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free method to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings, suggesting that practitioners should incorporate multiple decompiler views rather than relying on a single tool.

title: FlexLAM: Resolving the Bottleneck Trade-off in Latent Action Learning
summary: Latent actions provide a compact interface between action-free video and downstream decision-making, yet existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck. We identify a bottleneck trade-off: overly tight codes can discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while overly loose codes preserve additional transition variation that must be resolved when alignment labels are scarce or narrowly distributed. FlexLAM replaces this fixed capacity with variable-length latent actions trained by nested dropout, yielding prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed, without new architectures or losses. A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and under a low-return single-task alignment stress test, indicating that FlexLAM is not merely adjustable at inference time but learns a better latent-action interface at the same token budgets. The same model supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining, and FlexLAM improves Ego4D transition reconstruction. These results suggest that variable-length latent actions are an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces.

AI.tldr: FlexLAM introduces variable-length latent actions via nested dropout, replacing fixed-capacity bottlenecks in Latent Action Models. This allows prefix-valid codes that capture essential transition structure first and add detail as needed, matching or surpassing fixed-capacity LAMs at every token budget without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck, creating a bottleneck trade-off: overly tight codes discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while overly loose codes preserve extraneous variation that is hard to resolve when alignment labels are scarce or narrowly distributed. The authors aim to resolve this trade-off without introducing new architectures or loss functions.
AI.method: FlexLAM replaces the fixed-capacity bottleneck with variable-length latent actions trained using nested dropout. This produces prefix-valid codes, where earlier bits capture compact transition structure and later bits add detail progressively. The approach requires no new architectures or losses and supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining.
AI.result: A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and a low-return single-task alignment stress test. FlexLAM also improves transition reconstruction on Ego4D and supports inference-time budget adjustment without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Variable-length latent actions serve as an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces. FlexLAM learns a fundamentally better latent-action interface at identical token budgets, not merely an adjustable one.

title: Repository-Level Solidity Code Generation with Large Language Models: From Prompting to Fine-Tuning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in general-purpose code generation, but their effectiveness in specialized software domains remains underexplored. Solidity smart contracts represent a high-stakes domain where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics remain insufficient for repository-level Solidity generation, where models must synthesize complete contracts from natural language requirements. To address this gap, we introduce SolidityBench, a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts paired with natural language descriptions. We also propose SolidityScore, a Solidity-aware semantic metric that emphasizes domain-critical constructs such as security modifiers, contract declarations, and Solidity-specific keywords. Using this benchmark, we evaluate representative code LLMs, including Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama, across zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and supervised fine-tuning. The results show that general-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, retrieval-augmented generation performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive benchmark for repository-level Solidity code generation and shows that high-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts.

AI.tldr: SolidityBench introduces a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts with natural language descriptions and SolidityScore, a domain-aware semantic metric. Evaluation of multiple LLMs across prompting strategies reveals that supervised fine-tuning with high-quality domain data yields the most reliable smart contract generation.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at general code generation but remain underexplored in specialized, high-stakes domains like Solidity smart contracts, where code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks are insufficient for repository-level generation.
AI.method: The authors introduce SolidityBench (5,470 repository-level contracts with NL descriptions) and SolidityScore (a semantic metric weighting Solidity-specific constructs like modifiers, contract declarations, and keywords). They evaluate Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama under zero-shot, Chain-of-Thought, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
AI.result: General-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. RAG performs best among non-parametric methods, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. SFT achieves the largest improvement by internalizing domain constraints into model parameters.
AI.conclusion: High-quality domain-specific data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated Solidity smart contracts. The benchmark and metric fill a critical evaluation gap for repository-level smart contract synthesis.

title: GLARE: A Natural Language Interface for Querying Global Explanations
summary: While global explanations are crucial for understanding vision models across datasets, classes, and decision contexts, their complex and monolithic nature often hinders practical exploration. Because users typically seek targeted answers to specific questions rather than static artifacts, we present an LLM-based interactive interface that provides natural language access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers. The system's core LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. This enables flexible aggregation without exposing users to low-level representations. For each query, the interface outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations, and intent-aligned visualizations. We evaluate the system on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Our results demonstrate that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based interactive interface that translates natural language questions into SQL queries over local explanation data, enabling flexible, accessible exploration of global explanations for black-box image classifiers with statistics-augmented responses and visualizations.
AI.motivation: Global explanations for vision models are crucial but complex and monolithic, hindering practical exploration. Users need targeted answers to specific questions rather than static explanation artifacts, yet existing global explanation methods lack flexible, natural language-based interactive access.
AI.method: The system uses an LLM as a mediator to translate natural language questions into structured SQL queries over aggregated local explanation data (e.g., LIME, SHAP). It outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses paired with intent-aligned visualizations, shielding users from low-level representation details.
AI.result: Evaluation across intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors demonstrated that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated natural language querying is an effective paradigm for making global explanations more accessible and usable, bridging the gap between monolithic explanation artifacts and the targeted, question-driven needs of human users in XAI contexts.

title: Image Encryption Algorithm Based on Convolutional Neural Networks and Dynamic S-Box Generation
summary: The paper proposes a dynamic approach to image encryption, combining the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and classical cryptography to improve the security and flexibility of image encryption. The main concept is to create adaptive Substitution boxes (S-boxes) based on characteristics that are learned by a trained CNN. The CNN-based S-boxes can be relied on for more non-linearity, uniqueness, and input image dependence than the conventional fixed S-boxes because they are susceptible to the linear and differential attacks. This dynamic behaviour enhances the confusion property and makes it more resistant to statistical and structural attacks. The encryption algorithm consists of CNN-based feature extraction and the creation of a personalised S-box to replace the pixels. Entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI enable security assessment of generated S-boxes based on the CNN, indicating that the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional ones.

AI.tldr: A dynamic image encryption method is proposed that uses CNN-learned features to generate adaptive, image-dependent S-boxes, replacing fixed classical S-boxes to enhance non-linearity and resistance to linear/differential attacks, with security validated through standard metrics.
AI.motivation: Traditional fixed S-boxes in image encryption are vulnerable to linear and differential cryptanalysis. The authors aim to introduce dynamism and input-dependence into the substitution step to strengthen the confusion property and resist statistical and structural attacks more effectively.
AI.method: A CNN is trained to extract features from the input image. These learned characteristics are then used to dynamically generate a personalized, adaptive S-box for that specific image. The encryption algorithm performs pixel substitution using this CNN-based S-box. Security is evaluated via entropy, histogram analysis, correlation coefficients, NPCR, and UACI.
AI.result: The CNN-generated S-boxes demonstrate high non-linearity, uniqueness, and input dependence. Security assessments (entropy, histogram, correlation, NPCR, UACI) indicate that the proposed scheme offers superior resilience and flexibility compared to traditional fixed S-box encryption methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining CNN-based feature extraction with classical cryptography to create adaptive S-boxes yields a more secure and flexible image encryption scheme, effectively mitigating vulnerabilities associated with static substitution boxes.

title: Spectral DPPs via NEPv: A Scalable Continuous Relaxation of Determinantal MAP for Diversity-Aware Data Selection
summary: Selecting a small, diverse, high-quality subset from a massive pool of candidates is a recurring primitive in modern machine learning -- data curation and coreset selection for training and fine-tuning large models, active-learning batch acquisition, prompt and exemplar selection for in-context learning, retrieval diversification, and experimental design. Determinantal Point Processes (\DPP s) give a principled, well-calibrated notion of diversity for this task, but their \emph{MAP} objective -- pick a size-$k$ subset $S$ maximizing $\logdet(L_S)$ -- is NP-hard, and the standard greedy and sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in the ground-set size $n$. This cost is prohibitive precisely in the data-centric regime where diversity matters most, where $n$ ranges over millions to billions of candidate examples, features, or embeddings. We recast \DPP-MAP as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, and show that its first-order optimality conditions form a \emph{Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency} (\NEPv) of a previously unstudied form. This \NEPv\ admits a self-consistent field (\SCF) iteration with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee, giving a principled iterative solver where the diversity objective drives an eigenvector-dependent operator. The resulting algorithm, \OurMethod, requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel and runs in time $O\!\big((ndk+nk^2)\,t\big)$ for a small number of iterations $t$, scaling near-linearly in $n$ and integrating directly with low-rank and feature-map kernels common in ML. This paper focuses on the relaxation, solver, and scaling analysis; full real-data benchmarking is left to a planned empirical study.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates NP-hard DPP MAP inference (subset selection maximizing log-determinant) as a continuous optimization over the Stiefel manifold, deriving a novel Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). An SCF-style iteration with spectral-gap contraction guarantees yields an algorithm (OurMethod) that runs in near-linear time O((ndk+nk²)·t), scaling to millions/billions of items.
AI.motivation: DPP MAP inference is the principled approach for diverse subset selection in modern ML (coreset construction, active learning, in-context example selection, retrieval diversification), but exact MAP is NP-hard, and standard greedy/sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in ground-set size n. When n reaches millions or billions — precisely where diversity matters most — these costs become prohibitive.
AI.method: The authors recast discrete DPP MAP (maximize logdet(L_S) over size-k subsets) as a continuous optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold. They derive first-order optimality conditions that take the form of a novel Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). This NEPv is solved via a self-consistent field (SCF) iteration, with a spectral-gap-based local convergence (contraction) guarantee. The method requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel matrix, avoiding full materialization.
AI.result: The resulting algorithm (OurMethod) achieves O((ndk + nk²)·t) time complexity for t iterations, scaling near-linearly in n. It integrates naturally with low-rank and feature-map kernels commonly used in ML. The paper provides the relaxation framework, solver derivation, and scaling analysis.
AI.conclusion: The continuous relaxation via Stiefel manifold optimization and the NEPv/SCF solver offers a principled, scalable approach to DPP MAP inference. The paper focuses on theoretical development; empirical benchmarking on real data is deferred to future work.

title: Beyond Static Endpoints: Tool Programs as an Interface for Flexible Agentic Web Services
summary: In the agentic web era, LLM-based agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, yet most interfaces remain \emph{static endpoints} that poorly express long-horizon workflows with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. We present ToolPro, which represents an agent's tool intent as an \emph{executable tool program} that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. ToolPro combines constraint-guided program construction, effect-aware replay for exactly-once state-modifying calls, and a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. We instantiate ToolPro over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing and evaluate it on diverse workflows of real-world applications. ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4\% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1\%, with larger gains under higher network latency and workflow complexity.

AI.tldr: ToolPro introduces executable tool programs that encode multi-step agent workflows (loops, conditionals, joins, retries) to replace static endpoint calls, reducing latency by up to 53.4% and client traffic by up to 96.1%.
AI.motivation: In the agentic web era, LLM agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, but most interfaces are static endpoints ill-suited for expressing long-horizon workflows involving loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. Stepwise calling across the network incurs high latency and bandwidth overhead.
AI.method: ToolPro represents agent tool intent as an executable tool program that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. It employs three key techniques: (1) constraint-guided program construction to synthesize valid programs, (2) effect-aware replay ensuring exactly-once execution for state-modifying calls, and (3) a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. The system is instantiated over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing.
AI.result: Evaluated on diverse real-world application workflows, ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1%, with larger gains observed under higher network latency and increased workflow complexity.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from stepwise API calling to executable tool programs substantially improves performance for agent-driven web service interactions, particularly in high-latency and complex workflow scenarios.

title: From 50K to 8.2 Million in 24 Hours: Vozinha's Algorithmic Consecration and the Multilingual Making of World Cup Visibility
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; v0.1 pilot preprint. Dataset and evidence package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20722235
summary: We present a multilingual computational discourse analysis of how language constructed the algorithmic consecration of Vozinha, the 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper, after Spain 0-0 Cape Verde at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The study contributes a multilingual corpus in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French; a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestion with human validation; and an analysis of cross-lingual narrative diffusion across discourse phases. We treat the platform follower count itself, narrated as "50k to 8M", as a linguistic object: a circulating and narratable proof of visibility rather than a mere measurement. The follower-growth timeline is used only as contextual metadata: we reconstruct a conservative phase structure, not a continuous API-native series, and type every datapoint by value class, confidence, and evidence type. The only exact primary scraper anchor is 8,235,652 followers at 2026-06-16 15:47 UTC; all other figures are reported as estimated ranges or thresholds, including an estimated pre-match baseline of 45k-56k. Findings suggest that distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese mobilization, Spanish crisis, English nation-making, and a shared platform-metric spectacle through which peripheral athletic performance became globally visible. As a v0.1 pilot, the paper releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline, while flagging full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement as planned work.

AI.tldr: A multilingual discourse analysis of how four languages framed the viral fame of Cape Verde's 40-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha after a 2026 World Cup draw against Spain, introducing a narrative frame taxonomy, annotation pipeline, and cross-lingual diffusion analysis while treating follower-count growth as a narratable linguistic object rather than mere metrics.
AI.motivation: To investigate how distinct linguistic communities construct algorithmic consecration—the transformation of peripheral athletic performance into global visibility through platform metrics—and to understand cross-lingual narrative diffusion, using the viral case of Vozinha's follower surge from ~50k to ~8M as a natural experiment.
AI.method: Construction of a multilingual corpus (Portuguese, Spanish, English, French); development of a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestions with human validation; conservative phase-structure reconstruction of the follower-growth timeline (not continuous API data), with each datapoint typed by value class, confidence, and evidence type; cross-lingual frame distribution analysis across discourse phases.
AI.result: Distinct languages carried distinct dominant frames: Portuguese mobilized around national pride, Spanish centered on crisis narratives, English framed the event as nation-making, and all languages participated in a shared platform-metric spectacle. The follower count itself functioned as a circulating, narratable proof of visibility across all four languages.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that algorithmic consecration is linguistically mediated: the same platform event is narratively constructed differently across languages, with platform metrics serving as a shared spectacle. As a v0.1 pilot, the paper releases schema, taxonomy, guidelines, and timeline, with full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement planned as future work.

title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
summary: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, yet its black-box nature remains a key roadblock to deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools, such as Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), are ill-equipped for NCO, whose decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary definition. To close this gap, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), to our knowledge, the first framework for interpreting NCO policies by distilling black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios. EPB employs an LLM to autonomously evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. EPB works through an iterative framework: Block I fixes program bank capacity and introduces a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme that couples numerical gradients for student router updates and textual gradients for LLM-based program revision; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate EPB's effectiveness and broad applicability, where the distilled program portfolios largely match original performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

AI.tldr: EPB introduces a framework that distills black-box neural combinatorial optimization models into interpretable, human-readable program portfolios using LLM-driven program evolution with hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent and adaptive capacity management.
AI.motivation: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) models achieve strong performance but suffer from a black-box nature that hinders deployment and scientific understanding. Existing interpretability tools like Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) fail for NCO because NCO decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack a predefined concept vocabulary.
