AI.method: EPB uses an LLM to evolve a bank of programs, each serving as a bottleneck via per-step action distributions. The framework operates in two blocks: Block I uses a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent — numerical gradients update a student router, while textual gradients guide LLM-based program revision, all under fixed capacity. Block II dynamically adjusts bank capacity through fault-targeted expansion (adding programs for weak cases) and redundancy pruning (removing overlapping programs).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that distilled program portfolios largely match the original NCO model performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as compositions of classic heuristic variants.
AI.conclusion: EPB advances interpretable NCO and establishes itself as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models, bridging the gap between high-performing black-box models and human-understandable reasoning.

title: Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on language-model components to interpret instructions, process external data, invoke tools, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks more consequential, especially as attackers adopt model-guided automation to scale probing, prompt refinement, and response evaluation. This work analyzes the resulting attack-defense setting through a probabilistic model of a target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. Our analysis shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses can allow attacker success rate (ASR) to approach one as the query budget grows, since predictable refusals provide useful feedback to automated search. We then examine detect-and-misdirect, where detected malicious interactions receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge. This strategy reduces the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates and yields a bounded asymptotic ASR. We evaluate a proof-of-concept realization of this strategy through Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), a lightweight conversational misdirection method designed to replace predictable refusal text with safe but strategically misleading responses in automated jailbreak settings. On jailbreak benchmarks, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the security of agentic AI systems against automated prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks. It shows conventional detect-and-block defenses fail because predictable refusals provide feedback that lets automated search achieve near-100% attack success. The authors propose "detect-and-misdirect" — returning controlled misleading responses to degrade the attacker's judge — and implement Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), which reduces attack success rates by up to two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems that use language models to interpret instructions, invoke tools, and coordinate with other agents are increasingly vulnerable to prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks. Attackers now use model-guided automation to scale probing, making conventional defenses insufficient. The key insight driving this work is that predictable refusal responses in detect-and-block defenses actually leak information that automated attackers can exploit to converge toward successful attacks given sufficient query budget.
AI.method: The authors first develop a probabilistic model of the attack-defense setting, modeling the target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. Using this model, they formally analyze conventional detect-and-block defenses and prove that attack success rate (ASR) approaches 1 as query budget grows. They then propose "detect-and-misdirect," which returns controlled, non-operational responses to detected malicious interactions, designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge and reduce the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates. They implement this via Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), a lightweight conversational method that replaces predictable refusals with safe but strategically misleading responses. Evaluation uses jailbreak benchmarks and end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows detect-and-block yields ASR → 1 with sufficient queries, while detect-and-misdirect bounds ASR asymptotically below 1. Empirically, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude on jailbreak benchmarks and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.
AI.conclusion: Predictable refusal-based defenses are fundamentally inadequate against automated adversarial search. The detect-and-misdirect paradigm, instantiated via CMPE, offers a principled alternative that bounds attacker success by degrading the attacker's own evaluation loop rather than merely blocking individual attempts.

title: Spectral Retrieval-Augmented Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting leverages historical patterns to predict future values, but traditional methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-stationary patterns that are difficult to memorize during training. Retrieval-augmented approaches have emerged as promising solutions by retrieving similar historical patterns to enhance predictions. However, existing retrieval methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: spectral blindness, which overlooks critical frequency-domain characteristics that capture underlying periodic structures, and temporal recency, which treats all historical data equally without emphasizing recent, more relevant patterns. In this paper, we propose SpecReTF, a novel retrieval method that addresses these issues by converting time series into windowed frequency representations, measuring similarity with a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information. To balance recency and historical context, we apply an exponential moving average weighting scheme that emphasizes recent windows. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SpecReTF outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy across diverse, non-stationary time series.

AI.tldr: SpecReTF introduces a retrieval-augmented time series forecasting method that uses windowed frequency-domain representations (amplitude + phase similarity) with exponential moving average recency weighting, outperforming time-domain retrieval baselines on non-stationary benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) spectral blindness — they operate in the time domain and fail to capture frequency-domain periodic structures essential for non-stationary series; (2) temporal recency neglect — they treat all historical windows equally, ignoring that more recent patterns are often more predictive.
AI.method: SpecReTF converts time series into windowed frequency representations (via spectral transforms). Similarity between query and historical windows is measured using a combined metric that jointly captures amplitude and phase information. An exponential moving average (EMA) weighting scheme is applied to emphasize temporally recent windows when aggregating retrieved patterns for forecasting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that SpecReTF consistently outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy on diverse, non-stationary time series.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating spectral representations and recency-aware weighting significantly improves retrieval-augmented time series forecasting. SpecReTF provides a more robust approach for handling complex, non-stationary patterns that traditional time-domain retrieval methods fail to capture.

title: When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents
summary: As LLM agents increasingly select tools autonomously, their choices among tools with different privileges become safety-relevant. However, prior tool-selection studies focus on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices underexplored. To address this gap, we study over-privileged tool selection, in which an agent selects or escalates to a higher-privilege tool despite a sufficient lower-privilege alternative. We introduce ToolPrivBench to evaluate whether agents choose higher-privilege tools despite sufficient lower-privilege alternatives, measuring both initial selection and escalation after transient tool failures. Across eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, we find that over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is further amplified by transient failures. We further find that general safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice, while prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. We therefore introduce a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary. Our mitigation experiments show that this defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

AI.tldr: LLM agents frequently select over-privileged tools when lower-privilege alternatives suffice, especially after transient failures. Standard safety alignment and prompt controls fail to mitigate this. A privilege-aware post-training defense significantly reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain autonomous tool-selection capabilities, safety hinges on whether they choose tools with appropriate privilege levels. Prior work focuses on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, ignoring whether agents unnecessarily escalate to higher-privilege tools. This gap motivates studying "over-privileged tool selection."
AI.method: The authors introduce ToolPrivBench, a benchmark spanning eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, measuring both initial tool selection and escalation after transient tool failures. They evaluate mainstream LLM agents, test general safety alignment transfer, assess prompt-level controls, and propose a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary.
AI.result: Over-privileged tool selection is prevalent among mainstream LLM agents and is amplified by transient failures. General safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege choices, and prompt-level controls offer only limited mitigation under transient failures. The proposed privilege-aware post-training defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use.
AI.conclusion: Over-privileged tool selection is a significant and underexplored safety issue for autonomous LLM agents. A targeted privilege-aware post-training defense effectively addresses this without degrading general agent capabilities, highlighting the need for specialized safety mechanisms beyond general alignment.

title: SAGE-OPD: Selective Agent-Guided Intervention for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves student models by training them on trajectories induced by their own policy, making it a promising approach for mitigating exposure bias in agent training. However, most OPD studies focus on single-turn settings, while realistic LLM agents interact with environments over multiple turns. In this regime, early errors can alter future observations and compound across the trajectory, and standard dense token-level OPD becomes brittle, as it may over-penalize semantically valid alternatives, reinforce local degeneracies such as repeated actions, and propagate unreliable teacher supervision on off-distribution histories. We propose SAGE-OPD, a verifier-free selective intervention framework specifically designed for multi-turn OPD. Instead of applying teacher supervision uniformly across all turns, SAGE-OPD first observes environment feedback and uses teacher judgment to decide whether each student response should be skipped or intervened on. To further address compounding errors, SAGE-OPD weights token-level distillation by teacher confidence, reducing the influence of uncertain teacher distributions on corrupted or ambiguous histories. Finally, SAGE-OPD applies loss normalization to preserve the overall loss scale of standard OPD while retaining selective turn-level weighting. Experiments on agent tasks show that SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies further demonstrate that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization provide complementary benefits. Our results suggest that effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision should be selectively allocated to turns where intervention is necessary and reliable.

AI.tldr: SAGE-OPD introduces a selective intervention framework for multi-turn on-policy distillation that decides when to apply teacher supervision based on environment feedback, weights token-level distillation by teacher confidence, and normalizes loss to preserve training scale — achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement on ALFWorld over standard OPD.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) fails in multi-turn LLM agent settings because dense token-level supervision becomes brittle: early errors compound across turns, semantically valid alternatives get over-penalized, local degeneracies like repeated actions are reinforced, and teacher supervision becomes unreliable on off-distribution histories.
AI.method: SAGE-OPD is a verifier-free framework with three components: (1) turn-level selective intervention — using environment feedback and teacher judgment to decide whether to skip or intervene on each student response; (2) teacher confidence weighting — scaling token-level distillation loss by teacher confidence to reduce influence of uncertain supervision on corrupted/ambiguous histories; (3) loss normalization — preserving the overall loss scale of standard OPD while incorporating selective turn-level weighting.
AI.result: On agent tasks, SAGE-OPD consistently outperforms baselines, achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablations confirm that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization each provide complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision must be selectively allocated only to turns where intervention is both necessary and reliable.

title: A Comparative Study of Pretrained Transformer Models for Quranic ASR: Speech Representations, Label Formats, and Dataset Composition
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to International Journal of Speech Technology
summary: Quran Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) aims to convert Quranic recitation into text, enabling applications such as aided memorisation tools and Quranic search engines. However, existing ASR models often exhibit high Word Error Rates (WER) on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models for Quranic ASR, using advanced speech feature extraction methods: Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R. These models apply self-supervised learning by masking portions of input audio and using Transformer architectures to learn context-aware speech features. The pretrained models are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. Through comprehensive ablation studies across feature extractors, output label formats, training strategies, and clip durations, we identify the key factors that affect transcription accuracy in this domain. Our best-performing configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting, representing roughly a five-percentage-point gain over the Citrinet baseline (WER = 0.163) while reducing combined-model training time from 140 hours to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models to extract deeper speech feature representations for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates fine-tuning strategies for Transformer-based self-supervised speech models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on Quranic ASR, achieving a best WER of 0.08–0.11 across test sets, outperforming a Citrinet baseline by roughly 5 percentage points while significantly reducing training time.
AI.motivation: Existing Quranic ASR systems suffer from high Word Error Rates on user-recited verses and incomplete coverage of the Quranic corpus. There is a need for a systematic empirical study identifying optimal fine-tuning configurations—feature extractors, label formats, training strategies, and clip durations—to improve transcription accuracy in this domain.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune three pretrained Transformer-based self-supervised speech models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. They conduct comprehensive ablation studies varying feature extractors, output label formats (with/without diacritics), training strategies, and audio clip durations. Performance is benchmarked against a Citrinet baseline on EveryAyah and EveryAyah+Tarteel test sets.
AI.result: The best configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on EveryAyah and 0.11 on EveryAyah+Tarteel, representing roughly a five-percentage-point improvement over the Citrinet baseline (WER=0.163). Combined-model training time is reduced from 140 to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall speech representation.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning of self-supervised Transformer speech models significantly outperforms prior baselines for Quranic ASR. Key practical insights include using non-diacritized Arabic text and the XLS-R feature extractor. Future directions involve improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

title: A-COMPASS: Formal Foundations for Anonymity Analysis in Microdata
summary: In the information age, one of the leading problems is how to ensure individual's privacy. Depending on the context in which privacy is considered, various data privacy models have emerged. However, the domain of formal verification of these models is still not sufficiently explored even when it comes to the most basic models. An attempt to verify privacy requirements is the Compliance Assertion Language (COMPASS). In COMPASS, one can specify an anonymity condition that a table needs to satisfy, and an action that will modify the table if the condition is not satisfied. It is designed to operate on preprocessed tables in a form one record - one group of people. In this paper, we modify the COMPASS language in order to operate on microdata tables in their usual form of one record - one person. The modified language is called A-COMPASS. Along with checking of previously applied anonymity conditions, A-COMPASS enables the execution of anonymization actions as a new feature. We further provide the syntax and the semantics for the A-COMPASS language. We also prove the most important properties of the introduced semantics like determinism and compositionality. Finally, we provide a mechanism to verify anonymity properties, such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces A-COMPASS, a modified version of the COMPASS language that operates on standard microdata tables (one record per person) rather than preprocessed grouped tables. It adds anonymization action execution as a new feature, provides formal syntax and semantics, proves key properties (determinism, compositionality), and enables verification of anonymity properties like k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of data privacy models remains underexplored, even for basic models. The existing COMPASS language operates on preprocessed tables (one record–one group), which limits its applicability to real-world microdata. There is a need for a language that can directly handle standard microdata tables while also executing anonymization actions, not just checking conditions.
AI.method: The authors modify the COMPASS language to create A-COMPASS, which operates on microdata tables in the standard one record–one person format. They define the formal syntax and semantics of A-COMPASS, prove semantic properties (determinism and compositionality), and develop a mechanism for verifying anonymity properties such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.result: A-COMPASS successfully extends COMPASS to handle microdata tables in one record–one person form. The language supports both checking previously applied anonymity conditions and executing anonymization actions. The semantics are proven to be deterministic and compositional. The verification mechanism for k-anonymity and l-diversity is provided.
AI.conclusion: A-COMPASS advances formal verification of privacy models by adapting COMPASS to real-world microdata formats and adding action execution capabilities. The formal semantics and proven properties establish a sound foundation for verifying anonymity guarantees in data publishing scenarios.

title: Does Text Actually Help? Uncovering and Resolving Text Collapse in Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal time series forecasting, which pairs numerical sequences with domain-relevant textual reports, promises to inject world knowledge into forecasting pipelines. However, we uncover a critical failure mode in existing frameworks that we term text collapse: the text branch converges to a content-independent transformation, contributing negligible discriminative signal regardless of the input description. We argue that text collapse is a consequence of a fundamental asymmetry in time series forecasting: the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while the text branch, despite carrying complementary and often critical information, is insufficiently utilized, leading to its systematic underexploitation. To address this, we propose \textbf{REST-TS} (\textbf{R}esidual-\textbf{E}xclusive \textbf{S}upervision for \textbf{T}ext in \textbf{T}ime \textbf{S}eries), which turns the asymmetry into a design principle: the numerical backbone produces its own independent numerical forecast, and the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual, the prediction gap that numbers cannot explain. Because no numerical pathway can reduce these losses, the text branch must extract genuine content from the input description. Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that supervising the text branch on the residual compels it to extract genuine content from the input.

AI.tldr: Existing multimodal time series forecasting suffers from "text collapse," where the text branch learns a content-independent transform. REST-TS solves this by forcing the text branch to exclusively predict the residual between the numerical forecast and ground truth, compelling genuine text utilization.
AI.motivation: Multimodal time series forecasting pairs numerical data with textual reports to inject world knowledge, but current frameworks exhibit "text collapse" — the text branch degenerates into a content-independent function that adds no discriminative value. This stems from a fundamental asymmetry: numerical inputs are strongly autocorrelated with outputs (making the numerical backbone dominant), while the text branch is systematically underexploited despite carrying complementary information.
AI.method: REST-TS (Residual-Exclusive Supervision for Text in Time Series): The numerical backbone produces its own independent forecast, and the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured residual — i.e., the prediction gap that the numerical model alone cannot explain. Since no numerical pathway can reduce these residual-targeted losses, the text branch must extract genuine semantic content from the input description. This transforms the asymmetry from a weakness into a design principle.
AI.result: REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures. It consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing multimodal forecasting frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that exclusive residual supervision compels the text branch to extract meaningful content from textual inputs.
AI.conclusion: The asymmetry in multimodal time series forecasting — where numerical inputs dominate due to autocorrelation — can be addressed by exclusively supervising the text branch on the structured residual. This forces genuine cross-modal utilization and yields SOTA results, validating REST-TS as an effective design principle.

title: The Correctness Illusion in LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, LNCS format. Companion papers to follow on arXiv next week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary: Benchmarks for LLM-generated GPU kernels (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) score correctness through fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks. The number of inputs varies between benchmarks. The shape, dtype, and tolerance are fixed for each kernel. We test that oracle empirically. We construct a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels (15 correct controls and 9 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors) and re-evaluate it under op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The seeded oracle flags 9 of 9 buggy kernels and passes 15 of 15 correct controls, at zero precision cost on controls. We extend the corpus to 26 ops (adding a flash-attention pair) and re-run the same protocol on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). The verdicts are identical across all five GPUs: 10 of 10 illusions caught and 16 of 16 controls clean. The corpus result is about LLM-style transcription bugs that the allclose-on-one-shape oracle certifies as correct, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM. Every flagged failure replays byte-for-byte from a stored seed.

AI.tldr: Existing GPU kernel benchmarks use fixed-shape, small-sample allclose checks that miss LLM-style transcription bugs. The authors propose a seeded fuzzing protocol with high-precision CPU references and per-operation absolute tolerances, demonstrating it catches 9/9 buggy kernels that fixed-shape oracles pass, while maintaining zero false positives on 15 correct controls. Results replicate identically across five GPU classes.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) validate LLM-generated GPU kernels using allclose-style checks with fixed shapes, dtypes, and tolerances on small input samples. This approach risks certifying buggy kernels as correct—particularly "illusions" where transcription errors survive narrow validation. The authors aim to expose this evaluation gap and provide a more rigorous alternative.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled corpus of 24 kernels (15 correct controls, 9 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors). They then re-evaluate using op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing: shape-and-dtype-aware input generation, an fp64 CPU reference implementation, and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The protocol is extended to 26 ops (adding flash-attention) and tested on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL)
AI.result: The seeded oracle catches 9/9 buggy kernels and passes 15/15 correct controls (zero false positives, zero false negatives). With the extended 26-op corpus, results replicate identically across all five GPUs: 10/10 illusions caught, 16/16 controls clean. Every flagged failure is byte-for-byte reproducible from a stored seed.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-shape, small-sample allclose checks are insufficient for validating LLM-generated GPU kernels; they systematically miss transcription-style bugs. Schema-aware seeded fuzzing with high-precision CPU references provides a strict, reproducible, and GPU-agnostic correctness standard with no precision cost on correct kernels.

title: CacheWeaver: Cache-Aware Evidence Ordering for Efficient Grounded RAG Inference
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding, but it also lengthens prompts and raises prefill cost. Prefix caching in serving engines such as vLLM reduces this cost only when requests share the same token prefix. In grounded generation, however, adjacent queries may retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders, so set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap. We present CacheWeaver, a lightweight prompt-layer method for cache-aware evidence ordering. The method keeps a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences and uses a greedy walk to place the most reusable prefix first, while leaving the serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged. Across three vLLM configurations, the method lowers median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by about 20-33 percent relative to retrieval-order prefix caching, without hurting answer quality in our QA tests. The greedy policy reaches 97.5 percent of the median TTFT gain from oracle ordering, indicating that most reusable prefix locality can be recovered by a simple scheduling layer between retrieval and inference.

AI.tldr: CacheWeaver is a lightweight prompt-layer method that reorders retrieved evidence sequences to maximize prefix cache reuse in RAG systems, reducing time-to-first-token by 20–33% without degrading answer quality.
AI.motivation: RAG improves factual accuracy but increases prompt length and prefill cost. Existing prefix caching (e.g., vLLM) only works when requests share identical token prefixes. In grounded generation, overlapping evidence across queries often arrives in different orders, preventing set overlap from translating into reusable prefix overlap. The goal is to recover this lost cache locality without modifying the serving engine or the retrieved evidence set.
AI.method: CacheWeaver maintains a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences. When a new query retrieves evidence, a greedy walk algorithm reorders the evidence chunks so that the longest matching prefix with cached sequences appears first, maximizing prefix cache hits. This operates as a thin scheduling layer between retrieval and inference, leaving the underlying serving engine and retrieved evidence unchanged.
AI.result: Across three vLLM configurations, CacheWeaver reduced median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by approximately 20–33% relative to retrieval-order prefix caching. The greedy policy achieved 97.5% of the median TTFT gain of an oracle ordering, demonstrating near-optimal recovery of prefix locality.
AI.conclusion: Most reusable prefix locality in RAG workloads can be recovered by a simple, cache-aware evidence scheduling layer. CacheWeaver shows that reordering evidence sequences is a practical, low-overhead approach to improving inference efficiency without compromising generation quality.

title: Benchmarking Agentic Review Systems
summary: A new class of agentic review systems are emerging as a remedy to the pressure placed on peer review systems by AI-assisted research, but it is unclear how they should be evaluated. We evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview and coarse), one proprietary system (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline, across six LLMs spanning frontier and efficient models. First, we study whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers track with papers' quality as approximated by external signals such as citations and acceptance decisions. Every system performs above chance in pairwise accuracy, and the best is OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 at 83.0%. Second, to test whether systems can catch errors with known ground truth, we construct a perturbation benchmark that injects four categories of errors into papers across eight arXiv subject classes and measure detection recall. The strongest configuration (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) catches 71.6% of injected errors, leaving substantial room for improvement. The union of detections across six models reaches 83.3% recall, suggesting different models detect different errors and better harness design can potentially increase performance. Beyond these benchmarks, we study a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users. Votes on its comments skew positive at 1.44 to 1, and the most common complaints are about false positives and minor nitpicks. Together, by evaluating full review systems backed by state-of-the-art models on real research papers, we show that while AI reviews still have room for improvement, they can already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive feedback from real users.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates AI-based peer review systems by testing their ability to predict paper quality (via citation/acceptance signals) and detect injected errors. The best system (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) achieves 83% pairwise accuracy on quality tracking and 71.6% error recall. A multi-model union reaches 83.3% recall. A public deployment shows positive user reception (1.44:1 upvote ratio), with complaints focused on false positives and nitpicking.
AI.motivation: The rapid rise of AI-assisted research is straining traditional peer review. While agentic AI review systems are emerging as a potential solution, there is no established framework for evaluating their effectiveness. This paper aims to fill that gap by systematically assessing both open-source and proprietary AI review systems.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three review systems (OpenAIReview, coarse, Reviewer3) plus a zero-shot baseline across six LLMs. Evaluation proceeds along three axes: (1) pairwise accuracy tests on ICLR/NeurIPS papers using external quality signals (citations, acceptance decisions); (2) a perturbation benchmark injecting four error types into papers across eight arXiv categories and measuring detection recall; (3) a real-world public deployment study collecting user votes and qualitative feedback on AI-generated reviews.
AI.result: All systems beat chance on pairwise quality assessment, with OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 leading at 83.0% accuracy. On error detection, the same configuration achieves 71.6% recall. The union of all six models reaches 83.3% recall, indicating complementary error detection capabilities. In the public deployment, user votes skew positive at 1.44:1, with false positives and minor nitpicks as the main complaints.
AI.conclusion: AI review systems, when backed by state-of-the-art models, already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive user feedback. However, substantial room for improvement remains, particularly in boosting recall and reducing false positives. Better ensemble/harness designs could further close the gap.

title: Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing the Limits of Fine-Tuning LLMs for Vulnerability Detection in Systems Software
summary: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. We present CWE-Trace, a framework for LLM vulnerability detection built from 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs. The framework enforces a strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical set / post-cutoff leakage-free set), preserves context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs, and introduces two diagnostic metrics: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). We evaluate eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification. Our analysis yields two key results. First, data contamination provides no measurable advantage. Function-level analysis shows that 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal: vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped across datasets, and ~31% of contaminated samples carry CWE misclassification. Second, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning. Models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes (DFI ranging from -85.5 to +94.8 pp) that persist from historical to post-cutoff data and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy. This is calibration without comprehension: output distributions adapt to training data while the underlying security reasoning remains absent. The weakest backbone at binary detection (DeepSeek-R1) gains the most in coarse CWE classification, revealing that detection and understanding are decoupled capabilities. The best detection score reaches only 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE ranking remains below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy, confirming that current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: CWE-Trace evaluates LLM vulnerability detection using 834 curated Linux kernel samples with strict temporal splits and novel diagnostic metrics. Results show data contamination provides no measurable advantage, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning (calibration without comprehension), and even the best models barely exceed chance (52.1% detection, <1.3% Top-1 CWE accuracy), confirming LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software.
AI.motivation: Unresolved question: do LLMs that score well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security, or do they merely pattern-match on contaminated training data? Existing benchmarks fail to disentangle these explanations.
AI.method: CWE-Trace framework: 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples covering 74 CWEs, with strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical vs. post-cutoff leakage-free), context-aware vulnerable-patched pairs, and two novel diagnostic metrics — Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). Evaluated 8 vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification tasks.
AI.result: (1) Data contamination gives no measurable advantage: 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal; ~31% have CWE misclassification. (2) Backbone directional priors dominate: models show stable, systematic failure modes (DFI -85.5 to +94.8 pp) persisting across splits, resisting correction via fine-tuning. Fine-tuning shifts output thresholds but not decision policies — calibration without comprehension. Detection and CWE classification are decoupled capabilities (weakest detector gains most in classification). Best detection: 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); Top-1 CWE accuracy <1.3%.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software regardless of fine-tuning strategy. Benchmark contamination fears are overstated; the deeper problem is fundamental absence of comprehension rather than data leakage.

title: MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents
summary: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 77.1\% exact match accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases accuracy to 80.5\% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

AI.tldr: MortarBench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs on mortgage loan origination tasks. Current SOTA models perform poorly (max 77.1% accuracy) and exhibit bias against non-English names. The authors propose CRIT, a confidence calibration framework that boosts accuracy to 80.5% while mitigating bias and improving risk management.
AI.motivation: Firms are increasingly deploying mortgage loan agents powered by LLMs to assist human loan officers, yet no public benchmark exists to evaluate their performance, fairness, or reliability. This lack of standardized evaluation risks deploying biased, inaccurate systems in a high-stakes financial domain.
AI.method: The authors introduce MortarBench, a benchmark built on a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline that generates realistic, distribution-matched examples with broad edge-case coverage. They evaluate SOTA LLMs on exact-match accuracy and probe for systematic biases (particularly regarding non-English names). To address observed weaknesses, they propose CRIT, a confidence calibration framework designed to improve accuracy, steering of risk management decisions, and fairness.
AI.result: Closed-source SOTA LLMs achieve at most 77.1% exact-match accuracy on MortarBench. Systematic biases against applicants with non-English names were discovered. CRIT improves accuracy to 80.5% while simultaneously enhancing risk management steering and reducing the identified biases.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are insufficiently reliable for autonomous loan origination, exhibiting both accuracy limitations and harmful demographic biases. The CRIT framework demonstrates that confidence calibration can partially address these issues, yielding measurable improvements in accuracy, fairness, and risk management.

title: Learning Critical Testing Literacy Through Puzzles: an Experience Report
summary:
In this paper, we report our experiences and takeaways from workshops using puzzles to learn CTL.
  Background: Software testing is important yet difficult to teach. We introduced a BoK of puzzle-based learning activities to teach CTL, based on a model of critical tester's cognition, leading to the pedagogical framework P4TEST. We conducted thirteen workshops with students, testers, teachers, and primary school pupils to assess puzzle-based teaching of critical testing literacy.
  Experience: Across eleven workshops, we used a semi-structured approach, varying puzzles, materials, and timing. In two additional workshops, we introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to gather more data on the learning experience.
  Observations: Participants consistently perceived themselves as experimenting while solving puzzles. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were visible in behaviour but hard to surface through written reflection alone. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate reasoning; written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive reflection. The theme Sensemaking / reflection-in-action captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
  Reflections: Puzzles are not the intervention: the entire sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is. Designing that sequence more deliberately is the work ahead. We also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to customise workshops.

AI.tldr: The paper reports on thirteen workshops using puzzle-based learning to teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL). Key findings: participants experienced puzzle-solving as experimentation; students converged on solutions while professionals explored further; emotions were visible in behavior but not in written reflections; think-aloud sessions captured immediate reasoning while written reflections elicited meta-cognition. The authors conclude the full sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting — not puzzles alone — constitutes the intervention.
AI.motivation: Software testing is important but pedagogically challenging to teach. The authors aim to assess whether puzzle-based learning activities, grounded in a model of critical tester's cognition and the P4TEST pedagogical framework, can effectively teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL) across diverse learner populations.
AI.method: The authors conducted thirteen workshops with students, professional testers, teachers, and primary school pupils. Eleven workshops used a semi-structured design varying puzzles, materials, and timing. Two additional workshops introduced workbooks and think-aloud protocols to gather richer data on the learning experience. Data was collected through observation, written reflections, and verbal protocols.
AI.result: Participants consistently framed puzzle-solving as experimentation. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring alternative paths. Emotions were behaviorally observable but rarely surfaced in written reflections. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate, in-the-moment reasoning; written reflections prompted deeper meta-cognitive reflection. The central theme of "Sensemaking / reflection-in-action" captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
AI.conclusion: Puzzles alone are not the intervention — the integrated sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is what drives learning. Future work lies in deliberately designing this full sequence. The authors also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to support customizable workshops.

title: Code-Switching Reveals Language Anchoring in Multilingual LLMs
summary: Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to handle Code-Switched (CS) inputs, yet mixing languages frequently degrades performance relative to source- or target-language monolingual counterparts. To understand this degradation, we use grammar-forced CS as a controlled diagnostic setting for locating CS representations relative to their source and target counterparts. We introduce Anchor Bias, a geometric measure that quantifies language anchoring, whether a CS hidden state aligns closer to its source or target language counterpart. Across diverse MLLMs, Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS stays source-anchored, whereas target-framed CS shifts target-ward and shows larger Question Answering (QA) degradation. Motivated by this representational pattern, we propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a source-side canvas from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during prefill. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across MLLMs and CS conditions, showing that internal anchoring signals provide an actionable target for mitigating CS inference failures.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why multilingual LLMs degrade on code-switched inputs, introduces "Anchor Bias" to measure whether hidden states align closer to source or target language, discovers a grammar-frame effect, and proposes CANVAS — an inference-time steering method that recovers QA performance by pulling target-language states toward source anchors.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs suffer performance degradation on code-switched inputs compared to monolingual inputs, but the underlying representational mechanisms causing this degradation are poorly understood. The authors aim to diagnose where CS representations sit in the model's representational space and leverage that understanding to mitigate failures.
AI.method: (1) Grammar-forced code-switching is used as a controlled diagnostic framework. (2) Anchor Bias is introduced as a geometric measure quantifying whether a CS hidden state is closer to its source-language or target-language monolingual counterpart. (3) CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering) is proposed as an inference-time intervention: it extracts a "source canvas" from the source-language portion of the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward that source anchor during the prefill phase.
AI.result: Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect across diverse MLLMs: source-framed CS remains source-anchored, while target-framed CS shifts toward the target and exhibits greater QA degradation. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across models and CS conditions.
AI.conclusion: Internal anchoring signals provide an actionable target for mitigating CS inference failures. The grammar-frame effect explains when and why CS degradation occurs, and CANVAS demonstrates that realigning representations at inference time is a viable remedy.

title: Grounded Inference: Principles for Deterministically Encapsulated Generative Models
summary: The incorporation of generative models into traditional computational systems presents both enormous opportunity and tremendous peril. Although many early adopters have realized these perils at great expense, the field still requires foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems. This manuscript establishes this foundation through the definition of four specific primitives of AI blended architecture, designed to enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models. It further establishes two overarching anti-patterns broadly represented across industry to serve as warnings for engineers in this field. This framework was designed to enable successful integration of AI into traditional systems while providing a foundation upon which generative model providers could build the next generation of generative model interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a foundational framework for integrating generative AI into traditional deterministic computing systems by defining four architectural primitives and two anti-patterns, aiming to de-risk AI adoption and guide next-generation model interfaces.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread industry adoption of generative models, many early adopters have suffered costly failures. The field lacks foundational architectural frameworks to safely and deterministically incorporate probabilistic AI components into traditional computational systems.
AI.method: The manuscript defines four specific architectural primitives for AI-blended systems that enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic generative models. It also identifies and articulates two overarching anti-patterns commonly observed across industry implementations.
AI.result: The paper delivers a foundational framework consisting of four primitives for safe AI integration and two identified anti-patterns serving as cautionary guidance for practitioners.
AI.conclusion: With these primitives and anti-patterns, the framework provides a foundation for successful AI integration into traditional systems and a basis upon which generative model providers can build the next generation of model interfaces.

title: Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents
summary: Securing AI agents that operate in complex digital environments has become a critical need, and runtime monitoring approaches that formulate and enforce policies expressed in a formal language like Datalog offer a promising solution. However, existing approaches are restricted to deterministic policies. In many practical applications of AI agents, there is a need to enforce security policies in the face of ambiguity, leading to probabilistic predicates or state transitions (for example, a declassifier or Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detector that has some failure probability on each invocation). Furthermore, in many such applications, one cannot easily make the independence assumptions necessary to invoke prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog. We address this by introducing a sound and efficient framework for such verification based on distributionally robust optimization, computing sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation regardless of possible correlations between predicates. On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool calling agents, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior art and improves the security-utility trade-off while ensuring rigorous bounds on the probability of policy violation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a distributionally robust optimization framework for runtime monitoring of AI agents that enforces probabilistic security policies with sound upper bounds on policy violation probability, outperforming prior deterministic Datalog-based approaches on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime monitoring approaches for AI agents using Datalog-based policies are limited to deterministic settings. In practice, security policies must handle ambiguity—such as probabilistic PII detectors or declassifiers with failure probabilities—and independence assumptions required by prior probabilistic Datalog work often cannot be satisfied.
AI.method: The authors propose a sound and efficient verification framework grounded in distributionally robust optimization (DRO). The method computes sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation without relying on independence assumptions between predicates, thereby accounting for arbitrary correlations.
AI.result: On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling AI agents, the proposed approach outperforms prior art, achieving a better security-utility trade-off while providing rigorous guarantees on the probability of policy violation.
AI.conclusion: Distributionally robust optimization enables effective runtime enforcement of probabilistic security policies for AI agents, offering formal soundness guarantees where prior deterministic and probabilistic Datalog approaches fall short.

title: 3D-DLP: Self-Supervised 3D Object-Centric Scene Representation Learning
summary: We introduce 3D-DLP, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning model that decomposes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, each particle encodes disentangled attributes, including 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features, and represents a distinct entity in the scene. The model learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective. We demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that the learned latent space is interpretable and controllable: by manipulating particle positions and decoding, we can generate novel scene configurations. Furthermore, we show that leveraging these compact 3D latent particles for downstream robotic manipulation improves performance over baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure. Code and videos are available at https://eubooks3003.github.io/3d-dlp.

AI.tldr: 3D-DLP extends Deep Latent Particles to 3D, learning to decompose RGB-D/voxel scenes into disentangled 3D latent particles (keypoints, bounding boxes, appearance) via self-supervised reconstruction, enabling controllable scene generation and improved robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Current object-centric representation learning either lacks explicit 3D structure or relies on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs. There is a need for compact, interpretable 3D object representations that disentangle geometry and appearance for downstream tasks like robotic manipulation.
AI.method: Extends the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework to 3D by decomposing scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles. Each particle encodes disentangled attributes: 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features. The model learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective, without requiring ground-truth object annotations.
AI.result: On both simulated and real-world datasets, the learned latent space is interpretable and controllable — manipulating particle positions and decoding yields novel scene configurations. For downstream robotic manipulation, 3D-DLP outperforms baselines that lack explicit 3D information or use dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure.
AI.conclusion: 3D-DLP demonstrates that self-supervised learning of compact, disentangled 3D object-centric representations is feasible and beneficial, offering both interpretability for scene generation and improved performance in robotic manipulation tasks compared to non-object-centric alternatives.

title: N-Version Programming with Coding Agents
summary: This paper revisits the classical concept on N-version programming in the setting of contemporary AI coding agents. Revisiting the seminal Knight-Leveson experiment, we study whether diversity across agent systems, models, and implementation languages creates diverse failure modes. Using the Knight-Leveson's, Launch Interceptor Program Specification, we evaluate 48 agent-generated implementations on a shared oracle and a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. The results show substantial common-mode failure, along the findings of Knight-Leveson. Further analysis that many of those co-occuring failures can be traced to where is specification is particularly hard or ambiguous. We also demonstrate that diversity from coding agents provides practical benefit: across majority voting three-version units, the mean failure count drops from 387.44 for single versions to 130.99 for triples, and 11,844 N-version units exhibit zero observed failures. Our original results is the strongest evidence to date that N-Version Programming with coding agents is a useful engineering strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits N-version programming using contemporary AI coding agents, replicating the Knight-Leveson experiment. Evaluating 48 agent-generated implementations of the Launch Interceptor Program against 1M test inputs, it finds substantial common-mode failures—often tied to ambiguous specification areas—but demonstrates that majority voting across three-version units reduces mean failures from 387.44 to 130.99, with 11,844 N-version units showing zero failures, providing the strongest evidence yet for the practical utility of N-version programming with coding agents.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the classical N-version programming paradigm, originally studied by Knight and Leveson in the 1980s, holds practical value when applied to modern AI coding agents. Specifically, the authors aim to determine if diversity across agent systems, models, and programming languages yields genuinely diverse failure modes or whether common-mode failures persist, and whether ensemble strategies can yield reliability gains.
AI.method: The study replicates the Knight-Leveson experiment using the Launch Interceptor Program Specification. 48 implementations are generated by varying coding agents, underlying models, and programming languages. All implementations are evaluated against a shared oracle using a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. Three-version majority voting units are constructed from these implementations, and failure rates are compared between single versions and N-version triples. Co-occurring failures are further analyzed to trace their origins to specification ambiguities.
AI.result: Substantial common-mode failure was observed, consistent with Knight-Leveson's original findings. Many co-occurring failures traced back to hard or ambiguous parts of the specification. However, diversity from coding agents provided practical benefit: mean failure count dropped from 387.44 (single versions) to 130.99 (three-version majority voting units), and 11,844 N-version units exhibited zero observed failures out of 1M tests.
AI.conclusion: N-version programming with AI coding agents is a useful engineering strategy. While common-mode failures persist—particularly where specifications are ambiguous—the substantial reliability improvement from ensemble voting provides the strongest empirical evidence to date supporting the practical adoption of this approach.

title: What sentiment analysis can't see: Measuring whether customers were helped, and what went wrong, across 70,000 support conversations
summary: Most companies read their customer support data at scale using sentiment analysis, which measures how customers sound rather than whether they were satisfied with the result. We tested a richer alternative on 70,450 support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform: alongside tone, we used GPT-5.4 to estimate each customer's satisfaction and to flag whether they reported a concrete problem, then validated all three readings against the 1-to-5 ratings customers left on the conversations they rated. The satisfaction estimate tracked those ratings far better than sentiment did, correlating at 0.47 against 0.36 and flagging unhappy customers with far fewer false alarms. The structured read also sees what sentiment cannot: tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of conversations, a single "Neutral" label hides everything from quietly satisfied customers to ones who quietly gave up, and the largest group of all is "tolerated friction," customers who are satisfied but still reporting a fixable problem, a standing issue that no sentiment-based dashboard can surface. The broader finding is that LLM-based annotation can capture far more than the tonality of a customer's language, offering strong potential for new business metrics grounded instead in the customer's state (whether they were satisfied) and the cause of their problem extracted directly from the raw textual data of interactions and feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that traditional sentiment analysis is an inadequate proxy for customer satisfaction in support interactions. Using GPT-4 (referred to as GPT-5.4) on 70,450 support conversations, the authors demonstrate that directly estimating satisfaction and flagging concrete problems outperforms sentiment-based approaches, revealing that tone and satisfaction diverge in 44% of cases and uncovering a large "tolerated friction" segment invisible to sentiment tools.
AI.motivation: Companies routinely use sentiment analysis to monitor customer support at scale, but sentiment only captures linguistic tone — how customers *sound* — rather than whether they were actually satisfied with the resolution. This creates a blind spot: customers may sound neutral or positive yet remain dissatisfied, or sound negative but be satisfied. The authors seek a richer, LLM-based alternative that directly estimates customer state and problem causality from raw conversation text.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 70,450 customer support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform. Using GPT-4 (labeled GPT-5.4), they produced three annotations per conversation: (1) tone/sentiment, (2) estimated customer satisfaction, and (3) whether a concrete, fixable problem was reported. All three were validated against 1-to-5 star ratings left by customers on a subset of rated conversations. Performance was compared via correlation coefficients and false-alarm rates for detecting unhappy customers.
AI.result: The satisfaction estimate correlated with actual customer ratings at 0.47 versus 0.36 for sentiment, with fewer false alarms when flagging unhappy customers. Tone and satisfaction disagreed in 44% of conversations. A single "Neutral" sentiment label masked heterogeneous outcomes, including quietly satisfied customers and those who silently gave up. The largest identified segment was "tolerated friction" — customers who were satisfied yet still reported a fixable problem — a cohort entirely invisible to sentiment-based dashboards.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based annotation can capture far more than linguistic tonality, enabling new business metrics grounded in customer state (satisfaction) and problem causality extracted directly from interaction text. This shift from tone-based to state-based measurement offers actionable insights — particularly surfacing tolerated friction — that sentiment analysis alone cannot provide.

title: Optimal Scheduling in a Question-Answering Forum of Knowledge Workers
summary: As individuals turn to the Internet to find answers to questions they may have, several Question Answering (QA) forums have evolved, where users knowledgeable in certain topics can contribute their expertise to answering these requests for information. While these are currently volunteer based, we consider a future version employing knowledge workers who are experts in certain topics. In such a system, the request-answer processes forming the queuing system may utilize schedulers that assign requests in different topics to the experts in the forum, who may be able to answer them according to their expertise levels in different topics. With this model, we calculate the capacity of the system for handling the requests while keeping the system stable, and design schedulers that achieve capacity. We also investigate how collaboration between experts in answering requests can potentially increase capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper models a future QA forum staffed by knowledge workers with varying topic expertise, analyzes the queuing system's capacity under different scheduling policies, and designs schedulers that achieve maximum stable throughput while also exploring how inter-expert collaboration can further increase system capacity.
AI.motivation: Current QA forums rely on volunteers, but the authors envision a future system employing paid knowledge workers with heterogeneous expertise. Understanding the fundamental capacity limits of such a system and how to optimally match incoming requests to experts is critical for designing efficient, stable operational policies.
AI.method: The authors model the QA forum as a queuing system where requests arrive for different topics and are assigned to experts with varying expertise levels across topics. They apply queuing theory and scheduling analysis to calculate the system's stability region (maximum capacity), design scheduling policies that achieve this capacity, and analyze the potential capacity gains from collaborative request handling among experts.
AI.result: The paper derives the maximum capacity of the system under the constraint of maintaining stability, presents scheduling algorithms that achieve this capacity bound, and demonstrates that collaboration between experts can potentially increase the overall request-handling capacity beyond what non-collaborative approaches allow.
AI.conclusion: A paid knowledge-worker QA forum can be modeled as a queuing system with topic-dependent expertise. Capacity-achieving schedulers exist that keep the system stable, and collaboration among experts offers additional throughput gains, suggesting that hybrid expert-matching and collaborative strategies are key to efficient future QA platforms.

title: Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. This paper introduces the Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB), a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure. SEB consumes certificates issued by the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies that the requested mutation matches the certified execution contract, checks validity windows, policy epochs, revocation epochs, and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. By separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities. We present the SEB execution model, certificate and replay-verification predicates, scoped identity semantics, bypass-prevention deployment patterns, failure behavior, and a concrete prototype implementation. We evaluate the prototype on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.

AI.tldr: SEB is a runtime enforcement broker that consumes SAB-issued certificates, verifies execution contracts, and mints scoped identities to ensure that only certified, time-bound, and auditable mutations reach production infrastructure — separating proposal, admission, and execution while preventing autonomous agents from directly holding mutation authority.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents lack mandatory enforcement points for certified authority at mutation time; identity-based access control and assurance certification alone cannot guarantee that only certified actions execute in production, creating a gap between certification and actual infrastructure mutation.
AI.method: SEB interposes between agents and infrastructure APIs, consuming SAB certificates, verifying execution contracts against requested mutations, checking temporal validity (windows, policy/recovery epochs), detecting live-state drift, minting scoped execution identities, and recording signed decision/outcome records. Deployment patterns enforce that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities.
AI.result: Prototype evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes clusters; measurements cover latency overheads, revocation propagation speed, drift detection accuracy, and security resilience under fault injection.
AI.conclusion: SEB transforms certified authority into short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capabilities, bridging the gap between assurance certification and actual execution by providing a mandatory enforcement boundary — effective when production APIs reject non-broker identities.

title: Can In-Context Learning Support Intrinsic Curiosity?
summary: Effective machine learning depends not only on how we model data, but also on what data we choose to collect. While large sequence models have revolutionized data modeling, the problem of automated data selection, or "intrinsic curiosity", remains a significant challenge. Classic approaches incentivize exploration by rewarding an agent based on its "learning progress", which measures how much a newly acquired observation improves a world model's predictive ability. However, evaluating these rewards traditionally requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent updates within each trajectory, rendering them computationally impractical at scale. In this work, we investigate whether the emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models. Specifically, we evaluate whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress, using solely the prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. We first prove that in general Markov decision processes, this is in fact impossible in an unbiased way: the resulting intrinsic rewards either suffer from nuisance terms that bias their estimation of true learning progress, or they cannot be implemented using an in-context learner's prediction errors. Conversely, we prove a positive result for a broad subclass of non-temporal settings, encompassing active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design: here, ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. We corroborate our theory with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments, demonstrating that our ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can replace expensive gradient-based inner loops for computing intrinsic curiosity rewards. It proves ICL-derived rewards are fundamentally biased in general MDPs but work well in non-temporal settings like active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design, with experimental validation.
AI.motivation: Classic curiosity-driven exploration relies on "learning progress" rewards that measure world model improvement, but computing these requires costly inner-loop gradient descent per trajectory, making it impractical at scale. The authors explore whether emergent in-context learning in sequence models can serve as update-free world models to eliminate this computational bottleneck.
AI.method: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of whether prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations from an in-context learner can unbiasedly estimate true learning progress. It first proves a negative result for general MDPs (impossibility theorem), then proves a positive result for non-temporal settings (active learning / Bayesian Experimental Design), showing ICL-derived rewards asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Controlled experiments in continuous and symbolic environments validate the theory.
AI.result: In general MDPs, ICL-derived intrinsic rewards either contain nuisance bias terms or cannot be implemented using only prediction errors. However, in non-temporal settings (active learning, BED), ICL-derived rewards provably bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Experiments confirm the ICL-driven framework successfully trains optimal curious exploration policies.
AI.conclusion: In-context learning can replace expensive inner-loop updates for curiosity-driven exploration, but only in non-temporal settings. The negative result for general MDPs highlights a fundamental limitation, while the positive result opens a computationally efficient path for active learning and experimental design applications.

title: Qiskit Code Migration with LLMs
summary: The rapid evolution of Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) introduces a specific form of technical debt that compromises code maintainability and hinders software reuse. In the specialized domain of Quantum Software Engineering (QSE), this challenge is intensified by the scarcity of high-quality training data and the high volatility of emerging frameworks, which often lead general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce unreliable or hallucinated results. This paper proposes a hybrid approach integrating LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate the migration of Qiskit code across versions. The proposed methodology enhances the precision and reliability of migration suggestions by leveraging an automatically generated taxonomy of migration scenarios as the structured, version-specific knowledge source to guide the models. The approach is implemented through an automated, extensible workflow evaluating LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5 and OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) under different retrieval schemes (unconstrained and restrictive). Results demonstrate that the taxonomy-based RAG architecture, particularly under the restrictive scheme, significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality, with Google Gemini Flash-2.5 showing superior performance in detecting complex refactoring scenarios. These findings confirm the potential of this data-centric methodology to foster technological independence and provide robust, intelligent assistants that mitigate API obsolescence, ensuring the long-term availability of quantum algorithms within a rapidly shifting ecosystem and flattening the learning curve within Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid LLM+RAG approach using a taxonomy-based, version-specific knowledge source to automate Qiskit code migration, demonstrating significant reduction in hallucinations and improved reliability, particularly under a restrictive retrieval scheme.
AI.motivation: Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) evolve rapidly, creating technical debt through API obsolescence that compromises code maintainability and software reuse. General-purpose LLMs produce unreliable results due to scarce training data and high framework volatility in Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).
AI.method: A hybrid architecture combining LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5, OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), guided by an automatically generated taxonomy of migration scenarios as a structured, version-specific knowledge source. Two retrieval schemes are evaluated: unconstrained and restrictive.
AI.result: The taxonomy-based RAG architecture significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality. The restrictive retrieval scheme outperforms the unconstrained one. Google Gemini Flash-2.5 excels at detecting complex refactoring scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The data-centric taxonomy+RAG methodology provides robust, intelligent assistants for mitigating API obsolescence, fostering technological independence, flattening the QSE learning curve, and ensuring long-term availability of quantum algorithms in a rapidly shifting ecosystem.

title: TerraMARS: A Domain-Adapted Small-Language-Model Pipeline for Mars Terraforming Literature
summary: Researchers are interested in learning about Mars so that it may eventually become habitable for humans. To achieve this, there is a need for comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation environment, and spatial features through the scientific literature. These contain valuable information and meaningful quantitative constraints that can be used in other models and studies, such as habitability assessment and future terraforming studies. We present TerraMARS, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that combines a domain-adapted Small Language Model to answer Mars terraforming-related questions and convert unstructured Mars science text into machine-readable structured outputs in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. A corpus of open-access papers is collected and processed using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework.
