Google Gemma 3 1B was adapted to the domain using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The resulting pipeline generates both types of output and provides a foundation for integrating knowledge from scientific literature into downstream applications like digital twins and habitability modeling for Mars. The output from this pipeline looks promising, but further improvements are needed to increase extraction accuracy and factual consistency.

AI.tldr: TerraMARS is an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that uses a fine-tuned Small Language Model (Gemma 3 1B) with QLoRA to convert unstructured Mars scientific literature into structured JSON outputs and answer terraforming-related questions.
AI.motivation: To enable Mars habitability and terraforming studies, comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation, and spatial features must be extracted from unstructured scientific literature and converted into machine-readable formats for use in downstream models (e.g., digital twins, habitability assessment).
AI.method: A corpus of open-access Mars papers is processed through a multistage retrieval and chunking framework. Google Gemma 3 1B is domain-adapted via Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The end-to-end pipeline outputs both natural language answers and structured JSON.
AI.result: The pipeline generates promising structured outputs and answers to Mars terraforming-related questions, though further improvements in extraction accuracy and factual consistency are needed.
AI.conclusion: TerraMARS provides a viable foundation for integrating Mars scientific knowledge into structured downstream applications, but extraction accuracy and factual consistency remain areas requiring further refinement.

title: Beyond Entropy: Learning from Token-Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning; however, it faces a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates precipitate entropy collapse, leading to premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, whereas excessive Shannon Entropy maximization can cause entropy explosion, driving blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework, which shifts the optimization focus from scalar uncertainty to the distributional properties of token logits. By leveraging the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logits distributions, ICT identifies tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points for guiding effective exploration in LLM reasoning. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, proves that selectively updating on these tokens regulates policy concentration: it reduces the overall distribution uncertainty measured by Shannon entropy, while controlling probability concentration captured by second-order Rényi entropy. This dual effect prevents over-concentrated token generation from weakening exploration and effectively stabilizes the training landscape. Empirical results demonstrate that updating only the top 10% of unique tokens on Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B) models yields an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58%, with a maximum gain of 14.9%, over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines across seven benchmarks spanning math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.

AI.tldr: RLVR for LLM reasoning faces a stability trade-off between entropy collapse (premature convergence) and entropy explosion (incoherent exploration). The proposed ICT framework uses Jensen-Shannon divergence between token logit distributions to identify critical tokens for selective updating, theoretically grounded in Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, achieving up to 14.9% pass@4 improvement across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RLVR suffers from a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates cause entropy collapse (premature convergence to suboptimal strategies), while excessive Shannon entropy maximization triggers entropy explosion (blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning). No existing method satisfactorily resolves this entropy collapse–explosion dichotomy.
AI.method: The Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework shifts optimization from scalar uncertainty to distributional properties of token logits. It employs Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logit distributions to identify tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points. Only these top-k (e.g., 10%) unique tokens are selectively updated, theoretically proven to regulate both Shannon entropy (reducing overall distribution uncertainty) and second-order Rényi entropy (controlling probability concentration), thereby stabilizing the training landscape.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, 7B), updating only the top 10% unique tokens via ICT yields an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58% over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines, with a maximum gain of 14.9% across seven benchmarks (math, commonsense, Olympiad-level problems).
AI.conclusion: Selective token updating based on distributional divergence effectively balances exploration and exploitation in RLVR, preventing both entropy collapse and explosion. ICT provides a theoretically grounded, empirically validated solution for stabilizing LLM reasoning training.

title: From Efficiency to Leakage -- Privacy Backdoor in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple parties to collaboratively fine-tune language models for domain-specific tasks without sharing raw data. Since full model fine-tuning is often prohibitively expensive for FL clients, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto approach in practice, freezing the base model and training only a small set of adapters. In this paper, we show that a malicious parameter server can stealthily corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor that implicitly memorizes the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons, without degrading model utility. Concretely, our attack, NeuroImprint, assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains that each neuron is updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This design mitigates both cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing introduced by large local batches and stateful optimizers (e.g., Adam/AdamW) in language-model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the resulting isolated per-sample updates can be analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences. To understand the generality of our method, we implemented NeuroImprint on multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2) and evaluated it across four fine-tuning datasets spanning diverse domains. The results demonstrate that our attack can reconstruct 59% to 79% of all finetuning samples with high semantic fidelity.

AI.tldr: NeuroImprint is a novel privacy attack where a malicious FL parameter server stealthily crafts PEFT adapters to memorize client training samples in isolated neurons, then analytically inverts the per-sample parameter updates in closed form to reconstruct text with 59–79% success across diverse language models and datasets.
AI.motivation: Federated learning with PEFT is widely adopted for efficient collaborative fine-tuning, but the privacy risks from a malicious parameter server—capable of manipulating adapter weights—remain underexplored. Prior gradient inversion attacks fail against large-batch and stateful optimizer (Adam/AdamW) settings typical in LM fine-tuning, motivating a new attack vector.
AI.method: The attack, NeuroImprint, operates by: (1) assigning each client training sample a dedicated "memorization neuron" in the PEFT adapter; (2) constraining each neuron to be updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory, preventing cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing from large batches and Adam/AdamW; (3) after fine-tuning, analytically inverting the isolated per-sample updates in closed form to recover text embeddings; and (4) deterministically mapping embeddings back to token sequences. The method is implemented across BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2 on four domain-diverse fine-tuning datasets.
AI.result: NeuroImprint reconstructs 59% to 79% of all fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity across multiple model architectures and datasets, all without degrading model utility.
AI.conclusion: PEFT-based FL is vulnerable to a malicious server that can embed privacy backdoors into adapters via neuron-isolated memorization. The attack's closed-form invertibility and high reconstruction rates expose a serious privacy threat, challenging the assumption that PEFT inherently protects client data in federated settings.

title: Insulin4RL: Real-Time Insulin Management in the Intensive Care Unit for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (ORL) offers the potential to improve the quality of clinical decision-making using historical electronic health record (EHR) data. Current training and evaluative practices in this field rely heavily on EHR datasets that have been temporally discretised into fixed, regular time intervals. Discretisation creates fictional representations of complex clinical scenarios and compromises the generalisability of retrospective model evaluations. In this paper, we introduce Insulin4RL, a healthcare ORL dataset featuring naturally irregular inputs and actions from real clinical trajectories. Derived from MIMIC-IV, Insulin4RL comprises over 375,000 labelled decisions across 12,209 patients requiring insulin infusion titration in the Intensive Care Unit. The dataset can thus be used for research into ORL model performance under realistic clinical sampling assumptions. We provide a description of the dataset's structure and characteristics, baseline performance metrics using model-free offline reinforcement learning, and a standardised evaluation protocol using fitted Q-evaluation. We conclude with suggested areas for future research that could be addressed using this resource.

AI.tldr: Insulin4RL is a new offline RL benchmark dataset derived from MIMIC-IV, featuring naturally irregular clinical time series for insulin titration in the ICU. It provides over 375,000 labeled decisions across 12,209 patients and challenges the field's reliance on temporally discretized EHR data by enabling evaluation under realistic sampling assumptions.
AI.motivation: Current offline RL research in healthcare relies on EHR datasets that are temporally discretized into fixed, regular intervals. This discretization creates fictional representations of complex clinical scenarios and compromises the generalizability of retrospective model evaluations. There is a need for a benchmark that reflects naturally irregular clinical data sampling.
AI.method: The authors derive Insulin4RL from the MIMIC-IV database, curating real clinical trajectories of ICU patients requiring insulin infusion titration. The dataset preserves the naturally irregular timing of clinical observations and interventions. They establish baseline performance using model-free offline RL algorithms and propose a standardized evaluation protocol based on fitted Q-evaluation (FQE).
AI.result: The resulting dataset contains over 375,000 labeled clinical decisions from 12,209 patient episodes. Baseline offline RL performance metrics are reported, and a reproducible FQE-based evaluation framework is provided for consistent benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: Insulin4RL fills a gap in healthcare ORL by providing a realistic, irregularly-sampled benchmark. The authors highlight several directions for future research that can leverage this resource, emphasizing the importance of moving beyond discretized assumptions in clinical RL.

title: SysML Modeling of Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities
comment: Presented at the Workshop on Digital Twin Experiences and Model-Based Testing Methods, 12 June 2026, Västerås, Sweden, co-located with the 30th Ada-Europe International Conference on Reliable Software Technologies (AEiC 2026)
summary: Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) are emerging as a key organizational model for local and global sharing of renewable generation, storage, and flexible loads. Engineering Digital Twins of RECs is made difficult by the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data involved. In this paper, we take a first step toward a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for REC's Digital Twins. Starting from an industrially-validated REC domain model, we re-express a representative house subset in SysML using the open-source Modelio tool, yielding two Block Definition Diagrams - a device taxonomy and a community organizational view. We then discuss four semantic gaps that plain SysML leaves open and sketch how the SAREF4ENER ontology could be imported as a reference package to close them. Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins remains largely unexplored, and we position this paper as a first step along that line.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for Renewable Energy Community (REC) Digital Twins by modeling a representative house subset in SysML and identifying four semantic gaps that the SAREF4ENER ontology could bridge.
AI.motivation: Engineering Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities is challenging due to heterogeneous devices, contracts, and runtime data. Current approaches lack a systematic MBSE methodology, and the integration of formal ontologies with SysML for smart-energy Digital Twins remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors start from an industrially-validated REC domain model, re-express a representative house subset in SysML using the open-source Modelio tool, producing two Block Definition Diagrams (a device taxonomy and a community organizational view). They then identify four semantic gaps in plain SysML and sketch how SAREF4ENER ontology could be imported as a reference package to close them.
AI.result: The work yields two SysML Block Definition Diagrams that capture REC structure. Four semantic gaps are identified where plain SysML falls short, and a tentative mapping to SAREF4ENER is proposed as a remedy.
AI.conclusion: Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins is a largely unexplored but promising direction. This paper serves as an initial step toward an integrated MBSE-ontology workflow for REC Digital Twins.

title: FineREX: Fine-Tuned NER-RE for Human Smuggling Knowledge Graphs
summary: Court proceedings contain valuable evidence about human smuggling networks, but this information is often buried within unstructured, jargon-heavy legal documents. While large language models (LLMs) can support knowledge graph construction through automated information extraction, existing approaches rely on general-purpose models that are not tailored to the entity and relationship definitions required in this domain. We introduce FineREX, a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline built around a fine-tuned LLM for named entity recognition and relationship extraction (NER-RE). Using a manually annotated dataset of $512$ text chunks, FineREX achieves absolute improvements of 15.50% and 31.46% in entity and relationship F1-score, respectively, compared to a larger general-purpose baseline. These gains translate into higher-quality knowledge graphs, reducing legal noise by nearly half and lowering node duplication on long documents from 17.78% to 11.17%. By eliminating document rewriting and redundant extraction stages, FineREX also reduces end-to-end processing time by 50.0%. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning can substantially outperform larger general-purpose models while improving both the quality and efficiency of knowledge graph construction for illicit network analysis.

AI.tldr: FineREX is a pipeline using a fine-tuned LLM for named entity recognition and relationship extraction from legal documents on human smuggling. It outperforms larger general-purpose models by 15.50% (entity F1) and 31.46% (relation F1), while halving processing time, reducing legal noise by ~50%, and cutting node duplication from 17.78% to 11.17%.
AI.motivation: Court proceedings contain valuable intelligence about human smuggling networks, but extracting structured knowledge from unstructured, jargon-laden legal text is challenging. Existing LLM-based extraction approaches use general-purpose models not adapted to the domain-specific entity and relation schemas, resulting in noisy outputs and inefficient pipelines.
AI.method: FineREX is a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline centered on a fine-tuned LLM for joint named entity recognition and relationship extraction (NER-RE). The model is fine-tuned on a manually annotated dataset of 512 text chunks from legal documents. The pipeline eliminates document rewriting and redundant extraction stages present in prior approaches.
AI.result: Compared to a larger general-purpose baseline, FineREX achieves absolute F1 improvements of +15.50% for entities and +31.46% for relations. Knowledge graph quality improves: legal noise is reduced by nearly half, node duplication on long documents drops from 17.78% to 11.17%, and end-to-end processing time is reduced by 50.0%.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning substantially outperforms larger general-purpose models for knowledge graph construction in specialized domains like illicit network analysis, delivering gains in both extraction quality and pipeline efficiency.

title: AgentFinVQA: A Deployable Multi-Agent Pipeline for Auditable Financial Chart QA
summary: Financial chart question answering in regulated settings demands more than accuracy: practitioners must know which answers to trust before acting on them, and many institutions cannot send client data to external model providers. Yet existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused and opaque, and most assume proprietary API access; to our knowledge, none combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy compromise. We present AgentFinVQA, a multi-agent pipeline that decomposes each query into planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification, recording every step in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. On FinMME, AgentFinVQA improves $+7.68$ pp over a primary-backbone matched zero-shot baseline with a proprietary backbone (Gemini-3 Flash; 71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar $p \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-16}$), and $+4.84$ pp with open-weights Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served locally. The verifier's verdict also serves as a useful confidence signal (68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy on confirmed vs. revised answers), enabling human-in-the-loop review routing. Error analysis shows that question misunderstanding, legend confusion and extraction error account for nearly two-thirds of failures and are the categories least detected by the verifier, identifying clear directions for future work. Together these results show that auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical and that the open-weights system keeps most of the accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. We release our code to support reproducible evaluation.

AI.tldr: AgentFinVQA is a multi-agent pipeline for financial chart QA that prioritizes auditability and on-premise deployment. It decomposes queries into planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification, recording every step in a traceable packet. The system achieves significant accuracy gains over zero-shot baselines using both proprietary and open-weights backbones, while the verifier provides a useful confidence signal for human-in-the-loop routing.
AI.motivation: In regulated financial settings, practitioners need to know which answers to trust before acting on them, and many institutions cannot send client data to external model providers due to data residency requirements. Existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused and opaque, assume proprietary API access, and none combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy compromise.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline that decomposes each query into five stages: planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification. Every step per sample is recorded in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP). The system supports both proprietary backbones (Gemini-3 Flash) and open-weights models (Qwen3.6-27B-FP8) served locally, with the verifier providing a confidence signal by flagging answers as confirmed or requiring revision.
AI.result: On the FinMME benchmark, AgentFinVQA achieves +7.68 pp over a zero-shot baseline with Gemini-3 Flash (71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar p ≈ 1.1×10⁻¹⁶) and +4.84 pp with locally-served Qwen3.6-27B-FP8. The verifier yields 68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy on confirmed vs. revised answers. Error analysis shows question misunderstanding, legend confusion, and extraction error account for nearly two-thirds of failures and are the categories least detected by the verifier.
AI.conclusion: Auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical. The open-weights system retains most of the accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. The verifier's confidence signal effectively supports human-in-the-loop review routing, and error analysis identifies clear directions for future improvement.

title: Concept Flow Models: Anchoring Concept-Based Reasoning with Hierarchical Bottlenecks
summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enhance interpretability by projecting learned features into a human-understandable concept space. Recent approaches leverage vision-language models to generate concept embeddings, reducing the need for manual concept annotations. However, these models suffer from a critical limitation: as the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, information leakage increases, enabling the model to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations and undermining interpretability. In this work, we propose Concept Flow Models (CFMs), which replace the flat bottleneck with a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree. Each internal node in the hierarchy focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts, progressively narrowing the prediction scope. Our framework constructs decision hierarchies from visual embeddings, distributes semantic concepts at each hierarchy level, and trains differentiable concept weights through probabilistic tree traversal. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs, while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. Furthermore, CFMs yield stepwise decision flows that enable transparent and auditable model reasoning with hierarchical class structures.

AI.tldr: Concept Flow Models (CFMs) replace the flat bottleneck in Concept Bottleneck Models with a hierarchical decision tree to reduce information leakage. Each tree node focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts, progressively narrowing predictions. CFMs match flat CBM performance while improving interpretability through reduced effective concept usage and stepwise, auditable decision flows.
AI.motivation: Flat CBMs suffer from information leakage when the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, allowing models to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations, which undermines interpretability. A more constrained, structured bottleneck is needed.
AI.method: CFMs construct a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree from visual embeddings. Each internal node localizes a subset of discriminative concepts. The framework distributes semantic concepts across hierarchy levels and trains differentiable concept weights via probabilistic tree traversal, replacing the flat bottleneck.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks show CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. CFMs also produce stepwise decision flows enabling transparent, auditable reasoning with hierarchical class structures.
AI.conclusion: CFMs offer a compelling alternative to flat CBMs by structurally enforcing interpretability through hierarchical concept bottlenecks, successfully balancing predictive accuracy with reduced information leakage and enhanced reasoning transparency.

title: NRITYAM: Language Models Meet Art and Heritage of Dance
summary: Language models have become essential tools in shaping modern workflows. However, their global effectiveness hinges on a nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts. To address this gap, we present NRITYAM, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the cultural comprehension capabilities of language models in the context of global dance traditions. NRITYAM comprises 9,260 carefully curated question-answer pairs spanning 12 languages, making it the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. The dataset has been developed from the ground up through close collaboration with native dance artists and native speakers of the languages, who authored and validated culturally relevant questions specific to their regions. We evaluate a broad set of models, including large language models, small language models, multimodal large language models, and small multimodal language models. As a multilingual and multicultural benchmark, NRITYAM sets a new standard for evaluating the ability of AI systems to understand and reason about traditional performing arts. Detailed dataset samples are available at~\url{https://github.com/niladrighosh03/NRITYAM}.

AI.tldr: NRITYAM is a multilingual, multicultural benchmark of 9,260 QA pairs across 12 languages for evaluating language models' understanding of global dance traditions, built with native artists and speakers.
AI.motivation: Language models lack nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts, particularly in traditional performing arts. No comprehensive benchmark exists for evaluating cultural comprehension in dance across multiple languages and cultures.
AI.method: The authors constructed NRITYAM through close collaboration with native dance artists and native speakers, who authored and validated culturally relevant QA pairs. The benchmark spans 12 languages and covers both large and small language models, as well as multimodal variants.
AI.result: NRITYAM, with 9,260 QA pairs, is the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. It enables systematic evaluation of diverse model types — LLMs, SLMs, MLLMs, and small multimodal LMs — on their ability to understand and reason about traditional performing arts.
AI.conclusion: NRITYAM sets a new standard for evaluating AI systems' cultural comprehension in traditional performing arts, addressing a critical gap in socio-cultural evaluation of language models.

title: ORAgentBench: Can LLM Agents Solve Challenging Operations Research Tasks End to End?
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for multi-step tasks in executable environments, yet their ability to perform realistic operations research (OR) work remains unclear. Existing OR evaluations often decouple modeling from solving, rely on pre-formalized or text-only instances, and rarely test the full workflow from operational artifacts to validated decisions. In this work, we introduce ORAgentBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on challenging end-to-end operations research tasks. It contains 107 human-reviewed tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each packaged in an isolated environment with a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must write and run solution code, and their submissions are evaluated by hidden validators for schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Experiments with fourteen frontier agent-model configurations show that current agents remain far from reliable OR practice. The best agent passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks, and many feasible submissions still fall below the required quality threshold. Failure analysis further shows that errors are dominated by strategic weaknesses, including missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills increase hard-task feasibility, but do not reliably improve solution quality or pass rate. These results suggest that progress in OR agents requires moving beyond plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making.

AI.tldr: ORAgentBench is an execution-grounded benchmark with 107 human-reviewed OR tasks that evaluates LLM agents end-to-end — from natural-language briefs and multi-file artifacts through solution code execution to hidden validation. The best agent passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks, with failures dominated by strategic weaknesses in formulation, feasibility construction, and solution improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing OR evaluations decouple modeling from solving, rely on pre-formalized or text-only instances, and fail to test the full pipeline from raw operational artifacts to validated decisions. There is a gap in understanding whether LLM agents can perform realistic, end-to-end operations research work.
AI.method: The authors construct ORAgentBench, a benchmark of 107 tasks spanning diverse operational scenarios. Each task is packaged in an isolated execution environment containing a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must autonomously write and execute solution code. Submissions are evaluated by hidden validators on schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Fourteen frontier agent-model configurations are tested.
AI.result: The best-performing agent achieves only a 35.51% pass rate on all tasks and 20.59% on hard tasks. Many feasible submissions still fall below the required quality threshold. Error analysis reveals that failures are dominated by strategic weaknesses: missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills improve hard-task feasibility but do not reliably improve solution quality or overall pass rate.
AI.conclusion: Progress in OR agents requires moving beyond generating plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making. The gap between feasible solutions and high-quality solutions remains a critical challenge.

title: Algebraic Dead Directions in LayerNorm Transformers: A Forward-Pass-Only Diagnostic at LLM Scale
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Empirical companion to arXiv:2606.05957
summary: Pretrained transformers sit near singular minima of the loss, where the Fisher information metric degenerates along dead directions: directions in parameter space along which the directional Fisher vanishes. Locating such a direction normally needs a forward pass and an eigendecomposition of activations, or a sampling-based complexity estimate; none returns a direction computable from the network's parameters alone. We give one, for LayerNorm transformers. The inverse-scale direction $γ^{-1}/\|γ^{-1}\|$ of the LayerNorm affine is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance, for any input distribution, and induces a corresponding dead direction in parameter space. It is read from the LN scale parameter alone, with no forward or backward pass and no eigensolve: the cheapest dead-direction read, specific to LayerNorm. We test it on $14$ pretrained transformers ($9$ LayerNorm, $5$ RMSNorm; $160$M-$35$B; language and vision objectives). At random initialisation the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction (one forward pass, direct SVD) to four decimal places on $9/9$ LayerNorm models, and is correctly absent on $5/5$ RMSNorm models, which lack the mean-subtraction projector that creates it. On the trained checkpoint the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ${\sim}10^3\times$ and further dead directions open; the random-init-to-trained gap is a one-forward-pass, per-checkpoint readout of singular structure along the predicted coordinate. Two consequences follow in closed form: the residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on $13/14$ transformers measured on their own input distribution, the one exception (Gemma$4$-$31$B) a genuine dead direction the same read pinpoints; and the kernel direction's presence classifies a transformer's normalisation from the parameters alone.

AI.tldr: LayerNorm transformers contain a dead direction — an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm activation covariance — computable solely from the inverse-scale parameter γ⁻¹/‖γ⁻¹‖, requiring no forward pass, backward pass, or eigendecomposition. This direction deepens ~10³× during training and has downstream consequences for residual stream singular values and normalisation classification.
AI.motivation: Pretrained transformers sit near singular minima where the Fisher information metric degenerates along "dead directions." Existing methods to locate such directions require forward passes, eigendecompositions of activations, or sampling-based complexity estimates — none yields a direction computable from parameters alone. The authors aim to provide a parameter-only, analytically exact dead direction for LayerNorm transformers.
AI.method: The authors mathematically derive that the inverse-scale direction γ⁻¹/‖γ⁻¹‖ of the LayerNorm affine parameter is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance, for any input distribution. This follows from the mean-subtraction projector inherent to LayerNorm. They validate on 14 pretrained transformers (9 LayerNorm, 5 RMSNorm; 160M–35B parameters; language and vision objectives) by comparing the predicted direction against direct SVD at random initialisation and after training, measuring the eigenvalue deepening along this direction, and examining consequences for the residual stream's singular value preservation and normalisation classification.
AI.result: At random initialisation, the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction to four decimal places on all 9 LayerNorm models and is correctly absent on all 5 RMSNorm models. After training, the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ~10³×. The residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on 13/14 transformers; the single exception (Gemma 4-31B) is a genuine dead direction pinpointed by the same read. The kernel direction's presence classifies a transformer's normalisation type from parameters alone.
AI.conclusion: The inverse-scale direction provides the cheapest possible dead-direction readout — from LN scale parameters alone — specific to LayerNorm. It enables closed-form analysis of singular structure, serves as a per-checkpoint diagnostic, and can classify normalisation type without any forward/backward computation. The work establishes a principled link between LayerNorm's algebraic structure and the degeneracy of the Fisher information metric in pretrained transformers.

title: Token-Operations-Oriented Inference Optimization Techniques for Large Models
summary: Large model inference optimization serves as a key foundation for supporting the scalable, low-cost, and highly stable operation of large model services. Centered on token-oriented inference optimization technology, this paper proposes for the first time a four-layer technical architecture consisting of Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, and Compute-Network-Model Fusion. It systematically reviews the key technologies and current industry status across these four levels and analyzes the application value of related technologies in real-world business scenarios. This paper provides a practical technical path for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, ensuring the stability of token supply, and driving the transition of large model services from being merely callable to being operable.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a four-layer technical architecture for large model inference optimization centered on token-oriented strategies: Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, and Compute-Network-Model Fusion. It systematically reviews key technologies across these layers, analyzes their business value, and offers a practical path for reducing token costs, improving efficiency, ensuring supply stability, and enabling operational maturity of large model services.
AI.motivation: The scalable, low-cost, and highly stable operation of large model services currently lacks a unified optimization framework. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a structured technical architecture that moves large model services from being merely callable (usable) to truly operable (production-grade), with token-level economics as the central optimization target.
AI.method: The paper proposes a novel four-layer technical architecture: (1) Multi-model Fusion — combining multiple models for inference; (2) Model Optimization — techniques for optimizing individual models; (3) Compute-Model Fusion — co-optimization of computation and model structures; (4) Compute-Network-Model Fusion — joint optimization across computation, networking, and model layers. The work systematically surveys and reviews key technologies and industry practices at each layer.
AI.result: The paper delineates a comprehensive taxonomy of token-oriented inference optimization technologies spanning four architectural layers, maps them to industry practices, and demonstrates their application value in real-world business scenarios for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, and stabilizing token supply.
AI.conclusion: The proposed four-layer architecture provides a concrete, actionable technical pathway for transforming large model services from merely callable interfaces into fully operable, production-grade systems with optimized token economics. This framework serves as a foundation for scalable, cost-effective, and stable large model service deployment.

title: CombEval: A Framework for Evaluating Combinatorial Counting in Large Language Models
summary: We present CombEval, a dynamic benchmark for evaluating combinatorial counting in large language models. CombEval represents each problem as a typed Cofola specification over entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints, enabling controlled generation of natural-language counting problems with exact solver-verified answers. Unlike static collections, CombEval supports systematic variation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. We evaluate 11 LLMs under direct and code-augmented settings and find that models remain brittle on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Error analysis further identifies failures in constraint interpretation and counting principles. CombEval provides a diagnostic testbed for studying when and why LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning. The code and generated benchmark suites are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/YuxuZhou-CN/combination-problem-generation}.

AI.tldr: CombEval is a dynamic benchmark for evaluating combinatorial counting in LLMs, using typed Cofola specifications to generate natural-language problems with solver-verified answers. It supports systematic variation of object type, scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. Evaluation of 11 LLMs reveals brittleness on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relative positional constraints, and nested dependencies, with failures in constraint interpretation and counting principles.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for combinatorial counting are static collections that lack controlled, systematic variation and exact ground-truth answers. This limits diagnostic analysis of where and why LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning. A dynamically generated benchmark with verified answers is needed to isolate failure modes across different problem dimensions.
AI.method: CombEval uses typed Cofola specifications to model entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints. From these formal specs, it generates natural-language counting problems along with exact answers verified by a solver. The framework enables controlled manipulation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. Eleven LLMs are evaluated under both direct prompting and code-augmented (generation + execution) settings.
AI.result: LLMs exhibit consistent brittleness on four dimensions: ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Error analysis reveals two principal failure categories — misinterpretation of constraints and incorrect application of fundamental counting principles (e.g., overcounting/undercounting, misuse of permutations vs. combinations).
AI.conclusion: CombEval serves as an effective diagnostic testbed for combinatorial reasoning in LLMs, exposing systematic weaknesses that static benchmarks cannot isolate. The findings highlight that current models lack robust understanding of combinatorial structures, particularly when problems involve ordering, indistinguishability, relative constraints, or nested dependencies.

title: Calibrating Generative Models to Feature Distributions with MMD Finetuning
summary: Generative models can produce individually plausible samples while deviating substantially from a target set in the distribution of key features. For example, a model pretrained on broad drug-like chemical space may generate molecules whose molecular features differ from those of a therapeutic class of interest, such as known antibiotics. Correcting such distributional miscalibration is challenging: direct finetuning on the target set can overfit and does not control which features are matched. To fill this gap, we introduce kernel Calibrating Generative Models (kCGM). kCGM minimizes a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, with KL regularization to remain close to the pretrained model. On a target set of 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrifices chemical validity for feature-distribution matching, whereas kCGM improves target feature matching while increasing validity. We further demonstrate kCGM in protein and DNA generation tasks, showing it can adapt autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models using only feature-level supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/smithhenryd/cgm.

AI.tldr: kCGM introduces a kernel-based method to recalibrate generative models so their outputs match target feature distributions while preserving sample validity, outperforming direct finetuning on antibiotics, proteins, and DNA generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Pretrained generative models often exhibit distributional miscalibration — they produce individually plausible samples but deviate from the feature distribution of a specific target set (e.g., a therapeutic class). Direct finetuning on the target set leads to overfitting and provides no control over which features are matched.
AI.method: kCGM minimizes the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, combined with KL divergence regularization to keep the model close to the pretrained distribution. It operates using only feature-level supervision.
AI.result: On a target set of 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrificed chemical validity for feature matching, whereas kCGM improved target feature matching while also increasing validity. The method was further validated on protein and DNA generation tasks across autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models.
AI.conclusion: kCGM provides an effective, general-purpose framework for calibrating generative models to match target feature distributions without compromising sample quality or validity, applicable across diverse model architectures and data domains.

title: A Model-Driven Approach for Developing Families of Reinforcement Learning Environments
summary: Virtual training environments are software-intensive systems in which reinforcement learning (RL) agents learn, adapt, and demonstrate meaningful behavior. Virtual training environments offer a safe and cost-efficient alternative to training agents in real-world settings. However, to converge, most realistic RL problems require training in multiple, mostly similar but slightly different environments - i.e., families of environment variants. The typical development process of environment families is a labor-intensive and error-prone manual endeavor that does not scale well. To alleviate these issues, in this paper, we propose a model-driven approach for developing families of RL training environments. To obtain the family of environments, we develop an approach and prototype tool. In our approach, a hybrid genetic algorithm - a combination of population-based global search and heuristic local search - generates environment families. Mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations and are operationalized into a search process by a state-of-the-art model transformation engine. We demonstrate the soundness of our approach in a wildfire mitigation scenario and curriculum learning - a particular learning paradigm that relies on environment families.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-driven approach using a hybrid genetic algorithm and model transformations to automatically generate families of RL training environments, addressing the manual, error-prone development process. The approach is validated in a wildfire mitigation scenario using curriculum learning.
AI.motivation: Realistic RL problems require training across families of similar but slightly different environment variants. Manually developing these environment families is labor-intensive, error-prone, and does not scale, creating a need for automated generation methods.
AI.method: A model-driven approach where a hybrid genetic algorithm (combining population-based global search with heuristic local search) generates environment families. Mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations and operationalized through a state-of-the-art model transformation engine. A prototype tool implements this approach.
AI.result: The approach was demonstrated in a wildfire mitigation scenario using curriculum learning, showing soundness of the method for generating environment families.
AI.conclusion: The model-driven, search-based approach effectively automates the generation of RL training environment families, reducing manual effort and scaling to realistic problem complexities.

title: Clusters are All You Need: Pre-Training the Tsetlin Machine with Semantic Clusters from Language Models for Interpretability
summary: Pre-trained language models such as BERT achieve strong text classification performance but lack transparency, limiting their use in high-stakes settings. The Tsetlin Machine (TM) offers fully interpretable, clause-based reasoning but captures little semantic information, and prior attempts to bridge the two rely on static word embeddings that miss contextual meaning. We propose a semantic pre-training framework that transfers knowledge from a pre-trained language model into a TM without using embeddings. Text samples are grouped into semantically coherent clusters with K-means or Top2Vec, and the resulting cluster-sample pairs pre-train a non-negated TM with enhanced Type I feedback. The TM thereby learns interpretable semantic keywords that are fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Across five datasets, our method substantially outperforms vanilla and embedding-based TMs and reaches performance competitive with BERT while remaining interpretable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semantic pre-training framework that transfers knowledge from pre-trained language models into Tsetlin Machines (TMs) without using embeddings, achieving competitive performance with BERT while maintaining full interpretability.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained language models like BERT achieve high accuracy but are opaque black boxes. Tsetlin Machines offer full interpretability via clause-based reasoning but lack semantic understanding. Prior attempts to combine them use static word embeddings, which fail to capture contextual meaning. The motivation is to bridge this gap — transferring rich semantic knowledge from language models into TMs while preserving interpretability.
AI.method: The framework uses semantic clustering (K-means or Top2Vec) to group text samples into coherent clusters based on representations from a pre-trained language model. These cluster-sample pairs are then used to pre-train a non-negated Tsetlin Machine with enhanced Type I feedback. This pre-training allows the TM to learn interpretable semantic keywords (clause patterns), which are subsequently fine-tuned on downstream classification tasks. No word embeddings are used during TM inference.
AI.result: Across five datasets, the proposed method substantially outperforms both vanilla TMs and embedding-based TMs. It achieves performance competitive with BERT-level models.
AI.conclusion: Semantic knowledge from pre-trained language models can be effectively distilled into Tsetlin Machines through clustering-based pre-training, yielding a classifier that is both highly accurate and fully interpretable, making it suitable for high-stakes applications requiring transparency.

title: Think Again or Think Longer? Selective Verification for Budget-Aware Reasoning
summary: Test-time reasoning is increasingly used as a serving-time control knob, but extra reasoning is not uniformly valuable: it can repair failed attempts, waste compute on already-correct answers, or introduce harmful answer changes. We study this as a deployment allocation problem rather than a new-verifier problem. We introduce \sevra, Selective Verification for Reasoning Allocation, a serving-layer controller that decides whether to preserve a frozen solver's initial answer or invoke active verification. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B solver, we log intervention outcomes and train recoverability-aware gates from serving-visible attempt state. On \mathfive, selective verification reaches 76.3\% accuracy, compared with 75.5\% for always verifying, while reducing post-generation tokens by 26.8\% and harmful flips from 2.2\% to 1.0\%. However, an 8,192-token initial solve reaches 76.0\% accuracy with 28\% fewer total model tokens, showing that selective recovery is useful but not the best tested cost frontier. In frozen transfer to \gsm, the selective policy verifies only 3.0\% of examples, improves accuracy from 93.4\% to 94.5\%, and reduces verification tokens by 91.2\% relative to always verifying; again, a longer initial solve matches its accuracy with fewer realized tokens. On CommonsenseQA, always-on verification hurts, while Self-Consistency@5 improves accuracy at about five times the realized token cost. The resulting deployment rule is: tune the initial budget first, then use selective recovery when explicit checks, bounded retries, auditability, or regression-risk control matter.

AI.tldr: SEVRA is a deployment-layer controller that selectively invokes verification only when recoverable mistakes are predicted, reducing token waste and harmful flips compared to always-on verification. However, simply increasing the initial solve budget often matches or beats selective verification at lower cost, leading to a deployment rule: optimize initial budget first, then apply selective verification for auditability and regression control.
AI.motivation: Test-time reasoning (verification, self-consistency, etc.) is increasingly used as a serving-time control knob, but extra reasoning is not uniformly beneficial — it can fix errors, waste compute on already-correct answers, or introduce harmful flips. The authors frame this as a deployment allocation problem: given a frozen solver, when should a verifier be invoked to maximize accuracy while minimizing unnecessary computation and regression risk?
AI.method: The authors propose SEVRA (Selective Verification for Reasoning Allocation), a serving-layer gating mechanism. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B solver, they log intervention outcomes from verification attempts and train recoverability-aware gates based on serving-visible attempt state (e.g., solver confidence, trace features). The gate predicts whether verification is likely to repair an incorrect answer, and only invokes the verifier when expected benefit outweighs cost. The system is evaluated on MATH500, GSM8K, and CommonsenseQA, with comparisons against always-verify, never-verify, longer initial solves, and Self-Consistency@5 baselines.
AI.result: On MATH500, SEVRA achieves 76.3% accuracy vs. 75.5% for always-verifying, reduces post-generation tokens by 26.8%, and cuts harmful flips from 2.2% to 1.0%. However, an 8,192-token initial solve reaches 76.0% with 28% fewer total tokens. On GSM8K (frozen transfer), the gate verifies only 3.0% of examples, improves accuracy from 93.4% to 94.5%, and reduces verification tokens by 91.2% vs. always-verifying; again, a longer solve matches this accuracy with fewer tokens. On CommonsenseQA, always-on verification hurts performance, while Self-Consistency@5 improves accuracy at ~5× token cost.
AI.conclusion: The deployment rule distilled by the authors is: tune the initial solve budget first, then use selective verification when explicit checks, bounded retries, auditability, or regression-risk control are required. Selective verification is useful but not the best cost frontier — a longer initial solve is often more token-efficient.

title: Interactive Pareto navigation for deep multi-task learning
summary: In multi-task learning, handling an increasing number of objectives can quickly become challenging, both in terms of the computational resources and the decision maker's capacity to choose appropriate trade-offs. A widely used approach is thus to aggregate the individual losses in a single loss function by a weighted sum. This often fails to capture either the decision maker's preferences as a result of the shape of the Pareto front, or requires multiple adjustments and computations which becomes prohibitively expensive in deep learning applications. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework, Preference Pareto Exploration (PPE), which enforces the decision maker's preferences while accounting for the geometry of the Pareto set in an interactive exploration process. PPE is based on a predictor-corrector method that performs predictor steps tangential to the manifold of Pareto-optimal solutions, following the decision maker's preference. The subsequent corrector step results in a new trade-off reflecting this preference. To avoid explicit Hessian computations when characterizing the tangent space of the manifold, we employ a Krylov subspace method that relies solely on matrix-vector products. These products can be efficiently obtained via automatic differentiation, ensuring both efficiency and robustness throughout the optimization process. The method's functionality and performance are demonstrated using both toy problems and examples from deep learning.

AI.tldr: PPE is a predictor-corrector framework for multi-task learning that explores the Pareto front according to user preferences, using Krylov subspace methods to avoid explicit Hessian computations.
AI.motivation: Weighted-sum aggregation in multi-task learning often fails to capture decision maker preferences due to Pareto front geometry, and alternative methods require prohibitively expensive computations in deep learning contexts.
AI.method: PPE uses a predictor-corrector method: predictor steps move tangentially along the Pareto-optimal manifold following user preferences, corrector steps yield new trade-offs. Tangent space characterization employs Krylov subspace methods with matrix-vector products from automatic differentiation, avoiding explicit Hessian computation.
AI.result: The method demonstrates functionality and performance on both toy problems and deep learning examples.
AI.conclusion: PPE enables efficient interactive Pareto front exploration that respects decision maker preferences while remaining computationally feasible for deep learning applications.

title: AutoPass: Evidence-Guided LLM Agents for Compiler Performance Tuning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for code compilation tasks, but applying them to runtime performance tuning is difficult due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy runtime measurements. We present AutoPass, a multi-agent framework for compiler performance tuning that uses compiler and runtime evidence to guide LLM-generated optimization decisions. Rather than treating the compiler as a black box like prior auto-tuning schemes, AutoPass opens up the compiler to the LLM, enabling it to query compiler-internal optimization states and analyze the intermediate representation to orchestrate compiler options. The search process iteratively refines optimization configurations using measured runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and guide latency-improving edits. AutoPass operates in an inference-only, training-free setting and requires no offline training or task-specific fine-tuning, making it readily applicable to new benchmarks and platforms. We implement AutoPass on the LLVM compiler and evaluate it on server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64 systems. AutoPass outperforms expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods, achieving geometric-mean speedups of 1.043x and 1.117x over LLVM -O3 on x86-64 and ARM64, respectively.

AI.tldr: AutoPass is a multi-agent LLM-based framework that opens up compiler-internal states to guide optimization decisions, using runtime feedback to iteratively refine configurations. It achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.043× (x86-64) and 1.117× (ARM64) over LLVM -O3 without any training or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise for code compilation but struggle with runtime performance tuning due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy runtime measurements. Prior auto-tuning approaches treat the compiler as a black box, missing rich internal optimization state that could inform better decisions.
AI.method: AutoPass employs a multi-agent framework where LLM agents query compiler-internal optimization states and analyze LLVM intermediate representation (IR) to orchestrate compiler options. The search process iteratively refines optimization configurations using measured runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and guide latency-improving edits. It operates inference-only and training-free.
AI.result: On server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64 systems, AutoPass achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.043× and 1.117× over LLVM -O3, respectively, outperforming both expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods.
AI.conclusion: Opening up compiler-internal states to LLM-guided reasoning, combined with iterative runtime-feedback-driven refinement, enables effective and portable compiler performance tuning without the overhead of offline training or per-platform fine-tuning.

title: CREDENCE: Claim Reduction for Decomposition & Enhanced Credibility -- Semantic Metrics and Convergence Analysis
comment: 40 pages, 6 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to Language Resources and Evaluation
summary: Decomposing compound sentences into atomic, verifiable claims is a prerequisite for reliable automated fact-checking. Prior work has relied on token-overlap (Jaccard) metrics that systematically underestimate decomposition quality for paraphrastic claims, and has lacked formal termination analysis for the repair loop. We present Credence, a revised claim decomposition and evaluation framework addressing both shortcomings. Our contributions are: (1) Semantic-F1: we use BGE-large cosine similarity fidelity metric that resolves Jaccard's penalisation and improves downstream fact-checking accuracy; (2) Convergence theorems: we formally characterise four properties of the repair pipeline, establishing that rule-based repair is monotone and finitely terminating under an oracle parser assumption; LLM-based self-repair is provably non-monotone and requires an early-exit guard; (3) Three evaluation benchmarks spanning social-media, encyclopaedic, and news domains for cross-domain generalisation measurement; (4) Multi-model benchmarking across four decomposer models (3.8B-12B) and a closed API model. Experiments on SocialClaimSplit, WikiSplitBench, and ClaimDecompBench show that Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by +15-32pp. EPR ranges from 0.94 to 1.00 on SocialClaimSplit and WikiSplitBench, while ClaimDecompBench includes lower base EPR cases (down to 0.824) due to harder news-domain constructions, and rule-repair reduces the Atomicity Violation Rate (AVR) by 47-100% relative to the base model without degrading fidelity.

AI.tldr: Credence introduces Semantic-F1 (BGE-large cosine similarity) to replace Jaccard metrics for evaluating compound-to-atomic claim decomposition, provides formal convergence proofs for both rule-based and LLM-based repair pipelines, and benchmarks across three domains, showing +15–32pp improvement over Jaccard-F1 and 47–100% relative reduction in Atomicity Violation Rate via rule-based repair.
AI.motivation: Existing claim decomposition evaluation relies on token-overlap metrics (Jaccard) that penalise paraphrastic claims, underestimating decomposition quality and harming downstream fact-checking accuracy. Additionally, prior repair pipelines lack formal termination guarantees, risking infinite loops or degraded output.
AI.method: Credence proposes: (1) Semantic-F1 using BGE-large cosine similarity as a fidelity metric; (2) formal convergence analysis proving rule-based repair is monotone and finitely terminating under an oracle parser, while LLM self-repair is non-monotone requiring early-exit; (3) three cross-domain benchmarks (SocialClaimSplit, WikiSplitBench, ClaimDecompBench); (4) evaluation across four decomposer models (3.8B–12B) plus a closed API model, measuring Exact Parse Ratio (EPR), Atomicity Violation Rate (AVR), and fidelity.
AI.result: Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by +15–32pp across benchmarks. EPR ranges 0.94–1.00 on SocialClaimSplit and WikiSplitBench, dropping to 0.824 on harder news-domain ClaimDecompBench. Rule-based repair reduces AVR by 47–100% relative without degrading fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-F1 is a robust, paraphrase-tolerant alternative to Jaccard-based evaluation. Rule-based repair is provably convergent and effective at reducing atomicity violations, while LLM-based self-repair requires explicit early-exit guards due to non-monotonicity. Cross-domain benchmarking reveals news-domain claims as significantly harder, motivating future work on domain-adaptive decomposition.

title: Human-on-the-Loop Orchestration for AI-Assisted Legal Discovery
summary: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in electronic discovery (e-discovery), where compounding errors across multi-step reasoning chains can constitute legal malpractice. Unlike single-turn retrieval, agentic workflows operating over privileged document corpora exhibit a class of failure we term "trajectory collapse": an early misclassification silently propagates, rendering an entire privilege review invalid. This paper makes three contributions. First, we propose a structured taxonomy of agentic failures in legal information retrieval, organized by functional stage. Second, we introduce a four-layer verification architecture -- spanning planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty quantification -- designed to intercept these failures before they compound. Third, we present a preliminary simulation study on a synthetic e-discovery corpus that demonstrates how mandatory Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) escalation thresholds reduce privilege-waiver risk relative to fully autonomous baselines. Our results suggest that calibrated uncertainty thresholds can reduce privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% versus fully autonomous deployment, while routing fewer than one quarter of documents to attorney review.

AI.tldr: LLM agents in e-discovery suffer from "trajectory collapse," where early errors compound and invalidate privilege review. The paper proposes a failure taxonomy, a four-layer verification architecture with Human-on-the-Loop escalation, and shows via simulation that calibrated uncertainty thresholds reduce privilege-waiver risk by 61% while routing under 25% of documents to attorney review.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM workflows in e-discovery operate over privileged document corpora and exhibit compounding errors across multi-step reasoning chains. A single early misclassification can silently propagate, rendering entire privilege reviews invalid and constituting potential legal malpractice. This "trajectory collapse" problem lacks systematic characterization and mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The paper makes three contributions: (1) a structured taxonomy of agentic failures in legal information retrieval organized by functional stage; (2) a four-layer verification architecture spanning planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty quantification to intercept failures before compounding; and (3) a preliminary simulation study on a synthetic e-discovery corpus comparing mandatory Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) escalation thresholds against fully autonomous baselines.
AI.result: Calibrated uncertainty thresholds reduced privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% compared to fully autonomous deployment, while routing fewer than 25% of documents to attorney review, demonstrating a favorable risk-efficiency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Mandatory HOTL escalation with calibrated uncertainty thresholds provides a practical mechanism to mitigate trajectory collapse in legal AI agents, balancing risk reduction against human review burden in high-stakes e-discovery settings.

title: Techniques for Peak Memory Reduction for LoRA Fine-tuning of LLMs on Edge Devices
comment: Hassan Dbouk and Matthias Reisser contributed equally to this work
summary: Fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on an end-user's data offers personalized experiences while keeping data private, but faces severe memory constraints on consumer hardware. Peak memory during fine-tuning often exceeds device limits, especially for models with billions of parameters and long-context training data. This paper introduces a suite of complementary techniques to reduce memory footprint without sacrificing model quality: (1) base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, (2) memory-efficient checkpointing combining selective activation caching and disk offloading, (3) softmax approximation using semantically relevant token subsets, and (4) logits masking. Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B demonstrate up to $26\times$ and $28\times$ reduction in peak memory, enabling fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes four complementary memory-reduction techniques—base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, memory-efficient checkpointing with selective activation caching and disk offloading, softmax approximation via semantically relevant token subsets, and logits masking—to enable LoRA fine-tuning of multi-billion-parameter LLMs on consumer hardware, achieving up to 28× peak memory reduction on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B.
AI.motivation: LoRA fine-tuning on end-user data enables personalized, privacy-preserving LLM adaptation, but peak memory demands during training far exceed consumer hardware limits—especially for billion-parameter models with long-context data. Existing solutions address memory piecemeal, leaving a need for a comprehensive, integrated approach that preserves model quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce a suite of four techniques: (1) Base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization during forward/backward passes to reduce weight memory; (2) Memory-efficient checkpointing combining selective activation caching (storing only essential activations for gradient computation) with disk offloading of remaining states; (3) Softmax approximation that restricts attention computation to semantically relevant token subsets rather than the full sequence; and (4) Logits masking to reduce memory in the output projection layer.
AI.result: Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B show up to 26× and 28× peak memory reduction respectively, making fine-tuning feasible on resource-constrained consumer devices without sacrificing model quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed integrated memory-reduction techniques collectively enable practical, privacy-preserving LoRA fine-tuning of large models on consumer hardware, overcoming a critical barrier to personalized on-device LLM adaptation.

title: Probe-and-Refine Tuning of Repository Guidance for Coding Agents
summary: LLM-based coding agents need higher-level operational knowledge about a repository (which files house which subsystems, how to run the test suite, which workflows have historically led to wrong fixes) that does not exist in the code itself. Engineers typically maintain \texttt{AGENTS.md} files to supply this context as instructions for coding agents, but whether they help is contested: recent studies disagree on whether LLM-generated guidance improves or harms agent performance. In this paper we show that how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable, and introduce \emph{probe-and-refine tuning}: a procedure that uses synthetic bug-fix probes to iteratively diagnose and patch a repository's guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, with no agent loop or tool use during tuning. On SWE-bench Verified across four independent trials with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 200 steps, probe-and-refine achieves 33.0\,\% mean resolve rate vs.\ 28.3\,\% for the static knowledge base used to initialize it and 25.5\,\% for an unguided baseline ($p < 0.001$ for both probe-and-refine contrasts). The improvement comes from coverage rather than precision: refined guidance produces evaluable patches for 14.5 percentage points (pp) more instances while per-patch precision remains statistically constant ($\sim$59\,\%, $p = 0.119$), showing that improved guidance helps agents reach the correct file rather than improving the quality of the changes they make. Further, a step-budget experiment shows that guidance is what lets the agent use a larger step budget productively, and a cross-model experiment with NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B finds that the tuning loop degrades when the model cannot generate sufficiently diagnostic output, though per-patch precision remains constant even then.

AI.tldr: Probe-and-refine tuning iteratively improves AGENTS.md guidance files via synthetic bug-fix probes, boosting LLM coding agent resolve rates from 28.3% to 33.0% on SWE-bench Verified by expanding issue coverage (more evaluable patches) rather than improving per-patch precision.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents need repository-level operational knowledge (e.g., which files house which subsystems, how to run tests) that doesn't exist in code. Engineers use AGENTS.md files for this, but existing studies disagree on whether LLM-generated guidance helps or harms agent performance. The key insight is that how guidance is produced—not whether it exists—is the decisive variable.
AI.method: Probe-and-refine tuning: a procedure that uses synthetic bug-fix probes to iteratively diagnose and patch a repository's guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, with no agent loop or tool use during tuning. The process diagnoses where current guidance fails and refines it accordingly, evaluated on SWE-bench Verified across four independent trials with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 200 steps, plus a cross-model experiment with NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B.
AI.result: Probe-and-refine achieves 33.0% mean resolve rate vs. 28.3% for the static knowledge base and 25.5% for unguided baseline (p < 0.001 for both contrasts). The gain comes from coverage: refined guidance produces evaluable patches for 14.5 percentage points more instances, while per-patch precision remains statistically constant (~59%, p = 0.119). Guidance enables productive use of larger step budgets. With a weaker model (Nemotron-3-Nano), the tuning loop degrades when diagnostic output is insufficient, though per-patch precision still remains constant.
AI.conclusion: How guidance is produced is the decisive factor for coding agent performance. Probe-and-refine tuning reliably improves guidance by expanding coverage (helping agents reach correct files) rather than improving change quality. The approach is model-dependent: it requires the tuning model to generate sufficiently diagnostic output, but per-patch precision remains robust even when the tuning loop degrades.

title: Leverage Is Not Reach: A Control-Window Law for Single-Neuron Steering in Language Models
summary: Aligned language models gate behaviors such as refusal and language routing through sparse feed forward neurons, yet no theory predicts when a single neuron intervention controls a behavior coherently rather than collapsing the output. We develop a budget normalized control window framework for single neuron steering. A dose along one write direction reduces to one control coordinate: the alignment between the residual stream and the write, driven along a universal saturation curve in units of a coherence budget set by the residual norm divided by the write norm. Coherent control exists when a behavior trigger lies below the collapse ceiling. The same coordinate governs benign mode switches and refusal; the ceiling follows from weights and one generic forward pass, while triggers are measured at rollout. On fifteen held out neurons, the predicted ceiling has mean absolute error 0.14, about 0.07 in bulk layers, and the committed open or closed verdict holds on eleven against a ten of fifteen majority baseline. Closed cases expose three failure modes rather than violations: collapse before trigger, too little depth to propagate, or a normalization that caps how far one neuron can push. The law explains why local gradient attribution anti predicts control: true controllers write off the readout axis and carry a near zero first order gradient. A forward only contrastive screen made precise by the window recovers controllers that attribution misses. On refusal, the hardest case, intervention success is typed, not scalar: coherent bypass and strict actionable reach separate, so a neuron can flip refusal in fluent, on task text with no actionable content, and genuine actionable reach appears only for three of six audited Llama pivots and only at later rollout horizons. Single neuron steering is therefore a budgeted, typed audit of controllability rather than a fixed dose anecdote.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework—budget-normalized control window—that predicts when and why single-neuron interventions in language models produce coherent behavioral changes versus output collapse. The key insight: control reduces to a single coordinate (alignment between residual stream and write direction) following a universal saturation curve, governed by a coherence budget. The framework explains why gradient attribution fails to identify true controllers and enables a forward-only screening method that recovers them.
AI.motivation: Aligned language models exhibit gating behaviors (refusal, language routing) mediated by sparse feed-forward neurons, but no theory exists to predict when intervening on a single neuron yields coherent behavioral control versus collapsing the model's output. Existing practice relies on anecdotal single-neuron steering without understanding the conditions for reliable controllability.
AI.method: The authors derive a budget-normalized control window framework. A dose along a neuron's write direction reduces to one control coordinate: the alignment between the residual stream and the write vector, which follows a universal saturation curve. The curve is parameterized by a coherence budget (residual norm divided by write norm). Coherent control exists only when a behavior trigger lies below a collapse ceiling. The ceiling is predicted from weights and a single generic forward pass; triggers are measured at rollout. They validate on 15 held-out neurons, analyze failure modes, explain gradient attribution's failure, and develop a forward-only contrastive screen for controller discovery. The framework is applied to refusal, distinguishing coherent bypass from strict actionable reach.
AI.result: Predicted ceiling achieves mean absolute error of 0.14 across 15 held-out neurons (~0.07 in bulk layers). The committed open/closed verdict holds on 11 of 15 neurons against a 10/15 majority baseline. Three failure modes explain closed cases: collapse before trigger, insufficient depth for propagation, or normalization capping. Gradient attribution anti-predicts control because true controllers write off the readout axis with near-zero first-order gradients. The forward-only contrastive screen recovers controllers missed by attribution. On refusal, intervention success is typed rather than scalar: coherent bypass and actionable reach are separable; only 3 of 6 audited Llama pivots show genuine actionable reach, and only at later rollout horizons.
AI.conclusion: Single-neuron steering is properly understood as a budgeted, typed audit of controllability rather than a fixed-dose anecdote. The coherence budget framework provides a principled, predictive theory for when and how individual neurons can coherently control language model behavior, with practical implications for mechanistic interpretability and model auditing.

authors: V V N K Someswara Rao Koduri
title: TelcoAgent: A Scalable 5G Multi-KPM Forecasting With 3GPP-Grounded Explainability
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
summary: Key Performance Measurement (KPM) forecasting is essential for proactive network management of 5G and next-generation telecom networks. However, existing machine learning (ML) approaches face significant limitations in scalability and explainability, restricting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We propose TelcoAgent, a foundation model-based framework that enables accurate, scalable, and explainable forecasting of multiple KPMs across diverse network cells without the need for site-specific training.
