Specifically, the framework comprises three key components: (i) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) knowledge graph directly from specification documents, (ii) a scalable, time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline to deliver accurate, zero-shot forecasting, and finally (iii) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that provides actionable, domain-grounded diagnostics. Evaluated using a 3-month, real-world, city-scale 5G KPM dataset from a U.S.-based network operator, TelcoAgent demonstrates high forecasting accuracy for all 7 considered KPMs per cell across 200 cells, while delivering explainable insights and actionable instructions to address network degradations.

AI.tldr: TelcoAgent is a foundation model-based framework for 5G KPM forecasting that uses a three-agent pipeline combining a 3GPP knowledge graph, a time-series foundation model for zero-shot prediction, and a reasoning module for explainable diagnostics, achieving high accuracy across 200 cells without site-specific training.
AI.motivation: Existing ML approaches for KPM forecasting in 5G networks suffer from poor scalability (requiring site-specific training) and limited explainability, hindering real-world deployment for proactive network management.
AI.method: TelcoAgent consists of three components: (1) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3GPP knowledge graph from specification documents; (2) a scalable time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline for zero-shot forecasting; and (3) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that delivers domain-grounded, actionable diagnostics. The system is evaluated on a 3-month, city-scale real-world 5G KPM dataset from a U.S. operator across 200 cells covering 7 KPMs.
AI.result: TelcoAgent demonstrated high forecasting accuracy for all 7 KPMs across 200 cells, while simultaneously providing explainable insights and actionable instructions for addressing network degradations.
AI.conclusion: The foundation model-based approach effectively overcomes the scalability and explainability limitations of traditional ML methods for 5G KPM forecasting, enabling accurate, zero-shot predictions with domain-grounded diagnostics suitable for real-world network operations.

title: Tracking Representation Dynamics in Large Language Models with Persistent Homology
summary: Large language models are commonly aligned through supervised fine-tuning, yet little is known about how their internal representations evolve during this process. We study alignment dynamics using persistent homology by tracking the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. Across four transformer language models ranging from 1B to 7B parameters and three alignment objectives corresponding to helpful, harmless, and mixed training data, we find that the majority of topological reorganization occurs during the earliest stages of training. A dense checkpoint analysis reveals a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. We further show that different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, while instruction-tuned and pretrained models exhibit qualitatively different patterns of evolution. Our results suggest that persistent homology provides a complementary perspective on alignment, revealing representation-level changes that are not apparent from behavioral metrics alone.

AI.tldr: Using persistent homology to track activation space topology during LLM alignment fine-tuning, the authors find most topological reorganization occurs early in training with a transient peak followed by rapid stabilization, and that different alignment objectives produce distinct topological trajectories.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread use of supervised fine-tuning for LLM alignment, the evolution of internal representations during this process is poorly understood. Behavioral metrics alone cannot capture representation-level changes, motivating a complementary topological perspective.
AI.method: Persistent homology is applied to track the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. Four transformer models (1B–7B parameters) are studied under three alignment objectives (helpful, harmless, mixed). Dense checkpoint analysis captures fine-grained topological dynamics.
AI.result: The majority of topological reorganization occurs in early training stages, marked by a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. Different alignment objectives yield distinguishable topological trajectories, and instruction-tuned versus pretrained models show qualitatively different evolution patterns.
AI.conclusion: Persistent homology offers a valuable complementary lens on alignment, exposing representation-level dynamics invisible to behavioral metrics. The early-stage concentration of topological change and objective-specific trajectories suggest topology as a diagnostic tool for alignment processes.

title: AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning and generation abilities, but their fixed context windows limit long-term information accumulation and reuse across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems often construct memory in a coarse and unstable manner, relying on inefficient memory representations or unstable unconstrained updates. To address these challenges, we propose AtomMem, a long-term memory system designed for value-dense storage and stable memory evolution. AtomMem introduces a Fact Executor, which selectively extracts high value atomic facts from long form interactions to serve as highly efficient memory representations. Subsequently, AtomMem organizes these facts into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, capturing coherent episodic contexts and tracking dynamically evolving user attributes over time. During retrieval, the system activates an associative memory graph to connect fragmented memories. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark confirm that AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks, offering a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents.

AI.tldr: AtomMem is a long-term memory system for LLMs that extracts high-value atomic facts from interactions, organizes them into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, and uses an associative memory graph for retrieval, achieving SOTA on the LoCoMo benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs have fixed context windows that prevent long-term information accumulation across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems suffer from coarse, unstable memory construction with inefficient representations and unconstrained updates.
AI.method: AtomMem consists of three core components: (1) a Fact Executor that selectively extracts high-value atomic facts from long-form interactions as efficient memory representations; (2) hierarchical organization of facts into event structures (for episodic context) and temporal profiles (for tracking evolving user attributes); (3) an associative memory graph activated during retrieval to connect fragmented memories.
AI.result: AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LoCoMo benchmark across various reasoning tasks, demonstrating both scalability and economic viability for intelligent personalized agents.
AI.conclusion: AtomMem provides a scalable, value-dense, and stable long-term memory solution for LLM-based personalized agents, overcoming limitations of prior memory-augmented systems through atomic fact extraction, hierarchical organization, and associative retrieval.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Black-Box Uncertainty Estimation Methods for Large Language Models
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, their outputs often remain unreliable and may contain hallucinations, making uncertainty estimation (UE) essential for building trustworthy LLMs. In practice, many mainstream LLMs are only accessible through restricted APIs, where internal signals such as logits and hidden states are unavailable, making black-box UE especially important. However, existing work on black-box UE for LLMs remains fragmented in methodology and lacks a unified empirical comparison. To address this gap, we present a systematic review of black-box UE methods and organize them into five categories: verbalization-based, sampling-based, explanation-based, multi-agent, and hybrid methods. We further build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings. Our results show that no single method consistently dominates across all settings. Nevertheless, methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective, and hybrid methods that combine multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions. By releasing the benchmark data and a unified evaluation framework, we aim to facilitate reproducible comparisons and support future research, while our empirical findings provide practical guidance for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic review and empirical benchmark of black-box uncertainty estimation methods for LLMs, categorizing 24 methods into five types and evaluating them across 4 models and 4 datasets. Key findings: no single method dominates universally; answer-space reasoning/comparison and hybrid methods are generally most effective.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs are unreliable and prone to hallucination, making uncertainty estimation critical for trustworthiness. However, mainstream LLMs are often API-gated (black-box), preventing access to logits/hidden states. Existing black-box UE work is fragmented with no unified empirical comparison, motivating a systematic review and benchmark.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a systematic taxonomy organizing black-box UE methods into five categories: verbalization-based, sampling-based, explanation-based, multi-agent, and hybrid methods. They then build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings, using standardized metrics for comparison.
AI.result: No single method consistently outperforms across all settings. Methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are broadly effective. Hybrid methods combining multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions.
AI.conclusion: The field lacks a universal black-box UE solution. Answer-space reasoning/comparison and hybrid approaches are the most promising directions. The released benchmark and evaluation framework aim to enable reproducible research and guide future method development.

title: Predicting Mergeability of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Updates
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes it cheap to train many domain- and task-specific language model adapters, but whether two adapters can be merged is usually discovered only after both have been fully trained and evaluated. This late feedback is costly: adapters that are strong in isolation can interfere destructively once their updates are combined. We ask whether this outcome can be anticipated. We formalize adapter mergeability as the degree to which an adapter preserves its single-task utility after merging, and show that it can be forecast from signals measured in the first few percent of training -- chiefly how the low-rank updates and their gradients align across tasks and how much they disturb shared representations. We package these signals into MergeProbe, a lightweight predictor that estimates pairwise and set-level retention and turns the estimate into a concrete decision: merge directly, reweight, prune, or route. On MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark spanning math, code, science, instruction following, and safety, MergeProbe attains the best average and worst-case retention among strong interference-aware merge baselines while adding far less deployment overhead than full task routing. This turns LoRA merging from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem.

AI.tldr: MergeProbe predicts whether two LoRA adapters will interfere destructively when merged, using early-training signals (gradient alignment, representation disturbance) to forecast mergeability within the first few percent of training, transforming adapter merging from post-hoc trial-and-error into an anticipatory measurement problem.
AI.motivation: LoRA enables cheap training of many task-specific adapters, but merging them often causes destructive interference that is only discovered after full training and evaluation — a costly late-feedback loop. The authors aim to anticipate mergeability early in training to avoid wasting compute on incompatible adapter pairs.
AI.method: MergeProbe formalizes mergeability as the degree to which an adapter retains single-task utility post-merge. It forecasts this from early-training signals — specifically (1) alignment of low-rank update matrices and their gradients across tasks, and (2) disturbance to shared representations. These signals are packaged into a lightweight predictor that outputs pairwise and set-level retention estimates, which inform a concrete decision among four actions: merge directly, reweight, prune, or route.
AI.result: On MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark (math, code, science, instruction following, safety), MergeProbe achieves the best average and worst-case retention compared to strong interference-aware merge baselines, with significantly less deployment overhead than full task routing.
AI.conclusion: LoRA merging can be reframed from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem. Early-training signals are sufficient to reliably predict adapter compatibility, enabling proactive merging strategies that save compute and improve retention.

title: Prompt, Plan, Extract: Zero-Shot Agentic LLMs Workflows for Lung Pathology Extraction from Clinical Narratives
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Affiliations: (1) Department of Health Outcomes and Biomedical Informatics, College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA; (2) Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, Department of Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA; (3) College of Nursing, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
summary: Information extraction from pathology reports is essential for cancer staging, tumor registry population. Yet key data remains embedded in narrative reports, making manual extraction labor-intensive and error-prone. Traditional supervised Natural Language Processing pipelines address this through fully supervised Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction, but require expensive manual annotation and suffer cascading failures when upstream entities are missed. In this study, we developed a zero-shot, agentic workflow, and evaluated five open-source generative Large Language Models (LLMs) to populate 13 College of American Pathologists synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. We compared them against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework. The baseline achieved Micro-F1of 0.960, while the best zero-shot model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 (recall: 0.949), accurately extracting complex relations like Pathologic Stage without task-specific training. These results suggest that open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs are a low-cost solution for extracting lung pathology information.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot, agentic workflow using open-source generative LLMs was developed to extract 13 CAP synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. The best model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved a Micro-F1 of 0.893 (recall 0.949), competitive with a supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline (Micro-F1 0.960), demonstrating that open-source LLMs offer a low-cost, training-free alternative for pathology information extraction.
AI.motivation: Manual extraction of structured data from narrative pathology reports is labor-intensive and error-prone. Traditional supervised NER-RE pipelines require costly manual annotation and suffer cascading failures from missed upstream entities. The authors sought a zero-shot approach that eliminates annotation costs and avoids error propagation inherent in pipeline architectures.
AI.method: An agentic workflow was developed using five open-source generative LLMs evaluated in a zero-shot setting to populate 13 College of American Pathologists (CAP) synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. A novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework was introduced. The approach was benchmarked against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE pipeline baseline.
AI.result: The supervised GatorTron baseline achieved a Micro-F1 of 0.960. The best zero-shot model, GPT-OSS-20B, achieved a Micro-F1 of 0.893 with recall of 0.949, successfully extracting complex relational information such as Pathologic Stage without any task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs represent a viable, low-cost solution for extracting structured lung pathology information from narrative reports, approaching the performance of fully supervised methods while eliminating annotation overhead and pipeline error propagation.

title: MetaResearcher: Scaling Deep Research via Self-Reflective Reinforcement Learning in Adversarial Virtual Environments
summary: Deep research agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous information gathering and synthesis, yet their training remains constrained by the static nature of simulated environments, the limits of fact-retrieval-only task designs, and the inefficiency of outcome-based reinforcement learning. In this work, we propose MetaResearcher, a novel framework that scales deep research agent training across four synergistic dimensions. First, we introduce an Evolving Virtual World that injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation into the training environment, forcing agents to develop source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution skills. Second, we design Discovery-Oriented Tasks -- including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution -- that transcend simple fact retrieval and push agents toward genuine research behaviors. Third, we propose a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that jointly optimizes for answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity, directly addressing the repetitive action loop problem observed in prior work. Fourth, we introduce a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture comprising specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative research strategies through coordinated reinforcement learning. Built upon the LiteResearcher infrastructure, MetaResearcher requires zero marginal API cost for training while targeting substantial improvements in both benchmark performance (GAIA, Xbench-DS) and epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. We present the complete framework design, training methodology, and planned experimental validation.

AI.tldr: MetaResearcher proposes a multi-dimensional training framework for deep research agents featuring: (1) an evolving virtual world with temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation, (2) discovery-oriented tasks beyond fact retrieval, (3) a self-reflective meta-reward mechanism within GRPO to combat repetitive action loops, and (4) a heterogeneous multi-agent swarm architecture with specialized roles, all built on LiteResearcher with zero marginal API training cost.
AI.motivation: Current deep research agent training is limited by three key problems: (a) static simulated environments that fail to reflect real-world temporal dynamics, (b) task designs restricted to fact retrieval, which do not foster genuine research behaviors like hypothesis generation, and (c) outcome-based reinforcement learning that is inefficient and prone to repetitive action loops. The authors aim to overcome these limitations through a synergistic, multi-dimensional training framework.
AI.method: The framework scales training across four dimensions: (1) Evolving Virtual World — injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation to train source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution; (2) Discovery-Oriented Tasks — includes hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution tasks that go beyond fact retrieval; (3) Self-Reflective Meta-Reward — a mechanism within the GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) framework that jointly optimizes answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity; (4) Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm — specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models learn collaborative strategies via coordinated reinforcement learning. Training is built on the LiteResearcher infrastructure with zero marginal API cost.
AI.result: The paper presents the complete framework design and training methodology. Experimental validation is planned but not yet reported; the authors target substantial improvements on GAIA and Xbench-DS benchmarks, as well as enhanced epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions.
AI.conclusion: MetaResearcher offers a comprehensive blueprint for training more robust, genuinely research-capable agents by simultaneously addressing environment dynamics, task complexity, reward design, and multi-agent collaboration. The framework's zero-cost training paradigm and focus on epistemic robustness represent a significant architectural contribution, though empirical results are forthcoming.

title: Displacement Is Not Direction: Evaluating Fidelity Metrics for Quantized LLM Deployment
summary: Fidelity metrics, such as per-token KL divergence (KLD) against a high-precision reference, are often used in practice as low-cost proxies for benchmark quality. We test this practice on a 28-quant cohort of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and a 41-quant cohort of Devstral-Small-2-24B, evaluated across a suite of downstream benchmarks. We find that KLD is strongly correlated with benchmark score over the full cohort ($ρ=-0.72$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.86$ on Devstral, both with $p<0.001$). However, this relationship collapses to non-significance in the near-baseline silent zone ($ρ=+0.00$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.24$, $p=0.36$, on Devstral). This collapse persists across 14 measurement variants, including different KLD aggregations, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, and context lengths. At the per-prompt level, KLD has only weak failure-prediction power on code, with failed-vs-passed geometric-mean ratios in $[1.08,1.22]$ across five models on LiveCodeBench, and fails as a cross-model router, achieving only $42.3\%-49.4\%$ accuracy on disagreement prompts. We trace the collapse to a structural decomposition: KLD primarily measures the volume of disagreement with the reference, with silent-zone composite $ρ=+0.94$ ($p<0.001$) on Qwen and $+0.55$ ($p=0.03$) on Devstral, while its relationship to the direction of those disagreements is weak and task-conditional.

AI.tldr: KLD strongly correlates with benchmark scores across full quantization cohorts, but this correlation collapses to non-significance in the near-baseline "silent zone," because KLD primarily measures disagreement volume rather than direction.
AI.motivation: Challenge the common practice of using per-token KL divergence against a high-precision reference as a low-cost proxy for downstream benchmark quality, particularly in the practically relevant regime of near-baseline (mildly degraded) models.
AI.method: Evaluated two large quantization cohorts (28 quants of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 41 quants of Devstral-Small-2-24B) across downstream benchmarks. Measured correlation between KLD and benchmark scores over full vs. near-baseline cohorts. Tested 14 KLD measurement variants (aggregations, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, context lengths). Conducted per-prompt failure prediction on LiveCodeBench and cross-model routing experiments. Performed structural decomposition of KLD into disagreement volume and direction components.
AI.result: Full-cohort Spearman: ρ=-0.72 (Qwen) and ρ=-0.86 (Devstral), both p<0.001. Silent-zone: ρ=+0.00 (Qwen) and ρ=-0.24 (p=0.36, Devstral). Collapse persists across all 14 measurement variants. Per-prompt failure-prediction: geometric-mean ratios 1.08–1.22 (weak). Cross-model routing accuracy: 42.3%–49.4%. Disagreement volume vs. silent-zone composite ρ=+0.94 (Qwen) and +0.55 (p=0.03, Devstral); direction relationship is weak and task-conditional.
AI.conclusion: KLD is a reliable quality proxy only across large quality gaps; it fails in the near-baseline regime because it captures how much the model disagrees rather than whether those disagreements matter for task performance. Practitioners should not rely on KLD for fine-grained model selection among high-quality candidates.

title: Large Language Models Do Not Always Need Readable Language
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly prompted and interfaced with human-readable natural language, even when the intended reader is another model. This paper investigates whether semantic information can be encoded in compact, non-standard textual forms that sacrifice human readability while remaining recoverable by LLMs. We refer to this class of model-centric textual representations as BabelTele, approached here not as a fixed protocol but as an empirical probe into LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret such representations. Through readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires, and downstream task evaluations, we find that BabelTele can substantially depart from ordinary natural language while preserving core semantics for instruction-tuned LLMs. As a task-agnostic representational paradigm, BabelTele demonstrates high information density, maintaining 99.5% semantic fidelity even when the text volume is condensed to 27.9% of its original length. We further evaluate its semantic robustness in cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication. Results suggest that BabelTele can reduce context overhead while generally maintaining reliable downstream performance, although its effectiveness depends on the compressor-reader pair and task setting. These findings indicate that human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled, opening a path toward model-native representations in future exploration of LLM systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "BabelTele," a class of compact, non-standard textual representations for LLM-to-LLM communication that sacrifices human readability but preserves semantic recoverability. Experiments show BabelTele can condense text to 27.9% of its original length while retaining 99.5% semantic fidelity, demonstrating that human readability and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled.
AI.motivation: LLMs are typically prompted using human-readable natural language even when the intended reader is another model. The authors question whether this constraint is necessary and explore whether more compact, model-native textual representations can reduce context overhead while preserving semantics for downstream tasks.
AI.method: The authors empirically probe LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret non-standard textual representations (BabelTele) through: (1) readability diagnostics measuring departure from natural language, (2) model likelihood measures, (3) human questionnaires assessing interpretability, and (4) downstream task evaluations. They further test semantic robustness across cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication settings.
AI.result: BabelTele achieves 99.5% semantic fidelity while condensing text to 27.9% of its original length, demonstrating high information density. It maintains reliable downstream performance in agent memory and multi-agent communication scenarios, though effectiveness depends on the specific compressor-reader model pair and task setting.
AI.conclusion: Human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled. BabelTele opens a path toward model-native representations, suggesting future LLM systems could communicate via more efficient, non-human-readable protocols without significant semantic loss.

title: Understanding Key Features of Time Series Foundation Models from Epidemic Forecasting
summary: Seasonal influenza infects millions of people and causes substantial morbidity and mortality in the United States each year, making accurate short-term forecasting a core public-health need. Reliable forecasts of epidemic time series can inform vaccination timing, hospital staffing, and resource allocation, yet the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using influenza-like illness surveillance and influenza-associated hospitalization time series under both temporal and spatial generalization settings for 1-4-week-ahead prediction. We compare classical neural network architectures, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. Across tasks, we demonstrate that a mixture-of-experts model that fuses multiple pretrained forecasters achieves the strongest overall performance, indicating that heterogeneous pretrained representations provide complementary predictive information. Our results further show that numerical transformer-based models produce reliable forecasts, while pretraining provides the largest gains at longer horizons, particularly when the pretraining domain is mechanistically aligned with influenza dynamics. In contrast, LLM-based time series methods underperform relative to numerical forecasters in this setting. Finally, we examine hospitalization information as both an auxiliary covariate and a pretraining source. Hospitalization signals provide complementary improvements in selected settings and clarify when additional surveillance streams enhance the robustness of multi-horizon forecasting. These findings provide actionable guidance on model selection, pretraining strategy, and auxiliary-signal use for influenza preparedness.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting comparing classical neural networks, numerical transformers, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based approaches. A mixture-of-experts fusing pretrained forecasters achieves the best performance. Numerical transformers are reliable, pretraining helps most at longer horizons when domain-aligned, while LLM-based methods underperform. Hospitalization signals provide complementary value in selected settings.
AI.motivation: Accurate short-term influenza forecasting is a critical public-health need for vaccination timing, hospital staffing, and resource allocation. However, the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized, leaving a gap in actionable guidance for model selection and pretraining strategy.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using ILI surveillance and influenza-associated hospitalization time series under temporal and spatial generalization for 1-4-week-ahead prediction. Compared classical neural networks, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches, including a mixture-of-experts model fusing multiple pretrained forecasters. Also examined hospitalization data as auxiliary covariate and pretraining source.
AI.result: The mixture-of-experts model fusing heterogeneous pretrained forecasters achieved the strongest overall performance. Numerical transformer-based models produced reliable forecasts. Pretraining provided the largest gains at longer horizons, especially when the pretraining domain aligned mechanistically with influenza dynamics. LLM-based time series methods underperformed relative to numerical forecasters. Hospitalization signals provided complementary improvements in selected settings.
AI.conclusion: Findings provide actionable guidance on model selection (favor mixture-of-experts and numerical transformers over LLM-based approaches), pretraining strategy (domain-aligned pretraining is most beneficial at longer horizons), and auxiliary-signal use (hospitalization data offers complementary value) for influenza preparedness.

title: The Almost Intelligent Revolution: Options for Scaling Up Deliberation and Empowering People with AI
comment: Published in /Handbook of Democracy in the Era of Artificial Intelligence/ edited by Evangelos Pournaras, Srijoni Majumdar, Carina Ines Hausladen, and Dirk Helbing. 2026
summary: The increasing prominence of Large Language Models (LLMs) in public discourse presents both opportunities and challenges for democratic deliberation. While red teaming strategies help mitigate specific risks, broader concerns persist regarding linguistic constraints, biases, and the sycophantic tendencies of LLMs. This chapter explores how LLMs can be used to significantly scale up and democratise deliberation, particularly in fostering inclusivity and empowering traditionally marginalised groups. Drawing on concepts from Systemic-Functional Linguistics, the chapter examines how variations across language users (for example, with respect to socio-demographic groups) and across language use (for example, with respect to communicative functions) shape participation in AI-supported deliberation. The chapter presents AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their potential to scaffold argumentation, enhance access, and reduce the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms and biases which are embedded in prestigious registers. At the same time, the chapter cautions against both overclaiming, which leads to unrealistic expectations, and underclaiming, which risks missed opportunities for AI-assisted engagement. The chapter concludes by identifying future research directions to maximise the democratic potential of AI-assisted participation while embedding ethical safeguards to counteract the reproduction of linguistic inequalities.

AI.tldr: This chapter examines how LLMs can scale up democratic deliberation by fostering inclusivity for marginalized groups, using Systemic-Functional Linguistics to analyze how language variation (across users and functions) shapes AI-supported participation. It advocates balancing AI's potential against overclaiming and underclaiming, and calls for ethical safeguards against linguistic inequality.
AI.motivation: LLMs in public discourse create opportunities and challenges for democratic deliberation. While red teaming mitigates specific risks, deeper concerns about linguistic constraints, biases, and sycophantic tendencies remain unaddressed. There is a need to explore how LLMs can democratize deliberation at scale, especially for marginalized groups, while grappling with how language variation shapes participation.
AI.method: The chapter applies concepts from Systemic-Functional Linguistics (SFL) to analyze two dimensions of language variation: variation across language users (socio-demographic groups) and variation across language use (communicative functions). It reviews AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their capacity to scaffold argumentation, improve access, and counter exclusionary linguistic norms embedded in prestigious registers.
AI.result: AI-driven deliberation shows promise in scaffolding argumentation, enhancing access, and reducing the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms and biases tied to prestigious registers. However, risks of overclaiming (unrealistic expectations) and underclaiming (missed opportunities) must be carefully managed.
AI.conclusion: Future research should maximize AI-assisted democratic participation while embedding ethical safeguards to prevent the reproduction of linguistic inequalities. A balanced approach between optimism and caution is essential for realizing LLMs' democratic potential.

title: eCNNTO: A Highly Generalizable ConvNet for Accelerating Topology Optimization
summary: This work proposes an element-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to accelerate density-based Topology Optimization (TO), termed eCNNTO. TO generally undergoes a large number of iterations, where finite element analysis is performed in every iteration, leading to the efficiency bottleneck especially when dense meshes are used to achieve high-resolution designs. To address this limitation, eCNNTO is proposed to build upon Kallioras et al. (2020), where a Deep Belief Network (DBN) was trained for every element to predict its near-optimal density from its early history, thereby skipping the great majority of iterations and significantly accelerating the TO procedure. However, the method lacks spatial correlations among neighboring elements and may lead to disconnected features in the final structure. The proposed method employs CNN with residual connections to address this issue. On top of it, a novel training strategy is introduced to further enhance the optimization efficiency, where the training dataset consists of the final stage density histories rather than early ones. This change can also help reduce the required training data size. eCNNTO requires only a small dataset to train and yet it can be generalized to problems with largely different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, as well as non-design domains. In the end, the generalization capabilities and efficiency of eCNNTO are demonstrated through a variety of examples in two and three dimensions, achieving up to 90% and 97% reduction of iterations, respectively.

AI.tldr: eCNNTO proposes an element-based CNN with residual connections to accelerate density-based topology optimization by predicting final-stage densities from early optimization history, achieving up to 90% (2D) and 97% (3D) iteration reduction while preserving spatial correlations and generalizing across diverse problem configurations.
AI.motivation: Topology optimization is computationally expensive due to repeated finite element analyses across many iterations, especially for high-resolution designs. Prior work (Kallioras et al., 2020) used a Deep Belief Network per element to predict near-optimal densities and skip iterations, but it lacked spatial correlations among neighboring elements, leading to disconnected structural features. There is a need for a method that both accelerates TO and maintains spatial continuity.
AI.method: The authors propose eCNNTO, an element-based CNN with residual connections that captures spatial correlations among neighboring elements. Unlike prior DBN-based approaches that train on early-stage density histories, eCNNTO introduces a novel training strategy using final-stage density histories, which enhances optimization efficiency and reduces training data requirements. The method trains on a small dataset yet generalizes to varying boundary conditions, loading cases, domain geometries, mesh resolutions, and non-design domains.
AI.result: eCNNTO achieved up to 90% reduction in iterations for 2D problems and up to 97% reduction for 3D problems. The method demonstrated strong generalization across diverse problem configurations, including different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, and presence of non-design domains, all while requiring only a small training dataset.
AI.conclusion: The element-based CNN with residual connections and final-stage density history training effectively overcomes the spatial correlation limitation of prior element-wise DBN approaches, enabling highly efficient topology optimization with significant iteration reduction and robust generalization across varied problem settings.

title: Advances in Scientific Machine Learning for Coupled Fluid Flow and Transport
summary: This chapter reviews recent advances in Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) for modeling coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena governed by the incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport equations. Such systems, found in applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection, feature strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior that make high-fidelity simulations computationally expensive. To address this, the chapter surveys state-of-the-art SciML methods for building efficient surrogate models, including linear reduced-order techniques based on Singular Value Decomposition (such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition) and nonlinear neural network approaches like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and $β$-Variational Autoencoders ($β$-VAEs). It first covers the authors' work combining these models with High Performance Computing strategies, including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening (AMR/C) and scientific floating-point data compression. It then presents two new contributions: surrogate modeling of turbidity currents via PINNs, and the extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows using $β$-VAEs. Governing equations and representative benchmarks, including lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, illustrate these methodologies. The chapter is intentionally long, covering both the mathematical and physical foundations of coupled fluid flow and the computational aspects of state-of-the-art modeling. Overall, it demonstrates how SciML enables fast, accurate approximations of complex coupled systems within the specific data regimes and modeling assumptions considered, while substantially reducing computational cost relative to full-order simulations. Broader capabilities such as real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain active research directions whose feasibility depends strongly on the problem at hand.

AI.tldr: Surveys SciML techniques—including POD/DMD, PINNs, and β-VAEs—for building computationally efficient surrogate models of coupled incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport flows, with new contributions on PINN-based turbidity current modeling and β-VAE extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal convection.
AI.motivation: Coupled fluid flow and transport systems (e.g., turbidity currents, thermal convection) involve strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale physics, rendering high-fidelity full-order simulations prohibitively expensive. There is a need for efficient surrogate models that preserve accuracy while dramatically reducing computational cost.
AI.method: Reviews linear reduced-order methods (SVD-based, including DMD) and nonlinear neural network approaches (PINNs, β-VAEs). Integrates these with HPC strategies: Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening (AMR/C) and scientific floating-point data compression. Introduces two new applications: (1) PINN-based surrogate modeling of turbidity currents, and (2) β-VAE extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from Rayleigh-Bénard thermal flows. Uses lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection as illustrative benchmarks.
AI.result: Demonstrates that SciML surrogates achieve fast, accurate approximations of coupled fluid-transport systems under specified data regimes and modeling assumptions, with substantial computational savings versus full-order simulations. PINNs effectively model turbidity currents; β-VAEs successfully extract disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal convection.
AI.conclusion: SciML enables efficient surrogate modeling of computationally expensive coupled flow-transport problems. Broader capabilities like real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain open challenges, with feasibility dependent on the specific problem context.

title: QMFOL: Benchmarking Large Language Model Reasoning via Quantifiable Monadic First-Order Logic Test Case Generation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant progress in reasoning, particularly in deductive reasoning, which is crucial for high-stakes decision-making. As models improve, evaluation benchmarks should evolve to keep pace. However, existing benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency.
  To address these issues, we propose QMFOL, an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with quantifiable and controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures using conjunction and disjunction patterns, enabling precise control over reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors. These structures are then translated into natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency ensured through round-trip verification using an external prover. Based on our framework, we build QMFOLBench, a benchmark comprising 2880 instances with 960 configurations across diverse logical and semantic dimensions. Evaluations on six large reasoning models (LRMs) and two LLMs show that performance degrades and computational overhead increases with rising logical complexity. Models perform better on True-labeled tasks than on False or Unknown ones, and exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation. Overall, QMFOL offers a scalable and reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

AI.tldr: QMFOL is an automated framework that generates monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures using conjunction/disjunction patterns, translates them to natural language via LLMs, and verifies consistency with an external prover. The resulting QMFOLBench (2880 instances, 960 configurations) reveals that model performance degrades with increasing logical complexity, and models show sensitivity to label type and semantic variation.
AI.motivation: Existing deductive reasoning benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and fail to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency. As LLMs improve, benchmarks must evolve to keep pace, requiring scalable, controllable, and reliable evaluation frameworks.
AI.method: QMFOL generates monadic first-order logic problems by: (1) constructing formal logical structures with tunable parameters—reasoning depth, width, label types (True/False/Unknown), and distractors—using conjunction and disjunction patterns; (2) translating these structures into natural language using LLMs; and (3) ensuring logical consistency via round-trip verification with an external automated prover (e.g., Z3). The resulting QMFOLBench contains 2880 instances across 960 configurations spanning diverse logical and semantic dimensions.
AI.result: Evaluation on six large reasoning models and two LLMs shows: (1) performance degrades and computational overhead (inference time/tokens) increases as logical complexity rises; (2) models perform better on True-labeled tasks than False or Unknown ones; and (3) models exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation in problem presentation.
AI.conclusion: QMFOL provides a scalable, reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with precise, quantifiable control over complexity, enabling more rigorous and fine-grained evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

title: REDACT: A Systematically Controlled Multilingual Benchmark for Personal Information Detection
summary: Benchmark infrastructure for personally identifiable information (PII) detection remains limited: existing corpora cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and do not show which surface conditions cause detector failures. We present REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,427 records, 324,078 entity annotations, 51 entity types, 4,127 surface-form patterns, and 25 languages across 9 scripts. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes: domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, and co-occurrence. Three entity-level metadata fields (disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier) enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate or per-type F1. From the full benchmark, we evaluate five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,000 records. Aggregate F1 masks an architecture-dependent failure structure: the rule-based detector performs poorly on the highest-stakes data, including HIGH-sensitivity categories (recall 0.07) and non-verbatim disclosure forms, while the LLM detectors remain more robust, with the HIGH tier as their strongest sensitivity slice. A three-model reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment corroborates that sensitivity-tier assignment is the task's hardest axis. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and stratified evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: REDACT is a multilingual PII detection benchmark with systematic control over nine generation axes, 51 entity types across 25 languages. Evaluation of five detectors reveals aggregate F1 masks critical failure patterns: rule-based systems fail on high-sensitivity entities, while LLMs prove more robust, with sensitivity-tier assignment being the hardest axis.
AI.motivation: Existing PII detection benchmarks are limited in entity type coverage, lack systematic control over generation conditions, and fail to reveal which surface conditions cause detector failures. This obscures critical weaknesses, particularly for high-stakes, high-sensitivity data.
AI.method: The authors construct REDACT using a strength-2 covering-array sampler controlling nine axes (domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, co-occurrence). The benchmark comprises 13,427 records with 324,078 entity annotations, 51 entity types, and 4,127 surface-form patterns across 25 languages/9 scripts. Three entity-level metadata fields — disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier — enable stratified evaluation. Five detectors (rule-based Presidio, GLiNER, OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are evaluated on a locked stratified 1,000-record sample.
AI.result: Aggregate F1 conceals architecture-dependent failure structures. The rule-based Presidio achieves only 0.07 recall on HIGH-sensitivity categories and struggles with non-verbatim disclosure forms. LLM-based detectors are more robust, with the HIGH sensitivity tier as their strongest slice. A reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment confirms sensitivity-tier assignment as the hardest axis of the task.
AI.conclusion: Systematically controlled benchmarking with fine-grained metadata is essential for exposing PII detector weaknesses. LLM-based approaches significantly outperform rule-based systems on high-stakes, high-sensitivity PII detection. The benchmark, schema, prompts, and evaluation harness are publicly released.

title: The Tao of Agency: Autotelic AI, Embedded Agency and Dissolution of the Self
summary:
Most artificial intelligence systems are built on the assumption that goals are exogenous and specified by the designer. Exploring what happens when an agent begins generating its own goals opens the field of autotelic AI. Agents are expected not merely to pursue objectives but to discover them. In this article, we trace its consequences through intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness; the last of which is found to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embeddedness individuates the agent at the cost of revealing that the individuation is non-unique, such that the same dynamics admit many valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self.
  The deepest problem with autotelic AI is therefore not how the agent generates goals, but how it generates and relativizes the self to which the goals are assigned. The agent must believe in its own boundary in order to act, and see through that boundary in order to understand. We consolidate these developments into a single framework and extend it along three directions: a quantum formulation in which the agent-environment cut becomes physical, a philosophical reading against non-dual contemplative traditions, and a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.

AI.tldr: This paper explores autotelic AI—agents that generate their own goals—and argues that the deepest challenge is not goal generation but self-individuation: how an agent defines and relativizes the self to which goals belong. Embeddedness is necessary but not sufficient for autotelic agency, as it reveals multiple valid self-boundaries. The authors propose a unified framework extending into quantum formulations, non-dual philosophy, and LLM-based implementation.
AI.motivation: Most AI systems treat goals as externally specified by designers. The paper challenges this by examining what happens when agents generate their own goals (autotelic AI), arguing that the core unresolved problem is not goal generation itself but the more fundamental issue of how an agent constitutes and relativizes its own identity—the "self" that owns those goals.
AI.method: The paper traces consequences of autotelic agency through several conceptual lenses: intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness. It consolidates these into a unified framework and extends it along three trajectories: (1) a quantum mechanical formulation where the agent-environment cut is physical rather than merely conceptual; (2) a philosophical analysis drawing on non-dual contemplative traditions; and (3) a concrete instantiation using LLM-based agents.
AI.result: Embeddedness is found to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embedding the agent reveals that individuation is non-unique—the same underlying dynamics admit multiple valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self. The key tension is that the agent must believe in its own boundary to act, yet see through that boundary to understand.
AI.conclusion: The deepest problem in autotelic AI is not goal generation but self-generation and self-relativization. The agent must simultaneously reify and deconstruct its own boundary. The paper's unified framework connects this insight to quantum physics, non-dual philosophy, and practical LLM-based agent architectures.

title: On the QUEST for Uncertainty Quantification via Highest Density Regions
comment: 27 pages, of which 10 are main text. Contains 7 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm in total
summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for reliable decision-making in safety-critical applications in probabilistic machine learning. For regression problems, dominant scalar UQ approaches - notably, those based on proper scoring rules - measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk. This can lead to counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. We propose an alternative framework, in which uncertainty is characterised by the volume of the most probable subset of a distribution's support. QUEST (Quantifying Uncertainty via highest dEnSiTy regions) is a novel approach to UQ based on the concentration of Lebesgue measure at a distribution's peak(s), evaluated at one or more values of a robustness parameter $α$. We establish connections between our measures and classical statistics from information theory and economics. We show that, unlike popular alternatives based on proper scoring rules, QUEST measures of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty satisfy a set of axioms adapted from the UQ literature, including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks confirm that QUEST performs favourably against standard measures such as variance and differential entropy.

AI.tldr: QUEST introduces a new uncertainty quantification framework based on highest density regions (HDRs), measuring uncertainty via the Lebesgue volume of a distribution's most probable subset. Unlike pointwise scoring rule approaches, QUEST satisfies key axioms (monotonicity under spread, location invariance) and decomposes into epistemic and aleatoric components, outperforming variance and differential entropy on selective prediction benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Dominant scalar UQ methods for regression use proper scoring rules that measure pointwise predictive risk, which yields counterintuitive results when the target statistic diverges from the conditional expectation. There is a need for an axiomatized UQ framework that better captures distributional concentration.
AI.method: QUEST characterizes uncertainty via the Lebesgue measure volume of a distribution's highest density regions at one or more levels of a robustness parameter α. This is rooted in the concentration of probability mass at distributional peaks. The authors establish connections to information theory and economics, and axiomatically decompose uncertainty into epistemic and aleatoric components.
AI.result: QUEST measures satisfy desired axioms: monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts, unlike proper scoring rule-based alternatives. Selective prediction benchmarks show QUEST compares favorably against variance and differential entropy.
AI.conclusion: QUEST provides a principled, axiomatically sound alternative to pointwise UQ methods, with theoretical grounding in HDR volume and practical advantages in selective prediction tasks.

title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
summary: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit--DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

AI.tldr: A pronunciation assessment framework using only native speech, combining SSL-based token surprisal with transcript-guided alignment (Text2DUnit-DTW), achieving near-supervised performance without requiring labeled non-native data.
AI.motivation: Traditional automated pronunciation assessment requires costly labeled learner error data or non-native corpora. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency by building a lightweight system trained solely on native speech resources, optionally calibrated with minimal scored samples.
AI.method: Learner speech is discretized via an SSL encoder and K-means codebook into acoustic tokens. A token language model trained on native speech computes surprisal (higher values signal phonotactic deviation). A novel Text2DUnit-DTW module predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens via dynamic time warping, producing error-sensitive alignment features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused through simple regression for final scoring.
AI.result: On SpeechOcean762, Pearson Correlation Coefficient improves from 0.60 (surprisal-only) to 0.66 with transcript guidance, approaching supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC confirms consistent improvements.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight, native-only training framework effectively assesses pronunciation quality by combining phonotactic surprisal with transcript-guided acoustic alignment, offering a viable alternative to systems requiring expensive labeled learner data.

title: PhysDrift: Bridging the Embodiment Gap in Humanoid Co-Speech Motion Generation
summary: Humanoid robots require co-speech motions that are not only expressive and speech-aligned, but also physically executable under embodiment constraints. Existing co-speech generation pipelines are predominantly human-centric: motions are first generated in human-body representations such as SMPL-X and subsequently retargeted to humanoid robots. In this work, we identify a fundamental embodiment gap in this paradigm, where the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts embodiment consistency during motion transfer and physical execution. Through extensive analysis, we show that although retargeting can preserve coarse motion semantics, it significantly compresses motion diversity and weakens prosody-motion synchronization, limiting expressive humanoid behaviors. To address this problem, we first propose IK-EER, a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting. Building upon the curated robot-native motion dataset, we further introduce PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech without relying on intermediate human-body representations. Unlike conventional human-centric pipelines, PhysDrift maintains embodiment consistency throughout both training and inference while incorporating physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics. Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an "embodiment gap" in human-centric co-speech motion generation pipelines for humanoid robots, proposes IK-EER for curating robot-native motion data, and introduces PhysDrift, a framework that directly generates executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech without intermediate human-body representations, improving alignment, plausibility, and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing co-speech motion generation pipelines generate motions in human-body representations (e.g., SMPL-X) and then retarget them to humanoid robots. This human-centric paradigm introduces an "embodiment gap": the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts embodiment consistency, compresses motion diversity, and weakens prosody-motion synchronization during retargeting and physical execution.
AI.method: Two-stage solution: (1) IK-EER — a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting to build a robot-native motion dataset. (2) PhysDrift — an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech input, bypassing intermediate human-body representations, while incorporating physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability compared to conventional human-centric pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Direct robot-native co-speech motion generation (PhysDrift) eliminates the embodiment gap inherent in human-centric retargeting pipelines, enabling humanoid robots to produce expressive, physically executable, and temporally aligned co-speech motions suitable for real-time interaction.

title: Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery
summary: Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level structural causal model (SCM) captures the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM. Existing applications of this notion largely follow a hypothesis-testing paradigm: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then evaluates if the low-level system implements it. We study the complementary problem of learning a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. Our contributions leverage hypotheses from low-rank causal discovery, and can be summarized as follows: (1) we show that observations generated by a low-rank graph induce latents that form a causal abstraction, (2) we provide identifiability results about these latents, and (3) we propose a practical objective to learn this high-level SCM.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to learn high-level causal models (causal abstractions) directly from low-level observational data, moving beyond the traditional hypothesis-testing approach. It leverages low-rank causal discovery to show that low-rank graphs induce latent variables forming a causal abstraction, provides identifiability results, and proposes a practical learning objective.
AI.motivation: Existing work on causal abstraction is largely confirmatory: an expert hypothesizes a high-level model and then tests whether the low-level system implements it. The complementary, more challenging problem — automatically learning a high-level causal abstraction from low-level data — remains underexplored. This paper aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The authors leverage the framework of low-rank causal discovery. Under the assumption that the low-level causal graph has low-rank structure (i.e., the connectivity matrix is low-rank), they demonstrate that this induces latent variables which naturally form a valid causal abstraction of the low-level system. They derive identifiability results for these induced latents and formulate a practical optimization objective for learning the high-level SCM from observational measurements.
AI.result: The paper provides three main contributions: (1) a proof that observations from a low-rank causal graph induce latent variables that constitute a valid causal abstraction, (2) formal identifiability guarantees for these latent variables, and (3) a tractable objective function for learning the high-level SCM in practice.
AI.conclusion: The authors establish a principled connection between low-rank causal discovery and causal abstraction learning, showing that high-level causal models can be learned from low-level data under low-rank assumptions, with identifiability guarantees and a practical algorithm.

title: GEMS: Geometric Constraints Enable Multi-Semantic Superposition in LLMs
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code and logs are available at: https://github.com/LuLu663939/gems-multi-semantic-steering
summary: Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate hidden states at inference time without retraining. Existing methods handle only single-direction injection; when multiple semantic directions are superposed without constraints, the model collapses. We show that this collapse decomposes into two independently acting sources: distributional deviation, where additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers and drive activations outside the training distribution, and directional interference, where non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. These two sources define the design constraints that any training-free multi-directional intervention must address. As one instantiation of these principles, we propose GEMS, a training-free method that maps each source to a corresponding geometric constraint: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection for distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization for directional interference. On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves accuracy at 98% (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%; on Wikitext-2, the same injection incurs only 2.2% PPL increase. Component ablation isolates the causal role of each constraint, and layer-level probes confirm that orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B.

AI.tldr: Activation steering for multi-directional control fails due to distributional deviation and directional interference. The authors propose GEMS, a training-free method using norm-preserving superposition and real-time orthogonalization to enable concurrent multi-directional steering without model collapse.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods only handle single directions; superposing multiple semantic directions without constraints causes model collapse. The authors aim to decompose the collapse mechanisms and derive principled design constraints for training-free multi-directional intervention.
AI.method: The collapse is decomposed into (1) distributional deviation — additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers, pushing activations out of distribution, and (2) directional interference — non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen. GEMS addresses both: norm-preserving weighted superposition with targeted attention-pathway injection handles distributional deviation, while real-time orthogonalization (Gram-Schmidt-based) mitigates directional interference. Causal ablation and layer-level probing validate each constraint.
AI.result: On GSM8K, three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserve 98% accuracy (baseline 92%) vs. 4% for unconstrained addition. On Wikitext-2, the same injection yields only 2.2% PPL increase. Component ablation confirms each constraint's causal role; probes confirm orthogonalized signals reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Multi-directional activation steering is feasible without retraining when two geometric constraints — norm preservation and orthogonalization — are enforced. GEMS provides a principled, scalable, training-free framework applicable across model scales and architectures.

title: Advancing DialNav through Automatic Embodied Dialog Augmentation
summary: For embodied agents capable of physical interaction, the capability to create and understand dialog is crucial to ensure both safety and effectiveness. While DialNav~\cite{han2025dialnav} provides a framework for holistic evaluation of the dialog--execution loop in photorealistic indoor navigation, its performance remains limited by a critical scarcity of training data (2K episodes). To address this, we propose an automatic generation pipeline, and construct the \textbf{RAINbow} dataset, a large-scale training dataset with 238K episodes for DialNav. Our pipeline converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog and creates cost-efficient and high-quality dataset. Then, we introduce two additional complementary advances to unlock the data's full potential: (1) Dual-Strategy Training, a navigation training scheme to align the navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop, and (2) a localization model that leverages VLN knowledge. By combining these complementary solutions, our model substantially outperforms the baseline in success rate on both \textbf{Val Seen} (58.24, \textbf{+89\%}) and \textbf{Val Unseen} (29.05, \textbf{+100\%}) splits, establishing a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper presents RAINbow, a large-scale 238K-episode training dataset built via an automatic pipeline that converts existing VLN data into multi-turn dialog, addressing DialNav's data scarcity. Combined with Dual-Strategy Training and a VLN-enhanced localization model, the approach achieves substantial improvements (+89% on Val Seen, +100% on Val Unseen), setting a new state of the art.
AI.motivation: DialNav provides a framework for evaluating dialog–execution loops in photorealistic indoor navigation for embodied agents, but its performance is severely limited by scarce training data (only ~2K episodes). The authors aim to overcome this bottleneck by generating large-scale, high-quality training data to unlock better dialog-aware navigation capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose three complementary advances: (1) an automatic generation pipeline that converts existing Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) datasets into multi-turn dialog, producing the RAINbow dataset with 238K episodes; (2) Dual-Strategy Training, which aligns navigation training with the dynamic dialog–navigation loop; and (3) a localization model that leverages VLN knowledge to improve spatial understanding.
AI.result: The combined method substantially outperforms the DialNav baseline: Success Rate on Val Seen reaches 58.24 (+89% improvement) and on Val Unseen reaches 29.05 (+100% improvement), establishing a new state of the art on the DialNav benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The critical bottleneck of training data scarcity in dialog-aware embodied navigation can be effectively overcome through automatic dataset generation. When paired with targeted training strategies and knowledge transfer from VLN, large-scale synthetic dialog data enables substantial performance gains and robust generalization to unseen environments.

title: IHBench: Evaluating Post-Interruption Recovery in Voice Agents with Structured Workflows
summary:
Voice agents deployed in structured workflows (customer service, healthcare scheduling, account management) must handle frequent user interruptions while maintaining progress through multi-step procedures. Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models focus on the timing of interruptions: barge-in detection, endpointing, and turn-taking dynamics. They leave unmeasured what happens after the interruption: does the agent resume the workflow at the correct step? Does it address the user's interjection? Does it avoid re-delivering content the user already heard?
  We introduce IHBench (Interruption Handling Benchmark), a benchmark that evaluates post-interruption recovery in voice agents executing state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled points mid-utterance, with per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. Each interruption is scored on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality.
  We evaluate 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and the open-weight community. Models vary widely, and recovery quality depends strongly on the interruption type. Across our experiments, closed-weight models are consistently more robust to interruptions than open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade roughly 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and show no audio-versus-text modality gap, whereas the open-weight models lose ground on all three. A human study validates the LLM judge against human annotators, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge indicates that recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis.

AI.tldr: IHBench is a new benchmark evaluating how voice agents recover after user interruptions in structured multi-step workflows across 10 enterprise domains. It tests 27 audio-language models on task fulfillment and recovery quality across 6 interruption types, finding closed-weight models significantly more robust than open-weight ones.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for speech models focus exclusively on interruption timing (barge-in detection, endpointing, turn-taking) but neglect what happens after the interruption — whether the agent resumes at the correct workflow step, addresses the user's interjection, and avoids repeating already-heard content. This gap is critical for voice agents deployed in structured enterprise workflows like customer service and healthcare scheduling.
AI.method: The authors introduce IHBench with state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled mid-utterance points. Per-interruption evaluation rubrics are auto-generated alongside the data, scoring each interruption on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality. 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and open-weight communities are evaluated. A human study validates the LLM judge, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge is conducted.
AI.result: Closed-weight models consistently outperform open-weight ones: they win more often on task fulfillment, degrade approximately 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and exhibit no audio-versus-text modality gap. Open-weight models show degradation across all three dimensions. Recovery quality depends strongly on interruption type. Cross-benchmark analysis indicates recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis from what AudioMultiChallenge measures.
AI.conclusion: Post-interruption recovery is a distinct and underexamined capability axis for voice agents that existing benchmarks fail to capture. Closed-weight models demonstrate substantially greater robustness, and IHBench provides a validated framework for measuring and improving this capability in speech-capable models.

title: Source-Grounded Data Generation for Text-to-JSON Learning
summary: From financial filings to clinical records, legacy industries rely heavily on long, unstructured documents to store high-value information. Reliably extracting this information into structured, machine-readable representations is a key prerequisite to making the contents accessible to automated systems. JSON is a natural target for such structured extraction, yet constructing reliable and scalable text-to-JSON training data remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration), a source-grounded data generation pipeline that constructs reports and JSON schema by using LLMs for scalable synthesis while validating ground-truth values against the underlying spreadsheet. Evaluations on STAGE-Eval, our source-grounded benchmark with an 851-example test set, show that STAGE produces stronger training data than existing approaches. This improves Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.

AI.tldr: STAGE is a data generation pipeline that creates text-to-JSON training data by grounding LLM-synthesized reports and JSON schemas against spreadsheet sources, significantly improving structured extraction performance (Qwen3-4B exact match: 31.37% → 74.27%).
AI.motivation: Legacy industries rely on long, unstructured documents containing high-value information that needs to be extracted into structured machine-readable formats like JSON. However, constructing reliable, scalable text-to-JSON training data remains a major challenge due to the difficulty of ensuring ground-truth accuracy at scale.
