AI.method: The authors propose STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration), a source-grounded data generation pipeline. It uses LLMs to synthesize reports and corresponding JSON schemas, then validates the ground-truth values by cross-referencing them against the original underlying spreadsheet data, ensuring factual accuracy of the generated training examples.
AI.result: On STAGE-Eval (an 851-example source-grounded benchmark), STAGE-generated training data substantially outperforms existing approaches. Fine-tuning Qwen3-4B improves exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.
AI.conclusion: Source-grounding via spreadsheet validation is an effective strategy for generating high-quality text-to-JSON training data, enabling reliable structured information extraction from unstructured documents at scale.

title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
summary: Achieving dexterous robotic manipulation in the real world heavily relies on human supervision and algorithm engineering, which becomes a central bottleneck in the pursuit of general physical intelligence. Although emerging coding agents can generate code to automate algorithm search, their successes remain largely confined in digital environments. We conjecture that the missing abstraction to automate robotics research is a repeatable feedback loop for real-world policy improvement: reset the scene, execute a policy, verify the outcome, and refine the next iteration. To bridge this gap, we introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework for coding agents that instantiates this physical feedback routine with four core modules: an Environment module (EN) for automatic reset and verification, a Policy Improvement module (PI) that launches policy refinement, a Rollout module (R) to evaluate policies with one or multiple physical robots operating in parallel, and an Evolution module (E) in which coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This closed-loop system transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure, minimizing human effort while allowing fair ablations across training recipe and agent variants. Powered by ENPIRE, frontier coding agents can autonomously train a policy to achieve a 99% success rate on challenging, dexterous manipulation tasks, such as organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use, a process that further accelerates when we dispatch an agent team on a robot fleet. Our results suggest a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advancing robotics in the physical world.

AI.tldr: ENPIRE is a closed-loop harness framework that enables coding agents to autonomously improve real-world robotic manipulation policies through a repeatable physical feedback loop (reset → execute → verify → refine), achieving 99% success on dexterous tasks like pin box organization, zip-tie fastening, and tool use — all while minimizing human supervision.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous manipulation research is bottlenecked by heavy reliance on human supervision and manual algorithm engineering. While coding agents excel at automating algorithm search in digital domains, they lack a physical feedback loop — the ability to reset scenes, execute policies, verify outcomes, and iteratively refine — which is the missing abstraction needed to automate robotics research in the physical world.
AI.method: The authors introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework with four modules: (1) **Environment (EN)** — automatic scene reset and outcome verification; (2) **Policy Improvement (PI)** — launches policy refinement; (3) **Rollout (R)** — evaluates policies using one or more physical robots in parallel; (4) **Evolution (E)** — coding agents analyze execution logs, consult literature, and improve both training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable, iterative optimization loop.
AI.result: Using ENPIRE, frontier coding agents autonomously trained policies achieving a 99% success rate on challenging dexterous manipulation tasks (organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, tool use). Performance further accelerated when deploying an agent team across a robot fleet for parallel evaluation.
AI.conclusion: ENPIRE offers a practical and scalable pathway for deploying coding agents to autonomously advance real-world robotics, dramatically reducing the human effort required and enabling fair ablation studies across training recipes and agent variants.

title: Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity
summary: Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report that a probe's MCS to a reference probe trained on the out-of-distribution (OOD) data near-perfectly linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC (R^2 = 0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove this general phenomenon in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

AI.tldr: Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between a probe and an OOD-trained reference probe linearly predicts OOD AUROC (R²=0.98). The paper extends this finding across models/layers/domains and proves it analytically: under class-balanced Gaussian projections, both MCS and OOD AUROC are sigmoid functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), yielding linearity. The theory predicts when linearity breaks, confirmed empirically.
AI.motivation: Linear probes are commonly compared via Euclidean cosine similarity, but this metric is task-agnostic and ignores data covariance structure. MCS offers a task-aware refinement, yet its empirical success (near-perfect linear prediction of OOD AUROC) lacks theoretical explanation. The authors aim to provide rigorous theoretical grounding for this phenomenon and delineate its boundary conditions.
AI.method: The authors extend empirical validation of MCS across diverse models, layers, and concept domains. The core contribution is a closed-form proof: assuming balanced binary classes with Gaussian-distributed projections, both OOD AUROC and MCS to a reference probe are derived as sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's SNR on test data. Their monotonic relationship implies linearity. The theory also identifies conditions (non-Gaussianity, class imbalance, extreme SNR regimes) where linearity degrades, which are tested empirically.
AI.result: The linear relationship between MCS and OOD AUROC generalizes robustly across architectures, layers, and concept types. The closed-form derivation shows both quantities depend on SNR via sigmoid functions, explaining the linear mapping. Predicted failure modes (e.g., severe class imbalance, non-Gaussian projections) are empirically validated.
AI.conclusion: MCS is a theoretically justified and empirically effective replacement for Euclidean cosine similarity when comparing linear probes. Its SNR-grounded relationship to OOD performance makes it a principled diagnostic tool for interpretability research, with known boundary conditions for reliable use.

title: IHUBERT: Vector-Based Semantic Deduplication and Domain-Balanced Pretraining for Persian Resources
summary: Persian pretrained language models (PLMs) are still limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and by insufficient evaluation beyond standard classification and NER tasks. We present IHUBERT, a monolingual Persian PLM trained from scratch with the RoBERTa-base encoder (125M parameters) on a 45 GB curated subset of the Sepahr-Danesh collection (about 7-8B tokens). To improve corpus quality and reduce redundancy, we employ a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline that includes normalization, exact and near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for distribution balancing control across domains and registers. We additionally train a 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer on the full pretraining corpus to better capture Persian morphology and orthographic variation. IHUBERT is evaluated on seven Persian NLU benchmarks covering NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive question answering, and relation extraction, using task-standard metrics (entity-level F1, Macro-F1, EM/F1). IHUBERT achieves its strongest gains on extractive QA, ranking first on both PQuAD (F1 88.3542) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.0987), and attains the best result on FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). On NER and topic classification, it remains competitive (e.g., 0.8308 F1 on ParsTwiNER; 0.7953 Macro-F1 on DigiMag), while relation extraction remains the main remaining gap (0.6684 Macro-F1 on PERLEX). A controlled tokenizer ablation on the IHUBERT pretraining corpus shows that BPE yields slightly lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size, supporting our tokenization design. Overall, IHUBERT advances Persian language modeling through semantically curated large-scale pretraining and broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension-oriented tasks.

AI.tldr: IHUBERT is a monolingual Persian RoBERTa-base model trained on a 45GB semantically deduplicated corpus with a 139k BPE tokenizer, achieving state-of-the-art results on Persian extractive QA and NLI while remaining competitive on NER and topic classification.
AI.motivation: Persian PLMs suffer from limited high-quality pretraining data and narrow evaluation (mostly classification/NER). The authors aim to address both gaps through better corpus curation and broad NLU benchmarking.
AI.method: RoBERTa-base encoder (125M params) trained from scratch on 45GB of Sepahr-Danesh corpus (~7-8B tokens). Multi-stage preprocessing: normalization, exact/near-deduplication, anonymization, and vector-DB-based semantic deduplication for domain/register balance. A 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer is trained on the full corpus. Evaluated on seven Persian NLU tasks: NER, sentiment, topic classification, NLI, extractive QA, and relation extraction.
AI.result: Best: PQuAD F1 88.35, ParsiNLU-RC F1 49.10, FarsTail Macro-F1 0.8350. Competitive: ParsTwiNER F1 0.8308, DigiMag Macro-F1 0.7953. Gap: PERLEX relation extraction Macro-F1 0.6684. BPE tokenizer shows lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocab size.
AI.conclusion: IHUBERT demonstrates that semantically curated large-scale pretraining paired with a morphology-aware BPE tokenizer and broad multi-task evaluation advances Persian language modeling, with extractive QA and NLI benefiting most, while relation extraction remains a challenge.

title: Reward as An Agent for Embodied World Models
summary: While RL has become a promising tool for refining world models, existing methods largely rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, limiting exploration, behavioral diversity, and richer dynamic discovery. In this work, we challenge this conservative paradigm. We argue that the core limitation is not exploration itself, but the lack of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without reliable verification, expanded exploration becomes highly susceptible to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without achieving genuine improvement. To evaluate this motivation, we instantiate our method in embodied world models, where physical plausibility, and task completion provide a rigorous testbed for scalable RL under complex dynamics. On the verification side, we introduce Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts. On the exploration side, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification through DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. By unifying Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO, we enable RL on a more reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling, effectively mitigating reward hacking while yielding significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, thereby demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges conservative exploration in RL-based world model refinement, arguing the core issue is not exploration itself but the lack of reliable verification. It proposes two complementary components: (1) Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework for robust verification under distribution shifts, and (2) DynDiff-GRPO, a dynamic-aware rollout diversification method that expands action-space exploration. Together, they enable broader, safer exploration with significant accuracy gains across multiple world models.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for refining world models rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, which limits exploration, behavioral diversity, and discovery of richer dynamics. The authors argue that the fundamental bottleneck is not exploration per se, but the absence of reliable verification strategies. Without such verification, expanding exploration leads to reward hacking — policies exploit imperfect reward signals rather than achieving genuine improvement. This motivates the need for robust verification mechanisms that can support and validate broader exploration.
AI.method: The paper introduces two main components: (1) **Reward as an Agent** — an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals, mitigating reward hacking under distribution shifts. (2) **DynDiff-GRPO (Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification)** — a method that explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. These are unified into a single framework, instantiated in embodied world models where physical plausibility and task completion serve as rigorous testbeds.
AI.result: The unified approach of Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO yields significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models. The framework effectively mitigates reward hacking while enabling substantially diversified sampling, demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.
AI.conclusion: Broader exploration in RL-based world model refinement is viable and beneficial, but only when paired with reliable verification. The proposed agentic reward framework and dynamic-aware rollout diversification together provide the necessary verification-exploration synergy to overcome the limitations of conservative paradigms and achieve scalable, genuine improvements in world model accuracy.

title: Latent Confounded Causal Discovery via Lie Bracket Geometry
summary: Recent work on Kan-Do-Calculus (KDC) has established that the boundary between passive observation and active intervention in causal inference is a category-theoretic bi-adjunction, with interventions modeled by left Kan extensions and conditioning by right Kan extensions. This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms under latent confounding, building on the information-geometric and categorical consequences of KDC. In smooth statistical settings, Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields; failures of these fields to close under Lie brackets become computable Frobenius residuals, which we interpret as witnesses of failed visible integrability and possible latent or unmodeled structure. Our first algorithm, BRIDGE (Bracket Residuals for Interventional Discovery and Geometric Estimation), combines an interventional density or Radon-Nikodym-ratio engine with a geometric screen that proposes a high-recall family of admissible arrows, identifies non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and passes the reduced family to downstream score-based or differentiable discovery routines. The second algorithmic contribution, Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM), learns amortized intervention fields and factors latent curvature spectrally, exposing the direct Lie-space endpoint toward which BRIDGE points. A detailed set of experiments show that both algorithms are capable of discovering causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential space of possible DAGs by many orders of magnitude. This paper introduces a new paradigm in causal discovery, where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two causal discovery algorithms—BRIDGE and Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM)—that leverage Kan-Do-Calculus and information geometry to detect latent confounders. BRIDGE uses Frobenius bracket residuals (non-closing Lie brackets) to identify latent obstructions, while SKFM learns amortized intervention fields and spectrally factors latent curvature. Both dramatically reduce the DAG search space.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery under latent confounding suffers from a super-exponential DAG search space. The authors exploit the category-theoretic bi-adjunction in Kan-Do-Calculus—where left Kan extensions model interventions and right Kan extensions model conditioning—to derive geometric signatures of latent structure. Failures of local causal vector fields to close under Lie brackets provide a principled, computable signal for unobserved confounding.
AI.method: The paper develops two algorithms: (1) BRIDGE, which computes Frobenius residuals from Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures, screens for non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and feeds a reduced arrow set to score-based discovery; (2) SKFM, which learns amortized intervention fields via flow matching and performs spectral decomposition of latent curvature to directly identify the Lie-algebraic endpoint that BRIDGE approximates.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate both algorithms successfully recover causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the DAG search space by many orders of magnitude compared to exhaustive search.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a new paradigm where latent causal structure is inferred directly from the differential geometry of intervention-induced flows, grounding causal discovery in the category-theoretic and information-geometric foundations of Kan-Do-Calculus.

title: Self-Preference Is Weak or Absent in Verifiable Instruction-Following Revision: A Four-Model Test Under Genuine Authorship
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly review and revise text, including their own. A documented self-preference bias (models favoring their own generations when acting as judges) raises the question of whether models also resist valid corrections to their own writing. We test this in a setting where "valid" is decided not by another model but by a deterministic verifier: instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model writes a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it; the model then accepts or rejects that edit either as the genuine in-context author or as a fresh model that sees the draft neutrally. Across four mid-tier model families and 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons, we find no detectable self-preference: authors reject verified-good fixes to their own drafts at essentially the same rate as fresh models judging the same drafts (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). A self-skepticism hint from a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. The one robust observation is qualitative: when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of their stated reasons are flaw-catching rather than preference, that is, about the character of rejections, not an elevated rate. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.

AI.tldr: LLMs do not exhibit a statistically significant self-preference bias when evaluating verified corrections to their own writing. Authors accept valid fixes at essentially the same rate as neutral judges (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]), and rejections are overwhelmingly based on perceived flaws rather than preference.
AI.motivation: Prior work documents a self-preference bias in LLMs when judging text quality (models favor their own outputs). This raises the concern that models might resist valid corrections to their own writing, undermining the utility of LLM-driven revision pipelines. The authors test this using a deterministic verifier (IFEval) rather than another model as judge, isolating the effect from confounds of model-based evaluation.
AI.method: The experiment uses instruction-following revision on the IFEval benchmark. A model writes a draft; the IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it. The model then decides to accept or reject the edit under two conditions: (1) as the genuine in-context author, or (2) as a fresh model seeing the draft neutrally. Comparisons are made across 4 mid-tier model families with 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons total. A smaller pilot had hinted at a self-skepticism effect, which was tested for replication.
AI.result: No detectable self-preference bias: authors reject verified-good fixes at essentially the same rate as fresh models (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). The self-skepticism hint from the pilot did not replicate at scale. Qualitatively, when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of stated reasons are flaw-catching rather than preference-based. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded given the sample size.
AI.conclusion: Self-preference bias does not manifest in the setting of deterministic, verifier-confirmed corrections to LLM-generated drafts. Models do not systematically resist valid edits to their own writing. Rejection behavior, when it occurs, is driven by claimed flaw detection rather than egoistic preference, though the study cannot rule out small effects below ~13 percentage points.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates multi-agent orchestration architectures (DAG Plan & Execute vs. ReAct) across enterprise scales (up to 200 agents), finding that scale-induced agent discovery noise—not task complexity—dominates performance degradation. A Task Manager with priority inference, event merging, and preemption is introduced to enable continuous operation, reducing high-priority latency by 14–75% and improving related-event correctness by >20pp at enterprise scale.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI requires continuous event monitoring and multi-agent coordination, but existing multi-agent systems are designed for discrete request-response workflows and have not been rigorously evaluated at realistic enterprise scales (hundreds of agents). The gap between academic assumptions and production needs motivates this systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The authors benchmark two prevalent agent orchestration architectures—DAG-based Plan and Execute (structured, dependency-graph planning) and ReAct (iterative reasoning-and-acting)—across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80 agents), and Enterprise (~200 agents). They also propose a Task Manager component that enables continuous operation through three mechanisms: priority inference from event context, semantic merging of related events to reduce redundancy, and preemption of lower-priority tasks for urgent ones.
AI.result: Scale dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at Persona scale but degrade significantly at Enterprise scale, with agent discovery noise identified as the primary bottleneck. Simple tasks degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan & Execute offers higher precision and better parallelization at smaller scales but suffers from overhead that worsens at scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent orchestration for enterprise AI must be designed with scale-induced discovery noise as a first-class concern. Continuous-operation mechanisms like the proposed Task Manager are essential for production deployment. Architecture selection involves a precision-vs-robustness trade-off that shifts unfavorably for structured planning approaches as agent pools grow large.

title: SEAGAN: domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a flexible framework for learning from scientific data linked through physical, biological, or functional relationships. One promising domain is plant physiology, where measured responses often arise from multiple interacting processes whose exact separation remains difficult even with manual intervention. In plant physiology, a key example is the A-Ci curve, which relates net CO2 assimilation rate (Anet) to leaf intercellular CO2 concentration (Ci) and is used to estimate photosynthetic parameters in leaf and crop-canopy models. However, reliable estimation requires identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point, which remains a major source of uncertainty. Here, we formulate limitation-state identification along A-Ci curves as a graph-based node classification problem, with curve points as nodes. Domain-specific graph representations are created using distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The framework was evaluated against conventional learning baselines, graph-based architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark. Results on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states show that graph-based models improve classification, particularly near biochemical transition regions. The best-performing configuration, SEAGAN (domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes), integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieving an F1-score of 0.857 and an accuracy of 0.882. The results show that representing A-Ci curves as graphs improves biochemical limitation-state analysis, with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods providing the most effective strategy.

AI.tldr: GNN-based node classification on A-Ci curves for photosynthetic limitation-state identification. A new model, SEAGAN, combining process-aware features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted loss, achieves 0.857 F1 and 0.882 accuracy, outperforming baselines especially near biochemical transition regions.
AI.motivation: Identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each point of an A-Ci curve (net CO2 assimilation vs. intercellular CO2 concentration) is essential for estimating photosynthetic parameters, but remains a major source of uncertainty. Traditional methods struggle to reliably separate interacting physiological processes.
AI.method: The authors frame limitation-state identification as a graph-based node classification problem where curve points are nodes. Two graph construction strategies are used: distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The proposed SEAGAN model integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss. Evaluation is conducted on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states.
AI.result: Graph-based models improve classification over conventional baselines, particularly near biochemical transition regions. SEAGAN achieves the best performance with an F1-score of 0.857 and accuracy of 0.882.
AI.conclusion: Representing A-Ci curves as graphs with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods significantly improves biochemical limitation-state analysis in plant physiology.

title: HydraHead: From Head-Level Functional Heterogeneity to Specialized Attention Hybridization
summary: The quadratic complexity of attention poses a critical bottleneck for long-context processing, spurring interest in hybrid attention designs. Most open-source hybrid models adopt a layer-wise strategy. Yet, prior work has noted the inherent difficulty of integrating Linear Attention (LA) with Full Attention (FA), suggesting that the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. To probe this space, we conduct interpretability analysis and observe that layers exhibit block-wise functional similarity, while individual heads within the same layer display distinct functional specialization despite sharing input features. This head-level heterogeneity suggests that the head dimension provides a natural and principled granularity for fusing heterogeneous attention signals. Building on this insight, we introduce HydraHead, a novel architecture that hybridizes FA and LA along the head axis. HydraHead features two key innovations: (1) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and preserves FA only for them, and (2) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. By leveraging a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation, we achieve high-performance hybrid models with minimal training overhead. Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs in long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Crucially, trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5, a leading model of comparable size with a native context length of 256K. This highlights the significant scaling potential of head-level hybridization.

AI.tldr: HydraHead proposes hybridizing Full Attention and Linear Attention along the head dimension (rather than the conventional layer-wise approach), using interpretability-driven selection to preserve FA only for retrieval-critical heads and a scale-normalized fusion module to reconcile distributional gaps, achieving strong long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio with minimal training overhead.
AI.motivation: The quadratic complexity of Full Attention creates a bottleneck for long-context processing. Existing open-source hybrid models use layer-wise hybridization, but integrating Linear Attention with Full Attention is inherently difficult and the design space remains underexplored. The authors identify that layers show block-wise functional similarity while individual heads within a layer exhibit distinct functional specialization, suggesting head-level granularity as a more principled approach to hybridization.
AI.method: HydraHead introduces: (1) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that analyzes head functionality to identify retrieval-critical heads and applies FA only to those, while using LA for the rest; (2) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs; and (3) a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation to achieve high performance with minimal training overhead.
AI.result: Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs on long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning capability. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches the long-context performance of a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid at a much more efficient 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Trained on only 15B tokens, it achieves over 69% improvement over baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5 (a leading comparable-size model with 256K native context).
AI.conclusion: Head-level hybridization of FA and LA is a promising and underexplored design direction with significant scaling potential. The interpretability-driven approach enables highly efficient allocation of expensive full attention, achieving strong long-context performance at dramatically reduced computational cost compared to layer-wise hybrids.

title: Process-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Theorem Proving via Lean
summary: While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically has relied on a single binary verification signal, symbolic proof assistants in formal reasoning offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback. This gap between structured processes and unstructured rewards highlights the importance of feedback that is both dense and sound. In this work, we demonstrate that the Lean proof assistant itself can serve as a symbolic process oracle, supplying both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during training. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory. We incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods that balances outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 show that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet. Beyond empirical gains, our study highlights a broader perspective: symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time, but can also act as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward reinforcement learning frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using the Lean proof assistant as a process-level reward oracle for RLVR, providing dense tactic-level feedback (rather than binary outcome signals) during training. Incorporating structured rewards via first-error propagation and first-token credit into GRPO-style RL yields improvements over outcome-only baselines on formal theorem-proving benchmarks like MiniF2F and ProofNet.
AI.motivation: Traditional RLVR relies on a single binary verification signal (proved or not), but symbolic proof assistants like Lean generate rich, fine-grained structured feedback during proof elaboration — including which tactics are locally sound and where the first error occurs. There is a gap between this structured symbolic process information and the unstructured reward signals used in training. The authors aim to bridge this gap by using Lean as a dense, sound process-level reward oracle.
AI.method: Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration identifies both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step. These signals are converted into structured rewards: correct tactics receive positive credit, and the first erroneous step is explicitly penalized. These process-level rewards are integrated into a GRPO-style RL objective using two mechanisms — first-error propagation (propagating penalty from the first error backward) and first-token credit (assigning credit to the first token of each tactic) — to balance outcome-level and process-level advantages.
AI.result: Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 demonstrate that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, yielding performance improvements on the MiniF2F and ProofNet benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic proof assistants can serve not only as verifiers at evaluation time but also as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward RL frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

title: MassSpecGym in the Wild: Uncovering and Correcting Evaluation Pitfalls in AI-Driven Molecule Discovery
summary: Reliable benchmarking is critical for developing machine learning models for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) based molecule discovery. Subtle issues in experimental design and model evaluation procedures can degrade the trustworthiness of such benchmarks and lead to erroneous conclusions. We conduct a thorough review of model evaluation issues in the recent MS/MS machine learning literature, using the standard MassSpecGym benchmark suite as a case study to illustrate the impact of these issues. We find evaluation issues in at least 17 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption. We isolate three classes of failures: (i) data leakage, (ii) shortcut learning, and (iii) implementation bugs and metric divergence. Through extensive experimentation and code replication, we quantify the impact of these issues and show how they corrupt the evaluation standards MassSpecGym was designed to enforce. We distill our findings into recommendations generalizable to MS/MS challenges, benchmarks, and custom evaluation setups. We also release MassSpecGym v1.5, an implementation of our recommendations in the MassSpecGym benchmarking suite which addresses the failure modes identified in this audit. MassSpecGym v1.5 is publicly available at https://github.com/pluskal-lab/MassSpecGym.

AI.tldr: A systematic audit of MS/MS machine learning benchmarks reveals widespread evaluation issues — data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs — in 17 of 26 papers. The authors quantify these failures, provide best-practice recommendations, and release MassSpecGym v1.5 to address them.
AI.motivation: Trustworthy benchmarking is essential for progress in machine learning for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS)-based molecule discovery. The authors observed that subtle experimental design and evaluation flaws can undermine benchmark reliability and lead to incorrect scientific conclusions, motivating a systematic audit of the recent literature.
AI.method: The authors reviewed 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in its first year. They identified evaluation issues through code replication and extensive experimentation, categorizing failures into three classes: data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs/metric divergence. They quantified the impact of each failure mode on evaluation integrity.
AI.result: At least 17 of 26 papers (≥65%) contained evaluation issues. Data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs each corrupted benchmark scores in distinct ways, undermining the standardization MassSpecGym was designed to provide.
AI.conclusion: The authors distill findings into generalizable recommendations for MS/MS benchmarks and release MassSpecGym v1.5, which patches the identified failure modes to restore evaluation integrity.

title: Residual-Space Evolutionary Optimization via Flow-based Generative Models
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026 Workshop SPIGM, 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Data editing with generative methods typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search. However, these assumptions break down in flow-based settings, where edits are performed through forward and backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. We introduce residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that addresses this gap by combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. Building on the observation that conditional flow matching (CFM) can disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, our framework directly operates in residual space and separates two complementary search regimes: self-pollination performs local exploitation through feature-preserving residual refinement, and cross-pollination promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. As a proof of concept, we validate on MorphoMNIST, a benchmark dataset for counterfactual generation, and on crystal data, demonstrating that this exploration--exploitation decomposition provides a useful mechanism for balancing target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that combines flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms to handle non-differentiable or black-box objectives, decomposing search into self-pollination (local exploitation) and cross-pollination (exploration), validated on MorphoMNIST and crystal data.
AI.motivation: Existing generative editing methods require differentiable objectives and gradient-based search, which fail in flow-based settings where edits involve forward/backward integration and non-differentiable or black-box objectives. There is a need for a framework that enables flexible, optimization-based editing in such flow-based generative models.
AI.method: The framework leverages conditional flow matching (CFM) to disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals. It operates directly in this residual space with two complementary search regimes: (1) self-pollination, which performs local exploitation via feature-preserving residual refinement, and (2) cross-pollination, which promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. This is implemented through an evolutionary optimization algorithm.
AI.result: The framework was validated on MorphoMNIST (counterfactual generation benchmark) and crystal data (real-world scientific domain). Results demonstrate that the exploration-exploitation decomposition effectively balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to scientific applications.
AI.conclusion: The residual-space evolutionary optimization framework provides a useful, model-agnostic mechanism for flow-based generative editing with non-differentiable objectives, offering effective balance across alignment, preservation, and diversity in both image and scientific domains.

title: Hard or Just Unreached? Diagnosing the Sampling Blind Spot in Math-Reasoning Difficulty Estimation
comment: 9 pages of main paper, 4 figures and 5 tables in the main paper, with more in the appendix
summary: Math and science reasoning benchmarks rely on pass@k, the fraction of sampled chains that reach gold, as the canonical per-example difficulty signal. The same signal drives RL with verifiable rewards, math data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. We show this proxy has a persistent blind spot on its hardest stratum: on the eight free-form math cells we test (GSM8K and MATH across four open-weight models), 10.3-22.9% of the examples that no sampling seed solves in six tries are instead solved at matched compute by a six-chain deterministic regime. These are greedy decoding plus five cheap residual-stream perturbations applied via activation grafting, while greedy alone solves at most 6% on these math cells. Recovery scales with the additional budget, across perturbations whose mechanistic distinctness we verify across all twelve cells (cross-kind fix-set Jaccard <= 0.47 in every setup). Activation grafting is used as an intervention on internal representations, not a decoding method; we use it purely as a diagnostic and diversification tool, and our recovered items show that the pass@k= 0 % stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream rather than that the unmodified model reaches them under ordinary inference.

AI.tldr: Pass@k as a difficulty metric systematically misses hard-but-solvable problems: 10–23% of examples deemed unsolvable (pass@6=0%) are actually solvable using deterministic decoding with cheap residual-stream perturbations (activation grafting), revealing that the pass@k=0% stratum is structurally identifiable in the model's representations.
AI.motivation: Pass@k is the dominant proxy for per-example difficulty in math/science reasoning benchmarks, used to drive RL with verifiable rewards, data curation, and verifier training. The authors hypothesize that pass@k has a blind spot on its hardest stratum (pass@k=0%), where problems may be structurally solvable by the model but missed due to stochastic sampling alone.
AI.method: The authors compare stochastic pass@6 (six independent sampling chains) against a deterministic six-chain regime: greedy decoding plus five cheap residual-stream perturbations via activation grafting. Activation grafting is used purely as a diagnostic/diversification intervention on internal representations, not a decoding method. They test across eight free-form math cells (GSM8K and MATH × four open-weight models) and verify mechanistic distinctness of perturbations via cross-kind fix-set Jaccard (≤0.47 in all twelve setups).
AI.result: 10.3–22.9% of examples that pass@6=0% (no seed solves in six tries) are recovered by the six-chain deterministic regime. Greedy decoding alone solves at most 6% on these cells. Recovery scales with additional perturbation budget. Cross-kind Jaccard ≤0.47 confirms perturbation distinctness across all tested cells.
AI.conclusion: The pass@k=0% stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream; its existence reflects a limitation of stochastic sampling as a difficulty proxy, not a fundamental capability boundary of the model. Activation grafting serves as an effective diagnostic tool for probing this blind spot.

title: From Texts to Scores: Tracing the Emergence of Essay Quality Representations in Large Language Models
comment: This is a preprint of a manuscript currently under peer review
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have substantially transformed Automated Essay Scoring (AES), yet the internal mechanisms underlying LLM-based scoring remain poorly understood. In this work, we systematically analyze the hidden representations of eight LLMs across two English essay datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). Using linear probing, cross-prompt generalization, dimensionality reduction, and neuron-level analyses, we find consistent evidence that essay quality information is encoded in a linearly accessible form within LLM representations. These representations emerge progressively across layers, remain robust across prompting strategies, and partially transfer across essay prompts despite differences in scoring rubrics. In addition, nonlinear probes provide only marginal and inconsistent improvements over linear probes, suggesting that most essay quality information is already linearly decodable. We further identify individual ``essay scoring neurons'' whose activations strongly correlate with essay scores and whose behavior is sensitive to targeted intervention. Moreover, the layer-wise distribution of these neurons systematically shifts with essay length, with longer essays relying more heavily on deeper layers. Overall, our findings provide evidence that LLMs encode structured representations related to essay quality and offer new insights into the interpretability of LLM-based AES systems.

AI.tldr: Linear probing reveals that LLMs encode essay quality in linearly accessible hidden representations that emerge progressively across layers, transfer partially across prompts, and are mediated by identifiable "essay scoring neurons" whose layer distribution shifts with essay length.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread adoption of LLMs for automated essay scoring, the internal mechanisms driving their scoring decisions are poorly understood. The authors aim to open the "black box" and characterize how essay quality information is structurally encoded within LLM representations.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze hidden representations from 8 LLMs (including both open-source and proprietary models) across three datasets (ASAP++, CSEE in English; ENEM in Portuguese). They employ linear probing, cross-prompt generalization tests, dimensionality reduction (PCA), nonlinear probing (MLP) comparisons, neuron-level activation analysis, and targeted intervention experiments to identify and manipulate "essay scoring neurons."
AI.result: Linear probes consistently recover essay quality across all models and datasets, with performance emerging progressively across layers. Nonlinear probes yield only marginal, inconsistent gains. Representations partially transfer across prompts despite rubric differences. Individual neurons strongly correlating with essay scores are identified; their layer-wise distribution shifts toward deeper layers for longer essays. Targeted intervention on these neurons predictably alters scoring behavior.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode structured, linearly decodable representations of essay quality, offering evidence for interpretable internal mechanisms in LLM-based AES. This supports developing more transparent, controllable scoring systems and lays groundwork for mechanistic interpretability in educational NLP.

title: Multi-Head Attention-Based Feature Extractor Integration with Soft Actor-Critic for Porosity Prediction and Process Parameter Optimization in Additive Manufacturing
summary: Additive manufacturing process optimization requires precise parameter control to minimize defects such as porosity. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and susceptibility to local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision manufacturing tasks. This study addresses these limitations by employing a continuous action space combined with a novel architecture that integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor enhances the agent's ability to capture subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, enabling more effective exploration-exploitation balance for navigating value spaces with local minima. We validate our approach on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward values compared to standard RL methods including DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC. The proposed methodology achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining stability throughout training.

AI.tldr: A continuous-action Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) enhanced with multi-head attention achieves faster convergence and higher reward in optimizing laser powder bed fusion parameters for porosity minimization, outperforming DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL with discrete action spaces converges slowly and gets trapped in local optima, limiting precision in additive manufacturing process optimization. Continuous action spaces with better feature extraction are needed for handling low-dimensional inputs with subtle variations.
AI.method: Integration of a multi-head attention mechanism as a feature extractor within the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm operating in a continuous action space, applied to porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward compared to DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC, with maintained training stability.
AI.conclusion: The attention-augmented SAC with continuous actions effectively balances exploration-exploitation in low-dimensional feature spaces with local minima, enabling high-precision additive manufacturing parameter optimization.

title: Convex training of Lipschitz-regularized shallow neural networks
summary: In this work, we introduce a training procedure for shallow neural networks that promotes robustness against adversarial attacks. We solve a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program by introducing a convex restriction that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Our approach can be employed as a post-processing step by taking a pre-trained network as an initial solution to then solving the convex program whose optimal network is guaranteed to be no worse than the initial one. We illustrate the improvements of our training procedure with experiments using real world datasets for regression tasks under an adversarial setting. We show numerically that solving our proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. Additionally, we show that on certain datasets, networks obtained using our convex training program are both more accurate and robust with respect to adversarial attacks.

AI.tldr: A convex restriction approach is proposed for Lipschitz-regularized adversarial training of shallow neural networks, solvable to global optimality. It serves as a post-processing step that guarantees non-worse performance than a pre-trained network, yielding improved accuracy and robustness on regression tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard adversarial training for neural networks involves non-convex optimization, making it difficult to find globally optimal solutions. The authors aim to develop a method that promotes adversarial robustness with global optimality guarantees, particularly for shallow networks.
AI.method: The authors formulate adversarial training as a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized program. They derive a convex restriction (a convex program whose feasible set is a subset of the original) that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. The method is used as a post-processing step: a pre-trained network serves as initialization, and solving the convex program is guaranteed to produce a network no worse than the initial one.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world regression datasets under adversarial settings show that the convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. On certain datasets, the resulting networks are simultaneously more accurate and more robust against adversarial attacks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convex-restriction approach provides a principled, globally optimal post-processing method for improving adversarial robustness in shallow neural networks, outperforming existing methods in both objective value and robustness-accuracy trade-offs on regression tasks.

title: MedRLM: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence for Long-Context Clinical Reasoning, Sensor-Guided Screening, Evidence-Grounded Decision Support, and Community-to-Tertiary Referral Optimization
summary: Real-world clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous and longitudinal patient information rather than answering isolated medical questions. However, current medical large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems often rely on single-step prompting or retrieval, which can be fragile when clinical evidence is distributed across long electronic health records, medical images, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. This paper proposes MedRLM, a Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence framework for long-context clinical reasoning, sensor-guided screening, and community-to-tertiary referral support. Instead of compressing all patient information into one prompt, MedRLM treats the patient case as an external clinical environment that can be recursively inspected, decomposed, retrieved, verified, and synthesized. The framework coordinates specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, medical imaging, physiological sensor signals, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning. It further introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to connect patient-specific observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor-derived biomarkers, and referral criteria. A sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism activates deeper reasoning when abnormal physiological or behavioral patterns are detected, while uncertainty-gated refinement supports clinician review for high-risk or low-confidence cases. We also outline a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. MedRLM aims to move medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, and workflow-aware clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: MedRLM is a recursive multimodal clinical reasoning framework that treats patient cases as external environments to be iteratively inspected, decomposed, and synthesized by coordinated AI agents, moving beyond single-step QA toward auditable, workflow-aware decision support across EHR, imaging, sensors, guidelines, and referral planning.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs and retrieval-augmented systems rely on single-step prompting or retrieval, which fails when clinical evidence is fragmented across long EHRs, imaging, sensor streams, and guidelines. Real-world clinical decision support requires longitudinal, heterogeneous reasoning rather than answering isolated medical questions.
AI.method: MedRLM introduces four core components: (1) a recursive inspection framework treating the patient case as an external clinical environment; (2) specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, imaging, physiological sensors, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning; (3) a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory linking patient observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor biomarkers, and referral criteria; (4) a sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism for abnormal patterns and uncertainty-gated refinement for high-risk or low-confidence cases.
AI.result: The paper outlines a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets covering EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes, though concrete experimental results are not yet reported in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: MedRLM aims to advance medical AI from static question answering to auditable, multimodal, workflow-aware clinical decision support, with recursive reasoning and uncertainty-aware safeguards for real-world deployment.

title: LOKI: Memory-Free Null-Space Constrained Lifelong Knowledge Editing
summary: Lifelong knowledge editing aims to efficiently and sequentially update language models over time, as new knowledge becomes available or when the model makes mistakes, while preserving acceptable performance on past knowledge. One unresolved challenge is that existing methods modify a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge samples, reducing flexibility and increasing catastrophic forgetting. Another is requiring access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing to obtain data statistics. To address these challenges, we introduce LOKI, a novel approach that uses dynamic layer selection based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of the model weights, bypassing the requirement for previous knowledge access. We show that LOKI achieves superior performance to existing approaches across a wide variety of experiments, achieving up to a 14\% improvement in average accuracy.

AI.tldr: LOKI introduces dynamic layer selection via Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion with null-space projected gradient updates for lifelong knowledge editing, outperforming existing methods by up to 14% in average accuracy without requiring access to previous knowledge.
AI.motivation: Existing lifelong knowledge editing methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they modify a fixed set of layers for all knowledge samples, which reduces flexibility and exacerbates catastrophic forgetting; (2) they require access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing for data statistics, which is impractical in real-world sequential update scenarios.
AI.method: LOKI employs two core mechanisms: (1) dynamic layer selection per knowledge sample using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to identify which layers are most relevant for a given update; (2) projecting gradient updates onto the null-space of the model weights, which constrains updates to directions that minimally interfere with previously learned knowledge, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting without needing access to past data.
AI.result: LOKI achieves superior performance compared to existing lifelong knowledge editing approaches across diverse experimental settings, with up to a 14% improvement in average accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic layer selection via HSIC combined with null-space projection is an effective strategy for lifelong knowledge editing, offering both improved accuracy and reduced catastrophic forgetting while eliminating the need for access to prior knowledge samples.

title: ReNikud: Audio-Supervised Hebrew Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion
summary: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion for Modern Hebrew is needed for applications like text-to-speech (TTS), but is challenging due to the language's abjad writing system, which leaves vowels largely unwritten, creating substantial ambiguity. Standard approaches first predict vowel diacritics (nikud) to produce International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, but this is limited: vocalization data is scarce and laborious to produce, it does not specify features such as lexical stress, and it reflects formal grammatical rules rather than everyday spoken pronunciation. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction, meanwhile, struggles on limited data and fails to exploit the character-level alignment characteristic of abjads. Our method, ReNikud, overcomes these limitations with two key insights: (1) Weak audio supervision via a phoneme-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) pseudo-labeling pipeline on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, yielding phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias. Results on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the new targeted MILIM benchmark for spoken Hebrew show that ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods. We will release our code and trained models to support further work on Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

AI.tldr: ReNikud introduces a Hebrew G2P system that uses ASR pseudo-labeling on thousands of hours of unlabeled audio to capture natural spoken pronunciation, combined with a pseudo-vocalization architecture enforcing character-level alignment, outperforming prior SOTA on existing and new benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern Hebrew G2P is challenging due to its abjad writing system (vowels largely unwritten), scarce vocalization data, and the mismatch between formal grammatical nikud and everyday spoken pronunciation. Existing approaches either rely on limited, labor-intensive vocalization data or struggle with direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction on small datasets.
AI.method: (1) Weak audio supervision: A phoneme-based ASR pipeline pseudo-labels thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, producing phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) Pseudo-vocalization architecture: Predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias that exploits the abjad structure.
AI.result: ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the newly introduced MILIM benchmark, which specifically targets spoken Hebrew.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging weak audio supervision and a character-aligned pseudo-vocalization architecture effectively addresses data scarcity and pronunciation naturalness in Hebrew G2P. Code and trained models will be released.

title: Multi-Granular Attention-Driven Reinforcement Learning Framework for Web Intelligent Enhancement Systems
comment: 2026 3rd International Conference on Integrated Intelligence and Communication Systems (ICIICS), 6 Pages
summary: From the past few years, web intelligent enhancement systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous and dynamic web data to deliver personalized, context-aware services. However, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning models often struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving web environments. In this research, a Multi-Granular Attention-based Reinforcement Web Intelligent Enhancement System (MGAR-WIES) is proposed to address the challenges by integrating semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Initially, heterogeneous web data comprising structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources are collected and preprocessed for generating unified feature representations. These representations are transformed into a dynamic semantic graph, where entities and their relationships are modeled by using graph embeddings enhanced by attention mechanisms for capturing both local relevance and global contextual dependencies. Subsequently, an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy leverages the attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions like content recommendation, navigation optimization, and service adaptation. Finally, the continuous online feedback is further integrated to update graph representations and learning policies in real time by ensuring sustained adaptability and performance. The proposed MGAR-WIES acheived better results in terms of accuracy (80%) when compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Proposes MGAR-WIES, a system combining semantic graph modeling, multi-granular attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning to deliver personalized, context-aware web services from heterogeneous, dynamic web data, achieving 80% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML, DL, and RL models struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving web environments that rely on heterogeneous and dynamic data for personalized services.
AI.method: Heterogeneous web data (structured, semi-structured, unstructured) is collected, preprocessed into unified feature representations, and transformed into a dynamic semantic graph with attention-enhanced graph embeddings capturing local and global context. An adaptive multi-agent RL strategy then leverages these attention-aware semantic states to optimize actions (recommendation, navigation, service adaptation), with continuous online feedback updating graph representations and policies in real time.
AI.result: MGAR-WIES achieved 80% accuracy, outperforming existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Integrating semantic graphs, attention mechanisms, and adaptive RL effectively addresses semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability challenges in dynamic web environments, yielding superior accuracy for intelligent web enhancement.

title: Pitch Spelling Jazz Lead Sheets, Solo Transcriptions, Classical Piano and Monophonic Scores
summary: We present an algorithm for pitch spelling and key estimation. Given an input in MIDI-like format, containing information on note pitches (expressed in semitones relative to the lowest reference note) and bar boundaries, it estimates the appropriate note names, a global Key Signature, and a local scale for each bar. This related information elements are evaluated jointly during two stages of optimisation. During an initial 'modal' stage, a probable scale is proposed for each bar, minimising the number of accidentals to be printed in the printed score with a shortest-path search. Then, during a second stage called 'tonal', these local scales are used to estimate the Key Signature and note names that would result in the best musical notation for the entire piece. We present evaluations conducted on datasets comprising a variety of digital musical scores: jazz lead sheets taken from the Real Book, transcriptions of recordings of jazz soli and bass lines, traditional tunes, as well as classical scores for piano and monophonic instruments. Our procedure was originally designed for use in music transcription, specifically for building digital collections of jazz solos transcribed from audio recordings, for the purposes of music analysis, teaching and the preservation of cultural heritage. This method should also prove useful for other tasks related to the processing of musical notation. Furthermore, to this end, we have defined new distances between various common jazz scales, which may be of some interest to musicological studies.

AI.tldr: A two-stage algorithm for joint pitch spelling and key estimation from MIDI input: first a modal stage assigns local scales per bar via shortest-path minimization of accidentals, then a tonal stage estimates global key signature and note names. Evaluated on jazz, traditional, and classical scores, with new jazz scale distance metrics.
AI.motivation: Music transcription from audio to notation requires accurate pitch spelling (assigning enharmonic note names) and key signature estimation. Existing approaches often treat these separately, but they are interdependent. The authors aim to support building digital collections of jazz solos for analysis, teaching, and cultural heritage preservation, requiring robust, joint estimation that handles diverse musical genres.
AI.method: A two-stage optimization algorithm: (1) Modal stage: for each bar, a local scale is selected from a predefined set by minimizing the number of accidentals required, formulated as a shortest-path search over possible scale sequences across bars. (2) Tonal stage: using the local scales, a global Key Signature and enharmonic note spellings are estimated to optimize overall notation quality for the entire piece. New distance metrics between common jazz scales are introduced to inform scale transitions.
AI.result: Evaluated across multiple datasets including Real Book jazz lead sheets, transcribed jazz solos and bass lines, traditional tunes, and classical piano and monophonic scores. The method demonstrates effectiveness across these varied musical styles.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of pitch spelling and key estimation via a two-stage modal-tonal approach is effective across diverse musical genres. The method is well-suited for automated music transcription pipelines, particularly for jazz heritage projects. The newly defined jazz scale distance metrics may also benefit musicological research.

title: Efficiently Representing Algorithms With Chain-of-Thought Transformers
summary: The increasing popularity of \emph{reasoning} models -- language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer -- is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the \emph{Word RAM} model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on $\bigO(\log n)$-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: \emph{Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms?} For instance, can they sort $n$ items in $\bigO(n \log n)$ steps or run Dijkstra's algorithm in $\bigO(E + V \log V)$ steps? We answer affirmatively, up to poly-logarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: \emph{continuous} CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a \emph{hybrid} architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT \emph{can} efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in $n$. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a ``flat'' instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions -- in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms (the standard model for algorithm design) with only poly-logarithmic overhead, in contrast to prior results about simulating Turing machines which incur quadratic overhead.
AI.motivation: Prior theoretical work showed CoT transformers can simulate Turing machines (thus are computationally universal), but Turing machines are a poor fit for algorithm design. Real algorithms are designed in the Word RAM model (random-access memory, unit-cost operations on O(log n)-bit words), which can be exponentially faster than Turing machines. The open question is whether CoT transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms — e.g., sorting in O(n log n) steps or Dijkstra's algorithm efficiently — or whether they are inherently limited by their sequential, Turing-machine-like nature.
AI.method: The authors prove efficient simulation in three transformer settings: (1) finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, (2) continuous CoT where reasoning takes vector form, and (3) a hybrid architecture with transformer layers atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. They show these architectures can simulate any Word RAM algorithm with poly-logarithmic overhead, reducing to log-squared for flat instruction sets and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions.
AI.result: CoT transformers can simulate Word RAM algorithms with only poly-logarithmic overhead in n — a dramatic improvement over the quadratic overhead required for Turing machine simulation. For flat instruction sets, the overhead drops to O(log² n), and for multiplication-free flat instructions, merely O(log n). This covers practical algorithms like sorting and Dijkstra's algorithm running in near-optimal time.
AI.conclusion: CoT transformers are not merely Turing-complete; they can efficiently simulate the Word RAM model that underpins practical algorithm design. This provides much stronger theoretical justification for chain-of-thought reasoning, bridging the gap between computational theory and practical algorithmics, and showing that CoT reasoning can match the efficiency of standard algorithmic frameworks up to small poly-logarithmic factors.

title: CzechDocs: A Multiway Parallel Dataset of Formatted Documents for Minority Languages in Czechia
summary: We present CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, and PDF) covering Czech and minority languages used in Czechia-primarily Ukrainian and English, with smaller portions of Vietnamese, Russian and other languages. The dataset is designed to support the evaluation of machine translation systems that aim to preserve document formatting during translation. We provide a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation on a validation subset of the dataset. This validation split, together with the evaluation toolkit, is publicly released for further research. A held-out test split will be reserved for a future shared task focused on document-level translation with formatting preservation.

AI.tldr: CzechDocs is a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, PDF) for Czech and minority languages in Czechia, designed to evaluate format-preserving machine translation systems.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of evaluation resources for machine translation systems that preserve document formatting (HTML, DOCX, PDF) during translation, particularly for Czech and minority languages spoken in Czechia.
AI.method: Creation of CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset spanning three document formats across Czech, Ukrainian, English, Vietnamese, Russian, and other minority languages. A validation subset with an evaluation toolkit is publicly released, while a held-out test split is reserved for a future shared task on document-level translation with formatting preservation.
AI.result: The paper provides a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation evaluated on the validation subset. The validation split and evaluation toolkit are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: CzechDocs fills a critical resource gap for format-preserving document-level MT evaluation. The held-out test split will serve as the basis for a future shared task, encouraging further research in this area.

title: BIM-Edit: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IFC-Based Building Information Modeling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to computer-aided design (CAD) to generate design artifacts from textual instructions. In engineering practice, this requires more than creating new geometry, models must also understand existing scenes, edit them correctly, and preserve semantics and relations.
