However, many CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models rather than editing existing ones, and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. We introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (BIM) represented in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format. BIM provides a challenging testbed because building models encode geometry together with semantic and relational structure. BIM-Edit contains 324 editing tasks spanning 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes. Tasks are expressed using three instruction categories - direct, spatial, and topological - covering both explicit and scene-grounded edits. We evaluate outputs along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Across evaluated LLMs, the best-performing model achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks. These results demonstrate a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the requirements of structured engineering design workflows.

AI.tldr: BIM-Edit is a new benchmark for evaluating large language models on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (IFC format), featuring 324 tasks across 11 real and 36 synthetic building models. The best LLM achieves only 49.5% average score across geometric, semantic, and topological metrics, revealing a substantial capability gap for structured CAD editing.
AI.motivation: Existing CAD benchmarks focus on generating new geometry from scratch rather than editing existing models, and they primarily evaluate geometric correctness while neglecting semantic and relational structure. Real engineering workflows demand models that can understand, edit, and preserve the rich semantics and topology of existing scenes — a gap BIM-Edit aims to address using IFC-based building models.
AI.method: The authors construct BIM-Edit, a benchmark of 324 natural-language editing tasks applied to 11 realistic BIM models and 36 synthetic scenes in IFC format. Tasks span three instruction categories: direct (explicit edits), spatial (position/location-based), and topological (connectivity/relationship-based). Model outputs are evaluated on three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency, producing an aggregated score.
AI.result: Across all evaluated LLMs, the top performer reaches only 49.5% average across the three metrics. No model fully solves more than 3.4% of the 324 tasks, indicating severe deficiencies in handling structured, multi-faceted BIM editing.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of structured engineering design workflows. BIM-Edit establishes a rigorous, multi-dimensional evaluation framework that highlights the limitations of LLMs in editing tasks requiring geometric precision, semantic understanding, and topological consistency simultaneously.

title: Efficient Neural Network Model Selection for Few-Class Application Datasets
summary: While much effort has focused on developing and benchmarking high-performance neural networks, less attention has been given to how dataset properties, known to practitioners, can guide efficient model selection. Neural models are typically evaluated on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten. To address this understudied but common setting, we develop a measure of classification difficulty based on data-side properties and show how it enables more efficient model selection for few-class datasets, where traditional approaches are less effective. We term this phenomenon "few-class distinctiveness". Our metric allows comparison of models and datasets 6 to 29$\times$ faster than repeated training and testing. Leveraging this insight, we extend scaled model families below the smallest published models, achieving greater efficiency at similar accuracy, for example models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Targeting resource-constrained applications, we demonstrate few-class model selection across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios, highlighting practical gains in efficiency without sacrificing performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "few-class distinctiveness," a data-side metric for measuring classification difficulty in datasets with few classes (≤10). This metric enables 6–29× faster model selection compared to repeated training/testing. Using this insight, the authors design smaller model variants that outperform existing compact models (e.g., 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano) while maintaining accuracy on mobile robot, drone, and IoT tasks.
AI.motivation: Most neural network research and benchmarking targets datasets with thousands of classes, but many real-world applications involve fewer than ten classes. Standard model selection approaches (repeated training and testing) are inefficient in this few-class regime, and the relationship between dataset properties and optimal model capacity is underexplored. The authors aim to formalize how data-side characteristics can guide efficient model selection for these common yet understudied settings.
AI.method: The authors propose a classification difficulty measure based on data-side properties that captures "few-class distinctiveness" — how separable classes are in feature space. This metric quantifies inherent dataset difficulty without requiring model training. By correlating this metric with model performance, they enable rapid model selection: comparing candidate architectures and datasets without repeated training. They also extend scaled model families downward (below YOLOv5-nano scale) to create ultra-compact models matched to the difficulty of few-class tasks.
AI.result: The proposed metric enables model and dataset comparisons 6 to 29× faster than traditional train-and-test cycles. Ultra-compact models designed using this approach achieve comparable accuracy to larger counterparts — e.g., models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Practical validation across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios demonstrates efficiency gains without sacrificing performance.
AI.conclusion: Data-side properties, formalized through few-class distinctiveness, provide a principled and computationally efficient basis for model selection in few-class settings. This approach bridges the gap between benchmarking practices (many classes) and real-world deployment (few classes), enabling better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for resource-constrained applications.

title: Actionable Activation Directions for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Misalignment Across Language Model Families
summary: Fine-tuning language models on insecure code induces emergent misalignment with poorly understood internal structure. We investigate whether this misalignment corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction shared across architectures. Across four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) finetuned identically, a difference-in-means direction achieves 99.6% separation of aligned and misaligned activations at each model's final layer. Causal steering by subtracting this direction reduces code spillover by 21-51 points, while a secure-code control confirms content specificity. Cross-architecture transfer via ridge regression maps yields large behavioral suppression (up to 46 points) but fails specificity controls as random and orthogonal directions perform comparably. We identify a two-tier specificity structure: within-model directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. An asymmetric transfer topology emerges, with Gemma and Qwen acting as geometric donors and Llama as a receiver. These findings define the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning on insecure code creates causally steerable misalignment directions within models, but cross-architecture transfer lacks specificity despite showing behavioral effects.
AI.motivation: To determine whether emergent misalignment from insecure code fine-tuning corresponds to a shared, causally actionable activation-space direction across model architectures, and to characterize the specificity limits of cross-architecture interventions.
AI.method: Four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) were identically fine-tuned on insecure code. Authors extracted a difference-in-means direction between aligned and misaligned activations at the final layer, performed causal steering via directional subtraction, tested cross-architecture transfer using ridge regression, and employed secure-code and random/orthogonal direction controls for specificity.
AI.result: Within-model: difference-in-means direction achieves 99.6% activation separation; causal steering reduces code spillover by 21–51 points with confirmed content specificity. Cross-model: ridge regression transfer yields up to 46 points of behavioral suppression but fails specificity controls — random and orthogonal directions perform comparably. An asymmetric transfer topology emerges: Gemma and Qwen act as geometric donors, Llama as receiver.
AI.conclusion: Misalignment directions exhibit a two-tier specificity structure: within-model directions are causally specific and actionable, while cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. Linear cross-architecture correction has fundamental specificity limits; within-model probing is recommended for auditing purposes.

title: Modularity-Free Conflict-Averse Training for Generalized PINNs
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a powerful framework for solving PDEs by embedding physical laws into differentiable objectives. Despite their advances, training PINNs remains fragile: recent conflict-averse optimization schemes alleviate gradient interference between residual and boundary losses, but we show that their effectiveness deteriorates as model capacity increases. In this paper, we identify a capacity-induced failure mode, where overparameterized networks undergo functional modularity, self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence toward Pareto-stationary points. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks demonstrate that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/heejokong/ModSync}.

AI.tldr: Overparameterized PINNs suffer from functional modularity, where the network self-partitions into task-exclusive modules that harm convergence. The authors propose ModSync, which penalizes task-exclusive connections to preserve cross-objective interaction, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: Conflict-averse optimization schemes for PINNs (e.g., mitigating gradient interference between residual and boundary losses) degrade as model capacity increases. The authors identify that overparameterized networks undergo "functional modularity," self-partitioning into modules dedicated to single tasks, which suppresses cross-objective interaction and prevents convergence to Pareto-stationary points.
AI.method: The paper proposes Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), a framework that integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse PINN training. ModSync penalizes task-exclusive (modular) connections in the network while preserving interaction-promoting pathways, effectively discouraging functional modularity and maintaining cross-objective coupling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks show that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy compared to existing conflict-averse training methods.
AI.conclusion: Functional modularity is a critical failure mode in overparameterized PINNs, and structural optimization via ModSync effectively counteracts it, enabling robust multi-objective training at scale.

title: OnDeFog: Online Decision Transformer under Frame Dropping
summary: In challenging real-world reinforcement learning applications, communication delays or sensor failures often cause frame dropping, in which the agent cannot receive the dropped states and associated rewards. To address the performance degradation caused by frame dropping, the Decision Transformer under Random Frame Dropping (DeFog) was developed by incorporating additional mechanisms into the decision transformer to tackle frame dropping. Although DeFog can mitigate performance degradation in frame-dropping environments, since DeFog is an offline learning method, it struggles to effectively generalize to novel states not adequately represented in the training dataset. In this study, we propose OnDeFog, which integrates the mechanisms in DeFog with the online decision transformer (ODT), an online reinforcement learning method that learns policies through direct environmental interaction. Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that our proposed OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments characterized by high dropping frame rate and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large amount of low-reward data.

AI.tldr: OnDeFog integrates DeFog's frame-dropping mechanisms into the Online Decision Transformer (ODT), enabling online policy learning that outperforms both ODT (in high frame-drop environments) and DeFog (on datasets with abundant low-reward data).
AI.motivation: DeFog addresses frame dropping in offline RL but fails to generalize to novel states unseen in the training dataset. Online methods like ODT can adapt through interaction, motivating the integration of DeFog's mechanisms into an online framework.
AI.method: OnDeFog combines DeFog's frame-dropping-specific mechanisms (designed for the Decision Transformer architecture) with the Online Decision Transformer (ODT), which learns policies through direct environmental interaction rather than static datasets.
AI.result: OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments with high frame-dropping rates and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing large amounts of low-reward data.
AI.conclusion: Integrating DeFog's frame-dropping mechanisms into an online learning framework (ODT) yields a robust agent that handles frame dropping effectively while maintaining the ability to generalize through environmental interaction.

title: The Register Gap: A Meaning Intelligence Framework for Nigerian Public Discourse
comment: Preprint. 12 pages, 2 tables. Supplementary materials: MIF Master Specification v2.0, Annotation Guidelines v1.0, and 30-item public calibration set with gold labels available from the author
summary: We introduce the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation and evaluation schema for Nigerian public discourse that separates surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Existing benchmarks for Nigerian languages, including NaijaSenti and AfriSenti, treat sentiment classification as a three-way polarity task (positive, negative, neutral). We argue that the dominant failure mode of AI systems on Nigerian discourse is not translation failure but context failure: the same utterance carries opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situation. The MIF operationalises this insight across nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. We construct a 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers, and evaluate a frontier language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions. The headline finding is the Register Gap: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) when the model receives the MIF schema in-context. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score increases by 5.4 points (73.2 to 78.6) under schema-informed prompting, with the largest practical gains in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points). We release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and the 30-item public calibration set to support reproducibility, while retaining a private holdout corpus for contamination-protected evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation schema for Nigerian public discourse that distinguishes surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Testing on a 30-item calibration dataset shows that providing the MIF schema to Gemini 2.5 Flash dramatically improves performance, particularly in register classification (+40 points), coded-subtext detection, and strategic action recommendation.
AI.motivation: Existing sentiment benchmarks for Nigerian languages (NaijaSenti, AfriSenti) reduce analysis to three-way polarity (positive/negative/neutral), ignoring the reality that identical utterances in Nigerian discourse can carry opposite pragmatic force depending on context. The authors argue the dominant AI failure mode is not translation but **context failure**, and current tools lack the dimensional richness to capture irony, coded subtext, register, and speaker intent.
AI.method: The authors designed the MIF with nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. They constructed a 30-item calibration dataset across four linguistic registers (Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, code-mixed). A frontier model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) was evaluated under two conditions: zero-shot prompting and schema-informed prompting (MIF provided in-context).
AI.result: The key finding is the **Register Gap**: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) with schema-informed prompting. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score improves from 73.2 to 78.6 (+5.4 points). Largest practical gains occur in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points).
AI.conclusion: Providing structured sociolinguistic context via the MIF schema dramatically improves LLM performance on Nigerian discourse understanding. The authors release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and public calibration set (withholding a private holdout for contamination-protected future evaluation) to support reproducibility and further research.

title: Implicit Semantic-Aware Communication Based on Hypergraph Reasoning
comment: This work is accepted at IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: Semantic-aware communication has emerged as a transformative paradigm for next-generation communication systems, shifting the fundamental goal from transmitting bit-level symbols to reliably recovering and understanding the semantic meaning of information. Previous studies have demonstrated that representing the semantic content of source messages as graph-based structures can significantly improve communication efficiency and the accuracy of semantic inference at the receiver. However, existing solutions typically employ graphs that capture only pairwise relationships, thereby neglecting higher-order implicit correlations commonly observed in real-world scenarios, such as group interactions, multi-entity associations, and complex relational contexts. This limitation reduces semantic expressiveness and makes semantic inference susceptible to ambiguity and performance degradation, particularly under noisy or corrupted channel conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework, HISR, which leverages hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities. In HISR, entities and their associated higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design not only disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate the over-smoothing effects commonly found in traditional graph embedding methods but also enables robust semantic inference even when partial information loss occurs during transmission. Numerical results show that the proposed HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HISR, a hypergraph-based semantic reasoning framework for semantic communication that captures higher-order relationships among entities, achieving up to 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic communication systems rely on graph-based representations that only capture pairwise relationships, neglecting higher-order correlations (group interactions, multi-entity associations, complex relational contexts). This reduces semantic expressiveness and causes inference ambiguity, especially under noisy channel conditions.
AI.method: The HISR framework represents semantic knowledge entities and their higher-order relations using hypergraphs (where hyperedges connect multiple entities simultaneously). Entities and relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts, which disentangles diverse semantic interactions and mitigates over-smoothing effects common in traditional graph embeddings.
AI.result: HISR achieves up to 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph-based semantic representations offer a superior alternative to traditional pairwise graphs for semantic-aware communication, enabling more robust and accurate semantic inference even under partial information loss during transmission.

title: Federated Bilevel Performative Prediction
summary: Federated bilevel optimization is widely used for nested learning problems across distributed clients, such as federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning under privacy and communication constraints. Most existing formulations assume fixed client data distributions, which can be violated by performativity, where deployed decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shift. We study federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper-level (UL) and lower-level (LL) objectives are evaluated under client-dependent, decision-dependent distributions. We formalize the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and provide sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. We then develop two federated methods to compute the FBPS solution: FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method based on federated hypergradient estimation with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines, and CNN-based classification further demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods in nonconvex neural network settings.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper and lower-level objectives suffer client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shifts. The authors define the Federated Bilevel Performatively Stable (FBPS) point, prove existence/uniqueness conditions, and propose two algorithms: FBi-RRM (linear convergence under contraction) and FBi-SGD (communication-efficient with convergence guarantees). Experiments on strategic regression, meta strategic classification, and CNN-based tasks validate the framework.
AI.motivation: Existing federated bilevel optimization assumes fixed client data distributions. However, in real-world deployments, decisions can reshape client behavior (performativity), causing decision-dependent distribution shifts. No prior work addresses performativity in the federated bilevel setting, where both upper-level (e.g., meta-learner) and lower-level (e.g., client adaption) objectives are affected by these shifts.
AI.method: The authors formalize the Federated Bilevel Performatively Stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective, establishing sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness. They develop two algorithms: (1) FBi-RRM, a repeated retraining method achieving linear convergence under a contraction condition on the performative sensitivity, and (2) FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method using federated hypergradient estimation with diminishing step sizes, with convergence guarantees when performative sensitivities are sufficiently small.
AI.result: Theoretical results establish convergence guarantees for both algorithms under stated conditions. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification empirically validate the predicted stability thresholds. The proposed methods demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines. CNN-based classification experiments further confirm practical effectiveness in nonconvex neural network settings.
AI.conclusion: Federated bilevel performative prediction is a principled framework for nested learning under client-specific distribution shifts. The proposed FBi-RRM and FBi-SGD algorithms provide effective solutions with theoretical convergence guarantees, and empirical results confirm their practical utility across both convex and nonconvex settings.

title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
summary: Effective Automated Essay Scoring (AES) are expected to support both reliable assessment and actionable instructional feedback. However, existing approaches often treat scoring and feedback as separate components: neural scoring models provide limited interpretability, while Large Language Model (LLM)-based feedback is typically insensitive to learners proficiency levels. To address this fragmentation, this work proposes PsyScore, a psychometrically-aware framework that integrates diagnostic assessment with instructional scaffolding through a shared latent ability representation. PsyScore comprises three key modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer that incorporates the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural architecture, enabling the precise estimation of student ability while maintaining psychometric interpretability, a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator, which conditions multi-agent feedback strategies on the diagnosed ability parameter to adapt instructional focus across different proficiency levels, and a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy that assesses feedback quality via pairwise preference judgements and student revision simulations. Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset demonstrate that PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while providing more pedagogically aligned feedback.

AI.tldr: PsyScore is a psychometrically-aware AES framework that unifies diagnostic scoring and adaptive feedback via a shared latent ability representation, using a neural IRT scorer, a ZPD-scaffolded feedback generator, and a multi-perspective evaluation strategy.
AI.motivation: Existing AES systems fragment scoring and feedback: neural scorers lack interpretability, and LLM-based feedback ignores learner proficiency levels. There is a need for integrated, psychometrically-grounded assessment that aligns scoring with pedagogically appropriate, proficiency-sensitive feedback.
AI.method: PsyScore integrates three modules: (1) a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer embedding the Graded Partial Credit Model into a neural network for interpretable ability estimation; (2) a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator that uses multi-agent strategies conditioned on diagnosed ability to adapt instructional focus; and (3) a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy combining pairwise preference judgments with student revision simulations.
AI.result: Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset show PsyScore achieves competitive automated scoring accuracy while delivering feedback that is more pedagogically aligned with learner needs compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Integrating psychometric measurement with instructional scaffolding through a shared ability representation enables AES systems to simultaneously produce reliable scores and proficiency-adaptive, actionable feedback.

title: Manifold Bandits: Bayesian Curriculum Learning over the Latent Geometry of Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a central approach for improving reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), where training efficiency depends critically on how problems are sampled during optimization. Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods typically prioritize prompts of intermediate difficulty, treating problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms and overlooking the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. In this work, we frame problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity: problems are related through the model's latent representation space, and sampling decisions can steer how learning signals evolve across that space. To operationalize this perspective, we introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and applies Bayesian learning to guide sampling. Empirically, we find that different sampling strategies induce non-trivial tradeoffs between productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). These results show that prioritizing difficulty alone is insufficient for strong downstream performance, highlighting the importance of incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling.

AI.tldr: The paper frames RL training problem sampling for LLMs as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity, proposes the Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC) framework using a hierarchical task tree and Bayesian learning, and shows that difficulty-based sampling alone is insufficient — structure and type-awareness matter.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods for RL-based LLM reasoning treat problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms, ignoring the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space where problems are related through the model's latent representations.
AI.method: The authors introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and applies Bayesian learning to guide sampling. They formulate problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit with endogenous non-stationarity, where sampling decisions influence how learning signals propagate across the latent representation space.
AI.result: Different sampling strategies reveal non-trivial tradeoffs among three dimensions: productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). Prioritizing difficulty alone does not yield strong downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling is critical for improving RL-based reasoning in LLMs. Difficulty-based heuristics alone are insufficient; a manifold-aware, hierarchical approach like BMC better balances the productivity–diversity–utility tradeoff.

title: CATCH-ME if you RAG: a dataset of Contextually Annotated multi-Turn Counterspeech against Hate and Misinformation Exchanges
summary: Online hate speech and misinformation frequently overlap, yet NLP research has mainly treated them in isolation. While LLMs represent a scalable solution for assisting humans in the generation of counterspeech for both threats, zero-shot models frequently generate repetitive and vague responses, underscoring the need for high-quality examples to steer model generation. However, existing counterspeech datasets against the overlap of hate and misinformation are scarce and limited to single-turn English dialogues, while real-life interactions span across multiple turns and languages. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dataset of dialogues tackling the intersection of hate and misinformation. To ensure factual grounding, the dialogues are also anchored in verified external knowledge (i.e., fact-checking articles and NGO reports) and include document- and chunk-level span annotations, making it directly applicable for RAG systems. Covering five languages and targeting hate directed at seven marginalized groups, this novel resource enables the training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first large-scale, multilingual, expert-curated dataset of multi-turn dialogues addressing the intersection of hate speech and misinformation, grounded in verified external knowledge with span-level annotations for RAG-based counterspeech generation.
AI.motivation: Hate speech and misinformation frequently co-occur, yet NLP research treats them separately. Current counterspeech datasets are limited to single-turn English dialogues, lack factual grounding, and fail to capture multilingual, multi-turn real-world interactions. LLMs need high-quality exemplars to avoid repetitive, vague zero-shot responses.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale, expert-curated multilingual dialogue dataset spanning five languages and targeting seven marginalized groups. Dialogues are anchored to verified external knowledge (fact-checking articles and NGO reports) with document- and chunk-level span annotations, enabling direct application in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems for training and evaluating counterspeech models.
AI.result: The paper delivers a novel resource — a multi-turn, multilingual counterspeech dataset grounded in verified knowledge — that enables training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models targeting the overlap of hate speech and misinformation.
AI.conclusion: By providing a multilingual, multi-turn, knowledge-grounded dataset, the work bridges a critical gap in counterspeech research, paving the way for more effective, context-aware, and factually accurate counterspeech generation models that can operate across languages and real-world conversational settings.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

AI.tldr: Introduces Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies how well predictive models respect logical rules, independent of predictive accuracy, applicable to any dataset and model over relational vocabularies, with automatic SQL-based computation for Horn rules.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation metrics (ranking quality, prediction error, classification accuracy) only measure predictive performance but fail to assess logical consistency of model outputs. In high-stakes domains like healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, respecting domain-specific constraints is as critical as accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension.
AI.method: RVS distinguishes between hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities). It operates over any dataset and any predictive model expressed with a relational vocabulary. Computation is automated via SQL queries generated from Horn rules. RVS can also evaluate dataset consistency and help identify poorly defined rules.
AI.result: Evaluated on three benchmarks (knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression) across rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic models. Results show that models with comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing behavioral differences invisible to standard metrics.
AI.conclusion: RVS fills a critical gap in model evaluation by adding a logical consistency dimension. It enables practitioners to detect rule violations, compare models beyond accuracy, audit training data, and refine rule sets, thereby promoting safer deployment of ML in high-stakes settings.

title: Learning universal approximations for partial differential equations with Physics-Informed Broad Learning System
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a central role in modeling complex physical, biological, and engineering systems. While traditional numerical solvers are robust, they often incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies, whereas recent Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative but frequently suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. To bridge this gap, this article proposes the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a novel backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization. We improved an algorithm within this framework to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently and provide a rigorous mathematical proof establishing the universal approximation property of PIBLS for these equations. Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy. This framework provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, offering a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: PIBLS reformulates PDE solving as direct least-squares optimization in a backpropagation-free framework, achieving 1–3 orders of magnitude speedup over PINNs with higher accuracy, and provides a rigorous proof of universal approximation for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical PDE solvers are robust but computationally expensive due to mesh dependencies. PINNs offer a mesh-free alternative but suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. There is a need for a framework that combines the mesh-free advantages of neural approaches with faster, more stable training.
AI.method: The authors propose the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a backpropagation-free framework that casts PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization problem. An improved algorithm within PIBLS is introduced to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently. A rigorous mathematical proof is provided for the universal approximation property of PIBLS for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.result: Experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs show PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PIBLS offers a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, serving as a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

title: Augmenting Game AI with Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Vision paper, published in Conference on Games 2026
summary: Immersion in video games depends not only on graphics, audio, and game mechanics, but also on the quality of in-game characters. Producing believable characters, or game AI, remains a significant challenge as behavioral complexity is hard to capture with hand-coded systems. Game AI is a source of immersion and engagement; however, the limitations stemming from the challenges of creating game AI often lead to frustration and the breaking of the illusion of realism within the game. The introduction of machine learning models opens the door to creating more believable, authentic, and relatable characters in games. The promise is that they either learn from interacting with the game, or from player data, to develop true human-like behavior. In this paper, we envision more applications of reinforcement learning for game AI in the future. For this to materialize, current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment across game genres. Therefore, we propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models with a set of requirements in mind that are suited towards game AI and game development. We present examples of games with reinforcement learning-augmented game AI and describe the practicalities of deploying player-facing machine learning agents in modern games. Furthermore, we identify bottlenecks and hard problems in these areas, which we believe offer promising research directions to accelerate the adoption of machine learning in game AI for the video game industry.

AI.tldr: This paper envisions broader adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) for game AI to create more believable characters. It proposes a training framework tailored to game development requirements, presents examples of RL-augmented game AI, discusses deployment practicalities, and identifies key bottlenecks and research directions to accelerate industry adoption.
AI.motivation: Hand-coded game AI struggles to capture behavioral complexity, leading to character inauthenticity that breaks immersion and causes player frustration. Machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning, promises more believable, human-like characters by learning from game interaction or player data, but current research limitations prevent broad deployment across game genres.
AI.method: The paper takes a vision and framework approach: it (1) proposes a reinforcement learning training framework with requirements specifically suited to game AI and game development pipelines; (2) presents case examples of games already using RL-augmented game AI; (3) analyzes practical deployment considerations for player-facing ML agents; and (4) systematically identifies bottlenecks and hard problems in the field.
AI.result: The paper identifies several bottlenecks: current RL research limitations that hinder cross-genre deployment, practical challenges in shipping player-facing ML agents in commercial games, and specific hard problems that remain unsolved. It also provides concrete examples of RL-augmented game AI already deployed in modern games, demonstrating feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning holds significant promise for transforming game AI into more believable, authentic characters, but realizing this vision requires addressing fundamental research bottlenecks. The proposed framework and identified research directions aim to bridge the gap between academic RL research and industry game development, accelerating adoption of machine learning in the video game industry.

title: An Information Theoretic Framework for Graph Novelty Generation via Latent Mixture Modeling
summary: We propose an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation, which aims to generate data that are distinct from existing patterns while preserving global structural consistency. Our approach embeds data into a latent space, models the latent distribution using finite mixture models, and generates novel samples by imposing explicit novelty and reliability conditions formulated in terms of description length. Specifically, novelty is enforced by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained by all existing mixture components, while reliability constrains their impact on the overall mixture structure under the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero with explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.

AI.tldr: Proposes an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation that uses finite mixture models in latent space, with novelty and reliability conditions based on Minimum Description Length (MDL), providing theoretical guarantees on misclassification rates and empirical validation on graph datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models lack a principled framework for generating graph-structured data that is both novel (distinct from training patterns) and structurally consistent (preserving global graph properties). There is a need for quantifiable risk control in novelty generation.
AI.method: Data is embedded into a latent space and modeled via finite mixture models. Novelty generation is formulated through two MDL-based conditions: (1) novelty condition — generated samples must be poorly explained by all existing mixture components (high description length under any single component); (2) reliability condition — the generated sample must not distort the overall mixture structure when incorporated, evaluated under the MDL principle. Theoretical convergence rates are derived for misclassification probabilities under appropriate threshold choices.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis demonstrates that with properly chosen thresholds, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero at explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets confirm the method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.
AI.conclusion: The MDL-based framework provides a theoretically grounded approach to graph novelty generation, offering both formal guarantees on error rates and practical empirical performance, bridging information theory and generative modeling for structured data.

title: Beyond Global Replanning: Hierarchical Recovery for Cross-Device Agent Systems
summary: Real-world computer-use tasks often span multiple applications and devices, requiring agents to coordinate heterogeneous environments under dynamic runtime failures. Existing multi-device agent systems support task decomposition and cross-device assignment, but recovery remains largely coarse-grained: when execution fails, they typically retry the same strategy, reassign the subtask, or revise the global plan, without systematically modeling the device-local strategy space. This limits their ability to distinguish failures that can be repaired within the current device from those that require cross-device replanning. We propose \textbf{H-RePlan}, a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents with unified API--CLI--GUI execution. H-RePlan equips each device with interchangeable execution strategies and separates device-local strategy recovery from orchestrator-level global replanning through a compact cross-layer failure abstraction. To evaluate this capability, we introduce \textbf{HeraBench}, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android devices and injects strategy- and device-level failures. Experiments show that H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, achieving higher completion, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rates while reducing the token cost required for reliable end-to-end success. These results demonstrate that scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution.

AI.tldr: H-RePlan is a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents that separates device-local strategy recovery from global replanning, evaluated on a new fault-injected benchmark (HeraBench) spanning Linux and Android, where it outperforms coarse-grained baselines in robustness and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-device agent systems handle failures coarsely—retrying the same strategy, reassigning subtasks, or revising the global plan—without modeling the device-local strategy space. This prevents them from distinguishing failures repairable within a device from those requiring cross-device replanning, limiting robustness in real-world cross-application, multi-device workflows.
AI.method: H-RePlan introduces a hierarchical replanning architecture: (1) each device is equipped with interchangeable execution strategies (API, CLI, GUI); (2) a compact cross-layer failure abstraction separates device-local strategy recovery (switching strategies within the same device) from orchestrator-level global replanning; (3) evaluation via HeraBench, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android and injects both strategy-level and device-level failures.
AI.result: H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines on completion rate, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rate, while also reducing the token cost required for reliable end-to-end success.
AI.conclusion: Scope-aware hierarchical recovery—distinguishing device-local from cross-device failure responses—is essential for robust multi-device agent execution.

title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
summary: Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ($128\times 128$) and AFHQ ($256\times 256$) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.

AI.tldr: Flow map models with a lookahead parameter t continuously span the distortion-perception tradeoff frontier in image restoration, interpolating between MMSE and perceptual-quality regimes without retraining or auxiliary models.
AI.motivation: Existing image restoration methods face a rigid distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff: low-distortion outputs are blurry, while perceptually sharp outputs lack fidelity. Current approaches require paired supervision, auxiliary models, or cumbersome hyperparameter tuning to traverse this frontier. The authors aim to provide a single-model solution that naturally and continuously spans the entire DP frontier.
AI.method: The authors leverage flow map models—an extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average flow field. They show that the lookahead parameter t in these models implicitly defines a one-parameter family of denoisers. For Gaussian targets, they prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier. They embed this mechanism within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) solver to handle general linear and nonlinear inverse problems, where t controls the tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency.
AI.result: A single trained flow map, without retraining, matches or surpasses specialized baselines at both the MMSE and perceptual extremes. Experiments on CelebA (128×128) and AFHQ (256×256) across multiple linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate the approach.
AI.conclusion: Flow map models provide a principled, continuous mechanism for navigating the DP tradeoff in both restoration and general inverse problems, unifying two previously disparate operating regimes within a single trained model.

title: StylisticBias: A Few Human Visual Cues Drive Most Social Biases in MLLMs
comment: Accepted to the non-archival workshops AI4Good and Culture x AI at ICML 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in personally and societally consequential settings, yet the visual cues that shape how these models judge people remain poorly understood. Prior work often compares different (groups of) individuals, making it difficult to separate appearance effects from identity differences. We introduce StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute-level social bias in MLLMs. We generate 500 photorealistic base faces and create about 50 single-attribute variations per face, producing about 25K images. This design keeps identity fixed and changes one visual attribute at a time. It lets us measure how specific cues shift model judgments. We evaluate six MLLMs across 25 binary social judgment scenarios. We find that age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. We further find that about 15 attributes account for nearly 80\% of the total variation, showing that bias is concentrated in a small set of visual cues. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments that are semantically aligned with appearance, especially socioeconomic and style-related judgments. We release StylisticBias as a benchmark for fine-grained bias evaluation in multimodal models. Code and dataset: https://github.com/timo-cavelius/StylisticBias and https://hf.co/datasets/shaghayegh/stylistic-bias-dataset.

AI.tldr: StylisticBias is a controlled benchmark using 25K photorealistic face images (500 base faces × ~50 single-attribute variations) to measure how visual cues like age, body type, and fashion style bias MLLM social judgments, finding that ~15 attributes account for 80% of judgment variation.
AI.motivation: Prior bias studies compare different individuals, confounding identity and appearance effects. There is a need to isolate how specific visual attributes—independent of identity—shift multimodal large language model judgments in socially consequential settings.
AI.method: The authors generate 500 photorealistic base faces and systematically vary one visual attribute at a time (e.g., age, body type, fashion style), producing ~25K images. Six MLLMs are evaluated across 25 binary social judgment scenarios, measuring attribute-level shifts while holding identity fixed.
AI.result: Age and body type dominate identity-level effects; fashion style and other cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. Approximately 15 attributes explain nearly 80% of total judgment variation. Sensitivity is strongest in semantically aligned judgments, particularly socioeconomic and style-related evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Bias in MLLMs is concentrated in a small set of visual attributes, with semantically aligned judgments most affected. StylisticBias is released as a benchmark for fine-grained, attribute-level bias evaluation in multimodal models.

title: Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence
summary: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a thermodynamic definition of intelligence as "lawful amplification of rare but valid futures" and proves that recursive self-simulation (a system modeling itself within the world) is necessary and nearly sufficient for achieving high intelligence under this measure, creating a universal scale applicable from passive matter to AI systems.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous, universal, and measurable definition of intelligence grounded in physics (thermodynamics) that applies across all systems — from simple feedback controllers to humans and AI — rather than relying on behavioral or task-specific benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors formalize intelligence thermodynamically as "rare-valid lift": the ratio of the probability of admissible outcomes under the system's policy versus passive dynamics. They then mathematically prove a necessity theorem (high rare-valid lift implies high-fidelity internal simulation of rare-valid futures) and a conditional near-sufficiency theorem (high simulation fidelity plus an effective policy yields lift approaching the actuation-limited optimum), establishing recursive self-simulation as the architectural core of thermodynamic intelligence.
AI.result: Two central results: (1) a necessity statement — high rare-valid lift is impossible without internal simulation identifying rare-valid futures with high fidelity; (2) a conditional near-sufficiency statement — when rare-valid fidelity is high and an effective policy exists, achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Together, these show recursive self-simulation is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but is architecturally necessary and nearly sufficient under the stated assumptions. The framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale spanning passive matter, feedback controllers, LLMs, humans as text generators, and Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling for Stable RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models by training reward models on preference data and optimizing policies to maximize predicted rewards. However, this pipeline faces two fundamental challenges: (1) reward models cannot signal when their predictions are unreliable, since they usually act as deterministic point estimators; and (2) modern group-based policy optimization can amplify unreliable reward signals, as exemplified by GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards during advantage computation. As policies explore increasingly diverse responses, these two limitations create a critical vulnerability: unreliable reward estimates may be granted disproportionate influence, triggering severe reward hacking. We propose Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM), which equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via quantile-based conformal prediction and reweights GRPO advantages through heteroscedastic variance decomposition. Experiments across HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF demonstrate that UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality compared to standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.

AI.tldr: UARM combines quantile-based conformal prediction for calibrated reward uncertainty with heteroscedastic variance-based advantage reweighting in GRPO, mitigating reward hacking and improving LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF suffers from reward models acting as deterministic point estimators without signaling prediction unreliability, and GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards amplifies unreliable signals, creating vulnerability to reward hacking as policy exploration diversifies.
AI.method: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM) integrates two components: (1) quantile-based conformal prediction to equip reward models with calibrated uncertainty estimates, and (2) heteroscedastic variance decomposition to reweight GRPO advantages, down-weighting high-uncertainty reward signals during policy optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF show UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and yields superior downstream alignment quality versus standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated uncertainty estimation in reward modeling combined with uncertainty-aware advantage reweighting effectively addresses the reward hacking vulnerability in RLHF, leading to more robust and aligned policy optimization.

title: Gender Bias in LLM Hiring Decisions: Evidence from a Japanese Context and Evaluation of Mitigation Strategies
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in hiring workflows, yet most research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has focused on English-language, Western-format resumes. This study examines whether pro-female gender bias extends to a Japanese corporate context and evaluates two practical mitigation strategies. Using a counterfactual resume design with 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes, 12 name pairs selected on linguistically grounded gender-signal criteria, and five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B), we conducted 43,200 API calls across baseline, prompt instruction, and privacy filter conditions. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model confirms a significant pro-female bias across all five models, replicating Western findings in a non-Western context. A prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produces no meaningful reduction in bias. A name-reliance analysis formally identifies the candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing the name from the prompt reduces the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected incompatibility between the privacy filter and GPT-4o's content safety filter, resulting in a 42% refusal rate, highlights a practical deployment challenge for name anonymization in LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit pro-female gender bias when evaluating Japanese-format (rirekisho) resumes, tests two mitigation strategies (prompt instructions and name anonymization), and finds that: (1) pro-female bias persists across all five tested LLMs, (2) gender-neutrality instructions are ineffective, (3) name removal nearly eliminates bias, confirming names as the primary gender signal, but (4) a GPT-4o safety-filter incompatibility causes a 42% refusal rate under the privacy filter condition, posing a practical deployment challenge.
AI.motivation: Prior research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has overwhelmingly focused on English-language, Western-format resumes, leaving a gap regarding whether such biases generalize to non-Western contexts like Japan, where resume formats (rirekisho) and gender-name conventions differ substantially. Additionally, practical mitigation strategies have not been rigorously evaluated in such settings.
AI.method: The authors employed a counterfactual resume design with 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes and 12 gender-paired names selected on linguistically grounded gender-signal criteria. They conducted 43,200 API calls across five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B) under three conditions: baseline, prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction, and a privacy filter (name removal). A crossed random-effects linear mixed model was used for statistical analysis, supplemented by a name-reliance analysis to isolate the causal channel of bias.
AI.result: Significant pro-female bias was confirmed across all five LLMs, replicating Western findings in the Japanese context. The prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produced no meaningful reduction in bias. Name-reliance analysis identified the candidate's name as the primary gender channel: removing the name reduced the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected interaction between the privacy filter and GPT-4o's content safety filter resulted in a 42% refusal rate, revealing a practical deployment obstacle for name anonymization.
AI.conclusion: Pro-female gender bias in LLM hiring evaluations is not confined to Western resume formats but extends robustly to Japanese rirekisho contexts. Simple prompt-based debiasing instructions are ineffective, whereas name anonymization effectively eliminates bias but introduces deployment friction due to LLM safety-filter conflicts. Practitioners must weigh these trade-offs when designing fair LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

title: Enhancing Graph Neural Networks Using Proximity Graphs for Dust Source Emission Forecasting
summary:
Accurate prediction of dust source emissions is critical for mitigating the significant environmental and health hazards posed by dust storms. Traditional forecasting methods often struggle to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of these phenomena.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that proximity graphs enable Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively model the intricate spatial and temporal relationships between data points. Specifically, we use proximity graphs--such as Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph--as the input for GNNs (including GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks, and Graph Attention Networks) to perform message passing.
  Our approach highlights the effectiveness of integrating proximity graphs with GNNs for robust and accurate dust source forecasting. To emphasize the importance of proximity graph representations, we compare our method against GNNs using random graphs for message passing. The results show that GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform those with random graphs and are also far superior to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model in dust source emission forecasting.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using proximity graphs (Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel, k-NN, Yao graphs) as input structures for GNNs (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) to forecast dust source emissions, demonstrating significant superiority over both random-graph GNNs and LSTM baselines.
AI.motivation: Accurate dust source emission prediction is critical for mitigating environmental and health hazards from dust storms, yet traditional forecasting methods inadequately capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics inherent in these phenomena.
AI.method: The authors use various proximity graph constructions (Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, Yao graph) as the adjacency structure input to multiple GNN architectures (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) for message passing. This is benchmarked against GNNs operating on random graphs and an LSTM model.
AI.result: GNNs employing proximity graphs significantly outperform GNNs using random graphs for message passing and are also far superior to the LSTM model in dust source emission forecasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating proximity graphs with GNNs provides a robust and accurate framework for dust source emission forecasting, underscoring the critical role that meaningful spatial graph representations play in capturing spatiotemporal dynamics compared to arbitrary or non-graph-based approaches.

title: Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of language-based tasks by leveraging both extensive parametric knowledge and in-context learning ability, enabling them to incorporate external information provided in the input prompt. However, the integration of external knowledge can introduce conflicts, not only between the model's internal parametric knowledge and the external information, but also among multiple pieces of external contexts. Existing approaches typically assume that either the model or the provided context is reliable, overlooking the possibility that both sources may contain errors, and avoid conflicts by privileging one source over the other, rather than actively resolving inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. Specifically, we first propose an adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval approach that employs a modified semantic entropy measure to quantify an LLM's confidence in its answer to a given query. Based on this confidence estimation, MACR either externalizes the model's internal knowledge as textual representations or retrieves relevant external knowledge when internal knowledge is insufficient, generating basic contexts for subsequent reasoning. Then we introduce an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents that, respectively, induce explicit rules, analyze potential conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across all available contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks, while also providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

AI.tldr: MACR is a multi-agent framework for resolving knowledge conflicts in LLMs, using semantic entropy to assess confidence, adaptive knowledge retrieval, and three specialized agents that induce rules, analyze conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across both parametric and external knowledge sources.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to LLM knowledge conflicts assume either the model or external context is reliable and avoid conflicts by privileging one source, rather than resolving inconsistencies. They overlook that both sources can contain errors and fail to handle conflicts among multiple external contexts.
AI.method: MACR uses: (1) an adaptive knowledge assessment module with modified semantic entropy to quantify LLM confidence and decide whether to externalize internal knowledge or retrieve external knowledge; (2) an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three agents — a rule induction agent, a conflict analysis agent, and a resolution agent — that collaboratively identify, analyze, and resolve conflicts across all available contexts.
AI.result: MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks and provides interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.
AI.conclusion: Moving beyond the binary choice paradigm and incorporating explicit multi-agent conflict resolution yields both superior performance and interpretability for LLM knowledge conflict resolution.

title: When, Where, and How: Adaptive Binning for Tabular Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Medical tabular data are ubiquitous in clinical research, but deep learning for tables remains underexplored because reliable labels often require costly expert adjudication, even though structured clinical variables are routinely available in tabular form. Self-supervised learning can leverage these unlabeled tables, and recent binning-based pretexts offer a promising inductive bias, but existing objectives fix a single global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision. We propose Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext for tabular SSL that couples discretization to learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks and the principles of curriculum learning, our method progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection and selects representation-aware splits to jointly improve value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features, and experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for linear probing and fine-tuning without dataset-specific discretization tuning. We further introduce a medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols to support reproducible progress in this underexplored domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/labhai/Adaptive-Binning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Adaptive Binning, a self-supervised learning method for medical tabular data that uses a training-adaptive discretization pretext with a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum, outperforming fixed global quantile binning on public medical tabular benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Medical tabular data is abundant but lacks labeled examples due to costly expert annotation. Existing self-supervised binning-based pretexts rely on a single fixed global quantile discretization and feature-agnostic supervision, failing to account for feature-specific value distributions and the spectral bias of neural networks (learning low-frequency patterns first).
AI.method: Adaptive Binning couples discretization to training through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Key components: (1) progressive discretization refinement per feature upon plateau detection; (2) representation-aware split selection that jointly optimizes value-space concentration and representation-space coherence; (3) a heterogeneity-aware objective that unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features. The method adapts bin boundaries during training as the model learns, starting coarse and gradually increasing granularity.
AI.result: Experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for both linear probing and fine-tuning, without requiring dataset-specific discretization tuning.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive Binning provides a principled self-supervised learning approach for medical tabular data by making discretization training-adaptive. The paper also contributes a standardized medical tabular SSL benchmark to enable reproducible progress in this underexplored domain.

title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
summary: Student-generated drawings are widely used in science education to assess learners' conceptual understanding in modeling-based tasks aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). However, scoring such drawings requires expert human judgment to interpret complex visual representations, making large-scale assessment costly to implement and sustain in classroom settings. In this work, we study automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings using a vision-based model. We evaluate a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation and propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal enables selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically while deferring uncertain cases for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, highlighting the value of confidence-aware methods for trustworthy educational assessment.

AI.tldr: A Vision Transformer with parameter-efficient adaptation and confidence-aware scoring is proposed for automated assessment of student-generated scientific drawings. The confidence signal enables selective automation, deferring uncertain cases to human review, improving scoring reliability while balancing coverage and risk.
AI.motivation: Student-generated drawings are widely used in NGSS-aligned science education to assess conceptual understanding, but scoring them requires costly expert human judgment, making large-scale classroom implementation unsustainable. Automated scoring is needed to reduce this burden.
AI.method: A Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation is evaluated for scoring student scientific drawings. A confidence-aware scoring framework is proposed that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions, enabling selective automation: high-confidence responses are scored automatically, while uncertain cases are deferred for human review.
AI.result: Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items demonstrate that the approach improves scoring reliability and supports a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
