AI.conclusion: Confidence-aware methods provide a trustworthy pathway for automated educational assessment of student drawings, enabling practical deployment by balancing automation with human oversight.

title: Neural Additive and Basis Models with Feature Selection and Interactions
comment: Accepted at PAKDD 2024. Code is available at https://github.com/shiralab/NAM-FS
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit attractive performance in various fields but often suffer from low interpretability. The neural additive model (NAM) and its variant called the neural basis model (NBM) use neural networks (NNs) as nonlinear shape functions in generalized additive models (GAMs). Both models are highly interpretable and exhibit good performance and flexibility for NN training. NAM and NBM can provide and visualize the contribution of each feature to the prediction owing to GAM-based architectures. However, when using two-input NNs to consider feature interactions or when applying them to high-dimensional datasets, training NAM and NBM becomes intractable due to the increase in the computational resources required. This paper proposes incorporating the feature selection mechanism into NAM and NBM to resolve computational bottlenecks. We introduce the feature selection layer in both models and update the selection weights during training. Our method is simple and can reduce computational costs and model sizes compared to vanilla NAM and NBM. In addition, it enables us to use two-input NNs even in high-dimensional datasets and capture feature interactions. We demonstrate that the proposed models are computationally efficient compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, and they exhibit better or comparable performance with state-of-the-art GAMs.

AI.tldr: NAM and NBM provide interpretable neural network-based generalized additive models but face computational bottlenecks with feature interactions or high-dimensional data. The paper introduces a feature selection layer to reduce costs, enable pairwise interactions, and maintain competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Standard NAM and NBM become computationally intractable when using two-input neural networks for feature interactions or when applied to high-dimensional datasets, due to the explosion in required computational resources. A mechanism is needed to mitigate this bottleneck while preserving interpretability.
AI.method: Introduce a feature selection layer into both NAM and NBM architectures. During training, selection weights are updated to identify and retain relevant features. This simple mechanism prunes unnecessary computations, shrinking model size and cost, and enables the practical use of two-input NNs for capturing feature interactions even in high-dimensional settings.
AI.result: The proposed models are computationally more efficient than vanilla NAM and NBM. They achieve better or comparable performance relative to state-of-the-art GAMs.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a trainable feature selection layer into NAM and NBM effectively resolves their computational bottlenecks, enabling scalable, interpretable modeling with feature interactions and high-dimensional data without sacrificing predictive performance.

title: Lagrange: An Open-Vocabulary, Energy-Based Sparse Framework for Generalized End-to-End Driving
summary: Scaling end-to-end autonomous driving to complex, open-world environments requires perceptual models that generalize to anomalous scenarios and planners that produce kinematically valid trajectories. Existing paradigms face a distinct dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization capacity. Dense models (e.g., occupancy networks), while geometrically robust, incur critical computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-level semantic reasoning. Conversely, sparse, query-based planners are efficient but reliant on closed-set definitions, rendering them vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) events. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer open-vocabulary reasoning, their autoregressive, discrete token generation fundamentally conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency control requirements of vehicle dynamics. To address this, we propose Lagrange, an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework based on Masked Latent Fields (MLF). Rather than relying on dense volumetric reconstructions or closed-set query mechanisms, Lagrange exploits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. We introduce an intent-driven masked cross-attention module that temporally filters irrelevant entities, decoding the attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field defined over spatial coordinates. By framing decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem spanning this energy field, we enforce strict compliance with vehicle kinematics while executing collision avoidance. Extensive offline evaluations on both standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange establishes a promising framework for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

AI.tldr: Lagrange proposes an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse autonomous driving framework using Masked Latent Fields (MLF). It leverages Vision-Language Models for class-agnostic semantic encoding and frames planning as Lagrangian action minimization over a continuous energy field, achieving both kinematic feasibility and generalization to anomalous/open-world scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving models suffer from a dichotomy: dense models (e.g., occupancy networks) are geometrically robust but computationally heavy and semantically limited, while sparse query-based planners are efficient but brittle to out-of-distribution events. VLA models offer open-vocabulary reasoning but their discrete autoregressive token generation conflicts with continuous vehicle control needs. A framework unifying open-vocabulary perception with kinematically feasible continuous planning is needed.
AI.method: Lagrange introduces Masked Latent Fields (MLF): (1) VLMs encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens; (2) an intent-driven masked cross-attention module temporally filters irrelevant entities; (3) attended tokens are decoded into an implicit continuous energy field over spatial coordinates; (4) decision-making is cast as a Lagrangian action minimization problem over this energy field, enforcing vehicle kinematic constraints during collision avoidance.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations on nuScenes (standard) and CODA (long-tail/anomalous) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange achieves robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible performance for open-world autonomous driving.
AI.conclusion: Lagrange establishes a promising framework that bridges the gap between open-vocabulary semantic understanding and kinematically valid planning, offering a viable path toward robust open-world autonomy without the computational burden of dense reconstruction or the brittleness of closed-set sparse models.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Squeeze-Excitation-like Attention
summary: We introduce SEA-PINN, a novel architecture that incorporates a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks to dynamically recalibrate the importance of neurons across layers. A key feature of SEA-PINN is its highly stable initialization. On 17 out of 20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN exhibit nearly negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, establishing a quasi-deterministic and favorable starting point for optimization. Notably, without employing Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activation functions, SEA-PINN attained competitive accuracy (83\% vs. 90\% improvement relative to FNN-PINN on the high-frequency case 7) as compared with TSA-PINN-a model specifically engineered for high-frequency problems via learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations. Furthermore, integrating SEA-PINN into TSA-PINN boosted performance by 42.49\%. These results underscore SEA-PINN as a lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation power, promotes more robust and efficient convergence, and strengthens the overall reliability of physics-informed learning.

AI.tldr: SEA-PINN integrates a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks, achieving quasi-deterministic initialization with near-zero variance, significantly reduced initial loss, and competitive accuracy on high-frequency problems without requiring Fourier features or periodic activations. It functions as a lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation, convergence robustness, and overall reliability.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from poor initialization stability, high variance in training outcomes, and difficulty capturing high-frequency components without specialized architectural modifications (e.g., Fourier features, periodic activations). The authors aim to address these issues with a lightweight, plug-and-play attention mechanism that improves both initialization and representation capacity.
AI.method: The proposed SEA-PINN architecture embeds a Squeeze-Excitation-like channel-wise attention mechanism into PINN layers. This dynamically recalibrates neuron-wise importance through learned scaling factors. The method emphasizes stable initialization, evaluated across 20 benchmark problems. It is also tested as a drop-in module combined with TSA-PINN (which uses learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations for high-frequency problems).
AI.result: On 17 of 20 benchmarks, SEA-PINN showed near-negligible variance and markedly lower initial loss, yielding a quasi-deterministic starting point. Without Fourier features or periodic activations, SEA-PINN achieved 83% improvement over FNN-PINN on high-frequency case 7, versus TSA-PINN's 90% improvement. When integrated into TSA-PINN, performance improved by an additional 42.49%.
AI.conclusion: SEA-PINN is an effective, lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation power, promotes robust and efficient convergence, and strengthens the reliability of physics-informed learning, both as a standalone enhancement and in combination with specialized high-frequency architectures like TSA-PINN.

title: Leveraging systems' non-linearity to tackle the scarcity of data in the design of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems
summary: Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) allows for the efficient building of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems (IFDS). On the other hand, DTL methods still heavily rely on large amounts of labelled data. Obtaining such an amount of data can be challenging when dealing with machines or structures faults. This document proposes a novel approach to the design of vibration-based IFDS using DTL in condition of strong data scarcity. A periodic multi-excitation level procedure leveraging intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems is used to produce images that can be conveniently analysed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to diagnose faults. A new data visualization method and its augmentation technique are proposed in this paper to tackle the typical lack of data encountered during the design of IFDS. Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A novel deep transfer learning approach for vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis under severe data scarcity, using periodic multi-excitation nonlinear responses visualized as images and analyzed by pretrained CNNs, with a new augmentation technique validated on a railway pantograph.
AI.motivation: Deep transfer learning for fault diagnosis still requires large labeled datasets, which are difficult to obtain for machinery and structures. There is a need for effective IFDS design under conditions of strong data scarcity.
AI.method: The authors propose a periodic multi-excitation level procedure that exploits intrinsic nonlinearities of real-world systems to generate images. These images are analyzed by pretrained Convolutional Neural Networks via transfer learning. A new data visualization method and an augmentation technique are introduced to address data scarcity.
AI.result: Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method for fault diagnosis under limited data conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables efficient vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis using deep transfer learning even with scarce labeled data, leveraging system nonlinearities and novel visualization/augmentation techniques.

title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Score Matching in Gaussian Mixtures via Reverse Fisher Divergence
summary: The score matching problem is a central training objective in modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems. A standard approach is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. However, recent results show that even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings, this objective can lead to undesirable and initialization-dependent convergence behavior. In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution. We analyze gradient descent (GD) for fitting Gaussian mixture models and show that this change in the objective leads to significantly better optimization properties. First, when the teacher distribution is a single Gaussian and the student is a Gaussian mixture model with fixed weights and identity covariances, we prove the global convergence of GD from arbitrary initializations. Second, we extend the analysis to the case where the teacher is also a Gaussian mixture model and prove global convergence guarantees under a global random initialization scheme and a $\widetildeΩ(1)$-separation assumption on the target means. In particular, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and we provide conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance. Our proofs rely on a new Lyapunov-based analysis of the gradient descent dynamics, showing that the reverse Fisher divergence has a much more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence.

AI.tldr: The paper studies reverse Fisher divergence as an alternative to forward Fisher divergence for score matching, proving that gradient descent on the reverse objective yields global convergence guarantees for Gaussian mixture models—unlike the forward objective which suffers from poor initialization-dependent behavior.
AI.motivation: Forward Fisher divergence (teacher expectation) can lead to undesirable, initialization-dependent convergence even in simple Gaussian mixture settings. The authors investigate whether reversing the expectation (student expectation) yields a better optimization landscape.
AI.method: The authors analyze gradient descent dynamics on the reverse Fisher divergence for fitting Gaussian mixture models. They employ a Lyapunov-based analysis to prove global convergence: first for a single-Gaussian teacher with a GMM student (fixed weights, identity covariances), then extended to a GMM teacher under a global random initialization scheme with a Ω̃(1)-separation condition on target means.
AI.result: Global convergence from arbitrary initialization is proven for the single-Gaussian teacher case. For the GMM teacher case, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and conditions are provided for convergence in total variation distance.
AI.conclusion: The reverse Fisher divergence exhibits a significantly more favorable optimization landscape than its forward counterpart, enabling global convergence guarantees that are absent for the forward objective.

title: SoftSkill: Behavioral Compression for Contextual Adaptation
summary: Agent skills are commonly deployed as natural-language Markdown files that encode answer policies, evidence-use habits, and task procedures. These files are readable and portable, but they are consumed indirectly: for each task instance, a frozen language model must translate a long textual artifact into generation-time behavior. This paper asks whether a natural-language skill can instead initialize a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model remains frozen. We propose SoftSkill, a frozen-backbone method that tunes such soft skills with next-token prediction and deploys them as latent behavioral priors at inference time. In our main single-round setting, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown skill tokens with a few virtual tokens. We further study agentic execution as a harder boundary case, where sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior. More broadly, the results suggest that some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls over how a frozen model enters the task.

AI.tldr: SoftSkill proposes replacing verbose natural-language Markdown skill files with a compact, trainable continuous prefix (soft skill) that controls a frozen language model's behavior at inference time. A length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves SearchQA by 8.3 points, LiveMath by 42.1 points, and DocVQA by 1.3 points over no-skill prompting, while outperforming SkillOpt by 5.2 and 12.5 points respectively with far fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Agent skills are typically encoded as long Markdown files that a frozen LLM must re-interpret per task instance, incurring substantial token overhead and relying on the model's in-context comprehension. The authors question whether such skills can instead be represented as compact, learnable continuous vectors that directly modulate the model's behavior without modifying the base model weights.
AI.method: SoftSkill tunes a short continuous prefix (e.g., length-32 virtual tokens) prepended to the input using next-token prediction on skill-relevant data, while keeping the base model entirely frozen. This soft delta is trained to serve as a latent behavioral prior. At inference, the learned prefix is deployed in place of the original Markdown skill instructions. The method is also tested on agentic execution via sparse trajectory imitation.
AI.result: A length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B yields: +8.3 pts on SearchQA, +42.1 pts on LiveMath, +1.3 pts on DocVQA over no-skill prompting. Compared to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves SearchQA by 5.2 pts and LiveMath by 12.5 pts, replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown tokens with just a few virtual tokens. Sparse trajectory imitation for agentic tasks provides useful but not yet robust compression of long-horizon procedural behavior.
AI.conclusion: Certain task skills are better represented as compact latent controls (soft prompts) rather than as additional Markdown text for inference-time reinterpretation. SoftSkill demonstrates that lightweight prefix tuning on a frozen backbone can effectively distill skill knowledge into a small continuous representation, outperforming text-based skill methods in both accuracy and token efficiency.

title: On the Oracle Complexity of Interpolation-Based Gradient Descent
summary: Recent work on first-order optimizers for empirical risk minimization (ERM) has suggested that smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data, rather than in the optimization parameters, can be leveraged to improve the oracle complexity of gradient descent (GD) methods. In this paper, we propose an inexact gradient method, piecewise polynomial interpolation-based gradient descent (PPI-GD), which approximates the full gradient in each iteration by querying the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain to construct polynomial interpolants of the resulting gradient samples over appropriately sized patches of the data domain. We analyze the oracle complexity of PPI-GD for strongly convex and non-convex loss functions when the data space dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples, and find it to outperform several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth. Furthermore, our analysis extends several techniques from the error analysis of bicubic spline interpolants to the setting of $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants which may be of independent interest in interpolation analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PPI-GD, an inexact gradient descent method that uses piecewise polynomial interpolation over equidistant data-domain points to approximate full gradients, achieving improved oracle complexity over standard GD variants for sufficiently smooth ERM loss functions when data dimensionality is polylogarithmic in sample size.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that leveraging smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data domain (rather than in optimization parameters) can improve oracle complexity of gradient methods. The authors seek to exploit this data-domain smoothness systematically via polynomial interpolation to reduce per-iteration oracle query costs while maintaining convergence guarantees.
AI.method: The proposed PPI-GD method queries the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain, constructs piecewise tensor-product polynomial interpolants of gradient samples over appropriately sized data patches, and uses these interpolants as inexact gradients. The analysis extends bicubic spline error analysis techniques to d-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants. Oracle complexity bounds are derived for both strongly convex and non-convex loss functions under the constraint that data dimension is bounded polylogarithmically in the number of samples.
AI.result: PPI-GD achieves improved oracle complexity compared to several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth with respect to the training data. The analysis also yields novel error bounds for d-variate tensor product polynomial interpolation, which may be of independent mathematical interest.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting data-domain smoothness via piecewise polynomial interpolation is a viable and principled strategy for reducing the oracle complexity of gradient-based ERM optimization, outperforming existing GD variants under appropriate smoothness and dimensionality conditions.

title: Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining
summary: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents easier to inspect, but it remains unclear whether such libraries can be mined from interaction data in a way that improves downstream policies. We study this question through a three-stage pipeline that segments GUI trajectories, clusters segments into candidate skills, and trains a skill-aware policy from the resulting annotations. The mined clusters are readable on the source benchmark: five of eight clusters have at least 0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels. However, readability does not imply transfer. GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5\% to 20.5\%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics. We therefore present the method as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether explicit skill libraries can be mined from GUI interaction trajectories to improve downstream policies. Through a three-stage pipeline (segmentation, clustering, skill-aware training), clusters achieve high purity against human labels, but skill-aware training via GRPO yields negligible policy improvements, revealing gaps in boundary detection, segment representation, and reward modeling.
AI.motivation: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents more inspectable and interpretable, but it is unclear whether such libraries can be automatically mined from raw interaction data in a way that actually improves downstream policy performance. The paper aims to test this assumption rigorously.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) segment GUI trajectories into candidate skill boundaries using a boundary detector; (2) cluster segments into candidate skills using an orderless segment representation; (3) train a skill-aware policy from the resulting cluster annotations using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an offline reward model. Evaluation spans InteraSkill Workflows, BrowseComp+, and source-domain metrics.
AI.result: Five of eight mined clusters achieve ≥0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflow labels, demonstrating readability. However, GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5% to 20.5%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement. The work is framed as a diagnostic study highlighting these specific failure points.

title: Matching Markets meet Cumulative Prospect Theory: Towards Optimal and Adversarially Robust Learning
summary: We study a multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem in the competitive setup with two-sided matching markets under a human centric decision making model. To capture human preferences, we use cumulative prospect theory (CPT) that weighs the actions of the agent in a nonlinear fashion using a ($α$-Hölder continuous) weight function. CPT has been widely used in behavioral economics and risk sensitive machine learning to emulate human preferences. We analyze the state-of-the-art learning algorithm with CPT weight distorted rewards and obtain a player optimal regret of $\mathcal{O}(K\log T \left(\frac{1}Δ\right)^{2/α})$, where $K$ denotes the number of arms, $T$ is the learning horizon, and $Δ$ represents (suitably defined) players' minimum preference gap. Noticing the dependence on $Δ$ to be sub-optimal, we further improve this regret by judiciously selecting the active set of arms during exploration, which removes the dependence on $K$ in the dominant term and achieves an improved (optimal) regret guarantees in the setting where the number of arms $K$ is significantly larger than the number of players $N$. In addition, we consider adversarial markets where the observed rewards of the agents may be corrupted. We propose and analyze algorithms for robust markets with CPT as risk sensitive measure in both settings where the total corruption budget is known and where it is unknown, and establish logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees in both cases.

AI.tldr: This paper studies multi-agent multi-armed bandit problems in competitive two-sided matching markets under Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT), achieving optimal regret bounds by smart exploration strategies, and extends results to adversarial settings with corrupted rewards.
AI.motivation: Traditional multi-agent bandit models assume rational, risk-neutral agents. However, real human decision-making exhibits nonlinear probability weighting and risk-sensitive preferences. CPT captures these behavioral nuances. The paper aims to design learning algorithms under CPT-distorted rewards in matching markets, where agents compete for arms (e.g., jobs, resources), and to handle adversarial reward corruption.
AI.method: The authors employ CPT with α-Hölder continuous weight functions to model distorted reward perceptions. They analyze a state-of-the-art learning algorithm under this distortion, yielding an initial player-optimal regret bound of O(K log T (1/Δ)^(2/α)). To remove sub-optimal dependence on Δ, they propose an improved algorithm that judiciously selects an active arm set during exploration, eliminating K from the dominant regret term. For adversarial markets, they design robust algorithms for both known and unknown total corruption budgets, using CPT as a risk-sensitive measure to maintain logarithmic regret guarantees.
AI.result: The initial algorithm achieves regret O(K log T (1/Δ)^(2/α)). The improved active-set exploration algorithm removes K-dependence in the dominant term, achieving optimal regret when K ≫ N. For corrupted settings, logarithmic player-optimal regret is established under both known and unknown corruption budgets.
AI.conclusion: CPT-based modeling effectively captures human-centric decision-making in competitive matching markets. The active-set exploration strategy yields optimal regret by decoupling from K, and robust algorithm variants maintain strong guarantees even under adversarial reward corruption, demonstrating practical applicability to real-world human-in-the-loop systems.

title: Rethinking Shrinkage Bias in LLM FP4 Pretraining: Geometric Origin, Systemic Impact, and UFP4 Recipe
summary: FP4 training promises substantial reductions in memory and computation cost for LLM pretraining, yet current FP4 hardware paths and recipes, including NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin-class systems and AMD MI350-series GPUs, remain centered on E2M1 data elements. In this study, we identify a fundamental limitation of that choice: non-uniform formats such as E2M1 inherently suffer from Shrinkage Bias, a systematic negative rounding error caused by the geometric asymmetry of their representable bins. We show that this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), providing a unified explanation for the training instability observed in existing E2M1-based FP4 recipes. In contrast, uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error and better convert the improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Based on this finding, we propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe that applies RHT to all three training GEMMs while restricting stochastic rounding to dY alone. On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies. Our results suggest that future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "Shrinkage Bias" — a systematic negative rounding error inherent to non-uniform FP4 formats like E2M1 — as the root cause of training instability in FP4 LLM pretraining. The authors propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe using E1M2/INT4 grids with Random Hadamard Transform and selective stochastic rounding, demonstrating superior BF16-relative loss across scales up to 124B parameters.
AI.motivation: FP4 training is promising for reducing LLM pretraining costs, and current hardware (NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin, AMD MI350) centers on E2M1. However, E2M1-based FP4 recipes exhibit training instability. The authors seek to explain and resolve this instability by examining the fundamental grid-geometry properties of 4-bit number formats.
AI.method: The authors first theoretically analyze representable bin geometry of E2M1 (non-uniform) versus E1M2/INT4 (uniform), identifying Shrinkage Bias as a systematic negative rounding error from geometric asymmetry. They show this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by Random Hadamard Transform (RHT). They then propose UFP4: a uniform 4-bit recipe applying RHT to all three training GEMMs with stochastic rounding restricted to dY only. Validation is conducted via long-run pretraining on Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B models, plus scaling-law analysis and ablation studies.
AI.result: UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation compared to strong E2M1-based baselines across all model scales. The scaling-law analysis and ablation studies support the finding that uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) better convert RHT's improved bucket utilization into higher quantization quality, directly addressing the Shrinkage Bias problem.
AI.conclusion: Future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1. The uniform format fundamentally avoids Shrinkage Bias and enables stable, high-quality FP4 pretraining when combined with RHT and targeted stochastic rounding.

title: SL-S4Wave: Self-Supervised Learning of Physiological Waveforms with Structured State Space Models
summary: Modeling long-sequence medical time series data, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), poses significant challenges due to high sampling rates, multichannel signal complexity, inherent noise, and limited labeled data. While recent self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, based on various encoder architectures such as convolutional neural networks, have been proposed to learn representations from unlabeled data, they often fall short in capturing long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. Structured state space models (S4) excel at long-sequence modeling, but existing S4 architectures fail to capture the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. In this work, we propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a tailored encoder built on structured state space models. The encoder incorporates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels, enabling the capture of both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SL-S4Wave (1) consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines in a challenging arrhythmia detection task, (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples, showcasing strong label efficiency, and (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, highlighting its capacity to model complex temporal dynamics in long sequences that most existing approaches fail to efficiently model, and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types, underscoring its robust cross-domain generalization. We additionally evaluate SL-S4Wave on multiple EEG tasks, achieving superior performance over strong baselines, demonstrating generalizability of our approach beyond cardiac waveforms.

AI.tldr: SL-S4Wave is a self-supervised learning framework for long-sequence medical time series (ECG/EEG) that combines contrastive learning with a structured state space (S4) encoder featuring multi-scale global convolution, achieving state-of-the-art performance in arrhythmia detection with strong label efficiency, long-sequence modeling, and cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing SSL methods for medical time series (e.g., ECG) struggle to capture long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. While S4 models excel at long-sequence modeling, current S4 architectures fail to handle the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms, motivating the need for a tailored S4-based SSL framework.
AI.method: The authors propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework with a custom S4-based encoder. The encoder employs multi-layer global convolution with multiscale subkernels to jointly capture fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms.
AI.result: SL-S4Wave consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and SSL baselines on arrhythmia detection, achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples (strong label efficiency), maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types, and generalizes to multiple EEG tasks with superior performance.
AI.conclusion: SL-S4Wave demonstrates that a properly tailored S4 architecture combined with contrastive SSL can effectively model long, noisy, multichannel physiological time series, offering strong performance, label efficiency, and cross-modal generalizability across both cardiac (ECG) and neural (EEG) domains.

title: Interpretable Sperm Morphology Classification via Attention-Guided Deep Learning
summary: Male infertility is a major cause of couple infertility, often linked to abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning models offer automated analysis, most lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. This study proposes an attention-guided deep learning framework for sperm morphology classification. We combine a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to focus on key areas of the sperm head, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Evaluated on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, our model achieves accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9% (macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948), outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0. Furthermore, we use Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight features influencing the model's decisions. The results demonstrate that this accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework combining EfficientNet-B0 with CBAM attention for interpretable sperm morphology classification, achieving 90.2% and 93.9% accuracy on SMIDS and HuSHem datasets, with Grad-CAM++ visualizations for clinical transparency.
AI.motivation: Male infertility is a leading cause of couple infertility, often associated with abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning enables automated sperm analysis, existing models lack interpretability, hindering clinical adoption. There is a need for accurate yet transparent frameworks that clinicians can trust.
AI.method: The authors propose an attention-guided framework that integrates a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). CBAM sequentially applies channel and spatial attention to emphasize discriminative regions of sperm head images. Model decisions are interpreted post hoc using Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight salient morphological features.
AI.result: On the SMIDS dataset, the model attained 90.2% accuracy with a macro F1 score of 0.913. On the HuSHem dataset, accuracy reached 93.9% with a macro F1 score of 0.948. These results surpass both a baseline SimpleCNN and a standard EfficientNet-B0 without attention.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided framework delivers both high classification accuracy and interpretability, making it a practical, transparent tool suitable for deployment in clinical fertility settings for automated sperm morphology assessment.

title: Adversarial Bandit Optimization with Globally Bounded Perturbations to Convex Losses
summary:
We study adversarial bandit optimization in which the loss functions may be non-convex and non-smooth. In each round, the learner selects an action and observes only the loss incurred at that action. The loss consists of an underlying convex and $β$-smooth component and an adversarial perturbation that may be chosen after observing the learner's action. The perturbations are subject to a global budget controlling their cumulative magnitude over time.
  This framework extends the globally budgeted, post-action perturbation model from underlying linear losses to general convex and $β$-smooth losses. For this broader class, we establish expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget.
  To establish these guarantees, we modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm and develop an analysis that controls the additional regret caused by the perturbations. In the absence of perturbations, our results reduce to regret guarantees for the standard bandit convex optimization setting with $β$-smooth losses.

AI.tldr: This paper extends adversarial bandit optimization with global budget constraints on post-action perturbations from linear to convex, β-smooth loss functions, providing expected regret guarantees that explicitly account for the perturbation budget.
AI.motivation: Existing work on globally budgeted, post-action adversarial perturbations in bandit optimization has been limited to linear loss functions. The authors aim to generalize this framework to convex and β-smooth losses, which capture a much broader class of practical problems, and to understand how the perturbation budget affects regret in this richer setting.
AI.method: The authors modify a standard bandit convex optimization algorithm to handle post-action adversarial perturbations. They develop a novel regret analysis that decomposes and bounds the additional regret attributable to perturbations, leveraging the β-smoothness property to control estimation and optimization errors under non-convex, non-smooth loss observations.
AI.result: The paper establishes expected regret bounds that explicitly characterize the effect of the global perturbation budget for convex, β-smooth losses. In the perturbation-free case, the results recover standard regret guarantees for bandit convex optimization with β-smooth losses.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully extends globally budgeted post-action perturbation models from linear to general convex and β-smooth losses, with regret guarantees that cleanly separate the effects of the underlying smooth optimization problem from the adversarial perturbation budget.

title: Context-Aware Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling of IVF Laboratory Environmental Conditions
summary: IVF pregnancy rates are routinely modeled using patient-level variables, while high-resolution laboratory environmental data remain underutilized. We show that this is a missed opportunity. Rather than relying on raw sensor averages, we engineer 55 context-aware temporal features, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed, that capture the dynamics of incubator microenvironments. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic, these features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw averages. We then train a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that shares environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European clinic via partial pooling, while preserving site-specific baselines. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the model achieves R2 = 0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal.

AI.tldr: Engineered temporal environmental features from incubator sensors significantly outperform raw averages for IVF pregnancy rate prediction. A hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model with partial pooling transfers this signal across clinics, achieving R²=0.86 and 64% error reduction on held-out data from a different continent.
AI.motivation: Current IVF prediction models focus heavily on patient-level variables while neglecting high-resolution laboratory environmental data (temperature, humidity, etc.). Raw sensor averages are insufficient to capture the dynamic microenvironment conditions that may affect embryo development and pregnancy outcomes. The authors aim to demonstrate that structured, context-aware environmental features contain clinically meaningful and transferable predictive signal.
AI.method: 1) Feature engineering: 55 context-aware temporal features derived from incubator sensor data, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence windows, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed. 2) Hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression with partial pooling, allowing environmental effect estimates to be shared between an Asian clinic (61 weeks of training data) and a Northern European clinic while preserving site-specific baselines. 3) Cross-validation comparison against raw sensor averages (3-5% error) and held-out evaluation on the Northern European clinic data.
AI.result: The 55 engineered features reduced cross-validated prediction error to 1.27% (vs. 3-5% for raw averages). The hierarchical Bayesian model achieved R² = 0.86 on held-out Northern European clinic data, with a 64% error reduction in the 35–39 age group compared to a naive baseline.
AI.conclusion: Structured environmental monitoring of incubator microenvironments yields clinically meaningful and transferable predictive signal for IVF pregnancy rates. Context-aware temporal features capture dynamics that raw averages miss, and hierarchical Bayesian partial pooling enables cross-clinic generalization, challenging the standard practice of using only patient-level covariates.

title: Score Approximation for Diffusion Models on Arbitrary Low-Dimensional Structures
summary: The remarkable success of score-based diffusion models has spurred significant efforts to establish their theoretical foundations. However, existing complexity bounds for score approximation rely heavily on restrictive assumptions like Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports, which are routinely violated by the singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters inherent to real-world perceptual data. This work establishes a universal score approximation theorem that works for any distribution supported on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension $d$. Using a novel discrete-mixture formulation, we prove that the score function can be approximated with a ReLU network whose complexity grows exponentially only with $d$, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. Combined with existing theories on accurately solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, our work shows that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, explaining their competence in real-world generative tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a universal score approximation theorem for diffusion models that works for any distribution supported on compact sets with finite upper Minkowski dimension d. Using a discrete-mixture formulation with ReLU networks, it shows score approximation complexity grows exponentially only with d (intrinsic dimension), not ambient dimension, breaking the curse of dimensionality and explaining why diffusion models handle irregular, non-smooth real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical complexity bounds for score approximation in diffusion models rely on restrictive assumptions—Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports. Real-world perceptual data routinely violates these assumptions through singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters. The authors aim to close this gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel discrete-mixture formulation and prove a universal score approximation theorem. The score function is approximated using a ReLU network, with complexity scaling exponentially in the upper Minkowski dimension d of the support (an intrinsic dimension measure), rather than the ambient dimension. This is combined with existing backward diffusion SDE theory for arbitrary compact distributions.
AI.result: The ReLU network's complexity grows exponentially only with the intrinsic dimension d, not the ambient dimensionality, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality that plagued prior bounds.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models can readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, which provides a theoretical explanation for their strong empirical performance in real-world generative tasks. The work significantly relaxes the restrictive assumptions of prior theory.

title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
summary: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how language models interpret in-context compliance demonstrations for jailbreaking, finding that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable, preference optimization is critical for safety, demonstration ordering exhibits recency bias, and refusal behaviors interact differently with in-context learning across models.
AI.motivation: Prior work establishes that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak models, but the mechanisms remain poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize what models actually extract from different types of compliance demonstrations, moving beyond merely demonstrating that jailbreaking works to understanding how it works.
AI.method: The authors mix benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and test three hypotheses across four language models. They analyze how demonstration composition, ordering, refusal behavior, and training methodology (particularly preference optimization) influence harmful compliance rates.
AI.result: Benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. Preference optimization is the critical training stage preventing benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance. Demonstration ordering shows strong recency bias. Models differ in refusal interactions: some adopt demonstrated formatting even while refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal.
AI.conclusion: The paper moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works. What models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

title: ADaPT: Token-Level Decoupling for Efficient Large Reasoning Models
summary: Large reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought to achieve strong performance, but applying such reasoning uniformly incurs high computational cost. Existing efficiency-oriented methods attempt to shorten or mix reasoning strategies, yet often degrade reasoning capability. We identify the root cause as sequence-level coupling between efficiency incentives and correctness optimization, which implicitly penalizes long but correct reasoning trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Adaptive Dual-Process Thinking (ADaPT), a token-level dual-process framework that explicitly decouples efficiency and correctness signals during training. ADaPT introduces a mode-selection token to control fast and slow reasoning, applying efficiency-related rewards exclusively to this token to avoid penalizing correct long reasoning while encouraging efficiency when appropriate. Moreover, ADaPT enables precise and continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off at inference time: by adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token, a single trained model can smoothly move along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ADaPT decouples efficiency and correctness signals at the token level via a mode-selection token, enabling adaptive fast/slow reasoning without penalizing correct long chains-of-thought, and allows continuous Pareto-optimal trade-off control at inference.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chain-of-thought but incur high computational cost. Existing methods that shorten or mix reasoning strategies degrade reasoning capability because they couple efficiency incentives with correctness optimization at the sequence level, implicitly penalizing long yet correct reasoning trajectories.
AI.method: ADaPT introduces a token-level dual-process framework with a dedicated mode-selection token that governs fast vs. slow reasoning. During training, efficiency-related rewards are applied exclusively to this token, decoupling efficiency signals from correctness optimization. At inference time, adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token enables precise, continuous navigation along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier using a single trained model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance, with smooth and controllable trade-offs along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Token-level decoupling of efficiency and correctness via a mode-selection token effectively resolves the sequence-level coupling problem, enabling adaptive reasoning that preserves performance while reducing cost. The approach provides a practical mechanism for controllable efficiency-performance trade-offs in large reasoning models.

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
summary:
LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
  We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python.
  We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

AI.tldr: Multi-LCB extends the Python-only LiveCodeBench (LCB) to 12 programming languages by transforming existing Python tasks into equivalent cross-language versions, preserving LCB's contamination controls. Evaluation of 24 LLMs reveals Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and significant multilingual performance gaps.
AI.motivation: LiveCodeBench is a popular contamination-aware code-generation benchmark but is restricted to Python only, leaving unaddressed the question of whether LLMs can generalize across diverse programming languages — a critical requirement for real-world software engineering.
AI.method: The authors introduce Multi-LCB by transforming Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks across twelve programming languages while fully preserving LCB's contamination controls, evaluation protocol, and format compatibility. The benchmark is designed to automatically track future LCB updates for sustained relevance.
AI.result: Evaluation across 24 instruction and reasoning LLMs revealed three key findings: (1) evidence of Python overfitting, where models perform disproportionately well on Python compared to other languages; (2) language-specific contamination patterns; and (3) substantial disparities in multilingual programming performance.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LCB establishes a rigorous new benchmark for multi-language code evaluation that directly addresses LCB's primary limitation, exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities and enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence.

title: Compositionality Emerges in a Narrow Depth-Connectivity Regime: Architecture Constraints and Solution Manifolds
summary: Compositionality is believed to be the foundation for generalization, enabling models to reuse meaningful primitives in novel combinations. Yet, models trained with standard gradient-based optimization rarely, and often only weakly, exhibit compositional internal structure, and it remains unclear how or why such compositionality forms. In this work, we show that compositionality emerges in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot. Along the connectivity axis, compositionality only appears in some specifically sparse networks, heavily depends on which connections remain rather than on weights' sparsity alone. Along the depth axis, compositionality emerges within a narrow, target-dependent regime, peaking at specific depths, while both shallower and deeper networks fail. When either the depth or connectivity condition is violated, gradient descent silently converges to fractured solutions rather than compositional ones. To discover and exploit this emergence, we introduce (i) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity and (ii) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate where compositionality is most likely to appear. Finally, we support these empirical findings with a theoretical framework based on compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds, explaining why compositional solutions are reachable only in a narrow depth-connectivity regime.

AI.tldr: Compositionality in neural networks emerges only within a narrow sweet spot of both connectivity sparsity and network depth. Outside this regime, gradient descent converges to non-compositional "fractured" solutions. The authors propose similarity-based pruning and a depth heuristic to recover and predict this emergent structure, supported by theoretical analysis.
AI.motivation: Compositionality is considered fundamental to generalization, yet standard gradient-based training rarely yields models with compositional internal structure. The authors aim to understand how and why compositionality forms, and to develop practical methods to discover and exploit it.
AI.method: The authors systematically investigate the joint effect of network connectivity (sparsity and specific connection patterns) and depth on the emergence of compositional solutions. They introduce two practical tools: (1) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity by pruning based on weight similarity rather than magnitude, and (2) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate the depth at which compositionality is most likely to emerge. A theoretical framework using compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds is developed to explain the empirical findings.
AI.result: Compositionality emerges only in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot: along the connectivity axis, it appears in specifically sparse networks and depends on which connections remain, not merely weight sparsity; along the depth axis, it peaks at specific, target-dependent depths, with both shallower and deeper networks failing. Violating either condition causes gradient descent to silently converge to fractured, non-compositional solutions.
AI.conclusion: Compositional structure in neural networks is not a generic product of gradient-based learning but requires specific architectural conditions — a narrow regime of sparse connectivity and appropriate depth. The proposed SP pruning and depth predictor offer practical means to induce and locate compositionality, while the theoretical framework provides explanatory grounding for these phenomena.

title: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
summary: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit introduces a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that stores pronunciation corrections as latent token-level perturbations in a Modern Hopfield Network, achieving 92.7% relative reduction in Phoneme Error Rate on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns without retraining or degrading general speech quality.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching TTS systems produce high-quality zero-shot speech but remain static after deployment, meaning pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist indefinitely unless the model is retrained — a costly and impractical requirement. There is a need for an adaptation mechanism that can incorporate corrective feedback on-the-fly without modifying model weights.
AI.method: FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space when corrective pronunciation feedback is provided. These corrections are stored in a Modern Hopfield Network functioning as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, stored corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching so that previously unseen but morphologically similar proper nouns can benefit from prior corrections.
AI.result: On a curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns spanning 18 language families, FlowEdit reduced target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Each correction completes in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit demonstrates that frozen flow-matching TTS models can be effectively adapted for pronunciation corrections through latent embedding edits stored in associative memory, enabling life-long improvement without weight updates or degradation of general synthesis quality.

title: Towards Graph-Based Deep Learning for Map Generalization: Insights from Building Footprints Simplification and Aggregation
summary: Map generalization remains one of the fundamental tasks in cartography, especially for the simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints. This study presents the first exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to both tasks, reformulating simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. We evaluate representative graph neural network architectures (GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE) on multi-scale building datasets, showing that GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strengths in link prediction accuracy, while also revealing persistent challenges in precise node movement prediction. Beyond quantitative performance, the results highlight that aggregation poses greater complexity and challenges than simplification, underscoring the difficulty of capturing higher-level spatial relationships in map generalization with current deep learning approaches. Although limitations such as data imbalance and the need for post-processing remain, the study provides valuable insights and methodological directions for advancing automated map generalization with deep learning approaches.

AI.tldr: First exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to building simplification (node movement prediction) and aggregation (link prediction), finding GraphSAGE strongest for aggregation but both tasks remain challenging, especially aggregation.
AI.motivation: Map generalization, particularly simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints, remains a fundamental cartographic challenge. The authors aim to explore whether graph-based deep learning can address these tasks in a unified framework, moving beyond traditional algorithmic approaches.
AI.method: Reformulation of building simplification as node movement prediction and building aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. Three representative graph neural network architectures — GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE — are evaluated on multi-scale building datasets.
AI.result: GraphSAGE shows relative strengths in link prediction (aggregation), but precise node movement prediction (simplification) remains problematic across all architectures. Aggregation proves more complex and challenging than simplification, indicating current deep learning approaches struggle to capture higher-level spatial relationships.
AI.conclusion: While graph-based deep learning shows promise for automated map generalization, persistent challenges — including data imbalance, post-processing requirements, and difficulty modeling higher-level spatial relationships — limit current applicability. The study provides methodological directions for future work.

title: DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs
summary: Neurosymbolic systems such as DeepProbLog combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, but standard inference is associational. Counterfactual reasoning additionally requires a causal semantics for interventions and evidence. We introduce DeepSWIP, a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog programs. Using neural materialization, we reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, apply Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and compute counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, DeepSWIP is exact relative to the learned materialized FCM. The standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals identifies active neural probabilities and explains intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments on MPI3D confirm the transformation against a DeepTwin construction against 12,000 queries, as predicted and a 2.14$\times$ inference speedup from avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment shows that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands. Code is at https://github.com/saibib/deep_SWIP.

AI.tldr: DeepSWIP introduces a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog that enables exact counterfactual reasoning in neurosymbolic systems by reducing neural predicates to ProbLog choices via materialization, applying Single World Intervention Programs, and computing counterfactuals through weighted model counting.
AI.motivation: Standard inference in neurosymbolic systems like DeepProbLog is purely associational and lacks the causal semantics required for interventions and counterfactual reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a principled causal framework for neurosymbolic programs.
AI.method: The method reduces fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices via neural materialization, then applies Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs) to a single transformed program. Counterfactuals are computed by weighted model counting (WMC) under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions. The quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals is used to identify active neural probabilities and analyze intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. A DeepTwin construction serves as a correctness baseline, and an AIPW estimator addresses neural calibration degradation bias.
AI.result: Experiments on MPI3D validate the transformation against the DeepTwin baseline over 12,000 queries, achieving a 2.14× inference speedup by avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment demonstrates that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands.
AI.conclusion: DeepSWIP provides exact, efficient counterfactual inference for neurosymbolic programs by leveraging materialization and SWIP semantics. The framework also clarifies sensitivity issues in ProbLog conditionals and demonstrates the importance of proper causal estimation (AIPW) over naive plug-in approaches when neural components are miscalibrated.

title: Low-Energy Reduced RISC-V Instruction Subset Processor for Tsetlin Machine Inference at the Edge
comment: 6 pages, 6 Figures, Accepted in IEEE ISVLSI Conference 2026
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based machine learning approach that relies on simple bitwise operations and finite-state automata, which makes it attractive for edge AI deployments. Recent work has focused on co-processor and accelerator designs based on Tsetlin Machines (TMs). Although these designs achieve high performance, they typically depend on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, limiting flexibility and ease of programming. In this work, we present a domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor architecture and design flow tailored for TM inference. Leveraging the modular structure of RISC-V, we design a reduced instruction subset processor that retains programmability while targeting improved performance and lower energy consumption for TM workloads. Instruction profiling is employed to guide instruction reduction, followed by datapath and control path simplifications tailored to TM inference. Both the baseline RV32IM core and the proposed reduced core are evaluated across multiple datasets and compared with Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), which serve as a hardware-efficient baseline due to their reliance on bitwise operations during inference. Results show that TM achieves comparable or higher accuracy (e.g., up to 88.18% on CIFAR-2 compared to 60.0% for BNN) while reducing execution time by up to 98% across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves an average $29.7\times$ reduction in energy consumption, demonstrating its effectiveness for programmable and efficient edge AI systems.

AI.tldr: A domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor tailored for Tsetlin Machine inference is proposed, achieving up to 98% execution time reduction and 29.7× average energy savings compared to a baseline RV32IM core, while outperforming Binarized Neural Networks in accuracy on tasks like CIFAR-2 (88.18% vs 60.0%).
AI.motivation: Existing TM accelerator designs rely on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, which limit flexibility and ease of programming. There is a need for a programmable, efficient processor architecture that retains software flexibility while optimizing for TM inference workloads at the edge.
AI.method: The authors design a reduced instruction subset RISC-V microprocessor by profiling TM inference instructions, then simplifying the datapath and control path accordingly. The design flow leverages RISC-V's modular ISA structure. Both the baseline RV32IM core and the proposed reduced core are evaluated across multiple datasets and benchmarked against Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs).
AI.result: TM achieves superior accuracy over BNNs (e.g., 88.18% vs 60.0% on CIFAR-2). The proposed reduced RISC-V core reduces execution time by up to 98% and achieves an average 29.7× reduction in energy consumption relative to the baseline RV32IM.
AI.conclusion: The domain-specific RISC-V approach effectively combines programmability with hardware efficiency for TM inference, making it well-suited for edge AI deployments where both flexibility and low energy are critical.

title: LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents
summary: Policy-adherent tool-calling agents in customer-service domains must maintain task states across turns while calling tools and obeying domain policies. Task states consist of relevant facts, identifiers, constraints, and conditions observed through user interaction and tool calls. In standard agents, task states are not represented separately. Observations, tool returns, and policy instructions are placed in the prompt, leaving agents to reconstruct the relevant states from the prompt each time they decide what to do next. This design makes state management implicit, creating two common failure modes. An agent may retrieve the right facts but later ground its decision in stale, missing, or incorrect information; and a syntactically valid tool call may still violate a domain policy that depends on the current task state. We introduce \textsc{LedgerAgent}, an inference-time method for tool-calling agents that maintains observed task states in a separate ledger and renders the states into the prompt. The ledger is also used to check state-dependent policy constraints before environment-changing tool calls are executed, blocking policy violations. Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, \textsc{LedgerAgent} improves average pass\textasciicircum{}k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.

AI.tldr: LedgerAgent introduces a separate ledger to explicitly maintain task states for tool-calling agents, checking policy constraints before executing environment-changing calls. It improves pass^k over standard prompt-based approaches, especially under strict multi-trial consistency metrics.
AI.motivation: Standard tool-calling agents embed all observations, tool returns, and policy instructions directly in the prompt, forcing implicit state reconstruction at each decision step. This causes two failure modes: (1) agents may ground decisions in stale or incorrect information despite having retrieved the right facts earlier, and (2) syntactically valid tool calls can still violate domain policies that depend on the current task state.
AI.method: LedgerAgent is an inference-time method that maintains observed task states in a separate, explicit ledger. The ledger is rendered into the prompt so the agent always has access to current, accurate state. Additionally, before executing any environment-changing tool calls, the ledger is used to check state-dependent policy constraints, blocking calls that would violate domain policies.
AI.result: Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, LedgerAgent improves average pass^k over standard prompt-based tool-calling. The largest gains are observed under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state management via a dedicated ledger, combined with policy-constraint checking before tool execution, is an effective inference-time strategy for reducing state grounding errors and policy violations in tool-calling agents operating in policy-adherent customer-service domains.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing
summary: Reservoir computing offers a lightweight framework for forecasting dynamical systems but may struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to limited representational capacity. Conventional reservoir computing recurrently uses trainable reservoirs with hyperparameter sensitivity, while the next-generation reservoir computing removes recurrence at the cost of rapidly growing feature dimensions. Here, we develop Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing (KARC), which replaces reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. We rigorously show that KARC is a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), preserving the potential expressive capacity of KANs while admitting efficient closed-form training of reservoir computing. At comparable cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including partial differential equations. It can also be integrated with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation. This work thus establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, enabling efficient and high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting.

AI.tldr: KARC replaces reservoir computing's recurrent or high-dimensional feature spaces with explicit basis-function expansions based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. This yields a lightweight KAN design with closed-form training that outperforms existing reservoir methods on PDE benchmarks and can integrate with diffusion models for text-to-image generation.
AI.motivation: Reservoir computing is lightweight but suffers from limited representational capacity for long-range dependencies. Conventional RC uses sensitive hyperparameter-tuned recurrent reservoirs, while next-generation RC avoids recurrence at the cost of exploding feature dimensions. The authors seek a method that retains expressivity without recurrence or dimensional explosion.
AI.method: KARC replaces the reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem.
