This connects reservoir computing to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), preserving KAN expressive capacity while enabling efficient closed-form training (ridge regression) characteristic of reservoir computing.
AI.result: At comparable cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including PDE forecasting. It also successfully integrates with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: KARC establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, enabling efficient, high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting with closed-form training and strong empirical performance.

title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
summary: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models

AI.tldr: First application of cross-attention attribution (DAAM) to speech diffusion TTS, analyzing how individual style caption tokens influence acoustic output across 3,600 caption-transcript pairs, revealing layer-wise and temporal dynamics of style conditioning in CapSpeech-TTS.
AI.motivation: Style-captioned TTS lacks interpretability: it is unknown how individual words in natural language style descriptions affect acoustic output. This opacity hinders failure diagnosis and limits controllability improvements in expressive TTS systems.
AI.method: The authors adapt the DAAM (Diffusion Attentive Attribution Maps) framework from vision to speech, applying cross-attention attribution to CapSpeech-TTS. They extract per-token heatmaps across 25 transformer layers and 24 ODE (probability flow) steps. Analysis covers 3,600 combinations (120 style captions × 30 text transcripts), examining temporal variance of attention, correlation with F0/energy, layer-wise and step-wise attention dynamics, and attention entropy.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Style tokens exhibit lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning behavior. (2) Style attention correlates with prosodic features (F0 and energy). (3) Style conditioning peaks during early ODE steps and in deep transformer layers. (4) Attention entropy reaches a minimum at layer 17, coinciding with peak style importance, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical processing stage.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of how natural language style descriptions modulate cross-attention in speech diffusion models, establishing a methodology for diagnosing and improving controllable expressive TTS.

title: Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR): Function-Preserving SVD Compression for LLMs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Resource-Adaptive Foundation Model Inference (AdaptFM), Seoul, South Korea (non-archival)
summary: We present Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR), an SVD-based LLM compression framework that guides each weight matrix's low-rank approximation with a backward-signal influence metric. Starting from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W), AIR runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates influence element-wise under a monotone-descent guarantee. AIR is layer-local and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods: alone it exceeds ACIP, and AIR+LoRA outperforms it further. AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at <=60% parameter retention, matches its quality with ~90% less calibration data, and turns parameter savings into FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency gains.

AI.tldr: AIR (Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks) is an SVD-based LLM compression method that uses a backward-signal influence metric to guide low-rank approximation of weight matrices. It applies a single closed-form alternating least squares sweep with monotone-descent guarantee, achieving >18% perplexity improvement over SVD-LLM(W) at ≤60% parameter retention, matching its quality with ~90% less calibration data, and delivering FLOP, memory, and latency gains.
AI.motivation: Existing SVD-based LLM compression methods like SVD-LLM(W) rely primarily on activation-aware optimization but do not incorporate backward-signal (influence) information. This leaves potential compression quality on the table, since influence metrics can better identify which parameters matter most for downstream loss. The authors aim to close this gap with a method that integrates both activation and influence awareness in a principled, computationally efficient manner.
AI.method: AIR formulates each weight matrix's low-rank approximation using an influence metric derived from backward signals. The method starts from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W) and then runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates influence element-wise, with a monotone-descent guarantee. The approach is layer-local (each layer compressed independently) and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods like LoRA fine-tuning (AIR+LoRA).
AI.result: AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by more than 18% at ≤60% parameter retention. It matches SVD-LLM(W)'s quality while using ~90% less calibration data. As a standalone method it exceeds ACIP, and combined with LoRA it outperforms further. Parameter savings translate into concrete gains in FLOPs, peak memory, and per-token latency.
AI.conclusion: AIR demonstrates that incorporating backward-signal influence into SVD-based LLM compression yields significant quality improvements with less calibration data, while remaining computationally efficient (layer-local, closed-form ALS). Its orthogonal compatibility with methods like LoRA makes it a practical and effective compression framework.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift
summary: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: Expert-level calibration guarantees overall calibration for hard-routed MoEs under distribution shift, but not for soft-routed ones. The authors propose adversarial reweighting to enforce calibration of the routed aggregate, improving accuracy-calibration tradeoffs across diverse settings.
AI.motivation: While calibration is known to improve MoE ensembles, the theoretical conditions under which calibration benefits MoE models—particularly under distribution shift—are poorly understood. Understanding how routing mechanisms interact with expert calibration is critical for building trustworthy MoE models that generalize reliably.
AI.method: The authors analyze MoE calibration under distribution shift by examining hard-routed vs. soft-routed mechanisms. They prove that expert-level calibration is sufficient for overall calibration in hard-routed MoEs under a broad class of shifts, but not for soft-routed ones. To remedy this, they introduce an adversarial reweighting scheme that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate distribution under shift.
AI.result: Expert calibration suffices for hard-routed MoEs under distribution shift but fails for soft-routed models. The proposed adversarial reweighting method improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on challenging data subsets, across multiple model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Routing mechanism choice critically determines whether expert-level calibration propagates to the full MoE under distribution shift. Adversarial reweighting offers a practical solution for enforcing reliable calibration in soft-routed MoEs, enhancing both predictive accuracy and trustworthiness under shifted conditions.

title: Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Work in progress; we will continuously update the codebase and arXiv version
summary: This work presents a general framework for training large language models (LLMs) to "Connect the Dots" (CoD), a meta-capability required by long-lifecycle agents: as an LLM-based AI agent gets deployed in an environment, it solves a long sequence of tasks while continuously exploring the environment, learning from its own experiences, and iteratively self-updating its context about the environment, thereby achieving progressively better performance on future tasks conditioned on the updated context. Major components of the CoD framework include: (1) algorithm design and infrastructure for end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) with long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes; (2) tasks and environments for incentivizing and eliciting the targeted meta-capability in LLMs during training, as well as for faithfully measuring progress during evaluation. We present proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework, including a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment, as well as tasks and environments tailored to the targeted meta-capability (rather than domain-specific LLM capabilities or standard task-by-task RL). Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting, and demonstrate the potential for out-of-distribution generalization -- within the training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings -- of the elicited meta-capability. Our investigation of CoD connects several lines of prior works, and opens up new opportunities for advancing LLMs and AI agents. To facilitate further research and applications, we release our implementations at \url{https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/research/cod/examples/research_cod}.

AI.tldr: CoD introduces a reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to iteratively explore environments, update their internal context from experience, and improve at future tasks — a meta-capability essential for long-lifecycle AI agents.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM training paradigms treat each task independently (standard RL or supervised fine-tuning). Real-world autonomous agents, however, must operate over long horizons, accumulating knowledge across sequential tasks and self-improving through experience. The paper argues that LLMs currently lack this "Connect the Dots" meta-capability — the ability to learn from prior episodes and leverage updated context for better downstream performance — and proposes to cultivate it via end-to-end RL.
AI.method: The CoD framework comprises: (1) an end-to-end RL training loop with long rollout sequences that interleave "solve-task" episodes (where the agent acts in an environment) and "update-context" episodes (where the agent reflects on and integrates new information into its persistent context); (2) a GRPO-style (Group Relative Policy Optimization) RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment across the rollout; (3) custom-designed tasks and environments that specifically incentivize and measure the meta-capability of connecting information across episodes, rather than domain-specific skills or isolated task performance.
AI.result: Empirical results show that end-to-end RL under the CoD framework successfully elicits the targeted meta-capability. The trained models demonstrate out-of-distribution generalization: within training domains, across different unseen domains, and from CoD settings to Ralph-loop (observe-act-update) settings. The proof-of-concept implementations validate both the training methodology and the evaluation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: CoD provides a principled framework for training LLM agents that can autonomously accumulate and leverage environmental knowledge over long deployment horizons. It bridges multiple prior research threads (continual learning, open-ended RL, agent self-improvement) and opens new directions for building more capable, self-evolving AI agents. Code is open-sourced to facilitate further work.

title: Human-AI Agent Interaction in a Business Context
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure, submitted to Springer Nature
summary: As AI agents are increasingly integrated into core business processes, understanding and designing effective interaction patterns between humans and AI agents becomes crucial for value creation. This study identifies and evaluates principles and criteria for a positive User Experience (UX) with AI agents, along with methods for its measurement. We identify user expectations and needs to facilitate adoption, build trust, and support user-centered decision-making by development teams. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative techniques, we explore interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. The findings from this exploratory research serve as the basis to develop a survey experiment which evaluates the effectiveness of specific design elements on a larger scale. This foundational research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how to design effective human-AI agent interactions in business contexts by identifying UX principles, user expectations, and measurement methods. Using a mixed-methods approach, it combines qualitative and quantitative techniques to evaluate design elements, ultimately contributing to more intuitive human-AI collaboration.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become embedded in core business processes, there is a pressing need to understand how to design interaction patterns that foster adoption, trust, and user-centered decision-making. Without clear UX principles and evaluation criteria for human-AI agent interactions, value creation is hindered.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative techniques is employed. First, exploratory research identifies interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. These findings then inform the development of a survey experiment designed to evaluate the effectiveness of specific design elements at scale.
AI.result: The exploratory research yields identified interaction patterns, user expectations, and UX principles and criteria for human-AI agent interactions. These serve as the foundation for a subsequent survey experiment (described as future or ongoing work) to test design element effectiveness at a larger scale.
AI.conclusion: The research provides foundational contributions toward developing more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings, emphasizing the importance of understanding user needs to drive adoption and trust.

title: StreamKL: Fast and Memory-Efficient KL Divergence for Boosting Attention Distillation
summary: Attention distillation, which trains one attention distribution to match another by minimizing their Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, is widely used in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training. However, existing approaches materialize both attention distributions before computing the KL reduction, incurring $O(N_QN_K)$ memory and IO costs that become prohibitive at long context lengths. We present StreamKL, the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates this quadratic materialization. StreamKL derives a novel online formulation for the coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single one-pass forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. For the backward pass, StreamKL recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile, avoiding storage of quadratic intermediates. We further design and implement efficient GPU kernels with dedicated optimizations. Experiments show StreamKL delivers up to $43\times$ and $14\times$ speedups over baseline methods in the forward and backward passes, respectively. Most importantly, StreamKL reduces the extra HBM footprint of attention distillation from $O(N_QN_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling long-context distillation on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: StreamKL introduces the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates quadratic memory materialization, using an online streaming algorithm to reduce HBM footprint from O(N_Q N_K) to O(1) and delivering up to 43× forward and 14× backward speedups.
AI.motivation: Attention distillation via KL divergence is widely used across multiple domains (knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, sparse-attention LLMs), but existing methods require materializing both attention distributions before computing KL, incurring O(N_Q N_K) memory and IO costs prohibitive at long context lengths.
AI.method: StreamKL proposes a novel online formulation for coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single-pass forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. The backward pass recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile, avoiding quadratic intermediate storage. The method is implemented as optimized fused GPU kernels with dedicated hardware-aware optimizations.
AI.result: StreamKL achieves up to 43× speedup in forward pass and 14× speedup in backward pass over baseline methods. Critically, it reduces extra HBM footprint from O(N_Q N_K) to O(1), enabling long-context attention distillation on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: By eliminating the quadratic memory bottleneck of attention KL divergence, StreamKL unlocks scalable attention distillation for long-context models, making previously infeasible workloads practical on single-GPU setups.

title: VIMPO: Value-Implicit Policy Optimization for LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a central tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but current methods face a trade-off between simplicity and credit assignment. Group-relative methods such as GRPO avoid training a critic, but typically assign a trajectory-level advantage to every token. Actor-critic methods provide denser learning signals, but require a learned value function with its own training instability. We introduce VIMPO, a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized reinforcement learning. For autoregressive generation, the resulting value recurrence can be written in terms of policy-reference log-ratios and anchored by the terminal condition that no future reward remains at the end of a trajectory. This gives a simple value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards without training a critic. The same derivation also yields a critic-free actor advantage, allowing VIMPO to separate reward incorporation through the value loss from policy improvement through a PPO-style actor update. On mathematical RLVR benchmarks, VIMPO improves over GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with especially larger gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO retains a consistent advantage over GRPO, suggesting that policy-implied value optimization can provide finer credit assignment while preserving the practical simplicity of critic-free training.

AI.tldr: VIMPO introduces a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL. It uses a policy-implied value recurrence based on policy-reference log-ratios, enabling token-level credit assignment without training a critic. VIMPO outperforms GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and is more robust under noisy rewards.
AI.motivation: Current RL methods for improving LLM reasoning face a trade-off: group-relative methods like GRPO are simple but assign only trajectory-level advantages to every token (poor credit assignment), while actor-critic methods provide denser signals but suffer from training instability due to the learned value function. The goal is to achieve fine-grained credit assignment while preserving critic-free simplicity.
AI.method: VIMPO leverages the optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL to derive a policy-implied value function that does not require a separate critic. For autoregressive generation, this yields a value recurrence expressed in terms of policy-reference log-ratios, anchored by the terminal condition that no future reward remains at trajectory end. This produces a simple value loss incorporating outcome-level verifiable rewards. The same derivation gives a critic-free actor advantage, enabling a PPO-style actor update that separates reward incorporation (via the value loss) from policy improvement.
AI.result: VIMPO consistently outperforms GRPO on mathematical RLVR benchmarks including MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with particularly large gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy reward conditions, VIMPO retains a consistent advantage over GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Policy-implied value optimization can provide finer credit assignment than group-relative methods while maintaining the practical simplicity of critic-free training. VIMPO effectively bridges the gap between simple but coarse group-relative methods and denser but unstable actor-critic approaches.

title: Self-Adaptive Scale Handling for Forecasting Time Series with Scale Heterogeneity
comment: This is the full version of the paper accepted by the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF
summary: Current time series forecasting (TSF) research predominantly focuses on scale-homogeneous data, where different time series share similar numerical magnitude ranges. However, in real-world industrial scenarios such as financial product sales, different time series often differ by orders of magnitude (scale heterogeneity). Since these series share similar temporal patterns, joint modeling is desirable for better data utilization, yet existing scaling methods either compress low-scale signals (global normalization) or destroy semantic discriminability and amplify inverse-scaling errors (window-based scaling). This paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module that learns adaptive scale factors tailored to each input, preserving semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors. AS consists of Scale Calibrating (SC), which calibrates prior mean scaling factors through neural networks, and Scaling Selection (SS), which decides whether to apply calibration or retain the original factor, avoiding over-calibration. Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay show that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their performance. The code and dataset are available at the link https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module to address scale heterogeneity in time series forecasting, where different series differ by orders of magnitude. AS learns adaptive scale factors via Scale Calibrating and Scaling Selection, avoiding the pitfalls of global normalization and window-based scaling. It integrates into existing TSF models and improves performance on real-world financial datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing TSF research assumes scale-homogeneous data, but real-world industrial time series (e.g., financial product sales) often exhibit scale heterogeneity — series sharing similar temporal patterns yet differing by orders of magnitude. Joint modeling is desirable for data efficiency, but current scaling methods fall short: global normalization compresses low-scale signals, while window-based scaling destroys semantic discriminability and amplifies inverse-scaling errors.
AI.method: The AS module has two components: (1) Scale Calibrating (SC), which uses neural networks to calibrate prior mean scaling factors, and (2) Scaling Selection (SS), which adaptively decides whether to use the calibrated factor or retain the original, preventing over-calibration. The module is model-agnostic and can be plugged into popular TSF architectures.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay demonstrate that AS consistently improves the performance of popular TSF models when integrated.
AI.conclusion: The AS module effectively handles scale heterogeneity by learning input-tailored adaptive scale factors, preserving semantic discriminability and reducing inverse-scaling errors. It offers a practical, plug-and-play solution for industrial TSF applications with scale-diverse data.

title: Hierarchical Control in Multi-Agent Games: LLM-based Planning and RL Execution
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong performance in sequential decision-making, yet scaling to complex multi-agent environments remains challenging due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. We propose a hierarchical architecture where a pretrained large language model (LLM) acts as a centralized strategic controller that selects among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents, while RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. We evaluate this hybrid system in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and \emph{``Flat''} RL (end-to-end training without skill decomposition) baselines. The LLM+RL system achieves task performance statistically equivalent to hand-crafted BT (46.4\% vs 51.5\% win rate, $p=0.103$) while both significantly outperform Flat RL trained without skill decomposition. A user study ($n=15$) reveals that 60\% of participants perceive LLM+RL agents as the most human-like ($p=0.027$), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability. These results demonstrate that pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills, achieving competitive multi-agent coordination and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

AI.tldr: A hybrid system uses a pretrained LLM as a strategic controller that selects among specialized RL skill policies for multi-agent coordination, achieving competitive performance against hand-crafted behavior trees and superior human-likeness ratings.
AI.motivation: Scaling RL to complex multi-agent environments is difficult due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the challenge of learning coordinated strategies. The authors aim to leverage LLM reasoning to orchestrate pretrained RL skills, avoiding manual rule engineering while achieving both competitive performance and believable agent behavior.
AI.method: A hierarchical architecture where a pretrained LLM serves as a centralized strategic controller selecting among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents, while RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. Evaluated in a 2v2 King of the Hill competitive environment against behavior tree (BT) and Flat RL (end-to-end, no skill decomposition) baselines, with both quantitative win-rate comparisons and a human user study (n=15).
AI.result: The LLM+RL system achieved a 46.4% win rate versus the BT baseline's 51.5% (p=0.103, statistically equivalent), while both significantly outperformed Flat RL. In the user study, 60% of participants rated LLM+RL agents as most human-like (p=0.027), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills for multi-agent coordination, achieving competitive performance comparable to hand-crafted BTs and superior perceived believability, all without manual rule engineering.

title: Adaptive Distance-Aware Trunk Deep Operator Learning for Long-Span Roadway Bridges
summary: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated FE analysis computationally expensive for applications such as influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML approaches struggle to accurately capture these localized responses. To address this challenge, this study proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet for localized structural response prediction in large-scale bridge systems. The framework dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain using a KNN strategy, allowing the network to focus on structural influence zones. The trunk network is further enhanced using distance-aware features that encode the geometric relationship between the load and structural nodes. A physics-based full-field reconstruction is incorporated through a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation, enabling predictions at adaptive nodes to be extended to the entire structural domain. To enable scalable training, response data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that preserves the dominant global behavior while significantly reducing computational cost. The proposed framework is validated on both a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge. Results show that the method achieves FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%, while reducing the total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) by approximately 60x; excluding the post-processing reconstruction step, the AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM. In addition, the framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading configurations, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an adaptive-trunk DeepONet (AD-DeepONet) that uses KNN-based dynamic domain construction and distance-aware features to accurately predict localized structural responses in long-span bridges. A Schur complement formulation enables full-field reconstruction from adaptive node predictions. The method achieves FEM-level accuracy (<5% error) with ~60x total speedup and up to 10,000x inference speedup, validated on a benchmark bridge and the real-world Mussafah Bridge.
AI.motivation: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated full FEM analyses computationally prohibitive for tasks like influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML methods fail to accurately capture these localized responses, creating a need for a surrogate model that is both accurate in local regions and computationally efficient at scale.
AI.method: The proposed adaptive-trunk DeepONet framework dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain using a KNN strategy to focus on structural influence zones. The trunk network is enhanced with distance-aware features encoding geometric relationships between load and structural nodes. Full-field reconstruction uses a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation to extend predictions from adaptive nodes to the entire domain. Training data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that retains dominant global behavior at reduced cost.
AI.result: Validated on a benchmark bridge model and the Mussafah Bridge, the method achieves relative errors below 5% compared to FEM. Total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) is reduced by approximately 60x; excluding post-processing, AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude (10,000x) faster than FEM. The framework successfully generates full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary loading.
AI.conclusion: The AD-DeepONet framework demonstrates strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications, combining FEM-level accuracy with dramatic computational speedups. Its ability to handle arbitrary vehicular loading configurations and generate influence surfaces efficiently addresses a key bottleneck in bridge engineering practice.

title: What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Information-Theoretic Analysis
summary: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning within continuous hidden states, offering a promising alternative to verbose discrete reasoning traces. However, robust latent reasoning remains difficult because outcome supervision provides weak learning signals and leaves latent trajectories prone to semantic drift. In this work, we analyze Latent CoT from an information-theoretic perspective and identify this failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. We further decompose process supervision into two complementary dimensions: Trajectory Supervision, which injects dense stepwise reasoning signals, and Space Supervision, which preserves the semantic structure of the latent manifold. Our analysis shows that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space, whereas generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. To measure these effects, we introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies the mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. These findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision and suggest shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Supervision-in-Latent-CoT}{this repository}.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Latent Chain-of-Thought from an information-theoretic perspective, identifying a dual collapse problem (gradient attenuation + representational drift). It proposes decomposing process supervision into Trajectory Supervision and Space Supervision, introduces the Unified Latent Probe to measure mutual information between latent trajectories and reasoning steps, and demonstrates an Information-Performance Binding principle where reasoning accuracy depends on information fidelity preserved in the latent chain.
AI.motivation: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning in continuous hidden states, avoiding verbose discrete traces, but suffers from weak learning signals under outcome supervision, leading to semantic drift. The authors aim to diagnose why robust latent reasoning fails and to provide principled solutions grounded in information theory.
AI.method: The authors adopt an information-theoretic framework to analyze Latent CoT, characterizing failure as dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in latent space. They decompose process supervision into two dimensions — Trajectory Supervision (dense stepwise reasoning signals) and Space Supervision (preserving semantic structure of the latent manifold). They introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps, and contrast rigid geometric compression against generative reconstruction as a semantic anchor.
AI.result: Experiments reveal a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy is directly tied to the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. Generative reconstruction outperforms rigid geometric compression by providing a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision, advocating a shift from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. The ULP serves as a diagnostic tool for measuring latent reasoning quality.

title: Exploring the potential of AlphaEarth and TESSERA embeddings for Fine-scale Local Climate Zone Mapping: A case study across five cities in Switzerland
summary: Understanding urban spatial morphology is critical for climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable urban design, and Local Climate Zone (LCZ) mapping provides the basic framework for this. However, many cities still use coarse ~100-m resolution LCZ records, which are unsuitable for fine-scale urban research. In this study, precomputed embeddings from TESSERA (Feng et al., 2025) and AlphaEarth (Brown et al., 2025) are compared to traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) composites in five Swiss cities to see if they can upscale coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net. Three experiments assess multi-city transferability, the impact of higher-resolution reference data, and temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. We find that all datasets achieve strong performance with test data Intersection-over-Union (IoU) ranging from 0.59-0.69 and 0.77-0.82 in the first two experiments. TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings As expected, we find that the transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Overall, however, our results demonstrate the promising potential of embeddings derived from EO foundation models to reduce time consuming preprocessing, respectively, manual feature engineering tasks and to guide a universal deep learning-based LCZ mapping workflow. When combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net architecture, the embeddings enhance regional transferability and scalability, supporting the development of comprehensive and reproducible fine-scale LCZ maps for global urban climate applications Improving reference data quality remains the strongest lever for further accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: This study compares precomputed embeddings from two EO foundation models (TESSERA and AlphaEarth) against traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites for upscaling coarse ~100-m LCZ maps to 10-m resolution across five Swiss cities using an attention-based U-Net. TESSERA consistently outperforms other datasets, achieving IoU scores of 0.59–0.69 and 0.77–0.82 across experiments, though temporal transfer across years remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Many cities rely on coarse ~100-m resolution Local Climate Zone (LCZ) maps that are inadequate for fine-scale urban climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable design. The authors seek to determine whether embeddings from Earth observation foundation models can enable efficient upscaling to 10-m resolution while reducing manual preprocessing and feature engineering.
AI.method: The authors compare three input sources — TESSERA embeddings, AlphaEarth embeddings, and traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites — across five Swiss cities using a location-aware attention U-Net architecture. Three experiments are conducted: (1) multi-city transferability, (2) impact of higher-resolution reference data, and (3) temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. Performance is evaluated using Intersection-over-Union (IoU).
AI.result: All datasets achieved strong IoU: 0.59–0.69 in multi-city transferability and 0.77–0.82 with higher-resolution reference data. TESSERA consistently outperformed both S1S2 and AlphaEarth. Temporal transfer across different years proved challenging, remaining an open problem. Reference data quality emerged as the strongest lever for further accuracy improvement.
AI.conclusion: EO foundation model embeddings, particularly TESSERA, show strong potential to simplify and universalize fine-scale LCZ mapping workflows at 10-m resolution. Combined with a simple attention U-Net, they enhance regional transferability and scalability for global urban climate applications. Improving reference data quality is identified as the most impactful path for further gains.

title: Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis using a Multimodal Approach with 3D MRI and PET
comment: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible neurodegenerative disorder and a leading cause of death worldwide. Early diagnosis plays an important part especially at the Mild Cognitive Impairment stage, where timely intervention can help slow its progression before it advances to AD. Neuroimaging data, like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, can help detect brain changes early by providing structural and functional brain changes related to the disease. Yet, many multimodal models still fuse MRI and PET with static concatenation and apply identical computation to all subjects, which limits robustness to patient/site heterogeneity and can waste computation. To address these limitations, we present the first study of combining 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies - concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention - and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier that performs input-adaptive routing, activating only the most informative experts per case. Finally, we utilize Grad-CAM to visualize disease-related regions, ensuring model interpretability. Experiments are performed across three binary classification tasks (NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD). Results show that GMU achieves accuracies of 80.46 % (NC vs. MCI) and 95.47 % (NC vs. AD), while gated self-attention attains 82.08 % on MCI vs. AD. Ablations show that removing the MoE consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks. These findings underscore the value of input-adaptive, multimodal modeling for AD diagnosis by leveraging the complementary nature of MRI and PET.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multimodal framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis that combines 3D CNN feature extractors with three fusion strategies (concatenation, GMU, gated self-attention) and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts classifier for input-adaptive routing, achieving strong performance across three binary classification tasks using MRI and PET data.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal models fuse MRI and PET via static concatenation and apply uniform computation to all subjects, limiting robustness to patient/site heterogeneity and wasting computation. There is a need for input-adaptive, efficient multimodal modeling for early AD diagnosis.
AI.method: The authors combine 3D convolutional feature extractors with three multimodal fusion strategies: concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention. A sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier performs input-adaptive routing, activating only the most relevant experts per case. Grad-CAM is used for interpretability. Evaluated on three binary classification tasks: NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD.
AI.result: GMU achieved 80.46% accuracy on NC vs. MCI and 95.47% on NC vs. AD. Gated self-attention attained 82.08% on MCI vs. AD. Ablation studies showed that removing the MoE classifier consistently degraded accuracy across all tasks.
AI.conclusion: Input-adaptive multimodal modeling leveraging complementary MRI and PET data, particularly with MoE routing and advanced fusion strategies, significantly benefits AD diagnosis. The approach improves robustness to heterogeneity and computational efficiency.

title: Comparative Study of Neural Surrogate Architectures for Autoregressive Prediction of Internal Battery States
summary: The Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model resolves internal electrochemical states in lithium-ion batteries with high fidelity. However, the numerical solution of its governing equations is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment, limiting scalability from individual cells to pack and fleet-scale applications. While machine learning surrogates can substantially reduce inference latency through GPU acceleration, most existing approaches learn solution approximations tied to specific operating conditions rather than learning generalizable state-evolution dynamics. This work presents a systematic comparison of four neural network architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators that predict full DFN internal states across a wide range of operating conditions. To ensure a controlled architectural comparison, all models are trained under a unified framework using multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning, isolating the impact of spatial inductive bias. Results demonstrate that the U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, while providing a 5.38x speed-up over the numerical solver. These findings highlight spatial inductive bias as a critical determinant of surrogate performance, advancing the development of surrogates for internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

AI.tldr: Compares four neural architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) as autoregressive surrogates for the DFN battery model. U-Net achieves 3% nRMSE after 300-step rollouts with 5.38× speedup, demonstrating spatial inductive bias as critical for learning generalizable state-evolution dynamics rather than condition-specific approximations.
AI.motivation: The DFN model is too computationally expensive for real-time use at pack or fleet scale. Existing ML surrogates learn condition-specific approximations rather than generalizable dynamics. The authors aim to systematically identify which neural architectures best capture state-evolution operators that generalize across diverse operating conditions.
AI.method: Four architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, Fourier Neural Operator) are formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators predicting full DFN internal states. All models are trained under a unified framework with multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning to isolate the effect of spatial inductive bias. Performance is evaluated via 300-step autoregressive rollouts across all internal state variables.
AI.result: U-Net achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, with a 5.38× speed-up over the numerical solver. Its multi-scale feature hierarchy outperforms the other architectures, demonstrating that spatial inductive bias is a critical determinant of surrogate performance.
AI.conclusion: Spatial inductive bias, as embodied by U-Net's multi-scale hierarchy, is essential for building accurate and generalizable DFN surrogates. This advances the development of internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

title: PaAno+: Multiscale Encoding and Cross-Variable Attention for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time-series anomaly detection has significant practical value for industrial and medical monitoring, as well as other critical domains. Current Transformer- and large-model-based detection approaches incur excessive computational overhead, while existing lightweight alternatives are constrained by insufficient feature extraction and inadequate modeling of dependencies across multivariate variables. To mitigate the above drawbacks, this study develops a lightweight, efficient anomaly detection model, dubbed PaAno, within the patch-oriented representation learning paradigm. In the encoder module, a multiscale feature-extraction backbone is constructed using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields to capture hierarchical temporal characteristics; subsequent cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation, combined with residual connection optimization, further stabilizes feature representation learning. A cross-variable fusion attention module is embedded to explicitly characterize inter-variable correlations, empowering the model to identify anomalous patterns amid intricate operational conditions. Moreover, a novel pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting is customized to uncover intrinsic structural properties of time series, and triplet loss is leveraged to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced feature discrimination. Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrate that the proposed PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, yielding significant performance gains across evaluation metrics, including VUS-PR, relative to the original PaAno. Leveraging a compact network design, the presented model achieves favorable computational efficiency, enabling deployment on resource-limited terminals for real-time anomaly inference.

AI.tldr: PaAno is a lightweight patch-based anomaly detection model that uses multiscale convolutional encoders, cross-scale attention aggregation, cross-variable fusion attention, and a novel temporal patch-window sorting pretext task with triplet loss to achieve state-of-the-art detection accuracy on TSB-AD while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for edge deployment.
AI.motivation: Current Transformer- and large-model-based anomaly detection methods are computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment, while existing lightweight models suffer from insufficient feature extraction and weak modeling of cross-variable dependencies in multivariate time series.
AI.method: PaAno employs: (1) a multiscale feature-extraction backbone using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields for hierarchical temporal features; (2) cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation with residual connections for stable representation learning; (3) a cross-variable fusion attention module to explicitly model inter-variable correlations; and (4) a novel self-supervised pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting, optimized via triplet loss to enhance patch embedding discrimination.
AI.result: On the TSB-AD benchmark, PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, with significant performance gains across evaluation metrics including VUS-PR, while maintaining favorable computational efficiency for deployment on resource-limited terminals.
AI.conclusion: PaAno demonstrates that a carefully designed lightweight architecture with patch-oriented representation learning, multiscale feature extraction, explicit cross-variable modeling, and self-supervised pretext optimization can match or exceed heavier Transformer-based methods in anomaly detection accuracy while enabling real-time inference on edge devices.

title: Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics
summary: Perception for action suggests that representations of the world should be shaped not by visual fidelity alone, but by their relevance for actions. At the same time, latent JEPA-style world models advocate learning compact predictive states from high-dimensional observations to facilitate the prediction of future states, but end-to-end training of these models is nontrivial because representations may collapse if our only goal is to construct a latent state that is easy to predict. We introduce a sensorimotor world model (SMWM): a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization. This single regularizer addresses both issues: it prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned representations. By forcing latent states to preserve information about the action underlying a transition, it biases the model toward the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment while discarding uncontrollable distractors. This yields stable latent world models trained from offline, reward-free trajectories, without frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers. Empirically, SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and enables competitive planning performance across simple 2D and 3D control tasks.

AI.tldr: SMWM proposes a sensorimotor world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization, which simultaneously prevents representational collapse and induces action-aligned latent representations, enabling stable learning from offline reward-free trajectories without auxiliary techniques like EMA or frozen encoders.
AI.motivation: Two key motivations: (1) Perception-for-action principles suggest representations should prioritize action relevance over visual fidelity; (2) JEPA-style world models aim to learn compact predictive states but suffer from representational collapse when trained end-to-end, since making states trivially predictable can lead to degenerate solutions. Existing remedies (frozen encoders, EMA, complex regularizers) add complexity. A unified solution addressing both the collapse problem and action-alignment is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce SMWM, a latent world model with a single inverse dynamics regularizer. The model learns to predict future latent states while the regularizer forces latent states to preserve information about the action that caused the transition. This biases representations toward controllable degrees of freedom and discards uncontrollable distractors. Training is end-to-end on offline, reward-free trajectories, without frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers.
AI.result: SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and achieves competitive planning performance on simple 2D and 3D control tasks, demonstrating that the inverse dynamics regularizer alone is sufficient for stable training and task-relevant representation learning.
AI.conclusion: Inverse dynamics regularization is a simple yet effective single mechanism that jointly solves representation collapse and action-alignment in end-to-end latent world model training, bridging perception-for-action principles with JEPA-style predictive architectures.

title: Quantile of Means: A Bonus-Free Ensemble Method for Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning
summary: Optimal Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically rely on carefully constructed count-based uncertainty estimates to drive exploration. Although theoretically sound, such estimates are hard to compute in practical settings and therefore offer limited insight for designing exploration heuristics. Meanwhile, ensembling has emerged as a practical approach, but remains without theoretical justification. Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, we propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Our simple count-free approach achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration in RL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs that achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds without relying on count-based uncertainty estimates, providing theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration in RL.
AI.motivation: Optimal RL algorithms depend on count-based uncertainty estimates that are theoretically sound but computationally intractable in practice. Ensembling has emerged as a practical alternative but lacks theoretical grounding. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration.
AI.method: Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, the authors propose a quantile-based ensemble method tailored to finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The approach is count-free and uses quantile statistics from an ensemble of value function estimates to drive exploration.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, matching the theoretical performance of count-based methods while being practically implementable.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based exploration can be theoretically grounded and achieve optimal regret guarantees in finite-horizon MDPs, closing the gap between practical heuristics and theoretical optimality in RL exploration.

title: When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital: Federated Conformal Risk Control via Risk-Curve Shrinkage
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the DeCaF Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees on segmentation quality by calibrating a prediction-set threshold on held-out data. In federated deployments, the standard approach pools calibration scores across sites into a single threshold. We provide the first quantification, on real multi-institutional brain tumor data (FeTS-2022, 1,251 subjects, 20 institutions), showing that this naive pooled CRC protects the average hospital but violates coverage at 40% of individual institutions, with the worst site exceeding the target false-negative rate by 7.8 percentage points. The naive alternative, per-site local CRC, largely restores coverage but inflates prediction sets by 83x, rendering them clinically useless. We propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n0 smoothly trades worst-case coverage for prediction-set efficiency; leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis identifies n0=19, achieving 2.7/20 violations at 2.0x stretch. We further show that direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets fails, concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals, and that the finite-sample correction term is essential: removing it triples violations. The marginal CRC guarantee is preserved by construction under the stated site-mixture assumption; per-site coverage is validated across four targets with three seeds. No patient-level images, masks, or per-volume scores leave any site.

AI.tldr: A shrinkage-based federated conformal risk control protocol is proposed to achieve per-institution segmentation quality guarantees without sharing patient data, addressing the failure of naive pooled CRC (40% site coverage violations) and the impracticality of per-site local CRC (83× prediction set inflation).
AI.motivation: Standard pooled CRC in federated settings only protects average performance and fails to guarantee coverage at individual institutions. Per-site local CRC preserves coverage but produces clinically useless, oversized prediction sets. There is a need for a federated approach that balances per-site coverage guarantees with prediction-set efficiency without sharing sensitive patient data.
AI.method: Each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a central server. The server computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site by shrinking site-specific thresholds toward a pooled estimate, controlled by a single hyperparameter n0. Leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis tunes n0. The method also incorporates a finite-sample correction term and preserves the marginal CRC guarantee under a site-mixture assumption. Direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets is also evaluated as an alternative.
AI.result: On FeTS-2022 (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions): pooled CRC violates coverage at 40% of institutions (worst-case +7.8 pp FNR). Per-site local CRC inflates sets by 83×. Shrinkage CRC with n0=19 achieves 2.7/20 violations at 2.0× stretch. Removing the finite-sample correction triples violations. Lagrangian budget optimization concentrates risk on vulnerable hospitals and fails.
AI.conclusion: The shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol effectively navigates the trade-off between worst-case coverage and efficiency, providing near-calibrated per-site guarantees while requiring minimal data transmission (G scalars per site) and preserving patient privacy.

title: Multi-Modal Contrastive Learning for Implicit Earth Embeddings via Location Tying
summary: Spatial prediction tasks are often limited by a lack of high-quality labelled ground-truth observations. To overcome this challenge, self-supervised pre-training is a possible solution, with contrastive learning dominant for location encoders. Those approaches usually align geographic coordinates with just one additional modality. We propose two multimodal contrastive learning architectures: Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying (MELT) and Sequential Alternating Location Training (SALT). These architectures expand this framework beyond two modalities by utilising unpaired geospatial data. Both methods are technically viable and match the performance of the strongest two-modality baseline (SATCLIP) across four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting that the chosen location encoder is the main limitation - the contrastive objective reaches its peak early, regardless of modality diversity or pre-training volume. MELT provides more stable training than SALT and presents a stronger foundation for future scaling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MELT and SALT, two multimodal contrastive learning architectures for geospatial representation learning that align location encoders with multiple unpaired modalities. Both match the strongest two-modality baseline (SATCLIP) but adding modalities does not consistently improve performance — the location encoder saturates early, suggesting it is the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Spatial prediction tasks suffer from scarce high-quality labelled data. Self-supervised contrastive learning is a promising solution, but existing methods align geographic coordinates with only one additional modality. The authors aim to scale contrastive location encoding to multiple modalities to determine whether multimodal diversity improves learned representations.
AI.method: Two architectures are proposed: MELT (Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying) ties all modality embeddings to a shared location encoder simultaneously; SALT (Sequential Alternating Location Training) alternates training between modality pairs. Both use unpaired geospatial data and contrastive objectives. Evaluation is conducted across four downstream tasks against SATCLIP and other baselines.
AI.result: Both MELT and SALT match SATCLIP performance across all four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities does not yield consistent improvements. The contrastive objective saturates early regardless of modality count or pre-training data volume, indicating the location encoder — not modality diversity — is the limiting factor. MELT provides more stable training than SALT.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal contrastive pre-training with unpaired geospatial data is technically feasible and matches two-modality baselines, but simply adding modalities does not help. Future work should focus on improving the location encoder itself rather than scaling modalities. MELT is recommended as the more stable foundation for such efforts.

title: Predicting gestational age at birth in the context of preterm birth from multi-modal fetal MRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA) https://melba-journal.org/2026:013
summary: Preterm birth is associated with significant mortality and a risk for lifelong morbidity. The complex multifactorial aetiology hampers accurate prediction and thus optimal care. A pipeline consisting of bespoke machine learning methods for data imputation, feature selection, and regression models to predict gestational age (GA) at birth was developed and evaluated from comprehensive multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI data from 333 control cases and 93 preterm birth cases. The GA at birth predictions were classified into term and preterm categories and their accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were reported. An ablation study was performed to further validate the design of the pipeline. Performance was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The pipeline achieves an R2 score of 0.13 and a mean absolute error of 2.74 weeks. It also achieves a 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity across folds. The predominant features selected by the pipeline include cervical length and statistics derived from placental T2* values. The confluence of fast, motion-robust and multi-modal fetal MRI techniques and machine learning prediction allowed the prediction of the gestation at birth. This information is essential for any pregnancy. To the best of our knowledge, preterm birth had only been addressed as a classification problem in the literature. Therefore, this work provides a proof of concept. Future work will increase the cohort size to allow for finer stratification within the preterm birth cohort. Our code is available at https://github.com/dfajardorojas/ml-for-preterm-birth-.

AI.tldr: A machine learning pipeline using multi-modal fetal MRI data (cervical length, placental T2* statistics) was developed to predict gestational age at birth, achieving 0.77 accuracy and 0.59 sensitivity for preterm birth classification. This represents the first regression-based approach to GA prediction, moving beyond prior classification-only methods.
AI.motivation: Preterm birth carries high mortality and lifelong morbidity risk, yet its complex multifactorial etiology hampers accurate prediction. Improved prediction would enable optimal clinical care and intervention planning.
AI.method: A bespoke ML pipeline with data imputation, feature selection, and regression models was developed using multi-modal fetal MRI data (morphological and functional) from 333 controls and 93 preterm cases. Gestational age at birth was predicted via regression, then classified into term/preterm categories. Performance was assessed via stratified 10-fold cross-validation with an ablation study for validation.
AI.result: The pipeline achieved R² = 0.13, MAE = 2.74 weeks for regression; classification yielded 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity. Dominant predictive features were cervical length and placental T2* statistics.
AI.conclusion: This work provides proof of concept that multi-modal fetal MRI combined with ML can predict gestational age at birth, representing the first regression-based approach to the problem (prior work only used classification). Future work requires larger cohorts for finer preterm stratification.

title: Computational Methods and Challenges in Cell-Free DNA Analysis for Multi-Cancer Early Detection
summary: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a promising avenue for non-invasive multicancer early detection (MCED), in that, it can enable multiple cancer detection simultaneously from a single blood draw, with particular sensitivity to cancers that currently lack established screening programs. Here we review the computational methods developed between 2022 and 2025 for cfDNA-based MCED. We focus on how fragmentomics and epigenetic features are extracted and analyzed to detect cancer at early stages. We first briefly outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then review classical statistical and machine learning approaches alongside deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. For each method we discuss biological interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical integration. Furthermore, we categorize the current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological while outlining open problems in the field. This review shows that multimodal ensemble approaches have the strongest promise for clinical integration and the highest readiness. However, for better assessment of future work and side-by-side comparison, standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting results will be crucial.

AI.tldr: This review surveys computational methods (2022–2025) for cfDNA-based multicancer early detection, covering fragmentomics and epigenetic feature extraction, classical ML and deep learning approaches, and argues that multimodal ensemble methods show the most clinical promise while standardization of evaluation protocols remains critical.
AI.motivation: Cell-free DNA enables non-invasive, simultaneous detection of multiple cancers from a single blood draw, especially benefiting cancers without established screening programs. The rapid development of computational methods between 2022–2025 warrants a focused review to assess progress, compare approaches, and identify gaps in the field.
AI.method: This is a literature review categorizing computational methods for cfDNA-based MCED. The review covers: (1) biological basis of cfDNA signals, (2) fragmentomics and epigenetic feature extraction pipelines, (3) classical statistical and machine learning approaches, (4) deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. Each method is evaluated on biological interpretability, validation strategy, and clinical integration readiness.
AI.result: Multimodal ensemble approaches demonstrate the strongest promise and highest readiness for clinical integration. Key challenges are categorized into technical, computational, and methodological domains. Standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting results is identified as crucial for future side-by-side comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal ensemble methods represent the current frontier in cfDNA-based MCED. Progress in the field will depend on establishing standardized evaluation benchmarks and transparent reporting practices to enable rigorous comparison of emerging computational methods.

title: Effective Dimension Governs Generalization in Quantum Kernel Vision Models
summary: Recent quantum vision models-quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks-report two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena: (i) ansatze with more, or more uniformly distributed, entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy rather than degrade it. These observations are currently treated as curiosities, discovered by grid search and explained, if at all, by hand. We show that both are manifestations of a single, measurable quantity: the \emph{effective dimension} $d_{\rm eff}$ of the (noise-shaped) quantum feature kernel. Working primarily with quantum-kernel vision models-a quantum feature map read out by a kernel classifier-we give a spectral account in which entanglement structure and quantum noise are two knobs that move $d_{\rm eff}$; in an overfitting regime, contracting $d_{\rm eff}$ acts as ridge-like regularization. We analyze the mechanism: an \emph{exact} decomposition of the depolarized kernel $K_p=(1-p)^2K+\tfrac{p(2-p)}{D}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ with $d_{\rm eff}(K_p)\to1$, a contraction result (and its boundary) for amplitude damping, a kernel-machine capacity bound, and a capacity/alignment risk decomposition; the monotone contraction operative in our entangled experiments is verified empirically, not proven in general. Along the one-parameter depolarizing family the collapse is instead exact by construction; we use it only to confirm the kernel decomposition to machine precision and at up to $12$ qubits, not as evidence for $d_{\rm eff}$. Amplitude damping contracts $d_{\rm eff}$ and lifts test accuracy by up to $+13\%$ along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect's sign flips between the over- and under-fitting regimes; noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. Our results organize two reported anecdotes into a single measurable principle for designing quantum-vision models.

AI.tldr: Two unexplained phenomena in quantum vision models—entanglement structure and quantum noise both improving generalization—are unified as manifestations of a single measurable quantity, the effective dimension of the quantum feature kernel. Working with quantum-kernel vision models, the authors provide a spectral account showing that both entanglement and noise act as knobs that contract effective dimension, serving as ridge-like regularization in overfitting regimes.
AI.motivation: Two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena have emerged in quantum vision models: (i) ansätze with more/uniformly distributed entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy. These have been treated as curiosities discovered by grid search without a principled theoretical explanation. The authors aim to provide a unified, measurable principle explaining both phenomena.
AI.method: The authors frame the analysis around quantum-kernel vision models (quantum feature maps read by kernel classifiers). They introduce the effective dimension d_eff of the noise-shaped quantum feature kernel as the unifying quantity. Key analytical contributions include: (1) an exact decomposition of the depolarized kernel showing d_eff(K_p)→1 under depolarization; (2) a contraction result for amplitude damping; (3) a kernel-machine capacity bound; (4) a capacity/alignment risk decomposition. Empirical verification is performed up to 12 qubits, with amplitude damping experiments showing up to +13% test accuracy gains along an inverted-U sweet spot that flips sign between over- and under-fitting regimes.
AI.result: Both entanglement structure and quantum noise are shown to be two knobs that move the effective dimension d_eff. In overfitting regimes, contracting d_eff acts as ridge-like regularization, explaining why more entanglement and injected noise can improve generalization. The depolarizing kernel decomposition is verified to machine precision up to 12 qubits. Amplitude damping contracts d_eff and lifts test accuracy by up to +13% along an inverted-U curve, with the effect flipping sign between over- and under-fitting regimes. Noise injection is shown to match an explicit spectral-filtering frontier.
AI.conclusion: The two reported anecdotes—entanglement improving generalization and noise boosting accuracy—are organized into a single measurable principle: the effective dimension of the quantum feature kernel. This provides a principled framework for designing quantum vision models, where tuning entanglement and noise levels controls effective dimension and thus regularization strength.

title: Learner-based Concept Drift Detection: Analysis and Evaluation
summary: Machine learning algorithms deployed for evolving streaming environments must handle the non-stationary data distributions, commonly referred to as concept drift. The presence of concept drift poses a major challenge for many real-world applications because it can severely degrade their predictive performance, hindering their ability to support robust decision-making. Consequently, the timely and efficient detection of drift events is critical for sustaining high accuracy over time. This study examines theoretically the concept drift characteristics and numerous drift detection algorithms across several categories. Furthermore, we evaluate their performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets exhibiting diverse streaming scenarios and drift characteristics, such as abrupt and gradual changes. This study aims to enhance understanding of the complex notion of concept drift characteristics and behavior of drift detectors, along with their applicability to diverse contexts.

AI.tldr: A theoretical and empirical study examining concept drift characteristics in streaming environments, categorizing and evaluating numerous drift detection algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets with various drift types (abrupt, gradual) to guide their application in non-stationary data contexts.
AI.motivation: Concept drift — non-stationary data distributions in streaming environments — severely degrades predictive performance in real-world applications, compromising robust decision-making. Timely and efficient drift detection is critical for maintaining high accuracy over time, yet the landscape of drift characteristics and detection algorithms lacks comprehensive theoretical and empirical characterization.
AI.method: The study conducts a theoretical analysis of concept drift characteristics and systematically categorizes numerous drift detection algorithms. It then performs an empirical evaluation of these detectors on both synthetic and real-world datasets that encompass diverse streaming scenarios and drift characteristics, including abrupt and gradual changes.
AI.result: The paper provides enhanced understanding of the complex nature of concept drift characteristics and the behavioral patterns of drift detectors across varying contexts. Performance results across synthetic and real-world datasets reveal the relative strengths and applicability of different detection categories under abrupt versus gradual drift scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes a structured framework for understanding concept drift and drift detectors, clarifying which approaches are suited to specific drift characteristics and application contexts, thereby aiding practitioners in selecting appropriate detection mechanisms for evolving streaming environments.

title: Boundary Embedding Shaping with Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Graph Structural Disentanglement
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at aggregating neighbor information for classification, yet their performance is hindered by graph structural entanglement, where spurious correlations from semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings. This challenge is most acute for nodes near class boundaries in the embedding space, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods largely treat all nodes uniformly, ignoring boundary vulnerabilities.
