In this paper, to improve classification performance, we tackle graph structural disentanglement by identifying boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning GNN plug-in module that selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal model parameter perturbation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms existing leading methods. Notably, BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.

AI.tldr: BES is a plug-in contrastive learning module for GNNs that identifies nodes near class boundaries and selectively suppresses spurious structural noise to improve classification and link prediction.
AI.motivation: GNN performance degrades due to graph structural entanglement, where semantically irrelevant neighbors introduce spurious correlations into node embeddings. This problem is especially severe for nodes near class decision boundaries, yet existing robust GNN methods treat all nodes uniformly, neglecting these boundary-specific vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning plug-in module for GNNs. BES identifies boundary-region nodes where structural noise is most damaging and applies targeted suppression of spurious neighbor correlations, refining decision boundaries with minimal parameter perturbation to the underlying GNN.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms leading methods. BES boosts GCN node classification accuracy by an average of 3.3%, with up to 5.0% improvement on WikiCS, and achieves superior link prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-region structural entanglement is the primary bottleneck in GNN classification. BES effectively addresses this through adaptive boundary-aware contrastive learning, yielding significant and consistent performance gains across multiple benchmarks and tasks.

title: Integrating national forest inventory, airborne lidar, and satellite imagery for wall-to-wall mapping of forest structure with computer vision
summary: Remote sensing is increasingly relied upon to deliver actionable science for forest and wildfire risk management across large landscapes. Wall-to-wall, annually updated maps are a persistent need for effective forest management. Many planning systems and data collections combine disparate data sources with different purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, which leads to confounding behavior in operational planning systems. We introduce the VibrantForests framework, developed and applied to map forest attributes and provide a coherent foundation for effective forest and wildfire planning. VibrantForests includes a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived samples and applied across the contiguous United States to concurrently generate estimates of canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter at 10-meter resolution. We demonstrate predictive capability spanning the full spectrum of forest conditions ranging from sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass. Results show that our model extends the range at which saturation is commonly encountered in comparable passive-sensor models, and reduces regression-to-mean behavior that commonly produces overestimation of forest attributes in small/sparse conditions and underestimation in large/dense conditions. The VibrantForests framework addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent wall-to-wall estimates of management-relevant attributes at annual cadence and 10m resolution.

AI.tldr: VibrantForests is a satellite-based framework that produces wall-to-wall, annually updated maps of five forest attributes (canopy cover, canopy height, biomass, basal area, quadratic mean diameter) at 10m resolution across the contiguous US, using lidar-trained models that reduce saturation bias and regression-to-mean errors commonly found in passive-sensor approaches.
AI.motivation: Current operational forest and wildfire planning systems rely on disparate data sources with varying purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, creating confounding behavior. There is a persistent need for coherent, wall-to-wall, annually updated forest attribute maps to support effective management across large landscapes.
AI.method: The VibrantForests framework uses a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived reference samples. It ingests passive optical satellite imagery and applies the trained model concurrently to estimate five forest attributes—canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter—at 10-meter spatial resolution across the contiguous United States.
AI.result: The model demonstrates predictive capability across the full spectrum of forest conditions (sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass). It extends the range at which saturation occurs in comparable passive-sensor models and reduces regression-to-mean behavior, mitigating overestimation in sparse/small conditions and underestimation in dense/large conditions.
AI.conclusion: The VibrantForests framework addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent, management-relevant forest attribute estimates at annual cadence and 10m resolution, providing a unified foundation for operational decision-making.

title: Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions
summary: The use of neural networks (NNs) is rapidly increasing, including in safety- and security-critical domains. To provide formal guarantees about NN behavior, many verification methods rely on optimizable linear relaxations of activation functions. However, existing techniques depend on hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. Extension to state-of-the-art activation functions therefore requires substantial manual effort. In contrast, our approach SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) is broadly applicable, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points. SLiR parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure that ensures sound upper and lower bounds over the input domain, enabling efficient optimization while maintaining correctness. Our experiments show that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: SLiR introduces a general, parameterized framework for generating sound linear relaxations of activation functions for neural network verification, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or critical points, eliminating the need for hand-crafted per-function relaxations and achieving up to 7.8x more verified properties than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing NN verification methods rely on hand-crafted linear relaxations tailored to each specific activation function. As novel activation functions emerge, this manual approach does not scale and creates a bottleneck for applying formal verification to state-of-the-art networks. A general, automated method is needed.
AI.method: SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure. Given only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points of the activation function, SLiR derives sound upper and lower linear bounds over the entire input domain. The relaxation parameters are optimizable, enabling efficient tightness tuning within verification frameworks.
AI.result: SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions. In verification experiments, it enables proving up to 7.8x more robust properties compared to state-of-the-art verification methods.
AI.conclusion: SLiR provides a broadly applicable, automated approach to generating sound linear relaxations for NN verification, significantly reducing manual effort while improving verification performance, making formal guarantees more accessible for networks using diverse activation functions.

title: Recurrent neural networks approximate continuous functions
summary: Classical approximation theorems ask for a new neural network whenever the target accuracy is improved. This paper studies the opposite possibility: can the network be chosen once and for all, and can accuracy be bought only by letting it run longer? We prove that this is possible for every continuous function on [-1,1]. More precisely, each such function is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The mechanism behind the construction is a new intermediate model, the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU). This model retains the algorithmic freedom needed to implement polynomial approximation schemes, while remaining rigid enough to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitude. The resulting convergence rates reflect the underlying polynomial approximation rates. We complement the construction with minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is not merely a proof artifact, but an unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and hidden dimension can uniformly approximate every continuous function on [-1,1] by simply running longer (i.e., increasing runtime), eliminating the need to redesign the network for better accuracy. A Turing machine with neural units (TMNU) intermediate model enables this construction. Minimax lower bounds confirm runtime is a fundamental resource, not an artifact.
AI.motivation: Classical neural network approximation theory requires constructing a new network (different architecture, weights, or size) whenever target accuracy is improved. The authors ask whether this is necessary, or whether a single, fixed network can achieve arbitrary accuracy simply through longer runtime — essentially decoupling accuracy from network design and making it purely a function of computational time.
AI.method: The authors introduce an intermediate abstraction called the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU), which combines the algorithmic flexibility of Turing machines (sufficient to implement polynomial approximation schemes) with sufficient structural rigidity to be simulated by ReLU RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitudes. A single fixed-weight, fixed-dimension ReLU recurrent network is constructed whose time evolution uniformly approximates any continuous function on [-1,1], with convergence rates matching the underlying polynomial approximation rates. Minimax lower bounds are derived to show runtime is an unavoidable resource.
AI.result: For every continuous function on [-1,1], there exists a single ReLU RNN with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension such that its time evolution uniformly approximates the function to arbitrary accuracy, with convergence rates reflecting polynomial approximation rates. Minimax lower bounds demonstrate that runtime cannot be circumvented — it is a necessary resource in the fixed-network approximation regime.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a paradigm shift in neural network approximation: accuracy can be "bought" purely through runtime rather than network redesign. The TMNU model serves as a bridge between algorithmic expressiveness and neural implementability. The complementary lower bounds rigorously justify that runtime is an essential, inescapable resource in this setting, not merely an artifact of the constructive proof.

title: Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs
summary: We develop QCPIKAN, the first quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Built upon Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers and parameterized quantum circuits, this hybrid framework embeds physical constraints into the training loss to enforce physical consistency. Our theoretical investigations grounded in approximation theory prove that this design accelerates high-frequency error convergence to an exponential rate and effectively mitigates numerical dispersion. We validate the framework across three typical seepage scenarios in porous media, including single-phase flow, component transport and two-phase flow. Compared with existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks, QCPIKAN achieves superior performance in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking and displacement front localization. This work provides a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs.

AI.tldr: QCPIKAN introduces a hybrid quantum-classical architecture combining Chebyshev-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with parameterized quantum circuits, embedding physical constraints to solve PDEs with exponential high-frequency error convergence. Validated on porous media seepage problems, it outperforms existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks in accuracy, error control, and front tracking.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks face limitations in high-frequency error convergence and numerical dispersion when solving PDEs. The authors aim to leverage the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem with Chebyshev polynomials and quantum circuits to overcome these bottlenecks, providing a more robust and efficient PDE solver for complex physical systems.
AI.method: The framework integrates Chebyshev-polynomial-based Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) layers with parameterized quantum circuits (PQC) in a hybrid classical-quantum architecture. Physical constraints (governing PDEs, initial/boundary conditions) are embedded into the training loss to ensure physical consistency. The theoretical analysis uses approximation theory to prove exponential convergence rates for high-frequency errors and mitigation of numerical dispersion. Validation covers three seepage scenarios: single-phase flow, component transport, and two-phase flow in porous media.
AI.result: QCPIKAN demonstrates superior performance over existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks across four metrics: (1) global prediction accuracy, (2) local error control, (3) dynamic evolution tracking, and (4) displacement front localization. Theoretical proofs confirm exponential high-frequency error convergence and effective numerical dispersion suppression.
AI.conclusion: QCPIKAN offers a robust and efficient hybrid quantum-classical framework for solving complex PDEs, with particular strength in porous media applications. The combination of KAN layers and quantum circuits provides a compelling alternative to conventional physics-informed neural networks.

title: Constrained hybrid modelling to predict microbial dynamics and organic matter turnover in soil systems
summary: Soil microorganisms control organic matter cycling and largely determine how soil systems can cope with and mitigate climate change and environmental threats. Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is therefore critical to predict carbon cycling in soils, albeit highly challenging to inform from data. One promising approach to improve their parametrisation is the integration of genomic data, yet modelling the complex and unknown relationship between genomes and the processes the microbes are driving is an unsolved problem. In this work, we present the first hybrid modeling framework for deriving biokinetic parameter values of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits based on DNA sequencing data. Our model predicts biokinetic parameters of the process-based model from genomic trait data with a neural network and integrates constraints from ecological theory and literature to ensure realistic behavior, even of non-observed state variables. We evaluate our method on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data, showing that our approach improves performance over multiple baselines and learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model effectively, even for small training datasets.

AI.tldr: A hybrid modeling framework that uses neural networks to predict biokinetic parameters of soil organic matter models from metagenomic trait data, constrained by ecological theory, enabling learning of unmeasurable dynamics even with small datasets.
AI.motivation: Soil microorganisms govern carbon cycling, but representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is challenging due to data scarcity and the complex, unknown relationship between genomes and microbial processes. Genomic data integration offers a promising but unsolved pathway for parameterization.
AI.method: A hybrid modeling framework that combines a process-based soil organic matter turnover model with a neural network. The neural network predicts biokinetic parameters from metagenome-inferred functional traits (DNA sequencing data). Ecological theory and literature-derived constraints are integrated to ensure realistic behavior of both observed and unobserved state variables.
AI.result: The method was evaluated on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data. It outperformed multiple baselines and effectively learned the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model, demonstrating robustness even with small training datasets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating genomic data into process-based models via hybrid neural network approaches is a viable and effective strategy for improving soil carbon cycling predictions, overcoming key limitations of traditional parameterization methods.

title: Critical Percolation as a Synthetic Data Model for Interpretability
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Neural networks learn features that reflect the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Synthetic datasets used to evaluate interpretability methods typically lack this structure, limiting their value as realistic toy models. To close this gap, we introduce a family of synthetic datasets consisting of hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional data space. The percolation data consists of sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters with a power-law size distribution. Latent variables modeling a taxonomic hierarchy generate each data point's target value. The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without requiring hyperparameter tuning. We leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to propose an almost linear-time algorithm to jointly sample a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition, enabling data generation at arbitrary scale. Using probing experiments, we find that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations. Together, sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability make critical percolation a principled testbed for interpretability research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a synthetic dataset based on critical mean-field percolation clusters with hierarchical latent structure, designed as a principled, analytically tractable testbed for neural network interpretability research. The data exhibits sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and supports linear decoding of ground-truth latent variables from network activations.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic datasets for evaluating interpretability methods lack the hierarchical, multi-scale structure characteristic of natural data, limiting their realism as toy models. There is a need for analytically tractable synthetic data that captures these structural properties to serve as a principled testbed.
AI.method: The authors construct a family of synthetic datasets using hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in high-dimensional space. They leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to develop an almost linear-time algorithm for jointly sampling random trees and their hierarchical latent decompositions. The data model has known critical exponents, fixing its properties analytically without hyperparameter tuning. Probing experiments are used to assess whether ground-truth latent variables can be decoded from neural network activations.
AI.result: The proposed percolation-based data model is analytically tractable with fixed critical exponents. The sampling algorithm enables data generation at arbitrary scale in near-linear time. Probing experiments demonstrate that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations.
AI.conclusion: Critical percolation, with its properties of sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability, constitutes a principled and effective testbed for interpretability research in neural networks.

title: On the Variance of Temporal Difference Learning and its Reduction Using Control Variates
summary: We analyze the variance of temporal difference (TD) learning using the phased setting with tabular representation, and show that one of the mechanisms behind its ability to reduce variance is by effectively aggregating over a larger number of independent trajectories. Based on this insight, we demonstrate that (1) the variance of TD is asymptotically bounded from above by Monte Carlo (MC) estimators, and (2) shorter horizon updates incurs less variance for a fixed number of samples. Beyond TD, we show that Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE), a method for estimating the advantage function, can be seen as a type of regression-adjusted control variate, which achieves a tighter bound on the variance compared to TD in the large-sample limit. Finally, we numerically illustrate the behaviors of these estimators with carefully designed environments.

AI.tldr: TD learning reduces variance by aggregating over more independent trajectories than MC; shorter horizons yield lower variance. DAE is shown to be a regression-adjusted control variate with even tighter variance bounds asymptotically.
AI.motivation: Understand the variance properties of TD learning and related estimators (MC, DAE) in the tabular, phased setting to provide theoretical guarantees on their relative variance behavior.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of asymptotic variance bounds in the phased tabular RL setting. TD variance is compared to MC, showing TD is asymptotically upper-bounded by MC variance. DAE is analyzed through the lens of regression-adjusted control variates. Numerical experiments in designed environments validate the theoretical findings.
AI.result: TD variance is asymptotically ≤ MC variance due to trajectory aggregation. Shorter-horizon TD updates incur less variance for fixed samples. DAE achieves a tighter variance bound than TD in the large-sample limit via control variate regression adjustment.
AI.conclusion: TD's variance reduction stems from aggregating independent trajectories; shorter horizons improve variance further. DAE provides even stronger variance reduction through regression-adjusted control variates, offering both theoretical and practical advantages.

title: Train, Retrieve, or Both? A Four-Arm Head-to-Head for Correct Statutory Citation on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act
summary: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need to be pointed at the provision of law that actually governs a question, with a correct statutory citation. We study this task on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) and its core regulation, asking the operator's question empirically: is fine-tuning enough, or is hybrid retrieval needed? We run a four-arm head-to-head on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (base zero-shot, LoRA SFT-only, RAG-only, and an SFT+RAG hybrid), scored on citation exact-match (section+subsection) over a small, human-verification-pending real eval set. The base model cannot cite the RTA and SFT-only mis-recalls sections; retrieval is essential and drives hallucination to zero by construction; and the SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. Its edge comes from SFT making provision selection more robust to the higher-recall candidate sets that hurt zero-shot RAG. Notably, this cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats a pipeline built on bigger, specialized retrieval models (a larger embedder and a cross-encoder reranker), and a larger/improved training set does not help either: strong statutory-citation performance here does not require specialized retrieval models or more data. The artifact zeroes hallucination and clears the lift-over-base bar but does not reach the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target. All results are on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set and are reported as preliminary.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or a hybrid approach is best for accurately citing statutory provisions from the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the study finds that SFT+RAG hybrid achieves the highest exact-match citation accuracy (0.481) with zero hallucinations, outperforming zero-shot, SFT-only, and RAG-only baselines. Retrieval is essential, and the hybrid approach using a cheap bge-small embedder matches or beats pipelines using larger specialized retrieval models.
AI.motivation: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need accurate statutory citations to the specific legal provisions governing their questions. The core empirical question is whether fine-tuning alone suffices for this legal citation task or whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is necessary.
AI.method: A four-arm head-to-head comparison using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: (1) base zero-shot, (2) LoRA SFT-only, (3) RAG-only, and (4) SFT+RAG hybrid. Evaluation uses exact-match scoring (section+subsection) on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set of questions about the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). The hybrid uses bge-small embeddings for retrieval.
AI.result: Base zero-shot cannot cite the RTA at all. SFT-only mis-recalls sections. RAG drives hallucination to zero by construction. The SFT+RAG hybrid achieves the highest exact-match score of 0.481 with zero hallucinated citations. SFT improves robustness to higher-recall candidate sets that degrade zero-shot RAG performance. The cheap bge-small hybrid matches or surpasses pipelines using larger specialized embedders and cross-encoder rerankers, and additional training data provides no further improvement.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval is essential for statutory citation tasks; fine-tuning alone is insufficient. An SFT+RAG hybrid with a small, cheap retriever yields strong performance without specialized retrieval models or large training sets. The system eliminates hallucination but falls short of the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target. All results are preliminary due to the small, human-verification-pending evaluation set.

title: Judging to Improve: A De-biased VLM-as-3D-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Generation
summary: A companion study established a de-biased, cross-model VLM-as-3D-judge that reliably ranks single-image-to-3D mesh quality where cheap geometry and CLIP proxies fall short. This paper asks: can that judge's preferences specialize a strong open generator, TRELLIS, on one asset class (furniture), cheaply and without human labels? Taking the judge from ranking to optimization is where the work lives. Pushing a VLM judge into the training and evaluation loop exposes failure modes ranking never triggered, so our contribution is an optimization-grade hardening of the judge: a training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) held distinct from an evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; position-bias correction; and fixes for three failure modes (image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs), with calibration evidence (clear-gap win-rate 0.83-1.0; base-vs-base ~0.5). Using this protocol as an independent evaluator, and working only from public models and data with lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation, we find our methods match the strong base rather than exceed it. Independent base samples carry essentially no learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate), so signal must be engineered by quality-contrastive construction. Across six adaptation methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, the most targeted - conditioner repair under severe degradation - reaches parity (0.50) with the base, while no method clears the >=65% win-rate target. The result is mechanistic: clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DIT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the locus that moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects. Matching a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is itself informative: exceeding it needs more than lightweight PEFT on public data, and the judge protocol is reusable.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a VLM-as-3D-judge's preferences can be used to cheaply specialize a strong open 3D generator (TRELLIS) on furniture assets without human labels. The core contribution is hardening the judge for optimization loops (fixing position bias, image overload, geometry-hiding renders, and reference-free judging failures), then testing six lightweight adaptation methods. Results show adaptation reaches parity with the base model but cannot exceed it, revealing mechanistic limits of cheap PEFT on public data.
AI.motivation: Prior work established that VLM judges can reliably rank 3D mesh quality where cheap geometry/CLIP proxies fail. However, repurposing such a judge from ranking into an optimization loop (to guide generator fine-tuning) introduces failure modes that ranking alone never encounters. The authors aim to bridge this gap by hardening the judge for optimization-grade use and testing whether its preferences can specialize a strong generator cheaply, with no human labels.
AI.method: The approach has two pillars: (1) Judge hardening — using separate training (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and evaluation (InternVL3-8B) judges to break circularity, applying position-bias correction, and engineering fixes for three failure modes: image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs. Calibration evidence includes clear-gap win-rate 0.83–1.0 and base-vs-base ~0.5. (2) Adaptation testing — applying six parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods across two input regimes and a severity sweep on the TRELLIS generator. Quality-contrastive construction is used to engineer learnable signal, since independent base samples have a 0.94 order-flip rate (near-random preference).
AI.result: No adaptation method clears the ≥65% win-rate target. The best method — conditioner repair under severe degradation — reaches parity (0.50 win-rate) with the base model. Flow-DiT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and clean inputs saturate the judge. The result is mechanistic: conditioning repair is the locus that actually moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects only. Matching but not exceeding a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is itself informative.
AI.conclusion: Matching a strong public-data base model via cheap, label-free VLM-guided adaptation is achievable but exceeding it requires more than lightweight PEFT on public data. The reusable judge protocol provides a foundation for future work. The key insight is mechanistic: where adaptation is applied (conditioner vs. flow-DiT) determines whether geometry actually changes.

title: CRAX: Fast Safe Reinforcement Learning Benchmarking
summary: Safety is a core concern for deploying reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving. While benchmarks have been central to progress in RL, existing safety benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics remain computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. To address this gap, we propose CRAX (Constrained RL Accelerated with JAX). Built on top of the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine with realistic 3D dynamics, CRAX leverages vectorized operations and hardware acceleration, yielding up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. The benchmark features six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each spanning three difficulty levels. Evaluating six popular safe RL methods shows that no single approach dominates across all tasks, and reveals the trade-offs between performance and safety. We find that curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer can improve performance over direct training in harder settings.

AI.tldr: CRAX is a JAX-accelerated safe RL benchmark using MuJoCo XLA physics, achieving ~100x speedups over CPU-based alternatives. It features 6 environment suites with 3 difficulty levels each and evaluates 6 safe RL methods, revealing performance-safety trade-offs and benefits from curriculum learning and safety transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing safe RL benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics are computationally slow (CPU-bound), which limits large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. There is a need for a fast, hardware-accelerated benchmark that maintains realistic dynamics while enabling efficient evaluation of safe RL methods.
AI.method: CRAX is built on the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine, leveraging JAX's vectorized operations and hardware acceleration (GPU/TPU). The benchmark provides six environment suites with three agent-specific tasks, each spanning three difficulty levels. Six popular safe RL algorithms are evaluated across these tasks, with experiments on curriculum learning (training across progressive difficulty levels) and safety transfer.
AI.result: CRAX achieves up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. Evaluation of six safe RL methods shows no single algorithm dominates across all tasks, highlighting context-dependent performance-safety trade-offs. Curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer strategies improve performance compared to direct training on harder settings.
AI.conclusion: CRAX fills a critical gap in safe RL research by providing a fast, scalable benchmark with realistic 3D physics. The findings emphasize that algorithm selection should be task-dependent, and that curriculum learning and safety transfer are effective strategies for improving safe RL performance in challenging settings.

title: Towards Modality-imbalanced Federated Graph Learning: A Data Synthesis-based Approach
summary: MultiModal Federated Graph Learning (MM-FGL) offers a natural collaborative training paradigm, but its practical deployment is challenged by two granularities of modality imbalance. Client-level imbalance occurs when certain clients lack entire modalities, while node-level imbalance occurs when individual nodes exhibit missing visual or textual attributes. While several relevant studies exist, our investigation reveals that they predominantly target graph-agnostic or centralized scenarios, rendering them difficult to adapt directly. To address these challenges, we formalize modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as an implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis problem. This paradigm recovers missing modal semantics directly within the representation space, thereby maximizing alignment with the original data's semantic distribution and mitigating the high variance induced by missing modalities. To this end, we propose FedMGS (Federated Modality-aware Graph Synthesis), which integrates three core components. The availability-aware graph encoder prevents missing modalities from contaminating local structural propagation. The prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities. The reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism regulates the impact of recovered latent representations prior to predictive readout. Extensive experiments on four tasks show that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines with gains up to 17.41% with best efficiency-performance tradeoff.

AI.tldr: FedMGS addresses modality-imbalanced MultiModal Federated Graph Learning by synthesizing missing modal semantics in latent representation space using availability-aware encoding, prototype-guided synthesis, and reliability-calibrated fusion, achieving up to 17.41% improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Practical deployment of MM-FGL faces two granularities of modality imbalance — client-level (entire modalities missing at certain clients) and node-level (individual nodes missing visual/textual attributes). Existing solutions target graph-agnostic or centralized settings and cannot be directly adapted to federated graph scenarios.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the problem as implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis. FedMGS comprises: (1) an availability-aware graph encoder that prevents missing modalities from corrupting local structural propagation; (2) a prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer that establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities; and (3) a reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism that regulates the influence of recovered representations before predictive readout.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across four tasks demonstrate that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving performance gains up to 17.41% while maintaining the best efficiency-performance tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: FedMGS effectively addresses both client-level and node-level modality imbalance in MM-FGL through latent semantic synthesis, overcoming limitations of prior graph-agnostic and centralized approaches with strong empirical results.

title: The Significance of Style Diversity in Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Generating high-utility synthetic data for intent classification typically requires human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings. In this paper, we propose a framework for synthetic dialogue generation that works entirely without human-annotated data, relying solely on intent definitions. Our proposed dialogue generation framework utilizes two different types of topic and style attributes to improve data diversity. Also, we propose two novel post-hoc stylization models called Univ and Exam to transform synthetic LLM-generated utterances into more varied, human-like linguistic styles. To enhance data quality, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge filtering process. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained using human-annotated training data. Crucially, the findings reveal that style diversity is more critical than topic diversity for synthetic data utility, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating style attributes during the generation process is more effective than post-hoc style adaptation.

AI.tldr: A framework for synthetic dialogue generation for intent classification that requires no human-annotated seed data, relying only on intent definitions. It uses topic/style attributes for diversity, two post-hoc stylization models (Univ and Exam), and LLM-as-a-judge filtering. Achieves up to 93.3% of human-annotated data performance, with style diversity proving more critical than topic diversity.
AI.motivation: In fast-paced industrial settings, human-annotated seed data for intent classification is often unavailable. Existing synthetic data generation methods typically depend on such seed data, creating a bottleneck. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency entirely by generating high-utility training data using only intent definitions.
AI.method: The framework generates synthetic dialogues solely from intent definitions without human annotations. It incorporates two types of attributes — topic and style — to enhance data diversity. Two novel post-hoc stylization models, Univ (universal) and Exam (example-based), are proposed to transform LLM-generated utterances into more varied, human-like styles. An LLM-as-a-judge filtering mechanism is employed to improve data quality by scoring and filtering generated samples.
AI.result: On both industrial and public datasets, the proposed approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained using human-annotated training data. Style diversity was found to be more critical than topic diversity for synthetic data utility, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Incorporating style attributes during generation proved more effective than post-hoc style adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Fully unsupervised synthetic dialogue generation from intent definitions is feasible and highly effective for intent classification. Style diversity is paramount for utility, and injecting style attributes during generation yields better results than post-hoc stylization. The framework offers a practical solution for industrial scenarios where annotated data is scarce or absent.

title: Direct Advantage Estimation for Scalable and Sample-efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) has been shown to improve the sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning algorithms. However, its reliance on full environment observability limits its applicability in realistic settings, and its requirement to model transition probabilities incurs substantial computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. In the present work, we address both limitations. First, we extend the theoretical framework of DAE to partially observable domains with minimal modifications. Second, we reduce its computational complexity by introducing discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities. We evaluate our approach on the Arcade Learning Environment and find that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) to partially observable environments and reduces its computational cost by using discrete latent dynamics models, demonstrating scalability and sample efficiency on the Arcade Learning Environment.
AI.motivation: DAE improves sample efficiency in deep RL but suffers from two key limitations: (1) it requires full environment observability, making it inapplicable to realistic partially observable settings, and (2) modeling transition probabilities imposes high computational overhead in high-dimensional observation spaces.
AI.method: The authors (1) extend DAE's theoretical framework to partially observable domains with minimal modifications, and (2) introduce discrete latent dynamics models to efficiently approximate transition probabilities, thereby reducing computational complexity.
AI.result: The proposed approach scales effectively with function approximator capacity and retains high sample efficiency when evaluated on the Arcade Learning Environment benchmark.
AI.conclusion: DAE can be successfully adapted to partially observable settings and made computationally tractable via discrete latent dynamics, broadening its practical applicability without sacrificing its sample efficiency advantages.

title: Pseudo-Feature Padding: A Lightweight Defense Against False Data Injection in Power Grids
summary: Deep Neural Networks DNNs have achieved remarkable accuracy in various tasks including their application in CyberPhysical Systems CPS for detecting False Data Injection Attacks FDIA during critical operations However the unique infrastructure of CPS makes DNNs vulnerable to exploitation by attackers aiming to evade detection Additionally the distinct nature of CPS presents challenges for conventional defense mechanisms against FDIA This paper proposes an innovative defense framework that strengthens DNNs against such attacks by introducing an additional input layer that performs padding in the input samples using pseudofeature values derived from the inputs statistical distribution This padding increases the input dimensionality in a randomized and dataaware manner making adversarial attacks computationally infeasible due to the nontransferable nature of crafted perturbations and the unpredictability of the padded structure Our method is lightweight modelagnostic and requires no modifications to the core architecture making it highly deployable in realworld CPS settings We evaluated our framework on critical power grid applications such as state estimation using the IEEE 14bus 30bus 118bus and 300bus systems Experiments under adversarial settings demonstrate that our padding strategy significantly improves model robustness with negligible impact on performance and effectively mitigates attacks that would otherwise bypass conventional defenses

AI.tldr: A defense framework for DNNs in CPS uses randomized, data-aware pseudo-feature padding to increase input dimensionality, making adversarial FDIA attacks computationally infeasible without modifying the core model architecture.
AI.motivation: DNNs deployed in Cyber-Physical Systems for False Data Injection Attack (FDIA) detection are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that evade detection. Conventional defenses are ill-suited to the unique infrastructure of CPS, creating a need for a lightweight, model-agnostic defense tailored to these environments.
AI.method: The framework adds an extra input layer that pads input samples with pseudo-features drawn from the input's statistical distribution. This randomized, data-aware padding increases input dimensionality, rendering adversarial perturbations non-transferable and the padded structure unpredictable, thus making attacks computationally infeasible.
AI.result: Evaluated on IEEE 14-bus, 30-bus, 118-bus, and 300-bus power systems for state estimation, the padding strategy significantly improved model robustness under adversarial settings with negligible performance impact, effectively mitigating attacks that bypass conventional defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed padding-based defense is lightweight, model-agnostic, requires no core architecture changes, and is highly deployable in real-world CPS, offering robust protection against adversarial FDIA.

title: On the Redundancy of Timestep Embeddings in Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models rely heavily on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate the denoising process across various noise scales. In this work, we challenge the necessity of these temporal signals by analyzing their impact on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. Beyond empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning. Our findings reveal a surprising robustness when timestep embeddings are completely removed. Extensive ablation studies on the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets show that these time-agnostic models can maintain high structural fidelity and even surpass their conditioned counterparts in competitive metrics, including FID, precision, and recall. Our analysis suggests these architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from the corrupted input under specific assumptions, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant. This study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and paves the way for more efficient and structurally focused generative architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the necessity of explicit timestep embeddings in diffusion models, demonstrating both empirically and theoretically that time-agnostic architectures can match or surpass conditioned counterparts on metrics like FID, precision, and recall on CelebA and CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models universally rely on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate denoising across noise scales. The authors question whether this temporal conditioning is truly necessary, aiming to simplify architectures and understand the fundamental role of time signals in diffusion training.
AI.method: The authors analyze the impact of timestep embeddings on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. They provide a theoretical framework proving that the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning under certain conditions. Extensive ablation studies are conducted on CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets, comparing time-conditioned and time-agnostic models across metrics including FID, precision, and recall.
AI.result: Time-agnostic models exhibit surprising robustness, maintaining high structural fidelity and even outperforming conditioned counterparts in FID, precision, and recall. The findings suggest architectures can implicitly infer noise scales directly from corrupted inputs, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant.
AI.conclusion: The study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms in diffusion models and opens the path toward more efficient, structurally focused generative architectures that eliminate the need for explicit timestep embeddings.

title: Neural network surrogates with uncertainty quantification for inverse problems in partial differential equations
summary: Inverse problems for differential equations arise throughout science and engineering, where one seeks to infer unknown model parameters from noisy or incomplete observations. Traditional numerical methods for these problems are often computationally expensive, particularly in Bayesian settings where evaluating the likelihood becomes costly for complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. To address this challenge, we introduce DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions, reducing overconfident inference when training data are limited. To evaluate the fidelity of the surrogate-induced posterior approximations in practice, we show that a short run of delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo can serve as an effective diagnostic. Across a range of numerical experiments, DeepGaLA delivers forward-model approximations with accuracy comparable to established Gaussian-process surrogates, while better maintaining efficiency as parameter dimension grows. Moreover, it can incorporate differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear settings. Overall, these results indicate that uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems.

AI.tldr: DeepGaLA is a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions for Bayesian inverse problems. It maintains efficiency in high-dimensional parameter spaces, matches Gaussian-process accuracy, and can incorporate differential-equation constraints. Delayed-acceptance MCMC serves as a diagnostic for surrogate-induced posterior fidelity.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical methods for inverse problems in differential equations are computationally expensive, especially in Bayesian settings where likelihood evaluation scales poorly with complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. Existing surrogates can help but may produce overconfident inferences when data are sparse.
AI.method: The authors propose DeepGaLA, a neural-network-based surrogate that provides uncertainty-quantified predictions for forward-model approximations. They employ delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo (DA-MCMC) as a diagnostic tool to evaluate the fidelity of the surrogate-induced posterior approximations.
AI.result: Across numerical experiments, DeepGaLA achieves forward-model accuracy comparable to Gaussian-process surrogates while scaling more efficiently with increasing parameter dimension. It also successfully incorporates differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear regimes.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates like DeepGaLA can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems, offering a practical path forward where traditional methods become prohibitive.

title: Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting: A Mechanistic Study of Representation Retention in Continual Learning
summary: Continual learning (CL) systems often forget previously acquired knowledge, yet the mechanisms driving forgetting remain hard to isolate in practice because real datasets entangle many factors. We present a controlled, toy-world framework that makes these mechanisms observable and testable. Using a synthetic generator-separator pipeline, we define ground-truth latent features, build tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap, and introduce measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional overlap among features). We then study retention dynamics-the temporal change of representation strength by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary task-level analysis based on effective rank characterizes how representational capacity is allocated across tasks. Our controlled experiments yield three takeaways. (1) Superposition tends to increase over time with transient dips at task boundaries, suggesting boundary-specific interference rather than steady drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition yet does not inevitably cause forgetting; when representations remain strong, forgetting can be reduced despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes. Together, these results nuance the common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting by showing that overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. Our toy analysis provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for CL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a controlled synthetic framework to study forgetting mechanisms in continual learning, using a generator-separator pipeline with tunable sparsity and measurable superposition. Key findings show superposition increases at task boundaries, sparsity-induced overlap does not inevitably cause forgetting when representations remain strong, and effective rank grows with sparsity, nuancing the simple "more superposition = more forgetting" intuition.
AI.motivation: The mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in continual learning systems are difficult to isolate in practice because real-world datasets entangle many confounding factors. There is a need for a controlled, observable, and testable framework that can disentangle representation strength, superposition, sparsity, and capacity allocation to generate falsifiable hypotheses about forgetting dynamics.
AI.method: The authors construct a synthetic generator-separator pipeline with ground-truth latent features, tunable sparsity, and task overlap. They introduce formal measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional feature overlap). Retention dynamics are studied by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary task-level analysis uses effective rank to characterize how representational capacity is allocated across tasks.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Superposition tends to increase over time with transient dips at task boundaries, indicating boundary-specific interference rather than steady representational drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces greater superposition but does not inevitably cause forgetting — when representations remain strong, forgetting can be mitigated despite feature overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank increases with sparsity, reflecting broader capacity utilization under sparse regimes.
AI.conclusion: The common intuition that increased superposition directly causes increased forgetting is overly simplistic. Instead, forgetting emerges from the interplay of superposition, representation strength, and capacity allocation. The proposed toy framework offers diagnostic tools and falsifiable hypotheses for advancing mechanistic understanding of continual learning.

title: Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: Equal advising: Daria Pugacheva and Fedor Ratnikov. Accepted to the ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI and PDEs
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, their performance suffers from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and strong sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the highly non-convex and multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. In this setting, the outer-loop hyperparameter search is a noisy and black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters, where classical local or gradient-based strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with their population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, provide a more robust mechanism for discovering promising configurations. We propose and investigate a two-stage approach based on evolutionary algorithms that combines exploration and exploitation parts of PINNs training to improve solution accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets. In the first stage, we perform low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate configurations, treating hyperparameter selection as a black-box outer-loop problem. In the second stage, only the most promising candidates are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine the solution. Evaluated on three popular problems, namely Advection, Klein-Gordon and Helmholtz equations, our method consistently outperforms standard training and achieves significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.

AI.tldr: PINNs face unstable training due to non-convex physics-informed loss landscapes. This paper proposes a two-stage evolutionary algorithm: a low-fidelity screening stage rapidly filters hyperparameter configurations, then only promising candidates undergo full training. The method outperforms standard PINN training on Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations under fixed computational budgets.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and high sensitivity to hyperparameters (both architectural and optimization-related) due to the highly non-convex, multi-term physics-informed loss. Hyperparameter search becomes a noisy black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters where gradient-based or local methods fail. Evolutionary algorithms offer population-based exploration suited to this mixed, non-differentiable search space.
AI.method: A two-stage evolutionary approach: Stage 1 performs low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate hyperparameter configurations (black-box outer-loop optimization). Stage 2 fully trains only the most promising candidates using standard gradient-based optimizers to refine solutions, all under a fixed computational budget.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms standard PINN training, achieving significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources across three benchmark PDEs: Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations.
AI.conclusion: Combining evolutionary exploration (for hyperparameter screening) with gradient-based exploitation (for solution refinement) effectively mitigates PINN training instability, yielding improved accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets.

title: Data Bias Mitigation under Coverage Constraints & The Price of Fairness
summary: Machine learning models have been shown to exhibit discriminatory outcomes or degraded performance for individuals at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes, such as race and gender. This stems in part from two interrelated challenges: the lack of principled measures for quantifying bias (potentially intersectional), and insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. We extend a recent bias mitigation framework to incorporate coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. Since achieving exactly zero bias for all groups may not be data efficient (meaning it may require large amounts of data), our solution trades small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency while satisfying coverage constraints. We also formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, and characterize the price of fairness, the minimum data modification cost, as a function of fairness tolerance. This is essential both for legal compliance, where regulations may mandate specific fairness thresholds, and for data governance, enabling practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification (particularly, data purchasing) costs. We evaluate our techniques on publicly available datasets, demonstrating that bias mitigation via our framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers, and that coverage constraints, while motivated by statistical considerations, are essential for preserving downstream ML performance.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a bias mitigation framework with coverage constraints to ensure sufficient representation of intersectional subgroups, formulates bias mitigation as an integer linear program, and characterizes the "price of fairness" — the minimum data modification cost as a function of fairness tolerance — enabling practitioners to trade off small bias approximation errors for greater data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models exhibit discriminatory outcomes at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes (e.g., race and gender). Two key challenges drive this: (1) a lack of principled bias quantification measures for intersectional groups, and (2) insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. Existing fairness frameworks struggle to balance bias elimination with data efficiency, and practitioners lack tools to navigate the cost-fairness trade-off.
AI.method: The authors extend a recent bias mitigation framework by adding coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. They formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program (ILP) that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, trading small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency. They also characterize the "price of fairness" — the minimum data modification cost as a function of fairness tolerance — providing a principled framework for legal compliance and data governance decisions.
AI.result: Evaluations on publicly available datasets show that the proposed framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers while reducing bias. Coverage constraints are demonstrated to be essential not only for statistical considerations but also for preserving downstream ML performance.
AI.conclusion: Coverage constraints are critical for effective intersectional bias mitigation. The ILP-based formulation and price-of-fairness characterization provide practitioners with actionable tools to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction, data modification costs, and predictive accuracy, supporting both legal compliance and data governance.

title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
summary: Mathematicians understand a PDE solution through mathematical structures rather than tables of computed values. Historically, this has been the product of mathematical analysis, carried out by hand for each problem individually. Neither numerical simulation nor neural networks produce those structures directly. We propose Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), a prior-guided framework in which an agent translates PDE theory, public problem constraints, and accumulated search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. The mathematical forms are refined under evolutionary search, while their continuous parameters are fit by gradient-based optimization. This makes the search an automated form of inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression. For problems with known analytical forms, ASYS recovers these forms naturally; for other problems, ASYS constructs analytical approximations which can guide mathematicians toward further analysis. In our experiments, across five problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, ASYS produces interpretable representations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, in settings where no closed-form description was previously available. ASYS shows the possibility of a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions, beyond handcrafted analytical solutions, mesh-based numerical solutions, and neural network approximations.

AI.tldr: ASYS is a prior-guided framework that combines agent-based translation of PDE theory with evolutionary symbolic search and gradient-based optimization to automatically discover interpretable analytical forms for PDE solutions, recovering known solutions and finding new approximate laws where none previously existed.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to understanding PDE solutions—manual mathematical analysis, numerical simulation, and neural networks—fail to directly produce the mathematical structures that mathematicians use to reason about PDEs. There is a need for automated methods that yield interpretable symbolic representations.
AI.method: ASYS uses an agent to translate PDE theory, problem constraints, and prior search experience into differentiable symbolic programs. These programs are refined via evolutionary search over their discrete forms while continuous parameters are optimized using gradients. This constitutes automated inductive-bias injection, distinct from blind symbolic regression.
AI.result: ASYS recovered known analytical forms for problems with existing solutions and constructed new analytical approximations for previously unsolved settings, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up.
AI.conclusion: ASYS demonstrates a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions that goes beyond handcrafted analytics, mesh-based numerics, and neural network approximations, offering interpretable symbolic forms that can guide further mathematical analysis.

title: Fisher-Geometric Sharpness and the Implicit Bias of SGD toward Flat Minima
summary: A widely held intuition in deep learning is that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly favors flat minima and that flat minima generalize better, but standard Euclidean measures of flatness such as the trace or maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, which undermines the theoretical foundations of this narrative. In this study we resolve this issue by grounding flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We define Riemannian sharpness mathematically and prove that it is invariant under smooth, function-preserving reparametrizations, which directly addresses the critique of Dinh et al. in the paper ``Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets''.We note that this invariance is a property of the true FIM; the diagonal empirical estimator used in practice (and in all experiments below) inherits invariance only approximately, and exact invariance under arbitrary reparametrizations would require structured estimators such as K-FAC. We formalize the gradient noise of mini-batch SGD as having a covariance structure proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the resulting stochastic differential equation, and then show that the probability mass is exponentially concentrated at Riemannian-flat minima. A PAC-Bayes generalization bound controlled explicitly by SR formally links this geometric bias to test performance. Our experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that SR reliably tracks generalization in ways that Euclidean sharpness does not, and that its scaling with $η/B$ matches the theoretical predictions. Together these results provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize.

AI.tldr: The paper grounds the "flat minima generalize better" intuition in Riemannian geometry by defining a reparametrization-invariant sharpness measure using the Fisher Information Matrix, derives theoretical links to SGD stationary distributions and PAC-Bayes bounds, and validates predictions empirically on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: Standard Euclidean sharpness measures (e.g., Hessian trace/max eigenvalue) are not invariant under function-preserving reparametrizations, undermining theoretical claims that SGD favors flat minima. Dinh et al. exploited this to show sharp minima can generalize, creating a need for an invariant sharpness notion.
AI.method: The authors define Riemannian sharpness as the trace of the product of the loss Hessian and the inverse Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) over the statistical manifold. They prove invariance under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations, model SGD noise covariance as proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the continuous-time Langevin diffusion, show exponential concentration at Riemannian-flat minima, and derive a PAC-Bayes generalization bound explicitly controlled by Riemannian sharpness.
AI.result: Riemannian sharpness is mathematically invariant under reparametrizations (exact for true FIM, approximate for diagonal empirical FIM). The stationary distribution of SGD concentrates probability mass exponentially at minima with low Riemannian sharpness. Experiments confirm Riemannian sharpness tracks generalization better than Euclidean measures and its scaling with η/B matches theory.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous, geometrically principled resolution to the reparametrization critique, establishing flatness—properly defined via the FIM—as a valid predictor of generalization grounded in both the implicit bias of SGD and PAC-Bayesian generalization theory.

title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents
summary: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. Second, we describe the practical design choices needed to make the 4-bit path robust, including asymmetric K/V treatment, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, QJL removal, and block-scale variants. Third, we present serving optimizations on AMD GPUs, including optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant, an FP4 approximation path that uses FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA support on CDNA4. On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant cuts P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47x in the cache-pressured late rounds (2.3x across all rounds) and raises output throughput by 1.63x over the FP8 KV baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper studies 4-bit KV-cache compression for multi-round agent workloads, designing a robust 4-bit pipeline (asymmetric K/V, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, block-scale variants) and introducing UltraQuant — an FP4 approximation using FP8 queries and native CDNA4 matrix instructions. On AMD GPUs, UltraQuant achieves 3.47× faster time-to-first-token in cache-pressured late rounds and 1.63× higher output throughput versus an FP8 KV baseline.
AI.motivation: Context-heavy LLM agents create a tension: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, placing extreme pressure on the KV cache. Serving throughput hinges on whether the system can keep GPUs utilized under high concurrency, and existing quantization schemes lack a holistic evaluation that jointly considers task quality, cache residency, and throughput in agentic workloads.
AI.method: The authors design a 4-bit KV-cache compression pipeline using TurboQuant-style rotation plus codebook quantization as a quality reference and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment baseline. Key design elements include asymmetric precision for keys vs. values, Walsh-Hadamard transform rotation, removal of QuIP-style QJL projections, and block-scale quantization variants. The serving system is optimized for AMD GPUs (CDNA4) with custom decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant: an FP4 approximation that retains FP8 queries, stores FP4 KV tensors with UE8M0 group scales, and leverages native scaled-MFMA instructions.
AI.result: On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant reduces P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47× in late (cache-pressured) rounds and by 2.3× across all rounds compared to the FP8 KV baseline. Output throughput increases by 1.63× over FP8 KV caching.
AI.conclusion: 4-bit KV-cache compression is viable and highly effective for agentic serving scenarios when quality, residency, and throughput are co-optimized. The UltraQuant FP4 path, enabled by AMD CDNA4's native scaled-MFMA support, provides substantial latency and throughput gains without sacrificing task quality, making it a practical deployment strategy for multi-round agent workloads under KV-cache pressure.

title: Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution
summary: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation may receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to distinguish stably effective operations from accidental hits. This paper formalizes the requirement as two structural conditions, alignability and comparability, and proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA). MAA constructs differential signals to make them comparable across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via EMA, and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. As a post-processing architecture, MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

AI.tldr: MAA addresses contradictory cross-batch feedback in trace distillation by enforcing alignability and comparability, using EMA-based signed evidence accumulation and semantic merging, achieving SOTA in 14/16 settings with 75% token reduction.
AI.motivation: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation can receive contradictory feedback across different batches, yet existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism. This prevents distinguishing genuinely effective operations from accidental successes.
AI.method: MAA formalizes two structural conditions: alignability and comparability. It generates comparable differential signals across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via Exponential Moving Average (EMA), and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. MAA functions as a post-processing architecture.
AI.result: MAA achieves best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.
AI.conclusion: MAA provides an effective, principled solution for cross-batch evidence accumulation in trace distillation, demonstrating that enforcing alignability and comparability enables robust identification of stably effective operations while drastically reducing computational cost.

title: Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving
summary: Mainstream LLM serving systems reuse prefix work mainly through paged or radix key-value (KV) caches. This is highly effective for high-throughput, high-concurrency serving, but it manages only one positional fragment of execution state: the KV cache. We study the opposite regime: low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive LLM agents, speech systems, and robot policies repeatedly branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. We introduce execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint and restore mechanism for the complete restorable state at a committed boundary. FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime whose evaluated NVIDIA CUDA backend runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. Because the live state is a closed set of named buffers, a capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the whole execution boundary, including KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, and metadata. This moves reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, showing that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond, and TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, the same correctness and structural properties hold. Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse.
