AI.tldr: FlashRT introduces execution-state capsules — a graph-bound checkpoint/restore mechanism that snapshots the complete LLM execution state (KV cache, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, metadata) into contiguous static buffers, enabling sub-millisecond fork/restore/rollback. Targeting low-latency, on-device serving, it achieves 3.9×–27× TTFT speedup over cold prefill, with byte-exact and token-identical restoration on an RTX 5090.
AI.motivation: Mainstream LLM serving systems optimize for high-throughput using paged/radix KV caches that reuse only one positional fragment of state. This breaks down in low-latency, small-batch, on-device scenarios (interactive agents, speech, robotics) where execution frequently branches, resets, interrupts, and re-enters under tight responsiveness budgets. The authors identify a missing serving point: explicit whole-execution-state reuse at committed boundaries rather than token-addressed KV fragments.
AI.method: FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime with an NVIDIA CUDA backend. It captures graph plans over contiguous, statically allocated named buffers with no block-table indirection. An execution-state capsule snapshots the complete closed set of named buffers at a committed boundary (KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, metadata). Capsules support snapshot, restore, fork, and rollback operations, shifting reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. Experiments run on RTX 5090, Jetson AGX Thor, and DGX Spark.
AI.result: On an RTX 5090: (1) Capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. (2) A KV-only ablation diverges, proving recurrent state is load-bearing. (3) GPU-resident snapshot/restore is sub-millisecond. (4) TTFT speedup over cold prefill ranges from 3.9× at 2k tokens to 27× at 16k tokens. Correctness and structural properties also hold on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark.
AI.conclusion: Execution-state capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary, latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse. This approach is well-suited for interactive on-device AI workloads where entire execution context must be rapidly saved, restored, or forked under strict latency constraints.

title: Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning
summary: Bayesian predictive inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, data efficiency, and robust generalization. However, exact inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations may remain computationally expensive or require restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context models have recently emerged as an amortized alternative by learning to map datasets directly to predictive distributions, but existing approaches are tightly coupled to the support of the training prior and lack explicit mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time, resulting in limited robustness under distribution shift. We introduce a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that explicitly represents prior information as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt its predictions across families of priors. On a suite of evaluations with increasing difficulty, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures, our method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. We further demonstrate its practical relevance on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/martianmartina/multi-task-bayesian-icl/.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that represents prior information as dataset prefixes, enabling adaptation to new priors at test time while matching oracle Bayesian performance at dramatically reduced computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing amortized Bayesian inference methods (e.g., Prior-Data Fitted networks and in-context models) are tightly coupled to the training prior's support and lack mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time. This causes limited robustness under distribution shift. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling test-time adaptation across families of priors.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-task in-context learning framework where a transformer is trained on sequences comprising both prior tasks and target tasks. Prior information is explicitly represented as a prefix of in-context datasets. The model learns to adapt its predictions across diverse prior families, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and those with high-dimensional latent structures, without requiring retraining or fine-tuning at test time.
AI.result: On evaluations of increasing difficulty — including out-of-meta-distribution priors and high-dimensional latent structures — the method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. It also demonstrates practical efficacy on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Amortized hierarchical Bayesian inference via multi-task in-context learning is both feasible and effective. Explicitly representing prior knowledge as dataset prefixes allows a single transformer to robustly handle distribution shifts and match exact Bayesian performance at a fraction of the computational cost.

title: Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy
summary: Differential privacy (DP) ensures rigorous individual-level privacy guarantees against even the most knowledgeable attackers, but its worst-case nature can impose a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. We introduce privacy via predictability, a fine-grained framework that explicitly incorporates the attacker's core knowledge, a compromised portion of the dataset generated by a stochastic process, and a specified family of queries. Predictability measures privacy leakage as the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information about unknown individuals after observing the algorithm's output, beyond what can already be inferred from the compromised data. We show that predictability and DP are generally incomparable: each can be small while the other is large. However, in the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised, and all binary queries are considered sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. More generally, predictability provides a finer-grained privacy metric tailored to specific sensitive information and specific attacker models. We introduce a general framework, using the generalized method of moments (GMM), to analyze asymptotic predictability when the compromised data is generated by a stationary, ergodic, mixing process. Using this analysis, we derive a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for ERM. Our approach is complementary to DP and can be used alongside DP to provide fine-grained privacy control.

AI.tldr: Introduces "privacy via predictability," a fine-grained privacy framework that measures leakage as the attacker's improved ability to predict sensitive information after seeing an algorithm's output, beyond what compromised data already reveals. Shows general incomparability with differential privacy, but a connection under worst-case assumptions. Provides asymptotic analysis via GMM for stationary mixing processes and applies it to ERM output perturbation.
AI.motivation: Differential privacy provides worst-case guarantees that can be overly conservative, imposing a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. The authors seek a finer-grained framework that incorporates the attacker's actual background knowledge (compromised data from a known stochastic process) and focuses on specific sensitive queries, enabling more tailored privacy protection without unnecessary utility loss.
AI.method: The framework defines predictability as the incremental prediction gain: the difference between the attacker's ability to predict sensitive information after vs. before observing the algorithm's output, formalized using mutual information or guessing probability. Asymptotic analysis uses the generalized method of moments (GMM) under stationary, ergodic, mixing assumptions on compromised data. This analysis is applied to design a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for empirical risk minimization (ERM).
AI.result: Predictability and differential privacy are generally incomparable (either can be small while the other is large). However, in the worst-case regime (all but one individual compromised, all binary queries sensitive), predictability implies mutual-information DP. The GMM-based asymptotic analysis enables practical calibration of noise in ERM output perturbation based on predictability rather than DP.
AI.conclusion: Predictability offers a complementary approach to DP, providing finer-grained privacy metrics tailored to specific attacker models and sensitive queries. It can be used alongside DP for more nuanced privacy control, balancing rigorous guarantees with improved utility in practical settings.

title: The Token Is a Group Element: On Lie-Algebra Attention over Matrix Lie Groups
summary: We place the attention token on the group: a token is an element $g_i$ of a matrix Lie group $G$ -- a bare transformation, with no feature payload and no external action $ρ(g)$ carrying it. To our knowledge this is the first attention construction whose tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements: their score is the closed-form algebra norm of the relative pose rather than a learned kernel, and it reaches the affine full-frame groups that every irrep- or surjective-exp-based method must exclude. We call it Lie-Algebra Attention. Once tokens are group elements, the rest follows with none of the usual representation-theoretic machinery. The relative geometry of a pair is canonical, $g_i^{-1} g_j$, so the pairwise invariant $w_{ij} = \log(g_i^{-1} g_j)$ is intrinsic rather than designed; equivariance under the diagonal $G$-action is tautological, and the cocycle condition holds automatically. The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm, $s_{ij} = -\|\log(g_i^{-1} g_j)\|_λ^2/τ$: the canonical proximity kernel under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product, with no irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernel. The construction applies to any matrix Lie group on a chosen logarithm chart containing the relative poses, including the non-compact non-abelian affine groups with scale and shear that no vector-token attention method reaches: neither the irrep tradition nor surjective-exp methods. Three sequence-completion experiments, on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2), bear this out: the closed-form score matches a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant and outperforms it on SE(2), using 50 to 80x fewer score parameters, while a vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: Lie-Algebra Attention replaces vector-valued tokens with bare matrix Lie group elements, using the canonical algebra norm of the relative pose as a closed-form attention score, achieving exact equivariance without irreducible representations or learned kernels, and extending to non-compact affine groups.
AI.motivation: Existing attention mechanisms either rely on irreducible representations (which cannot handle all groups, particularly non-compact affine groups with scale/shear) or surjective-exp-based methods (which also have group-coverage limitations). The authors aim to construct an attention mechanism where tokens are bare group elements, making equivariance tautological and eliminating representational machinery entirely.
AI.method: Tokens are elements g_i of a matrix Lie group G. The pairwise invariant is w_ij = log(g_i^{-1} g_j). The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm s_ij = -||log(g_i^{-1} g_j)||_λ²/τ under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product — a closed-form proximity kernel with no learned parameters. The construction works for any matrix Lie group with a chosen logarithm chart containing relative poses, including non-compact non-abelian affine groups.
AI.result: On SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2) sequence-completion experiments, the closed-form score matches or outperforms a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant (outperforming on SE(2)), while using 50–80× fewer score parameters. A vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Lie-Algebra Attention provides a simpler, principled attention mechanism for matrix Lie groups by treating tokens as bare group elements, achieving exact equivariance with a canonical closed-form score that generalizes to groups (like affine groups) inaccessible to prior vector-token methods.

title: Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction
summary:
A model is multicalibrated on a collection of group weights $G$ if it is calibrated -- i.e. unbiased even conditional on its prediction -- not just overall, but also after reweighting contexts by each $g \in G$. It is a useful property for many downstream applications and is a basic desideratum of trustworthy machine learning. Before this work, all predictors known to attain the minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity rate for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized, while deterministic predictors were known only with substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration was explicitly asked by [CLNR26] and implicitly in several prior works.
  We resolve this open problem by giving a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor. We then generalize the algorithm to produce optimal deterministic predictors that satisfy outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests. As an application, this also gives deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors with optimal sample complexity, resolving open problems posed by [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].

AI.tldr: This paper resolves an open problem in multicalibration by presenting the first deterministic algorithm that achieves the minimax-optimal sample complexity rate of Õ(ε⁻³), proving that randomization is not necessary for optimal multicalibration. The authors then generalize this to outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors.
AI.motivation: Prior to this work, all known predictors achieving minimax-optimal Õ(ε⁻³) sample complexity for ε-multicalibration were randomized; deterministic predictors suffered substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization was strictly necessary remained an explicit open problem posed by [CLNR26] and implicitly by several prior works.
AI.method: The authors construct a deterministic multicalibration algorithm that attains the minimax-optimal sample complexity rate. They then generalize this algorithmic framework to produce deterministic predictors satisfying outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests, extending to deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors.
AI.result: The paper gives a deterministic predictor achieving Õ(ε⁻³) sample complexity for ε-multicalibration — matching the minimax-optimal rate previously only attained by randomized predictors. This is extended to yield optimal deterministic predictors for outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors.
AI.conclusion: Randomization is not necessary for achieving optimal sample complexity in multicalibration. The deterministic algorithm resolves multiple open problems across multicalibration, outcome indistinguishability, omniprediction, and panprediction, establishing that deterministic approaches can match the theoretical guarantees of randomized methods.

title: How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?
comment: 20 main text pages and 6 pages of references and appendices
summary: LLM reasoning transparency is a critical affordance for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse and misalignment, and debugging surprising model behaviors. However, DiffusionGemma performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space; does this make its reasoning less transparent? We study this question by decomposing transparency into two components: variable transparency, whether we understand intermediate snapshots of a model's computational state; and algorithmic transparency, whether we can use these snapshots to reconstruct the process by which the model arrived at its outputs. Naively, DiffusionGemma has poor variable transparency: its opaque serial depth, the amount of serial computation that occurs in between interpretable model states, seems at first 28.6X higher than the corresponding autoregressive Gemma 4 model. However, we show that we can map the information flowing between denoising steps through an interpretable token bottleneck with no decrease in downstream performance. Treating these intermediate states as interpretable reduces the opaque serial depth to just 1.1X that of Gemma 4. Algorithmic transparency is harder for diffusion models than for autoregressive models because all token predictions in the canvas can change at every denoising step, giving the model the power to implement complicated distributed algorithms during the denoising process. To begin bridging this gap, we conduct a suite of interpretability case studies, uncovering initial evidence of novel diffusion-specific phenomena such as non-chronological reasoning, token and sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Finally, we test monitorability, a key application of transparency that measures whether model outputs are useful for downstream tasks. We find that DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether DiffusionGemma's continuous latent space computation reduces reasoning transparency compared to autoregressive models. By decomposing transparency into variable and algorithmic components, it finds that token-bottleneck mapping reduces opaque serial depth from 28.6X to 1.1X that of Gemma 4, while algorithmic transparency remains harder. Novel diffusion-specific phenomena are uncovered, and monitorability is found comparable between models.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning transparency is essential for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse, and debugging behaviors. DiffusionGemma performs much of its computation in continuous latent space, raising the question of whether this architectural choice inherently sacrifices transparency compared to autoregressive models like Gemma 4.
AI.method: The authors decompose transparency into two components: (1) variable transparency — understanding intermediate computational snapshots, quantified via "opaque serial depth"; (2) algorithmic transparency — reconstructing the reasoning process from those snapshots. They introduce a token-bottleneck mapping technique that projects information between denoising steps through an interpretable token representation without performance loss. They also conduct interpretability case studies and evaluate monitorability as a downstream application of transparency.
AI.result: Naively, DiffusionGemma exhibits 28.6X higher opaque serial depth than Gemma 4. The token-bottleneck approach reduces this to 1.1X. Algorithmic transparency proves harder for diffusion models due to all token predictions being mutable at each denoising step. Case studies reveal novel diffusion-specific phenomena: non-chronological reasoning, token/sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Monitorability is found to be similar between DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4.
AI.conclusion: DiffusionGemma's variable transparency can be substantially recovered through token-bottleneck mapping, nearly matching autoregressive transparency levels. However, algorithmic transparency remains a significant challenge requiring further investigation. The discovery of diffusion-specific reasoning phenomena suggests these models may employ qualitatively different computational strategies, and the comparable monitorability indicates practical utility is preserved.
